The Fellowship of the Ring is at its best when Tolkien’s worldbuilding and storytelling are doing the same work. The prose is excellent, the journey is compelling, and Middle-earth has a sense of reality that is difficult to fake. Its cultures feel distinct, its history feels ancient, and the world seems to extend far beyond whatever happens to be on the page at a given moment.

That realism comes from Tolkien’s extraordinary attention to detail, but it also creates the book’s main difficulty for me. There is so much mythology, history, poetry, language, geography, and reference to earlier ages that the novel sometimes asks the reader to become invested in the depth of Middle-earth before the immediate story has fully earned that investment. I know Tolkien’s larger mythology gives much of this material significance, but I think the fairest way to approach the book is to judge what it accomplishes here rather than rely on its reputation or on what a longtime fan already knows.

Some parts of the worldbuilding justify themselves immediately. The different cultures matter because they shape how characters understand one another, how they behave, and what they value. Other elements contribute more to the illusion of completeness than to the story itself. The maps are beautifully realized, but I never needed to consult one to understand the journey. The invented languages make the world feel more tangible, but I naturally read fantasy as though whatever language the characters speak has already been translated for me. These details have value; I just do not think all of them carry equal narrative weight.

I felt much the same way about the songs and poems. A number of them add real atmosphere or historical texture, but their frequency makes them less effective than they might have been. Used more selectively, I think they would have stood out as meaningful moments rather than becoming something I increasingly expected the story to stop for. The Tom Bombadil section produced a similar reaction. It broadens the sense of what Middle-earth contains, but within this particular novel it felt detached enough from the central story that I struggled to see why it needed so much space.

Still, I would not want Tolkien to strip all of this away, because the excess is clearly tied to the achievement. Middle-earth feels real precisely because it does not seem designed solely around the needs of the plot. It has songs that exist because people in this world sing them, histories that matter to its inhabitants whether Frodo understands them or not, and places that seem to have lives beyond the characters passing through them. That is a real strength.

For me, the issue is one of proportion rather than value. The story is mostly successful, the prose is often beautiful, and the world itself is remarkable. I simply think The Fellowship of the Ring is strongest when Tolkien allows that enormous mythology to deepen the story rather than compete with it.

"'I wish it need not have happened in my time,' said Frodo. 'So do I,' said Gandalf, 'and so so all who live to see such times. But that is not for them to decide. All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us".

Yet another book I’ve put off reading for many years. Mainly because I know Tolkien’s style doesn’t agree with me (much like Dickens). Having read The Hobbit a few years ago, I was prepared this time for the intensely descriptive passages and slow moving narrative. However, I found the first half of ‘The Fellowship of the Ring’ almost unbearably slow. So much so that I nearly abandoned it… nearly!

I’m not sure whether being so in love with Peter Jackson’s film adaptations plays a part in my struggle with the original source material. Perhaps knowing the outcome of a story that, at times, moves at a glacial pace is where the frustration comes from. However, I am still glad I persevered.

I found the narrative really picked up in the second half of the book. There were still sections that I felt just slowed everything down; but once Frodo reached Rivendell, I really did turn a corner.

I do love how descriptive Tolkien can be. But it can be a lot. Many of the parts where characters deliberate or retell things at length are my biggest bugbear. What takes two or three pages to tell can easily be done in a paragraph.

And don’t get me started on the songs - I have an irrational dislike for verse dropped into prose with no real need. Especially as some of Tolkien’s are in a made up language, giving nothing to the reader!

Today, no publisher would stand for it - this book (as well of all of Tolkien’s work, I’m sure) benefitted a little from the era in which it was written.

But… nobody can question Tolkien’s immeasurable talent for world-building. Indeed, the songs and long-winded characters play a crucial role in that. They immerse readers so deeply (even if unwillingly) that you do absorb much of Middle-Earth lore without realising. The accompanying maps give more understanding to the convoluted directions spouted on the long and perilous journey of the Fellowship.

Let’s not forget that Tolkien died with more than a dozen unpublished works, many of which were older than his most famous books. These show that he created an entire world - complete with history, legends, heroes and more - before Bilbo set foot out of his hobbit hole.

So yes - Tolkien’s style is a bit rich for me. But I can’t deny the genius of his creation. And so long as Hollywood keeps on adapting it all, I’ll continue to lap it up on screen. And maybe gradually make my way through the literature too.

There is definitely something about this book that pulls you in. One of my personal indicators of how much I’m enjoying a book is whether I think about it when I’m not reading, and that definitely happened here. I was invested in the journey, enjoyed the world and genuinely wanted to keep going.

It also made me realise again how well the movies adapted the story. There were even moments where I wondered whether I might actually prefer the movie, which is pretty rare for me.

My biggest issue, however: THE SONGS. I understand what Tolkien is doing with them. The Hobbits sing because it’s part of who they are, the Elves have their own songs and traditions, and together with all the different languages it adds another layer of history and culture to Middle earth. I can appreciate that kind of worldbuilding, but personally, it was just WAY too much. At some point it felt like half the book consisted of someone singing something, and I started skipping because it genuinely annoyed me. The same goes for longer passages in invented languages. A few words or sentences can add atmosphere, but when I don’t understand entire passages, it doesn’t make the world more immersive for me.

Apart from that, though, I really enjoyed finally experiencing this fantasy classic properly. The world is fascinating, the journey kept me interested and there’s clearly a reason this story has had such an enormous influence on fantasy.

“Vàng thật đâu cần reo ánh sáng,
Lang thang nào phải kẻ lạc đường.”


Điều mình thích nhất ở Chúa Nhẫn có lẽ là cách Tolkien xây dựng nhân vật. Hầu như chẳng ai có “bàn tay vàng”, cũng chẳng có ai đơn thuần là kẻ phản diện một chiều. Mỗi người đều có điểm mạnh, điểm yếu, nỗi sợ, sự do dự và những lựa chọn của riêng mình.

Nhân vật mình yêu thích nhất chắc chắn là Gandalf — người đâu vừa thông thái, điềm tĩnh, lại vừa có nét hóm hỉnh rất duyên.

“Một thầy phù thủy không bao giờ muộn, cũng không bao giờ đến sớm. Ông ấy xuất hiện chính xác vào lúc mình cần phải xuất hiện.”



Nhưng càng đọc, mình càng thấy gần như nhân vật nào trong Đoàn Hộ Nhẫn cũng đáng mến theo một cách rất riêng: từ sự trung thành và chân thành của Sam, nét vô tư của Merry và Pippin, cho đến những giằng co, yếu đuối rất “con người” của Frodo.

“Cháu chỉ ước sao chuyện này đừng xảy đến trong thời đại của cháu,” Frodo nói.
“Ta cũng vậy,” Gandalf đáp, “và tất cả những ai sống để chứng kiến những thời khắc như thế cũng đều mong như vậy. Nhưng đó đâu phải điều họ được quyền định đoạt. Điều chúng ta có thể quyết định, chỉ là sẽ làm gì với quãng thời gian đã được trao cho mình.”



Có lẽ vì vậy mà dù câu chuyện mang màu sắc sử thi, thế giới rộng lớn, hiểm nguy và đôi khi khá nặng nề, trải nghiệm nghe cuốn này của mình lại kỳ lạ thay rất thân thuộc và dễ chịu. Nó cho mình cảm giác giống như khi nghe Harry Potter: được bước vào một thế giới khác, đi cùng một nhóm nhân vật quen thuộc qua những khu rừng, quán trọ, con đường dài và những cuộc phiêu lưu, rồi dần dần cảm thấy họ giống như những người bạn.

Điểm duy nhất mình chưa thật sự thích là Tolkien đôi khi khá… dông dài (đặc biệt là khúc gặp Tom Bombadil). Có những đoạn miêu tả phong cảnh, lịch sử hay những bài hát khiến mình cảm giác câu chuyện đang đi rất xa trước khi quay lại với mạch chính. Và tất nhiên, mình vẫn hơi tiếc vì phần này có quá ít nhân vật nữ. Nên đây cũng là trường hợp hiếm hoi mình thích bản phim chuyển thể hơn truyện gốc.

Nhưng nhìn chung, Chúa Nhẫn là một cuốn sách mà càng đọc mình càng hiểu vì sao nó có sức ảnh hưởng lớn đến văn học fantasy đến vậy. Không chỉ vì thế giới Trung Địa đồ sộ, mà còn vì đằng sau chuyến phiêu lưu ấy là rất nhiều suy ngẫm về lòng can đảm, tình bạn, quyền lực, lòng thương xót và những lựa chọn mà một người bình thường phải đưa ra khi bị đặt vào những hoàn cảnh phi thường.

“Chẳng lẽ ngươi có thể ban cho họ sự sống hay sao? Vậy thì đừng vội vàng phán xét và ra tay kết liễu mạng sống của người khác. Vì ngay cả những kẻ khôn ngoan nhất cũng không thể nhìn thấy tất cả mọi kết cục.”

The intro, where Tolkien goes over hobbit history, was my favorite bit. I loved his observations on the development of hobbit culture and language throughout time, and their relationship to the outside world. For the rest, the Peter Jackson film feels more multidimensional: characters are more rounded and their friendships more vivid; the sense of danger and peril is on par with the book or better; and a lot of fluff is cut out, like the hobbits' first few dangerous encounters. These encounters, along with some of the world-building aspects, feel like filler detail, or unnecessary texture. They feel forced, and I'm sure to forget them. On to The Two Towers.

Listen, there are moments in this book that I think are truly fantastic, but there is no denying that Tolkien's writing style is overall pretty drab and detached. So, as incredible as some scenes are, when I was bored, I was lose-the-will-to-live kind of bored.

This is my first read of LotR; I watched the films once when they first came out. I don't have any kind of nostalgia and attachment to this world. The way people talk about the characters in LotR, I was expecting something more character-driven, and after reading a few chapters, I quickly had to readjust my expectations. For me personally, I don't find any of these characters all that interesting, and I'm not that invested in them.

Obviously, where Tolkien truly shines is in the world he has created. The lore and grand history are truly something masterful. I'm not always a fan of the way he delivers this world to me though. Again, his writing can be incredibly drab.

I'm surprised by how much I enjoyed his descriptions of the scenery though. I'm not always a fan of overly descriptive worlds, but here it was quite lovely. I also really enjoy the underlying eerie tension and atmosphere he is able to create when it comes to the riders and the ring, etc. The way it slowly gets more intense is great.

However, I'm not a fan of all the songs. This is completely a me thing. I never get on with songs in fantasy because they always sound terrible in my head no matter how I read them. Usually, I wouldn't factor in the songs in my ratings. I accept they aren't for me and tend to move on from them quickly. But here there are so many that it did actually start to hinder my reading experience.

For me overall, I really liked this. 3.5 stars is a good rating to me. I liked it. I just didn't love it.

Bora lá... Devo começar dizendo que eu queria muito entrar pro fã clube do Tolkien. Eu amo ler livros que são influentes pros seus respectivos gêneros, amo tentar entender o que faz deles tão especiais e imunes ao tempo. E no caso de Senhor dos Anéis, eu tinha um motivo a mais pra querer amar muito esse universo: eu conheço A fã número um do Tolkien e eu tinha prometido que eventualmente leria essa livro. Acontece que eu acabei não amando tanto quanto eu gostaria de ter amado.

Esse livro tem muitos méritos e características individuais que transformam ele em único e eu entendo o apelo que ele tem com os fãs de fantasia. O Tolkien claramente dedicou muito tempo e esforço em construir a Terra Média e todos os locais que os personagens visitam são organismos vivos, é muito especial a forma como a Natureza é vista e colocada nessa obra. Além disso, o uso da poesia como forma de complementar a narrativa é muito gostoso. Os personagens são interessantes e alguns muito cativantes (eu morreria por você, Sam Gamgi) e a relação de amizade e lealdade entre eles é muito bonita.

Dito isso, esse livro se arrastou muito pra mim e eu acabei auxiliando a leitura com o audiolivro pra me ajudar a engatar mais na história (deu certo, usei o audiolivro da Audible e o narrador era ótimo). Nem tudo nessa história está necessariamente diretamente conectado com o enredo principal e com o antagonista. Na verdade, o Tolkien usa bastante de momentos aleatórios do dia a dia pra construir a percepção da Terra Média e ao mesmo tempo que isso ajuda a enriquecer esse mundo, também faz a leitura ser mais cansativa. Pela maior parte do livro, não existe um senso concreto de objetivo, os personagens não tem muita certeza do que estão fazendo ou pra onde estão indo e nós vamos acompanhando as desventuras em série no meio do caminho. Não é a estrutura narrativa que eu mais gosto, como eu já tinha percebido em O Hobbit.

No fim, é um ótimo livro de fantasia que não funcionou tão bem pra mim. Ainda assim eu vou continuar a série e ver no que vai dar. Talvez o fato de já termos um objetivo estabelecido pra As Duas Torres faça esse livro ser mais empolgante pra mim.

Although the fellowship needs the help of every kind of person and every kind of place to make it through their journey, they BY FAR receive the most help from the elves. The material luxuries given to them by Elves and in Elf-Countries (such as excesses of food, or boats) are treated, I feel, as equally important as the resources they are given by other peoples (such as Tom Bombadill, or the horses they obtain in Bree). And they are, equally important. But frankly, the Elves can offer the fellowship something they cannot get anywhere else: rest. In fact, the fellowship feel so safe in Rivendell or Lorien that they spend entire weeks recovering from their journey, and they stay for so long because they do not feel a sense of urgency. The Elves, with advanced healthcare, and at this point military-grade defences, are able to give the fellowship a safety that they cannot obtain in The Shire or Bree. The help of the Elves is extremely great, and also at little cost to themselves: they give away healthcare cures and boats because they have them to spare, meanwhile the acquiring of even starved horses in Bree cost money. This first-world image of The Elves is interesting in contrast to the group of people they are most prejudiced against: Dwarves, who build a national identity around being working-class miners. While we can assume all settlements of people have a sort of class system (there are 'rich' and 'poor' hobbits), the Elves are not yet seen to do any kind of physical labour, unlike Hobbits, Men, and Dwarves, who clearly have job opportunities such as 'gardener', 'landlord', 'miner', or 'freelance poet' if you're Bilbo. I don't know if this is covered in The Hobbit or any extended works, but I think it's interesting that this group of people is demonstrably richer in every sense (time, money, resources, education) than every other group represented. Although the help of all groups is necessary, the expense of the Elves is the most minimal and yet goes the furthest. So when Boromir collapses in the want of the ring, calling for the 'strength to defend [ourselves]', you have to wonder what part the Elves have played in Middle Earth becoming so segregated that Boromir feels (correctly) an inferiority in the capability of Men's defence; the inferiority of the Hobbits defence, of even protecting themselves from natural predators in adverse weather. I don't think the Elves built their material wealth off the backs of peoples like The Hobbits, but there is a large disparity in the abilities of peoples to protect their homes, their lives, and engage in recreational arts. The Elves may not have caused this disparity through malice, but their refusal to engage in redistribution until the eleventh hour (and at so little expense) has, I feel, contributed to the rise of Sauron and the desire for power. #Aragorn hot as hell #Sam risks it all.

After a few months of reading very little, I wanted to revisit one of the most famous fantasy worlds in the world, a precursor and a major inspiration for countless novels today (and not just today). Coming back to the book, there were a lot of things that rubbed me the wrong way.

It's still one of the first works of modern fantasy written with the impact that came with it, and that also makes clear a whole set of clichés that have been repeated to death and have made this work age somewhat poorly. The textbook hero's journey (Frodo leaves a peaceful home, receives a call to adventure he initially rejects, a mentor pushes him to leave), the wise mentor who disappears right when he's needed most (Gandalf falling in Moria right before the book's final stretch), absolute good versus absolute evil, races with a fixed personality trait assigned to them. These were foundational elements back in 1954, but today, after seeing them recycled in Eragon, in The Wheel of Time, or in the countless imitators of the film trilogy itself, they feel predictable before they even happen.

It takes far too long for Frodo to actually leave the Shire. I'd forgotten how many times he runs into a Black Rider without there being any real confrontation. He dodges one by hiding under a tree root right after leaving Bag End, dodges another one on the way to Farmer Maggot's place, and still runs into another on the way to the ferry at Bucklebury. The first real physical clash with one doesn't happen until Weathertop, well into the book, and up to that point the Riders act almost politely, asking about a hobbit named Baggins at farmhouse doors instead of behaving like the terrifying servants of Sauron they're supposed to be.

On top of that, Frodo keeps moving from one safe haven and caretaker to the next. Farmer Maggot's farm, Tom Bombadil's house, the Prancing Pony in Bree, Elrond's house in Rivendell, that's four havens of calm before the Fellowship is even formed, and in most of them the same structure repeats itself, Frodo has a moment of temptation or fear with the ring, nothing serious happens, and the scene wraps up with a hearty meal or a song. It's an episodic structure that works almost like a string of linked fairy tales, and it delays the book feeling like a mission with real tension for a long time.

Pippin and Merry are two characters who, in this first book, might as well have been one. You can swap them in any scene and nothing changes, neither of them yet has a motivation, a doubt, or a way of speaking that sets him apart from the other beyond his name, something that does improve in later books but is pretty obvious here. The characters in general are fairly flat, and the way the book is written felt heavy to me on this reread. I don't mean Tolkien's famous landscape descriptions so much, those don't bother me, since they help me build my own mental picture of the places, but the conversations, which felt unnatural to me, as if no one ever spoke spontaneously but always in the tone of a speech. And the number of songs I skipped is staggering, there's nothing I hate more when reading.

I have an issue with the elves. They're presented as a wise, noble race, but in practice they act with an indifference that borders on selfishness. When Frodo runs into Gildor Inglorion and his group in the woods right after leaving Hobbiton, the elves basically tell him that chasing Black Riders isn't their problem and that everyone should mind their own business, despite the fact that they're talking to someone carrying the most dangerous object in the history of Middle-earth. Elrond, later on, decides much of the mission's fate at the Council with an authority nobody really questions, as if the other races were minors under his guardianship. They mind their own business, protect their own realms, and barely get involved in outside matters until the threat is knocking directly on their door, which is consistent with their detachment from death and time, but it turns a race presented as a moral example into a fairly passive one when it comes to actually acting.

The hobbits, meanwhile, are at times presented as benevolent, wonderful, almost innocent creatures, but as soon as they're in action it becomes clear, and they're described this way by other hobbits themselves, that they're fairly awful people, very much like humans in most of their pettiness and nowhere near as pure as they're initially made out to be. The clearest example is at Bilbo's birthday party, where a good chunk of the guests aren't there out of affection but out of interest in the presents, the Sackville-Bagginses have spent years waiting to get their hands on Bag End and don't hide their annoyance that Bilbo is still alive and around, and after Bilbo's disappearance the division of his belongings turns into a spectacle of greed among neighbors and relatives fighting over spoons and furniture. Nobody seems particularly concerned about Frodo or why he's leaving, only about what he leaves behind.

Then there's the infantilization. The rest of the world treats hobbits like children, basically because of their size, and what's striking is that when they're placed alongside characters of other races, they themselves start acting more childish too, as if the book itself were assigning them that role. I'd understand it if they were an isolated people with constantly childish attitudes due to their disconnect from the world, but that's not entirely the case, they have their own history, their own government, and their own fairly complex customs within the Shire. Frodo is a fifty-year-old man, not a teenager, and yet he often acts with the confusion and passivity of a young adult protagonist, giving in to panic or indecision at moments where, given his age and prior knowledge, he should already have considerably more composure (he knows the Shire's history, has traveled through Bilbo's books, and still behaves as if everything catches him off guard). That gap between the character's formal age and his narrative maturity is one of the things that takes me out of the story the most, along with how easily some dangers are resolved with barely any real effort from the protagonists themselves, and how little is actually explained about how the ring works beyond it being "frightening and tempting."

Despite all of this, I did enjoy it, not as much as the first time I read it many years ago, when I was much younger myself, but I enjoyed it. Being able to look at it with a more experienced and critical eye has been pretty revealing. All in all, it still strikes me as an excellent fantasy novel and a foundational work for understanding the genre as it exists today, but I noticed a lot of things, in the pacing, in the secondary characters, in the moral construction of its races, and in the infantilization of its protagonists, that make me a bit hesitant about rereading the following books.

Having been episodically enamored with Tolkien for over a decade, it’s a wonder I never tackled the books front to back. They sat on my shelf, mocking me with their thickness through the years. A thousand pages of wizards and elves and dwarves and hobbits and orcs and the like is a lot to carry around, so I began the excellent 48-hour fan-made immersive audiobook by Phil Dragash. I thought I knew the story, but I wholly underestimated the amount of wearily walking they do in this book. Every footfall has its own page. Peter Jackson led me to believe it took them a day or two to get from Hobbiton to Bree. Boy, was I wrong. This is what your grandfather says he did to get to school every day. This is a book about hiking with intermittent attempted robbery. The familiar favorites like the Prancing Pony, Weathertop, Rivendell, the Mines of Moria, Lothlorien, and Amon Hen drew me in as expected, but it took a lifetime to get there. The plot started moving at a comfortable pace after the Council of Elrond, but the casting and performances of the films really did a lot of legwork in characterizing the Fellowship’s personalities and dynamics. Only Gandalf, Sam, Aragorn, and occasionally Boromir (who only pops up once every few chapters to be devilish) seem like anybody by the end of the book. How is it that I care more about Bill, who is a horse, than three Hobbits? There’s much more to go, of course, but it’s a small start to a much larger story.

The core issue with this book is that Tolkien spends so much time building the world that the plot itself drags to the point of becoming a slog. It's exactly what makes this a classic, the world-building is unmatched, but that same instinct works against the pacing and makes long stretches genuinely hard to push through. The character work is uneven for similar reasons. We get real glimpses into a handful of characters, the hobbits, Gandalf, Aragorn, but most of the company remains largely unexplored, more names attached to the journey than people you actually come to know. Tolkien's biggest weakness shows up in the moments that should hit hardest. For all his mastery of prose and world-building, he simply cannot write emotion or action with any real force, and it leaves the story flat in exactly the places where you should feel excitement, drama, or genuine loss. It's genuinely surprising to say, but the movie outshines the book here, doing more with the emotional beats in a few scenes than the book manages across its entire length. Still, the world Tolkien builds is so singular and complete that it carries the book even through its weaker stretches, which is why this still lands as a solid read despite its flaws.

But the constant looming threat of the Black Riders really works, and that sense of creeping paranoia and panic is executed really well, even if the moment-to-moment stuff didn't always hold my attention.

I think the whole thing really comes together during the Lorien chapters late in Book Two. The beautiful sense of grief that suffuses the entire thing is a perfect capstone for the ideas and feelings that have been floating in the air up to that point. It makes everything up to that point, even the stuff that wasn't 100% working for me, make a different kind of sense when in service of those thematic threads. The whole book, in retrospect, feels centered around this idea of bearing witness to a world that's already ending, or at least changing so much that whatever comes next can't be the same thing. The little zoom-out moments, which happen almost constantly, reminding us that this is the last time that these characters will walk these paths, see these sights, breathe this air, are really really beautiful. It all sets up the grand stakes really well and leads perfectly into the sense of grim resolution that carries the big character choices at the ending.

Like, of course I knew that most of this book would contain people walking around. That’s like the entire premise. It just wasn’t very fun to read.
The characters are okay, they’re fun as a group but quite boring by themselves. They’re kind of one dimensional and don’t really have much personality outside of their *one personality trait* that each one has. Some of them were a bit annoying too, and at times I got pretty confused over who was who because there are just so many freaking names mentioned at all times. Especially in the parts with the elves. Can we slow down a bit and introduce these people some more? The female characters were also portrayed in a kind of icky way, but that’s unfortunately to be expected.
I do like the world building, even though that got confusing sometimes too, what with all the different place names and the map not being super helpful in the copy I read. I think Tolkien’s lore and everything he has created for this world is incredibly impressive and interesting and I am in awe that he managed to come up with all of this, especially so long ago.
I think my main gripes with this book ultimately boil down to the fact that I read a translation. The translation that I read is actually pretty infamous in my country, because it isn’t very good. It is known to have changed things around in the plot and I think the translator has made the language a lot more colourful and expansive than what it is in the original. I obviously can’t be sure of that claim since I haven’t read the original, but from what I’ve been able to gather from twenty minutes of research, I think the language is quite different from how Tolkien’s is. I read this translated because I was scared that I wouldn’t be able to understand the older language of the original, but now I kind of wish I had read it in English instead. Maybe I’ll eventually reread it as an audiobook in like ten years time in English. Now I will say, I don’t think the writing is bad in the translation. In fact, I enjoyed it. It is very colourful, but easily gets repetitive and annoying. The songs especially I found extremely annoying to get through, and at multiple points things are repeated over and over again and it was just boring to read. That bit at the start of the book where it is described in excruciating detail what presents Bilbo have given to everyone made me lose my mind. I’m not saying the translation is what made me have such conflicting feelings about the book, but I do think it played somewhat of a big part in it.
It’s interesting to see how different and at the same time similar the movie is to the book. Like I said, basically the entire first half of the book has been cut out of the movie and then patched together into what the film is. I think my final verdict is that I just cannot understand how such a boring book can create such an exciting and intriguing movie. It’s beyond me.

I don't really know how to rate this, but one thing is for sure, this book has been so acclaimed that I definitely expected better. Perhaps it gets better in the next books. I only started liking this story a bit when Aragorn appeared in chapter 10. And, even then, it only gets interesting enough for me to want to read it after they leave Rivendell. I honestly dislike Frodo and most of the Hobbits, at first their poor choices are understandable as they have never known danger and are not used to being careful and suspicious of everyone. Including 4 Hobbits in the fellowship is perhaps the least understandable thing that happens in this book. Frodo obviously has to be in it, and considering the ring tempts people, it is a good idea to have a very loyal friend go along (both to keep Frodo on the right path and to protect him from others who would be tempted), therefore Sam makes sense too. He never complains and displays an unfailing loyalty. HOWEVER Merry and Pippin make no sense, I don't see how they could help: they have not been trained to fight and have never used swords in their life, as Hobbits they have short legs (a downside in snow and probably walk slower due to said short legs) and eat like 3 people basically. They do not know any places they're going and have not even looked at the maps, neither has Frodo or Sam by the way, they seem to think they're going on vacation with how negligent they are in their preparations (no one uses their time in Rivendell to learn to fight or to memorize maps or anything at all that would be useful). 1 friend is understandable and probably needed but 3 ??? Especially when Frodo already considers Gandalf and Aragorn friends ! Just imagine how much better they could have done if instead of Merry and Pippin they had two other elves who have actual skills that would help ? Like one of the persons considered according to Gandalf is Glorfindel who actually saved their lives and fought several Nazgul and made them flee ! Perhaps Gandalf would still be with them if they had two more competent people with them. Let's be honest, after Rivendell Merry and Pippin literally are no help. They mostly complain about how hard it is and how they'll still follow Frodo everywhere.

I really hate books where characters are stupid or make stupid decisions: like Frodo hearing footsteps behind him the entire time in Moria and never mentioning it ?? Even if he thought it was a dream, we have established during the council that he saw Gandalf being imprisoned in one of his dreams, therefore his dreams are important anyway. Also, they make plenty of stupid decisions at the beginning when they leave the shire, like from the moment they realise the Black riders are after them, they should perhaps think for a second and come to the conclusion that getting drunk at the first occasion is NOT a good idea ? Especially Frodo and Sam who know what they're after.

Also, I absolutely did not see the need for so many songs and was quite annoyed when I had to read one but that's just my personal preference I guess (it could also be the french translation of those). Also so far I find the lack of woman in this world a bit jarring: the few are basically just beautiful aaaaand that's their only characteristic. The only one a bit useful is Galadriel and the only thing she does is show them a mirror that shows them stuff both Frodo and Sam are too stupid to actually use (like Sam sees what he knows is the future because he and Frodo have definitely not been where he saw them, but no he gets upset at what might be happening in the Shire?). And actual question: Galadriel has incredible powers and is very respected, so apparently women can hold high position in this world but somehow, the height of their usefulness is being pretty and nice?

Also there were several things that bothered me as someone who's a fan of hiking, like when they're caught in the snow, they don't even try to use the snow to make a shelter? they're just waiting around like 'Whelp guess we'll die'. Or when they make a fire but are always scared of giving away their position, they are ways to make a fire that won't smoke too much, I don't expect the Hobbits to know it, but SURELY Elrond and Gandalf should have sent at least one person who knows useful survival skills like that?? Maybe instead of two of the Hobbits? Also, all the walking at night, have you ever tried walking at night without a lamp ? Even with a strong lamp and on a large clear path I had a hard time walking at night because the place I was in was so full of mist I could not see anything. So I really would like an explanation on how they manage to go through fog at night and not get completely lost. Apparently they just have internal compasses because even underground in a maze with no light they can tell where the East is. I would like an explanation for that: How can they tell which tunnel goes which way ? It is never said and they never mention a compass or a spell that would tell them. Also, there are only two ways to cross the mountains?? I have a hard time believing that, surely there is another place where it's possible to cross even if there's no path? I mean a bit of climbing would have frankly been less dangerous than enemies looking to kill them and that would have been less predictable.

On an another note, why do we need to explain the entire genealogy of basically every character? Maybe it will be useful later, however, I see no possible reason to explain to us in detail how this town is close to this town you don't know, and this other town you don't know either, like it doesn't help us place the town since we don't know the other places mentioned and they don't appear on the map ?! Was the point just to show how complicated the world building is? I would have liked explanations that are relevant instead of name dropping names or places we'll never hear from again.

I really, really want to love Lord of the Rings; Tolkien’s writing is so descriptive that I sometimes get a bit lost.
I started to enjoy the book more as I got into the book and adjusted to Tolkien’s style of writing. He’ll write very descriptively (I’ve poked fun at how he will use a page to describe a patch of grass, and I found exactly that in the book) and he’ll also throw in some really important content all of the sudden! I’ve learned to read through everything but I only need to be deeply attentive for the more action-packed sections, which are very interesting!

One big question I had was why the book is called “The Fellowship of the Ring”, yet the team bearing the ring calls themselves “the Company”. I was waiting for “the Fellowship” title to appear for the group but it never did. In the last chapter Aragorn asked the Company, “What shall now become of our Company that has travelled so far in fellowship?” As the Company travelled together they grew close and experienced fellowship; this first book in the trilogy then, I suppose, is about the fellowship of the Company centered around the ring and their mission to destroy it.

It’s amazing how Tolkien imagined this whole, comprehensive fantasy world to the extent that maps are drawn up - close to the end of the book I learned how helpful it is to reference them. I think that rereading this book would be helpful because I definitely missed a lot. I enjoyed this book enough to continue on to read The Two Towers.

It took me about two months to finish the first 100 pages of the book, and the remaining I finished in a matter of days. The writing is nice, and the parallels with the gerat wars of humanity can be seen clearly. But I was confused as to why Frodo alone was chosen to be the ring-bearer, and had to rely on subreddits and youtube videos to get an idea on what him different from the rest of the fellowship (it could also be because I have ot read the Hobbit). It could also be because fantasy is not exactly a genre I like reading, and had not there been parallels of the war, I may not have gone through the book in the first place.

Regardless, I did find myself getting immersed in the book, and enjoyed reading the whole thing. And it has prompted me to want to read the remaining books in the trilogy. And that is why I think this is a good book, because it has made me want to read more about it.

So I’ve got complicated feelings about this book, and I’ve had them for 30 years now.

My first crack at Lord of the Rings happened when I was eight, fresh off my first read of The Hobbit, and it stopped me dead in my tracks. The tortuously slow beginning and hundreds of pages of mostly inconsequential self-indulgent wandering was just too much. The book would sit there on my bedside table with the bookmark halfway through for the next five years, until news of the upcoming movie adaptation pushed me into picking it back up to plow through it ahead of the premiere.

Given such a fragmented and rushed experience, the book didn’t make a huge impression on me. I picked up The Silmarillion afterwards, and its tragic beauty and mythic scale made it the book I would come back to repeatedly during my teen years. In the years to come, throughout my love affair with Tolkien’s mythos and Jackson’s movies, I never once reread the original trilogy.

So now, at last, I’ve taken the plunge. And it was… fine?

Tolkien is unquestionably a genius, of course. But even with all the beauty and depth here, I’m left with the feeling that this is a book stuck in the middle. It’s neither a straightforward adventure yarn like The Hobbit, nor a grand distant mythology like The Silmarillion, and instead ends up trying to do both at once. It just doesn’t work as well as either style on its own, and made for a somewhat frustrating reading experience.

I put off reading this for so long because I feared that, with its massive reputation, I’d be disappointed. And here we are.

I’m of two minds with this book. On one hand, it transformed the literary high fantasy, so its “tropes” can be forgiven, since it created the genre’s framework. In this way, it’s also notable how Tolkien embodies his influences, mimicking classic medieval literature. However, those influences aren’t regarded for their readability…

…which brings me to my next point. Through the lens of modern sensibilities, this is a drag. Yeah, J.R.R. Tolkien’s legendary interest in making languages/culture is amazing (really, the world-building is astounding) but it comes at the expense of a clunky narrative, pacing that screeches to a halt for lore drops, and flimsy characterization; he’s a linguist whose fiction is just a means of expressing his fascinations.

The caveat to all of this is that I love the LotR film trilogy, which—cynically—leaves me thinking that the greatest success of this book is the greater appreciation it gave me for how Peter Jackson adapted it.

Also, the moment Middle-Earth has indoor plumbing, I’m giving Tom Bombadil a swirly.

So why do people name him the father of fantasy?

His writing sticks to ideals that good guys are light and white and wear bright colours and bad guys are dark, broody, often foreigners to the main character and wear black… do you catch what I’m putting down?

I did really admire his world building. It’s immersive and there’s so much lore.

I went into The Fellowship of the Ring knowing next to nothing about the series outside of reading The Hobbit recently. It was fun to finally connect the dots on all the pop culture references and see the origins of so many core fantasy tropes. I enjoyed the slow introduction to the magic systems and the lore of the rings, especially seeing the contrast between Bilbo wearing his all the time and Frodo being cautious with it. The characters are great, and I am glad I am finally reading such an iconic piece of fantasy.

That said, I feel the pacing struggles to hold up in 2026 and the book does not always earn its page count. The intro is filled with random hobbit facts that feel disconnected from the main plot, and the narrative has a habit of getting bogged down. There is an abundance of talking about past events or planning future travels rather than experiencing the adventure directly. We spend time moving from place to place with characters discussing how difficult the journey is instead of taking the reader on that ride. I expect the movies will do more to bring the story to life and show the adventure, and I am excited to watch them. I do not dislike the story and plan to finish the trilogy, but the written format was a letdown compared to the hype.

Look, I hate to put such a low rating on a book as foundational as this one, but I just have to. And I’m probably being a little more generous than I actually feel.

This was a dull, slow, and repetitive book with entirely too much detail. And yet at the same time, not enough detail? Like all the detail went into the world building and not any in describing the emotions and the characterization of the characters.

“Frodo said nothing, but Sam looked scared.”

And I get it, this incredibly long book would be even more incredibly long with that additional characterization, but honestly I think I would prefer that. I mean compare above to the description of a mountain below:

“Only once before have I seen them from afar in waking life, but I know them and their names, for under then lies Khazad-dum, the Dwarrowdelf, that is now called the Black Pit, Moria in the Elvish tongue. Yonder stands Barazinbar, the Redhorn, cruel Caradhras; and beyond him are Silvertine and Cloudyhead: Celebdil the White, and Fanuidhol the Grey, that we call Ziralzigil and Bundushathur.”

(And it started a paragraph before and lasted another paragraph after)

And really, the world-building just did not do enough for me. I finished this novel with a great sense of relief; towards the end, Mr. Tolkien's detailed descriptions began to wear me down; but I can not bring myself to blame him or name him a deficient author. Rather, it is a deficiency within myself, this inability to enjoy the writing of one of the great masters in full.

Oh, but the parts I did enjoy! Farmer Maggot, the small-mindedness of the Shire, Frodo's foolishness in Bree, the domesticity of the opening Act, Elrond's House, and the forging of the Fellowship. Boromir's madness towards the end, drew my eye as well; I also enjoyed Lorien, that fair land of the immortal folk, but fairer still to me was the Lady Galadriel, and her mirror which foretold many things. The One Ring itself, its sinister creeping evil, its capturing of minds, was also fascinatingly rendered, and I do believe that Mr. Tolkien will have done it justice by the time I am through with his work.

But sadly, many of the descriptions after fair Lothlorien, and even during it, wearied me and set my mind a wondering so that, no sooner had I glanced at a sentence, then I forgot it. In this frustrating way, I drew towards the end; my imagination, my concentration, the crowning jewels of my reading ability, were withered down to dregs by the sheer descriptive force of Mr. Tolkien's writing.

But I can not cast this novel out, though a shadow lay over it ere its conclusion - for there were times when I read well, and with much enjoyment. Onto the sequels! though they may try me, still forever onwards! Let no man name me a faithless coward, giving farewell to a companion I have travelled many a league with! The shame would tear me all to pieces! Alas, for the easy times of comprehension!

Post-script:

The Shire and its inhabitants are much beloved to me. Bucolic, charming, prolific, and their hobbit holes are comfort itself! And old Tom Bombadillo!

🎶Tom Bombadillo and his Goldenberry🎶

Never a catchier tune have I heard! And there's more where that came from, for Good Mr. Tolkien has provided us with many a song and epic, and I am ever impressed by his rhyming. I also found Nature's depiction - Old Man Willow, the Mountain that would not let the Company pass, and the very rocks themselves - fascinating. We know trees are living, but Mr. Tolkien makes them truly sentient.

This is turning into rather a long post-script, and I must away! To a dark end or a future full of hope, I know not, but farwell, faithful reader, farwell!

"The Fellowship of the Ring" review: 2.5/5 stars

TLDR: I can see the greatness in flashes. I just spent too much of the book watching Tolkien gesture toward stakes instead of making me feel them.

Coming straight from The Hobbit, I was surprised by how much of The Fellowship of the Ring initially felt like Tolkien repeating his own formula at greater length: reluctant hobbit, vanished Gandalf, cryptic elves, enchanted forest, ancient songs interrupting the adventure, dangerous road, sudden rescue, restorative refuge. The opening is so front-loaded with Shire business and hobbit domesticity that, for a while, it feels less like the beginning of an epic than The Hobbit taking an extended victory lap.

That repetition might bother me less if Frodo were immediately compelling, but he remains strangely passive and opaque for much of the book. Bilbo, for all his comic simplicity, had a sharper dramatic contradiction: comfort-loving bourgeois hobbit versus latent appetite for adventure. Frodo is something else. He is less a psychological protagonist than a spiritual vessel, a bearer of burden rather than a lens through which the story becomes vivid. That is not inherently a flaw. It is a genuinely old-fashioned mode of storytelling. But the book asks me to care about home, history, doom, and moral weight before it has made me care much about Frodo himself.

The journey structure also wears thin. Too often, the book moves by accumulation rather than escalation: the hobbits are frightened, hungry, sleepy, or lost; an older and more powerful figure intervenes; the journey resumes. Read immediately after The Hobbit, Tolkien’s fondness for last-minute external rescue becomes impossible not to notice: Gandalf and the eagles there; Bombadil, Glorfindel, and the flood at the Ford here. After a while, danger starts to feel temporary. Hunger, pursuit, injury, exhaustion — all of it sits under the shadow of eventual sanctuary. Rivendell waits ahead like a pre-approved solution. Frodo is wounded? Rivendell will heal him. The company is starving? Rivendell will feed them. Gandalf is missing? Rivendell will explain him. The road rarely feels as if it extracts irreversible payment.

The Ring suffers from a related problem. We are told repeatedly that it is uniquely dangerous, corruptive, and world-ending, but for much of the book that danger is mediated through exposition and history rather than dramatized in the present. Gollum and Bilbo are evidence, but softened or indirect evidence; then Tom Bombadil handles the Ring like a trinket before its threat has fully landed. As a mythic exception, Bombadil may have a place in Tolkien’s cosmology. As narrative engineering, his timing is disastrous. He is a load-bearing exception introduced before the rule has been established, which makes him feel less like sublime mystery than premature deflation.

The same issue applies to Tolkien’s hierarchy of power. The Nazgûl are described as nearly unanswerable, but on the page they often function as spooky pursuers who can be delayed by fire, water, Elven presence, or sanctuary. The book frequently asks me to accept that certain beings are mighty, terrible, or spiritually significant because the tone insists they are. Sometimes that works. Often, especially early on, it feels like reverence before evidence: aura standing in for action.

The book improves substantially at Bree. Aragorn’s arrival injects social danger, consequence, and grim competence into what had started to feel like folkloric wandering. For the first time, the wider world feels not merely old and atmospheric, but politically and morally dangerous. The Prancing Pony gives the story friction: strangers, rumors, surveillance, bad judgment, and the sense that a mistake might actually matter.

The Council of Elrond is also much stronger than I expected. It works because characters with conflicting agendas argue rather than merely declare. Boromir’s skepticism forces Gandalf to produce evidence, and that reconstruction is the first time the Ring feels earned as the Ring, rather than simply announced as such. The scene gives the danger shape. It makes history argumentative instead of decorative.

Boromir himself is more interesting as an argument than as a character. His fall is telegraphed from his first scene; he never fully escapes being the marked “other guy” of the Fellowship. But his strategic position is not stupid. He exposes how strange and faith-based the Council’s plan really is: they possess the enemy’s ultimate weapon, refuse to use it, and decide instead to carry it into his own country. The narrative answers Boromir morally and metaphysically, but not always dramatically. “Using the Ring would damn the user” may be true in Tolkien’s world, but the mechanism is still more asserted than demonstrated.

Then comes Moria, where the book briefly becomes everything people say it is. The enclosed structure of the mines, preceded by the brutal crossing of Caradhras, creates tension the open road rarely manages. Gandalf suddenly has texture: irritable, arrogant, darkly funny, tired, formidable. He feels powerful rather than merely described as powerful. And the Balrog scene is electric. For once, the hierarchy of power is shown before it is explained. The room changes. The company reacts. Gandalf stands his ground and pays a price. This is the first rescue that does not feel cheap, because it costs something. Gandalf’s fall is the first genuine loss that lands, and it recontextualizes much of what came before.

Unfortunately, the book immediately hits the brakes again in Lothlórien. I understand what Tolkien is doing: grief, beauty, temptation, fading Elven grandeur, a preserved paradise outside ordinary time. But four chapters of suspended Elven dream-state after Moria’s earned stakes is too much. It is not that Tolkien cannot create awe. He plainly can. The issue is imbalance. He often spends his considerable power on atmosphere, genealogy, songs, reverence, and pastoral pause when the story is begging for dramatic pressure.

That is ultimately my problem with The Fellowship of the Ring. It is more rewarding as world and atmosphere than as plot. Its old-fashioned mode is not inherently bad, and its prose can be genuinely beautiful, but it asks for surrender before it has earned modern-style attachment. It wants the reader to be moved by scale, history, doom, and spiritual burden while its characters are still thin, its threats are often under-demonstrated, and its structure leans heavily on external rescue.

There are moments here I loved: Bree, the Council, Caradhras, Moria, Gandalf at his most cantankerous and magnificent, the Balrog. The highs are higher than anything in The Hobbit. But the low-voltage stretches are longer and more frequent, and the book repeatedly retreats into atmosphere when I wanted tension, consequence, or character. The ensemble is stronger than The Hobbit’s, but the point of view is weaker. Bilbo was interesting from page one. Frodo, for me, never quite became compelling on his own.

I can absolutely see why The Fellowship of the Ring is considered one of the most influential fantasy novels ever written. Tolkien created a world with incredible depth, history, languages, and cultures, and it’s clear how much care went into every detail.

That said, I found the reading experience surprisingly difficult. The book often spends pages describing landscapes, travel, songs, and historical details that didn’t always feel important to the immediate story. While I appreciate the worldbuilding, it frequently slowed the pacing to a crawl and made parts of the journey feel more like a history lesson than an adventure.

I also struggled to connect with some of the lore. There are many references to ancient events, places, and characters that clearly have significance, but as a first-time reader I often felt like I was missing context. I suspect that having a better understanding of Middle-earth beforehand, or even watching the films first, might have helped me appreciate these elements more.

As for the adventure itself, I found it less engaging than I expected. While there are memorable moments and a strong sense of atmosphere, the journey didn’t captivate me in the way other animal or fantasy adventures, such as Watership Down, have.

Overall, I respect what Tolkien accomplished and understand why the book is so beloved, but I found it easier to admire than to enjoy. I’m still interested in continuing the series, especially now that the foundations of the world have been established, but The Fellowship of the Ring was ultimately a mixed experience for me.

I finally did it! I finally read Fellowship! I've never read the books or even watched the movies, so I've been very intimidated by this series for a long time. Well, my friend finally bullied me into reading it.

I know three stars seems kind of blasphemous, but I don't mean it in a bad way. I enjoyed it, but it's also written in such a way that it was a bit of a struggle for me.

I will say I exist in a weird middle zone where I can understand why it's so beloved, but also why some people struggle with it. It is pretty dense. It's a history textbook. It's incredibly formal. It took me a decent while to read because it just took me longer to read. I couldn't get quite as attached and engaged with it because of the writing style, but honestly that's just how I am with all older works.

That being said, I knew the world-building was intense, I still wasn't prepared. At times it's almost overly so. A lot of this book really is characters just talking about the history and lore of this world. It's both extremely impressive and mildly tedious at times. Truly, a lot of this book is just people telling Frodo about the world and plot relevant stuff that happened without him.

I was honestly kind of surprised how little we actually get of the fellowship. It's not assembled until almost 300 pages in, and then only last about a hundred pages. I'm sure they'll band back together later, but still I was surprised how long it took to form. Then again, the first portion of the book was kind of funny to me because I went 'oh this is all stuff that got cut out of the movie isn't it?' and my friends did confirm as much. The pastoral traveling journey in the beginning was charming but I understand why it was cut for pacing issues with the movie. The pacing of the book, as is, is quite slow. It's a lot of going from one place to another and being told the lore of the world.

I can't say I'm madly in love with the book, to be honest. I did enjoy it. I do see why it's a classic. I'm obviously going to read the rest (but I do need a bit of a break because otherwise that'll be just too much). If anything, this has actually made me extremely excited for the movies. I think the movies will work a bit better for me, personally, as they seem to be more character driven and that's really my preferred kind of narrative. Still, I'm happy I finally read it.

The rite of passage in many fantasy readers journey, I had to read the place that started modern fantasy. For better or worse, I have watched the entire movie trilogy (extended cuts too!) so I am familiar with most of the story beats going into this first read. It's hard not to compare to the movies, as we as people love to compare. So while I did enjoy this book, I didn't love it like I did the movies.

Perhaps my brain is just rotted with social media and action movies that I couldn't enjoy the pacing of the book, but this felt slower than I enjoy. The sequence of going to the Prancing Pony felt far too long. The bits where they get attacked by trees and met Tom Bombadil was cool but afterwards I didn't feel much attachment to the events. Things happened, and all I felt was "neat." Which is strange because the opening birthday, the meetings at Rivendell and terrifying mines of Moria left me with strong feelings. But when I think about everything that lead to those points, eh, I don't know I just feel lukewarm.

The worldbuilding would probably be much more enjoyable on a reread. The prologue is extremely dense, as are other random chunks of world building. It's funny how we bag on modern books for "info dumping", but Tolkien feels a bit of an info dumper himself. The book was a mixed bag of information, some I thought was enjoyable and insightful for the chapter/scene, others felt thrown in. It feels sacrilegious to complain about one of the greatest fantasy worlds ever created, and yet I feel as though the way it introduced these elements were not always elegant.

Now the writing, of course, was extremely elegant. Tolkien has a way with words that make the experience feel whimsical and fun without removing any of the seriousness or impact of the world. I commonly came across phrases and words that I paused to appreciate. The way he explains setting and character interaction are flawless and flowing. He can paint such a pretty picture in my mind that lets me get lost in the world (funny how descriptive a scene where everyone is blindfolded can be!).

Along with all this comes an iconic cast. It’s strange visiting where tropes originate and seeing the first model and how they meld the archetype. Gandalf, Aragorn, Frodo, and Sam are just as enjoyable as the movies. What surprised me however were Merry and Pippin, who I felt were far more fleshed out and separated in personality. They felt stronger as characters compared to their movie counterparts. Along with that, other minor characters were interesting as they clearly had their own goals in the world, with larger implications obviously in action.

The book was enjoyable. I appreciate everything it has done for my favorite genre of literature. But the story itself? Good! One of my favorites? Nah. One of the better ones? Absolutely. And I will, under a scrap of shame, admit I enjoy other works quite a bit more.

A diferencia de 'El Hobbit', que me convenció 100%, 'La comunidad del anillo' me dejo algunos sentimientos encontrados.
Por un lado, es evidente por qué esta obra es tan influyente, el mundo que construye es tan inmenso, místico y memorable que llega a ser una obra maestra, sin embargo, mi experiencia de lectura no fue 100% satisfactoria.
Gran parte avanza a un ritmo bastante lento, cuando podría haber tenido más dinamismo, y no es solo por las extensas descripciones del entorno, que reconozco son hermosas en su mayoría, sino por algunos largos pasajes de transición como toda la historia de Tom Bombadil, la cual me pareció olvidable e innecesaria (con razón Peter Jackson la saca totalmente de la película, en el film ese personaje simplemente no existe).

En ese sentido, entiendo que el libro se centra en transmitir la idea del viaje y el paso de un mundo seguro a uno incierto, su objetivo es más contemplativo que de acción, pero aún así creo que hay partes que podrían ser prescindibles para aumentar la conexión emocional del lector para con la historia.
Aun así, el libro tiene momentos muy logrados: la sensación de peligro que se va construyendo gradualmente, la construcción de algunos personajes, los conflictos más directos como en Moria y el momento cumbre del puente Khazad-dûm, y sobre todo, esa sensación de que uno está frente a algo grande y cuidadosamente construido.

Su final abierto me pareció muy contenido, le faltó algo y es probable que tenga que ver con la conexión emocional que mencioné antes, el final no tiene cumbre (ésta sucede en el puente de Khazad-dûm), por lo cual, nos encontramos ante un final evocador y algo nostálgico pero muy sencillo para lo que pudo ser y carente de emociones fuertes que den un cierre inolvidable y conmovedor al lector en esta larga travesía que nos otorga el libro.

Volví a ver la película y contrariamente a lo usual, me gustó muchísimo más la película que el libro. Que gran trabajo de construcción de personajes hace el productor, y le puso toda la emoción que le faltó al libro, incluso modificó el final incluyendo el inicio de 'Las dos torres' porque el final del libro simplemente no hubiera funcionado en el film, y con ello, además de la tensión del puente de Khazad-dûm, trajo aún más tensión en un final inesperado, catártico y conmovedor, con el cual el apego a los personajes crece exponencialmente así como la avidez por seguir con la historia (algo que el libro no logra, al menos no en mi)

This book did not age well.

I’m a huge epic fantasy fan—sword-and-shield, big worlds, all of it. So I went into this expecting to feel that classic sense of sweeping adventure and deep immersion. But honestly, I didn’t get that from the book the way I thought I would.

What I did come away with, though, was a much stronger appreciation for the Peter Jackson films. That’s how I’ll always remember this story.

The book itself feels like a quaint, meandering sing-along from another time. It’s as if someone set out to tell a straightforward story—like running out for milk—but instead stopped at every park along the way, chatted with every passerby, and made sure to recount each interaction in detail. There’s a certain charm to it, but it can also feel slow and overly indulgent.

In the end, I can respect what it is, but it didn’t quite deliver the kind of epic experience I was hoping for.

This holds together better than the rambling epic journeys it inspired in other authors, I’ll give it that, but no matter how hard I try to soldier through Tolkien’s works because they’re classics… I simply do not like these books. I’m not generally a fan of the epic journey narrative, it loses me with the minute details that are there to fill out a world and hold no actual bearing on the plot (which is a stylistic choice and not a failing). It also fully loses me with the songs. There are so many. Holy shit. It’s also no fault of this book that I know the gist of the plot already through the movies, but I did find myself just yelling “get on with it already” partially because the pace feels glacial and partially because I already know what’s happening.

All that to say, I hated this. I’m giving it three stars regardless because I can acknowledge the time and love and effort that went into creating it and that it wasn’t badly crafted but simply isn’t for me. A lot of the fantasy elements pre-date this book, but it’s interesting to see its impact on other fantasy authors over time. That’s the only reason I’m even thinking of possibly finishing the next two books.

In this classic epic fantasy, Frodo is burdened with the task of returning the one ring to rule them all to the fires of Mordor before the dark lord Sauron gets to him first and makes all of Middle Earth his slaves. The task seems bleak, but Frodo is not alone. Along his quest, he reluctantly brings some Hobbiton shire friends Sam Gangee, Merry and Pippins. He accepts the help of the stoic but noble ranger Aragorn and of Gimlee and Boramir, the gritty but faithful dwarves. To balance this out, Frodo is also guided by soft spoken elf friend Legolas when the fellowship finally makes it way to Rivendell. In the end, the power of the corrupting ring is too great, even for Frodo’s well meaning company. He ultimately sets out to rid the ring with only the help of Sam as the task is to perilous to share and could alert the enemy.

I appreciate this book as the pinnacle work that started modern fantasy. However, I feel that the pacing is off and attention to detail exists in the wrong places. I will continue on with the series, but this is not a page turner. I will say that it’s cool to see the bridge between old and modern fantasy created in the 50s when Tolkien would’ve had much less inspiration to draw from other fantasy writers.

Middle-Earth is, without question, the most incredible imagination. But Tolkien is a frustratingly guffy writer. Things don’t get going until after The Council of Elrond — that’s 70% of the book largely spent side-questing. The 10/10 Peter Jackson film cleaves an entirely more streamlined narrative, which I acknowledge is purposefully prioritising drama. I also acknowledge Tolkien’s meanderings are equally deliberate in building an immersive and expansive escapist fantasy, and that Tolkien would probably dislike Jackson’s emphasis on the dramatic over the descriptive. I just prefer the clear momentum of the movies (and, honestly, lack the patience for Tolkien’s arguably excessive level of world-building).

As a lifelong reader, this one was really tough for me. I largely listened to the audiobook, so that might’ve skewed my perception, but this was the most long and drawn out opening book to a trilogy that I’ve ever read. On one hand, it was rich in description, is a case study in world building, and you can absolutely see the foundation being laid for the rest of the series. On the other hand, I was bored for about 87% of the book with very brief interludes of interesting action or dialogue pushing the plot forward. It makes perfect sense to me that Tolkien was an amateur historian and professor of Old and Middle English. Much of the book is about lineage, family history, explanations of topography and geography, and random bouts of poetry or singing to tell stories of old. This book was mostly just Frodo walking through different outdoor areas, making new friends, and eating meals. While masterfully written, I did not find this personally enjoyable. Thus, the almost two month timeline it took for me to read/listen.

I really wanted to love this one, I really did, but I think love is a bit of a strong word for how I feel about it.

Let's get the big thing out of the way. I think the Lord of the Rings films are excellent and are the main reason I picked the book up in the first place; but I think they also coloured my expectation of the book as they do streamline the plot.

I didn't hate it; please make that very clear. I thought there were some really great things in the story that I enjoyed. For example, I loved Tom Bombadil and Goldberry, and I was awfully curious about them and would have loved to hear more about them.

Bilbo's sarcastic notes to his relatives were delightfully catty and I would like more please. You know he'd do fantastic backhanded compliments.

I thought the party scene was entertaining. I also liked the descriptions of the places they went. It was detailed to the point where you could picture characters and their surroundings without it feeling too bogged down for the most part.

The main things I knew when going into the book was there was going to be a lot of walking, talking of walking/ where they're going and singing in it, but I severely underestimated how much apparently.

I also found certain bits of it a little repetitive at times to the point of mild distraction.

I was a little sad that Merry was somewhat forgotten throughout too. In all honesty, he felt like "the other one" that no-one could remember unless an event needed another hobbit to make a comment or do something for the others to react to. I did spend a good amount of chapters muttering "Well there's Frodo. Oh and good old Sam. Pippin's made an appearance; that's lovely. Where's Merry? Oh. This is another Merry-less chapter. Oh." Which was disappointing as again, I'm fond of the films and I appreciated all four of them and I hope when I get to the next two books, there's more for him to do.

Something I liked though, was Frodo's character. He has a heavy burden to carry and to be able to look into his mind was genuinely interesting. The inner thoughts of a character can really draw me in; something that can be hard done in different mediums.

I also liked that Sam; whether in book or film form, is my favourite. I enjoyed that he spoke plainly with honesty, that his devotion to Frodo overrode his want to go home to the Shire on more than one occasion, and that he was shown as compassionate without that being a great flaw. I dare say he was still my favourite in the whole story.

And, you get a true sense that Tolkien's real life inspired a lot of the mood of the book. The dread of the darkness invading places of peace gave a sense of foreboding that I appreciated and I think that helped carry it for me.

Overall, I genuinely appreciate that this is a well loved series of books (for good reason) and I think quests are a great plot point in books; however this just dragged for me more than I expected it to. I don't think it helped that I needed to have a Lord of the Rings dictionary to one side so I could understand the Elvish names easier. It just meant I had to start and stop a lot, but that's probably a me thing rather than a detriment to J.R.R. Tolkien's writing style so obviously I haven't taken that into account with my rating.

Will I read the next two? Probably at some point, but I think I need to put my feet up as I feel like I also walked as far as they did and this book has worn me out a little. And I plan to read something (hopefully) a little lighter first.

If approached as an exploration and expansion of a fully-realized world with deep, true history, a compelling read. If approached as an exciting, plotty adventure story, can be a slog. Refreshing to read a fantasy world that doesn’t feel thinly slapped-together.

Characters felt thin with the exception of Boromir, Gandalf (at times), and Gollum, who really carries the franchise and was the most exciting part of Fellowship despite having been on approx one page. Aragorn’s a cutout of a perfect hero, Frodo felt flat (though the first few chapters were strong), the hobbits felt sort of out of place. I liked Gimli and Legolas’ dynamic but didn’t get much of it. Sauron is literally just an empty shell of evil. Maybe that’s the point, but it didn’t work for me.

High points plotwise were Sam, Merry, and Pippin refusing to let Frodo leave the Shire alone, Strider’s aura in the inn, Khazad-Dûm, Gollum in the river, and Boromir in the last chapter. Low points were Tom Bombadil (wanted badly to like this part and couldn’t), the council of Elrond (could have worked if formatted differently), and Lothlorien.

The weakest point was the prose, which is something I was looking forward to, Tolkien being a linguist. Maybe I’ve been spoiled because the last two books I read were Lonesome Dove, in which the prose perfectly vanishes and leaves the action and dialogue to fly off the page, and Blood Meridian, which is scathingly dense but earned and poetic and probably the best-written novel I’ve read from a prose standpoint. Tolkien litters the page with semicolons and colons and dashes and exclamation points, which might be a sign of the time and the place it was written, but muddled things up for me and was especially jarring after reading Cormac McCarthy. In nearly half his sentences, he uses a semicolon when a comma would have been clearer. A couple random examples:

“ Hobbits are an unobtrusive but very ancient people, more numerous formerly than they are today; for they love peace and quiet and good tilled earth: a well-ordered and well-farmed countryside was their favourite haunt. “

In my mind, this could have been clean:

I really wanted this book to live up to the hype. For years, people have been shocked that I haven't read or watched Lord of the Rings. (Yes thank you I know Tolkien was also a linguist). But here's the thing. This book is a little dull. It's not bad! It's not bad by any stretch! But... it drags. There are so many moments that have no business being this drawn out. For every wonderful and memorable scene (Tom Bombadil is a standout here), there is an equally numbing and forgettable scene (I would name one but I've already forgotten them).

I will say this: I find Frodo awfully compelling. To be burdened with so great a burden, to alone be the one who knows the weight of such a duty, is a wonderful character hook to be given to such a simple man hobbit. He's a good man trying to do the right thing, at great, great personal cost. He's not a chosen one, there's no special prophecy about him, he's just an unfortunate lil dude who now has to save everyone. So awesome. But frequently he feels pushed to the side in favour of Tolkien's more exciting characters. He's a little underdeveloped, and I hope the next two books flesh him out more.

Aragorn, on the other hand, weirdly feels like the protagonist designed after the first draft of the book was written. There's almost this symbolic weight behind everything he does, as if Tolkien is trying to make some point every time his name appears on the page. I'm not complaining, it gives this regal man a sense of gravity. But I do find it detracts from Frodo. Merry and Pipin don't need to be particularly interesting; Sam is practically perfect, splashing after Frodo's boat in the last chapter (as is the rest of the fellowship); but Frodo's spotlight often feels stolen by Aragorn. It's hard to claim the book is about the Ring-Bearer and have the Heir of Isuldir be much more significant. But whatever, maybe I'm just griping over mismanaged expectations.

All that said, I am of course finishing the series, if only so that people who don't know what a conlang is stop telling me Tolkien made a conlang.
