After a few months of reading, I finally completed my book, The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring

I enjoyed it a lot. I read it in English this time around, like I did when re-reading The Hobbit. I also got a new version with a cover art that I really like. I’ll be getting the other books in this same style. I absolutely LOVE The Lord of the Rings.

I’ve seen the movies many times, and posted reviews of each one on Twitter. As well as The Hobbit (book and movies). As a child, after having read The Hobbit in Norwegian, I tried to read The Lord of the Rings too. I had this BIG fucking book containing all 3 books in it.

It must’ve been 1000 pages long. I spent so long reading it that the book started falling apart lol. And I never even finished the whole thing. I remember that I took forever to get to the end of the second book.

And as I started reading the third book, I was like “Fuck it, I’ve seen the movie, whatever” and gave up lmao. I guess I was sick of reading at that point. I stopped reading altogether for a few years, and I think that reading hiatus started around that time.

The Hobbit was fine, but I think LOTR was too heavy to read for me back then, and it felt overwhelming with such a massive thick book. Also, I feel like I read what the pages said, but I didn’t REALLY read the books.

I just tried to get through it, but I might not have been as concentrated. Because I always remembered The Hobbit (book) very well, which I read before LOTR. But I realize, now that I read Fellowship of the Ring as an adult, that I had forgotten nearly everything.

But man, I loved reading it this time around. It captured such a special vibe. Admittedly, I do think The Hobbit is better written. A lot of that has to do with the pacing and focus. LOTR is more all over the place.

You can definitely tell that Tolkien envisions a larger world this time around. It’s not just a potential one-off fairytale book like The Hobbit. It’s a huge living world full of mythos and lore.

While it’s so admirable to see all the work the author put into creating such a detailed universe, I do think it gets in the way of the storytelling for the specific plot of this book at times.

Telling a story and world-building often go hand in hand, but it’s important not to let the two get in the way of each other. Both are their own respective achievements.

It’s cool to do some light exposition to tell the readers about some lore every now and again if it’s related to the plot. If you can find a natural and relevant way to fit it in. But keep it short, and once again, relevant.

Sometimes, this book just spends entire pages on songs and poems or stories of ancient times that don’t really affect the story in any way. It’s more like, “Oh cool Middle-earth fun fact”. Lore exposition aside, I don’t like all the singing in general.

There’s too much of it, and I think it’s kinda weird for the characters to randomly start singing at various points in the book. Especially when they just make up all the lyrics on the spot. Big shock; I don’t like musicals. Now, in more appropriate settings, I wouldn’t mind.

Like how Bilbo likes to write songs as a hobby. And performing them in the House of Elrond in Rivendell as entertainment, etc. Or even singing in bars and taverns. I rather like the beginning of the book, such as I do with the film. Some would find it really slow, but I enjoy the peacefulness of the setting.

The descriptions of life in The Shire are lovely. I also quite like that they don’t do the whole flashback to the first war with Sauron where we learn all of the Ring’s backstory, etc., right away at the very beginning. They did this in the movie, and I don’t mind.

But it’s cool seeing it from a different angle in the book, where we don’t get to know everything right away. But we can gradually learn about the Ring and its true purpose and origin gradually with the characters throughout the book.

I believe I mentioned this in my book review for The Hobbit too, and it’s the case here as well. Even more so lmfao. Tolkien has a very… particular concept of time. You know when Gandalf leaves to do research on the Ring in the movie?

He was probably away for like a couple of days. Maybe weeks or a month at the very most, right? Oh, ok, it was a bit longer in the book, then? Big whoop. You’re probably thinking that he was away for multiple months or even a year in the book now. Lol, prepare yourselves…

Gandalf was away, doing research about the Ring, for 17 YEARS! WTF! 😂 I’m sorry, that’s just a ridiculous amount of time. It’s more realistic in the sense that it actually takes a while to travel across Middle-earth. But come on! Gandalf has a fast-ass horse.

And he could probably ride on all the direct roads without meeting much danger on the road. It’s not like when The Fellowship has to travel through a war-ridden land in secret… 17 years is the majority of how long I’ve fucking been alive 💀

If I were Frodo, I would hardly remember who tf Gandalf even was by the time he returned. Insanity. I can only assume they were inside the Mines of Moria much longer than in the movie as well, but I can’t recall.

They were in Rivendell for some time in the film, but definitely also longer in the book. Their pitstop in Lothlórien was a few days at most in the movie, and it was at least one or two whole weeks in the book.

They also traveled by boat down the river afterward for days on end in the book. They might’ve been paddling for an actual week somehow. The book spent an entire chapter when they were in boats on the river, I found that chapter pretty boring tbh.

I felt like I read through this book relatively quickly. I never really laid it aside for a longer period like with The Hobbit. I’m not a very fast reader, but I found myself reading almost daily, even if it was just a few pages.

So it’s definitely readable and interesting all throughout. The slowest part of the book, by far, was the whole Old Forest/Tom Bombadil arc. That whole part of the book lasts for three fucking chapters, and it feels very long.

The big problem is that it’s literally just a pointless side quest that prolongs the hell out of their journey. And it adds nothing to the story tbh. Again with this forced time and focus spent on lore stuff.

That entire arc and the character of Tom Bombadil is just a huge lore thing. Don’t get me wrong… Tom Bombadil - Very interesting character. Not an important story element worth spending time on, though.

Lol, I think Tolkien just created him shrouded in mystery to troll with us, as nobody understands wtf kinda creature he’s supposed to be, or how and why he can be that powerful. I absolutely understand why they didn’t include him at all in the movie.

And when they’re FINALLY leaving, they end up getting captured by these Barrow-Wight creatures, and so Tom needs to come back and save them AGAIN! Tolkien just wanted to stretch it out as much as humanly possible…

The Hobbit was focused on its own story, it didn’t spend chapters on random side quest stuff. Partly why I think it’s better written. Another reason, is that it’s more simplistic, but it never feels basic.

It’s written wonderfully, but Fellowship seems to try harder to sound poetic and complicated. I wanna feel totally confident that I know the meaning of what I read, so I do take the time to look up words whenever I don’t fully understand them.

I had to do that SO fucking often with this book. I’m not sure if it’s just written with a more “advanced” language because it’s old and they spoke a little differently back then, or if Tolkien was trying to show off this time around. My vocabulary got expanded at least.

Either way, The Hobbit is even older, and it wasn’t this complexly written. Still, it definitely worded its sentences in fancy ways. I prefer it nicely written, but not overly complicated just for the hell of it. LOTR still keeps it very atmospheric, though, and I appreciate that.

One thing it did do better in its writing, was descriptions. Sometimes in The Hobbit, I sort of struggled to envision how certain things were supposed to look and happen when reading it. I didn’t really meet this challenge in Fellowship of the Ring. I find one thing strange…

In this book, they hardly refer to the company as “The Fellowship of the Ring”, even though that is the book’s title. They are more commonly referred to as The Company of the Ring. I just think it’s more fitting to use what the actual title is.

They certainly do this in the movie. By the time the Hobbits finally get to Rivendell in the book, it must’ve been 20 years at the very least since Bilbo left The Shire.

When he and Frodo are reunited (I loved that scene), it turns out that Bilbo met up with some old Dwarf friends and traveled the journey to Erebor one more time. And when he eventually came back, he settled down in Rivendell.

I love that he actually redid his very first adventure. He certainly had A LOT of time to do so as well before Frodo arrived in Rivendell in the book. I’m glad he did something more exciting than chilling in Rivendell for 20 years. In the movie, he talked about wanting to revisit The Lonely Mountain, but didn’t actually do it because he had gotten too old.

But there wouldn’t have been time at all because everything didn’t take so ridiculously many years in the movie (which I prefer), so I guess it makes sense. One benefit of so many years passing, is that Bilbo and Frodo’s reunion is more impactful.

During the Council, there was an awesome scene in the book that didn’t happen the same way in the movie. This might be my favorite scene in the entire book… So Bilbo was part of the Council where they discussed what to do with the Ring. Which is only appropriate.

It’s weird that he wasn’t there in the movie. When they kept on talking about destroying the Ring and how it had to be taken to Mount Doom in Mordor through a dangerous journey… Bilbo was the first one who stood up. And he was like “Alright, alright."

"It’s only appropriate that the Hobbit who started all of this should be the one to end it.” And volunteered to be the ringbearer and take the Ring to Mordor. I LOVE this so much! Bilbo is my favorite character. Though, he’s close to being tied with Legolas.

Still, such a cool moment! He wasn’t allowed to go, because of his old age. And then Frodo said he’d do it. I get that this moment takes away from Frodo’s bravery, when he is indeed the protagonist in LOTR and not Bilbo.

So I understand changing it in the movie, if that was the reason. But I definitely prefer the book version either way. Frodo was still very brave imo. The book is split into two parts. The first book ends when they’re at the very gates of Rivendell.

The chapters also restart from 1 in Book 2. It’s not a big deal, but I would’ve preferred if they kept going with chapter 13 and onward in Book 2. It just gives me a better sense of how far into the book and story I actually am. The page number did continue from where it left off

I think I’d prefer no split at all, but they did it at an appropriate point in the story. The remainder of the book feels noticeably different. The second part is a bit shorter and much more fast-paced. I definitely prefer this part.

Although part 1 was more exciting in a weird way. It’s surely epic and interesting when we have this huge cast of awesome characters in “Book 2” with the Fellowship.

But I think “Book 1” felt more urgent and dangerous because they were only the four Hobbits being hunted by the dangerous Nazûls. Strider/Aragorn definitely helped, but they were still vastly outnumbered and alone in the wilderness.

Aragorn is so fucking cool, I loved it when they finally met up with him. It was also an interesting mystery why Gandalf hadn’t come to meet them. In the movie, we’re shown why.

In the book, you have to wonder until he reveals it himself when they’re reunited with him in Rivendell. His death in the book was sad as well. I kinda liked the Moria plot twist in the movie. They talk about Moria like it’s currently inhabited by Dwarves and is a strong fortress

Like another Rivendell but by Dwarves. They’re then shocked when they find all the corpses and the place is empty. But in the book, it seems like they know damn well that it’s abandoned and very perilous. I think I preferred the part on the mountain in the movie as well.

First of all, they communicate well that it is indeed Saruman who is toying with them, I like that. In the book, it almost seems like the mountain itself is against them. And that it may be of natural cause and bad luck. They also have that scene where Boromir picks up the Ring.

I like that they teased his temptation and fall over a longer period of time in the movie. They sorta do it in the book too, but I prefer how they did it in the movie. I also like that Aragorn got one last word with Frodo before they parted ways by the Great River in the movie.

Then again, I also like how bittersweet it is that they never had the chance in the book. The story also ends more abruptly in the book for some reason.

Frodo and Sam leave together and we don’t even get to know about the rest of them being attacked by orcs, or see the death of Boromir. I think showing the company splitting up even more, and the death of another major character really strengthens the ending.

And makes for a cool cliffhanger to inspire you to pick up the next book. The movie made a wise choice in including the first chapter of The Two Towers. Overall, I actually prefer the movie (the extended edition). Rarely the case when I read the original book.

The book is amazing, by all means. I loved it. Some elements, I wish they did keep in the movie. I found it strange how everybody sorta seemed to know about some type of dark lord from before, without really acknowledging it too much.

I thought it was teasing and buildup, but suddenly, they just started name-dropping Sauron. And that was it. They didn’t really go into detail about who or what he is, you just sorta get that he’s a powerful dark lord of sorts that created the One Ring.

Once again, it’s clear that the book is old when they VERY frequently use words like “queer”, clearly in a very different context than the modern one. Everybody’s queer in Middle-earth, it seems like 💀 I didn’t mind the amount of extra content this time around.

It was a bit lengthy, and while I was eager to rush through it and begin the actual story, all that info did strengthen my reading experience. It was a bit much with the extra content at the end of the book.

We don’t need a promo for every single other Tolkien Middle-earth book lol. One page kinda summing up other books would be more than sufficient. The maps were cool. I liked the few illustrations in the book too.

Also, I need to say something about how weird Gimli became towards Galadriel... Idk what even triggered that. Creepy ahh gift he asked for too. I understood that it was simply too strange to include in the movie. Fucking apparently, they did include it in the Extended Edition 💀

Need to add even more: Arwen was strangely absent from the book, this surprised me. She was hardly mentioned once while they were in Rivendell. The hints of anything romantic between her and Aragorn were very vague.

Some of her scenes on the road before Rivendell in the movie replaced her with an elf named Glorfindel in the book. Who was a cool character in his own right, by all means. But I can only assume Aragorn and Arwen’s romance exists at all in the books as well…

In the movies, they don’t really meet again between Rivendell in the first film and the very end of the third movie in Minas Tirith. So them not meeting at all in the first book is sort of a waste if they’re supposed to end up together.

And there aren’t exactly a whole lot of female characters in the movies. So it’s just even more ridiculous in the book lmao. I would’ve liked Arwen to play a much bigger role, and it’d make Aragorn more fleshed out if they showed his complex relation to her.

I have such mixed feelings about this. I reallyyyyy wanted to love “fellowship of the ring.” I don’t know if I did.

first off, I found it very hard to find a rhythm. the first and last 100 pages or so took so much willpower. all I needed was some genuine action, or even just some minor dialogue to keep me focused, which was surprisingly hard to come by. or at least it felt like it.

jrr tolkien is CLEARLY a very talented world-builder, but it seemed at times that he was too preoccupied in building the world than in furthering the active plot, like he got caught up in the vision and left the reader behind. it felt like 80% of this book was descriptions of the various natural landmarks and terrain of middle earth, and the cardinal directions in which they were all oriented. it was actually insane. perhaps if I were a more conceptual person it would have worked for me, but it didn’t, and i’m not. there is absolutely too much lore to hold on to in your brain. really all you need to know is that they’re heading southeast, and have to pass through a bunch of dangerous mountains first. I could’ve cut a good 150 pages right there. I don’t even think you need a map of middle earth, but if you had one you could cut even more.

that said, there is some gold in here. the whole tom bombadil thing left such a sweet taste in my mouth even despite the fact that it makes no sense. also, I love getting to know the characters. samwise gamgee is 100% in love with frodo and basically everyone knows it. I also think the commentaries on friendship and hardship are worth the slog. it feels both timely and timeless, to cherish good friends in times of evil.

overall, i’m left feeling grateful that peter jackson adapted it and turned it into the masterpiece that the LOTR movies are. I really think he did a wonderful job of picking through what’s important and what’s not. and the CASTING. I know this isn’t letterboxd but after reading this I’m truly impressed. I honestly think watching the movies first made it easier for me to get through this.

It is so hard to write a review for something that is such a classic. It also took me a whole month to read this book, which is very out of the ordinary for me, which is also making it hard to review. I always wondered why as a child I never got around to reading Lord of the Rings despite loving almost any fantasy book I was handed. But to be honest, I’m glad I didn’t end up reading this until adulthood, because I think as a kid I would have really struggled with it.

I’ve only done a little bit of reading into J.R.R. Tolkien’s background and beliefs, and I know there is a lot of discussion about how those things influenced his writing. I do know that he often drew inspiration from pagan epics, which often digress about names and places that the reader may not always be fully aware and the text does not take the full time to explain, which was probably the biggest thing I struggled with reading this book. Personally, as a reader I want to know every detail about the world I’m immersing myself in, so it was really tough to read entire passages and feel like I had no idea what was going on.

That’s not to say that the world building here isn’t great, because it is. One of the things I’ve grown to love about Tolkien’s writing is his clear appreciation for nature in his writing. The way he describes the forests and rivers and mountains the Frodo and the Company are journeying through are just so beautiful and unique, his grasp and control of language is truly amazing. Having read The Hobbit right before this I was at least able to recognize some of the places mentioned, but I did often wish I could read this book with a map of Middle Earth open in front of me.

The scale of this journey is pretty mind-blowing. I know that even though today The Lord of the Rings is often broken up into three books, it was originally written as a single work. That was important for me to keep in mind, because this did feel like a lot of exposition and a lot of cycles repeating: Frodo leaves a safe place, journeys for a long while on a road, encounters some kind of danger, finds help to get him to a safe place, repeat. That cycle happens at least 3 times in this book I would say, and finally at the end we kind of have our first break in that cycle when Boromir has his madness and Frodo takes off with Sam. Through those first three cycles Frodo covers so much distance and encounters so many hardships, it puts so many other epic journeys I’ve read to shame. It feels like the end of this book is finally putting up on the up and up toward the climax, although I have no doubt that will still take us some time to get to. But again, this is such a classic series and I’m excited to finally add it to my “Read” shelf.

I rated The Fellowship of the Ring 3 out of 5 stars. I feel a bit bad about the rating, but ultimately it just wasn’t the book for me.

I did really enjoy the characters, especially Tom Bombadil. He was one of the most unique and memorable parts of the book. I also liked Strider, who stood out as a strong and interesting character. I enjoyed seeing the Fellowship come together and follow their journey as a group, and their different personalities made their dynamic engaging.

The world building was also a highlight. Tolkien is very descriptive, and it adds a lot of depth to the setting, even if it sometimes slowed the pace.

That said, overall the pacing was a bit slow for me. There is a lot of traveling and dialogue, which at times made it feel like the story wasn’t moving forward very quickly. That made it harder for me to stay fully engaged throughout.

Overall, I did enjoy parts of it, especially the characters and world building, but the pacing kept it from fully grabbing my interest.

This was my first LOTR read since I'm an adult, so it somewhat hits differently. LOTR is a big part of my formative years, and a big part of pop culture in my generation. I love the universe Tolkien has created, and I love how these characters have spun off into different adaptations. So 3 stars might seem harsh, but I find myself again judging the classics against the absurd quality of current works.

As a fantastic story, Tolkien created fantastic settings. I'll use his word: queer. In his time, this was all part of the fantastic, it was what fantasy read like. But these days, we have emotionally true to life fantasy works that rip our souls out, and by comparison, The Fellowship of the Ring feels like a musical in a book. I admire the technical prowess to put so much story into song, but it doesn't feel true to life, nor reflects the setting and pacing of the story.

I never enjoyed Tom Bombadil, but this read left me sick of him. And that musical move of suddenly bursting into song gets overused in the book, but absolutely out off bounds with Tom Bombadil. Maybe this is more evident when you listen to the book, but nontheless, I love when a story feels so real that you immerse yourself into it, and this prevents me from doing so.

This being said, the ending of The Fellowship of the Ring is one of the best endings I've read to this day, in terms of balancing conclusion of the main story and launching a new adventure through a very reasonable and pleasing cliffhanger. It also follows one of the best moments in the book with that last minute raw confrontation. The ending is still at the top of the game, the rest of the book is starting to creep down with age, in my opinion.

Although it is a classic and holds a lot of nostalgia, there is a great deal of material in this book that drags. Parts seemed more of an outlet for Tolkien to write songs as opposed to furthering the plot of the story. Even still it is an enjoyable book and to see where many other series drew inspiration is still a good reading experience.

Después de visitar la tierra media en uno de los pioneros mas importantes de la narrativa fantástica, he de decir que este primer acercamiento me decepciono un poco , Tolkien al ser un estudiado lingüista dota de descripciones y cualidades únicas a sus personajes y mundo , siendo la comarca , Imladris, Khazad-dûm y Lothlórien las descritas en este primer libro, así como nos introduce a sus pasajes, hermosos y llenos de vida, en ellos tiende a ahogar al lector, somo expuestos a descripciones y costumbres un tanto redundantes que terminan por segar las posibilidades de profundizar algunos temas un tanto mas interesantes, los cuales como en Khazad-dûm se opta por obviar que el lector a tenido una previa introducción al rededor del silmarillion y otros relatos del propio autor. Lo cual diluye el worldbuilding en cierta medida, pero conforme avanzamos en las hojas encontramos una gran historia, tal vez sea de venir de sagas mas largas como el Cosmere, o con una escritura casi impecable como lo es Game of thrones, o de la lectura del primer libro de la Rueda del tiempo (que se podría decir que es el afinamiento de la propia Comunidad del anillo en si mismo). Que este libro en cuestión me dio sorpresas para bien o mal y ello se agradece, dado que vemos de primer mano el mundo que Tolkien creo para nosotros descrito de su mano, chocando con las adaptaciones de Peter Jackson, con ello nos quedamos en un viaje de 2 libros por delante para cerrar esta oda por el anillo de poder.

E un aburrimiento, una odisea. Demasiada caminata, demasiada descripción del paisaje. La historia de Tom Bombadil es una pérdida de tiempo total, igual que la subida a la montaña nevada. Un capítulo entero dedicado a la comunidad caminando para arriba y para abajo de una montaña sin ganar ni perder nada. El concilio de Elrond se alarga demasiado, con personajes básicamente construyendo la historia, y esas cosas me entran por un oído y me salen por el otro. La mayor parte de la sección de las minas de Moria es solo ellos caminando por una mina vacía durante varias páginas hasta que finalmente pasa algo interesante.

Básicamente, si te encanta la creación de mundos, La Comunidad del Anillo probablemente será tu libro favorito de la saga. Si prefieres una historia más centrada en la trama, que no se ande con rodeos, La Comunidad del Anillo probablemente te va a mandar a dormir.

La comunidad del anillo es, ante todo, una historia de delicadeza moral envuelta en epopeya. Tolkien no construye a su héroe desde la fuerza ni desde la gloria, sino desde la fragilidad: Frodo Bolsón es pequeño, sensible, silencioso, y precisamente por eso profundamente humano. En su figura, el heroísmo deja de ser estruendo para volverse resistencia íntima.

El camino de Frodo no nace del deseo de poder, sino de la capacidad de hacerse cargo. Su personalidad se teje con compasión, miedo y una voluntad serena que aprende a sostener el peso del mundo sin endurecer el corazón. A diferencia de los héroes tradicionales, Frodo no avanza para vencer, sino para preservar; no lucha por imponerse, sino por proteger lo que ama.

Tolkien nos ofrece así un héroe que crece hacia adentro. Cada paso que da lo aleja de la inocencia y lo acerca al sacrificio consciente. En La comunidad del anillo, el viaje no es sólo geográfico: es una transformación emocional y espiritual, donde la valentía se manifiesta en seguir caminando aun cuando el alma tiembla.

Desde una mirada femenina, el relato conmueve porque honra la ternura, la empatía y la fidelidad como fuerzas heroicas. Frodo nos recuerda que la verdadera fortaleza no siempre se ve, pero sostiene al mundo en silencio.

I can only compare it to the feeling of September, not quite fall already but definitely way long past the cozy summer. As we go on with this story it's very apparent that cold and tough times are waiting ahead. The best example of this in the book is Lothlorien who is not in its golden era anymore and an ending hasn't quite set in. It's in a limbo type of place at the moment. We hang on to the memories of the greatest times instead of accepting the surmise, instead of saying goodbye and moving on. Having the courage to say goodbye is a hard thing to acquire.

Det smärtar att recensera denna bok, för jag önskar verkligen att jag gillade denna bok mer än vad jag gör.

Någon introduktion till sagan om ringen behövs knappast. Jag kan inte påstå att jag är oerhört beläst i fantasygenrens historia, men boken är i populärkulturen så oerhört viktig än idag och den ligger i mångt och mycket som grund i så mycket fantasyverk än idag. Filmerna dessutom, är fullkomligt fantastiska.

Problemet med denna första bok är att den i mångt och mycket upplevs kastrerad jämfört med filmerna. Vad menar jag med detta?
Om jag förstått allt rätt så var J.R.R Tolkien en akademiker, och han arbetade på det litterära universumet som Sagan om Ringen tillhör, och där uppvisar boken sin största styrka: världsuppbyggandet. Namn, stämningen, och den underliggande historian som ligger till grund för berättelsen är oerhört kvalitativt genomförda. Man märker snabbt att mycket arbete och kärlek lades ned till detta, samt även hörnstenarna till berättelsen i sig, som i mångt och mycket är väldigt tilltalande.
Det boken faller på, därav mitt hyperbola kastrerad-uttryck, är att karaktärerna är så fruktansvärt platta. Sällskapet i boken på 8 karaktärer är så oerhört lika att det ofta är svårt att särskilja dem, med några få undantag. Samt, prosan är välvald för miljöbeskrivningar och för att skapa en mystisk stämning, men även den agerar bromskloss för att som läsare på något vis anknytas till dem. Att läsa denna bok har enbart givit mig mer respekt för Peter Jacksons tolkning i filmerna.

Kommer jag läsa resterande två delar i serien? Ja. Bör man känna till ovan innan man ger sig in i serien? Ja.
Jag hoppas att ett potentiellt högre tempo i de nästkommande böckerna kan hjälpa till att dölja de problem som del 1 uppvisar, men som denna bok står i synen av ett isolerat verk, så är den inte utan dess andel av problem.
Una rilettura, in questo caso era un ascolto. La nuova edizione con i nomi rivisitati mi ha disturbato un pochino. Ti diro' me lo ricordavo meglio.

I enjoyed this book a lot more than The Hobbit, but it didn’t start that way. The first half (or first ‘Book’ I suppose, as this book is split into two ‘Books’) felt spiritually very similar to The Hobbit, with our main characters setting out on a quest to travel across vast lands. Honestly, it initially felt like it was just retreading the same sort of story that was told in that book.

I’ve only read two Middle Earth stories, and I’m a little bit tired of the whole “protagonists find themself in grave danger, only to be saved at the last second by a friendly group who then welcome them into their home, feed them, top up their provisions, and then send them out renewed for the next leg of their quest” trope (off the top of my head there’s Farmer Maggot, Tom Bombadil, Bree, Rivendell, and Lothlórien in this book alone).

Thankfully it picked up significantly in the second half. The Council of Elrond, Gandalf vs the Balrog, and Boromir turning on Frodo all stood out as excellent chapters to me. Tolkien also does a good job of interweaving the lore of Middle Earth into the story without it feeling like a dump of exposition. I frequently found myself looking at the maps at the back of the book to get a bearing for where described events took place (something I feel helped with immersion and drew me into the world).

Overall I think this book starts a little dull, but settles into an engrossing story by its end.

So, if anyone has seen the movies and is planning to read this, I’d suggest going in with a different mindset: relax, take your time with each line, and go on a journey with the characters. I can see the reason why people love the story, and only imagine that will be proven more in the following books, but it is quite a difficult and often sloggy read. Bogged down with endless descriptions of geography and territory that slows down the progress of the story of the characters' journey, and often derailed by unnecessary poems (some even in Tolkien's made-up Elven language!), the amount of time and concentration required to get through this just may not be for everyone. There is a good story here, but it's often overshadowed by the very world-building for which the genre has become so well-known.

3.5 stars. After knowing about this book through pop culture for so long, it was really interesting to finally read it!

The Pros: Tolkien is the blueprint for so much fantasy that I grew up loving, like the Inheritance Cycle. Spotting all of the things that have been borrowed and reused was my favorite part of this read! I also really enjoyed the descriptive language. Middle Earth truly is a character in the story and it's beautifully described, especially the communities of the elves! There's a very strong vibe (for lack of a better word) to the entire book that's unique and immersive.

The Cons: I hate to say it, but for a grand fantasy adventure "The Fellowship of the Ring" is kind of boring. The plot moves slowly with the occasional burst of action, almost like the cycle of grinding and fighting you might go through in a video game. It's very different from a lot of the fast-paced modern fantasy I've read. There's also a lot of info dumping and telling vs. showing going on, which makes it difficult to remember the names of all of the places and people. Finally, with the exception of Sam, most of the characters are fairly one-note. The book is so focused on the scenery and the history that the characters seem to be simply vehicles to move you through the world. They talk about what's around them but rarely talk about themselves or each other in a way that gives them depth. The characters are what typically keep me hooked on a book, so that's been a real letdown for me. Hopefully everyone else rises to the level of Sam in books two and three.

Honestly, this book seems like ideal movie material, since in that format you can skip through the slow parts and easily turn the "telling" to showing. It's no wonder so many people are bigger fans of the movies than the books! I'm determined to finish the trilogy purely because it's so iconic, but if I didn't feel that way I'd be stopping here.

The OG fantasy series. Everybody knows Frodo Baggins, Samwise Gamgee, Aragorn and of course the infamous Gollum with his coined line. It's a household story, and yet I had never actually read it until now. You know the backstory: a young hobbit thrust onto a quest...except this time it's to destroy the very ring his mentor discovered 60 years earlier. Along the way, he joins a fellowship of dwarves, elves, hobbits and men. Quite poetic in its own right. My honest takeaways? I wasn't as enamored as I expected to be. Don't get me wrong, I can see exactly why it is a classic and why it shaped the genre, but I quickly realized that Tolkien is not a storyteller in the traditional sense. He is a worldbuilder through and through. He created languages, geography, history, lore, and even music. He reads more like a translator of Middle-earth than a narrator guiding a plot. That level of craft is astounding, although it slows the pacing in places where modern readers might crave more momentum more than lyricism. Even so, experiencing the depth of this world on the page, beyond Peter Jackson's aesthetic films, felt worthwhile. I'm excited to finish the trilogy, though I suspect I may remain more partial to the movies.

3.5 ⭐️ The prologue is an information dump overload that had my eyes crossing and wanting to DNF before even getting to the actual story. Pretty early on I realized that some of my favorite fantasy series must have been influenced by JRR Tolkien’s work — which is pretty cool. A few pitfalls slash observations during my first read: Tolkien loves words, lots and lots of flourishingly descriptive words, he veers towards convoluted dialogue, and he isn’t shy about writing longgggg ass chapters. There is no speed reading this, you have to take your time digesting every detail. I loved some chapters (The Shadow of the Past, Strider, The Council of Elrond, The Bridge of Khazad - Dum) and slogged through others (cough cough Tom Bombadil). All and all, I’m liking the lore but I’m not fully converted into the LOTR cult following, yet.

1. Demasiadas (y digo demasiadas) descripciones. Hay páginas enteras de paisajes, árboles o canciones que cortan totalmente el hilo.

E não é porque o livro é ruim, nada do tipo. O universo de Senhor dos Anéis é muito rico, vasto e completo. E a trama central da história é muito bem construída e pensada, Tolkien é genial.

Mas… é, inegavelmente, um livro muito cansativo. Quando comprei o box na Bienal, um amigo me disse que o início do Hobbit ia me fazer querer desistir, mas que era pra perseverar que valeria a pena. Agora percebi que ele se confundiu: o Hobbit é um livraço, tanto conteúdo que você quer ler tudo de uma vez. Na verdade ele estava falando do A Sociedade do Anel mesmo.

O que me fez empacar também foi a minha vida durante a leitura, arrumei um emprego quase em Mordor e fui demitido, perdi o ritmo e desanimei bastante.

Agora sobre o livro. Conhecemos todos os personagens lendários da saga, a narrativa de trajetória é muito legal e a “perseguição” do mal até então desconhecido nos deixa bem ansiosos pelo desfecho. Realmente se não fosse o excesso de detalhismo e os nomes infinitos seria um livro para devorar. As 3 estrelas são pelo quanto me prendeu, que não foi muito. No final eu já tava acelerando pra acabar.

The Fellowship of the Ring is a cornerstone of modern fantasy. Rich in worldbuilding, poetic language, and deep lore. Tolkien’s imagination feels endless, and his ability to make Middle-earth feel alive remains unmatched. The landscapes, the cultures and even the languages all breathe with history and purpose.

The pacing is slow, especially in the first half, and long stretches of description can make the story feel heavy. The dialogue often feels formal and old-fashioned, which adds charm for some readers but creates distance for others.

The book’s moral clarity: good versus evil, light versus dark can feel simplistic by today’s standards and the characters sometimes serve more as archetypes than complex individuals. Still, there’s something timeless about the journey, the friendships and the quiet heroism of Frodo and Sam.

Interesting that I liked the movie more -- but it's probably because I saw that first before listening to the audiobook.

This would have been a significantly more difficult read (and likely a lower rating) if not for the film, which I re-watched right before diving into this book. The book is rather slow moving (and at times boring), although the physical world of Middle Earth is richly described as we move through it. My biggest gripe is that I found it to be lacking in emotion/character depth – rarely do we get inside the minds and emotions of the characters we follow and it feels as though we are watching their journey from a distance rather than being on it with them.

I did enjoy reading it overall, but I think much of my enjoyment stemmed from my love of the films, which I think eliminated unnecessary plot points (Tom Bombadil), consolidated or improved others to build more suspense or streamline plot lines (building out Arwen’s character and relation to Aragorn, the decision to enter the mines of Moria), and generally fleshed out character development better.

Reading the books however did provide me with additional context on several plot points I didn’t fully understand from the film (Saruman’s betrayal, the Command power of the ring, the diminishing of the Elves) – though I am hoping for more elaboration on all of these topics in the next two books.

Lord of the Rings is a genre defining work with influence touching far and wide. This both raises it's status among readers while presenting difficulties for the modern reader. It's undeniably a corner stone of fantasy fiction (but I do think that Tolkien actually gets a little too much credit; there's still many people who seem to think Tolkien completely invented fantasy fiction which is completely 100% false). The problem is when a reader approaches these books today, they are approaching it from an environment that's so completely saturated with fantasy fiction ideas taken from these books that basically nothing here is very fresh. Most readers interested in fantasy will be familiar with literally every single thing in the book without having read it and then what are you left with exactly? Tolkien's writing. This is a weak point of these works for sure. Even for the time, most of the early fantasy writers were actually better writers than Tolkien. Tolkien's thing was the detailed world that he created and the way he handles the material in a hyper-literal documentary like depiction. He wants to detail with full academic rigor everything about this world. It's clear he put a lot of work into creating this world, but it's also clear how desperate he is to show you everything he's created whether or not it makes any literary sense to include it. It seems every character knows all about ancient history and wants to tell you all about it. There is endless telling and retelling from different characters' perspectives. Sure, there's plenty of good stuff in here but then quite a lot of it really isn't. If you compare him to earlier writers, you could say that a writer like Lord Dunsany compared to Tolkien are like the two different sides of fantasy writing. One is artful and lovely to read but shallow in world creation. The other is meticulous in detail and scope but fairly artless in writing ability.

Very little of Tolkien's descriptions can I actually imagine. Because he isn't really concerned with describing what the characters are seeing, he's just trying to direct you around the map he's created, hence the abundance of pointless cardinal directions and "on the left" and "on the right", and whatever, does he really think anyone cares? None of this matters. A better writer would just use descriptive language to evoke the feelings the characters have on seeing the landscape. So much of these books are taken up with long distance traveling but surprisingly very little of it brings to mind the actual experience of walking and traveling long distances. All the little minutiae you have to pay attention to when hiking or small things you notice around you is absolutely nowhere to be seen.

Anyway, this is the best book of the trilogy because it's mostly adventure and action. It never gets too bogged down with slow parts like the next book.

I wanted to love this. I really did. I've watched the movies multiple times and was excited to experience the full story through Tolkien's original text.

The pacing was solid until Rivendell. The journey to get there, the character introductions, the rising tension - all of that worked for me. But once we hit the Council of Elrond, everything ground to a halt.
I understand that Tolkien's world-building and lore are foundational to fantasy as a genre, and I respect what he created. But listening to extended genealogies, lengthy historical asides about who descended from whom, and constant songs/poems just doesn't work for me as a reader.

This isn't a criticism of Tolkien's quality - it's clearly masterful for readers who love deep world-building and historical detail. But I've realized I need emotional expressiveness and character-driven storytelling more than I need comprehensive lore. The narrative distance kept me from connecting with the characters the way I hoped I would.

I was in elementary school when the film adaptation of The Fellowship of the Ring came out, and I was a nerd with a bunch of nerd friends, and one of them bragged about having read the full trilogy (because he was a nerd). I thought the books sounded tedious and uninteresting, especially since there were Yu-Gi-Oh! duels and Pokémon games to play, so I just waited for the movies to come out like the bad little nerd I was. I saw the film trilogy a lot as a kid, The Fellowship of the Ring probably as many as 7 or 8 times, but I haven't seen any of them since I was in high school. I never really cared outside of liking fantasy movies and knowing that I was supposed to like those fantasy movies specifically. Then I went to college, developed Taste (tm), and by the time the godawful Hobbit movies came out (I have rarely been as bored as I was sitting through The Battle of the Five Armies, a solid -2/10 movie), I figured I didn't really care at all. Yet here I am, wanting to watch the trilogy again to see if I'd get more out of them as a proper adult, so I decided I might as well read the books first. So.

There's a lot to like about The Fellowship of the Ring. I really like how important music and storytelling is within the world of Middle Earth, and how much that says about its inhabitants. The characters of Legolas, Gamgee, and Merry and critically underdeveloped, but all the other central characters are fully fleshed out and fun. On the other hand, Tom Bombadil is just about the most annoying character I've ever read and I hate how much of the book is devoted to him. I think there was a meme on Tumblr back in the day about him being annoying, but I don't remember because I didn't care at the time. The pacing of Fellowship is inconsistent, where the scenes with a lot of exposition or dialogue just slog on and on. Tolkien gets a bad wrap for his overwrought descriptions, but I don't see that at all, I think it's fine. It's his exposition and dialogue writing that sucks.

All in all, I enjoyed reading The Fellowship of the Ring, but I also don't see why everyone's so obsessed with it. It's FINE, certainly better than most high fantasy, but I can't tell how much of my positive opinion is due to the fact that it's placed solidly in the cultural zeitgeist and how much is me actually enjoying it for what it is.

Three stars isn't the rating that anyone (myself included) wants to give this book, and maybe it doesn't deserve it. However, I would much rather be honest about my thoughts while reading, even if they are most definitely biased by a love for the film adaptation and the generations of fiction that came after The Fellowship of the Ring.

Tolkien is a master wordsmith, immersing readers in decadent descriptions, lush lore, and delightful dialogue that bounces and rambles with an almost musical quality. He really excels at narrating vistas and details and colorful conversations. My book club waxed poetic about the hobbits' stay in Bree, from how thoughtfully designed the inn was to the rowdy patrons. But by that point, I still wasn't sold on the story.

It wasn't boredom. I know that's probably a common complaint for the early chapters of Book One, but it wasn't what put me off. I was frustrated instead by what felt like a lack of consistency and consequences for our protagonists' stupid decisions. On the hobbits' walk to Bree, they do a terrible job of keeping it secret, keeping it safe. They make many mistakes on the road (and off of it), and yet no harm comes of it. Every time an enemy appeared, they got scared, but felt much better only a paragraph later because the sun was shining and they were singing. Why destroy the sense of dread so quickly? Why let bad behavior go unpunished? Why should we trust Gandalf's warnings, if nothing bad comes to pass? Without consequences, it felt less like a plot, and more like an account of someone's hiking trip.

My feelings on the matter did soften eventually, don't worry. But it wasn't until much later, in Rivendell, when I considered the happy-go-lucky attitude of those chapters as being a feature of unreliable narration. But it doesn't shake my main concern, that until the Barrow-downs they don't actually see a lick of consequences to actually sell the stakes. Ah, well.

Book Two, with the introduction of the Fellowship and their journey beginning, is much improved on this regard. However, I was still disappointed with this Book, but less so than Book One. Despite all the time we spend with the characters, and they spend with each other, I found that there isn't nearly enough character interaction to sell many of their relationships and their character arcs. In fact, there wasn't much to make me care for some of them at all. This is definitely where a lot of bias in favor of the movie comes in, I admit. The scenes we get where the characters are able to share a little joy or take care of one another in the movie really endear you to them; but in Tolkien's writing, it sometimes seems like they are being described as impersonally as the scenery. It's a shame, honestly.

Anyway. The book is good, for what it is. There's no use complaining that the author could have done better, blah blah blah, though I clearly have my opinions. It's still a genre-defining piece of fantasy, and decades of fantasy authors have been able to take Tolkien's style and improve upon it in ways that I like, and ways that I don't.

P.S. Despite everything I said about Book One, make no mistake: I'm a Tom Bombadil fan and will not be tolerating any slander of my boy.

Tolkien’s background as a philologist and medievalist infuses every page; Middle earth feels like a living history rather than a backdrop, almost reaching the point of overshadowing our characters so far. The landscapes, whether the shadowed woods of Lothlórien or the tomb-like darkness of Moria are painted with an almost poetic reverence. One of the most difficult reading experiences I’ve had. I feel scared to criticize this book, as it’s been hailed as one of the most influential pieces of fiction ever. But honestly it took me three months to get through it. Maybe I have terrible imagination, but my brain could only take ~30 pages a day of this. I had to put it down for a couple weeks, worried that it would be a never ending reading slump for me. It was hard to follow along and get immersed with the poetic writing style. I ended up skipping the songs, feeling like they were distracting to me. I had to reference ChatGPT after early chapter to help make sure I was following along to the whole picture of each chapter. As a nearly 30 year old man, this was a humbling experience like “Blood Meridian”.

HOWEVER - This is not to say that I thought this book was “bad”. I did enjoy certain aspects of reading it. Nearly every sentence would casually name drop a person/place that I would Google and find tons of lore on. I think I added at least a couple hours on the reading time due to getting lost in the rabbit hole of Middle Earth wiki pages. The descriptions of the Elvish lands were beautiful and I really enjoyed the brotherhood they formed throughout this journey. I’m really happy my copy came with occasional illustrations from the author himself. I just think maybe this is so dense for my brain that it’s not something I can enjoy passively or binge easily. If Brandon Sanderson is the Marvel equivalent of Fantasy novels, Tolkien feels like a silent film from the 1930s with beautiful imagery and so much creativity and imagination put into every scene shown. Unfortunately, I can’t ever imagine myself just sitting down and wanting to pick this up again unlike “The Hobbit”.

I’m honestly intimidated to continue the trilogy with how difficult this has been for me to enjoy thus far, but I feel like every reader should pay their respects knowing how influential this was to fictional story telling as a whole, and feel obligated to finish it out as a bucket list item. Maybe it’ll get better, or maybe take me another 6 months to get through it, but I’m hopeful to stick it out through the end.

They are on a month long journey and they barely have any conflicts. Even if they disagree on something it gets solved immediately.
The only real conflict happens between Frodo and Boromir at the end but it didn’t affect me at all because there was no relationship established between them. If they really bonded beforehand, it would have felt like a betrayal, but I just didn’t care for either of them.

Also Frodo does nothing. In the Hobbit, Bilbo at least had to prove himself worthy to the Dwarves and had to gain their trust. Here no one really doubts him, and he is just accepted as the ring bearer.

EN 🇬🇧 Okay soooo... hear me out!

I grew up obsessed with the Lord of the Rings movies. I love them, I quote them.. (Yes, including the extended editions, obviously.)
Tolkien’s world? Pure magic. Dreamlike!
So naturally, at some point I thought: “Time to read the actual books!”

I started with The Hobbit 5/5⭐, absolutely loved it.
Then came The Fellowship of the Ring…
…aaaand it took me a year and a half to finish.

Not because I didn’t want to read it. Or my reading time was limited, nooo. But because every time I picked it up, my brain entered sleep mode like an old Windows XP.

It’s slow. It’s heavy. And as much as I admire Tolkien’s world-building and the sheer scale of his imagination (I mean, languages, maps, history, the man built a whole damn universe), I just couldn’t fully connect with the writing style.

And honestly? I feel guilty about it. I wanted to love it. I really did.

Maybe it’s just that the book was written in another century, with a very different reading rhythm. I honestly don't know!

I can’t deny its greatness, it’s legendary. It's a fact. But for me? A tough read.

Will I read the next two? Definitely.
Will I suffer? Also definitely. 🙈

If I had picked up this book without being a fan of the films, I may have put it down after a few chapters. Much like the other reviews, it seems dull, doesn't paint a vivid image, and has little to no character development. However, I have seen the films, and am a huge fan. In a way, I represent the readers who read this book because of our love for the movie. Probably something that would turn the nose of a few people. It represents the impact Tolkien has had - even years into the future; Toilken is getting people who don't read to read - sure Peter Jackson played a part, but he didn't write LORD OF THE RINGS.

Starting this book was exciting. I looked forward to meeting the original Aaragon, the original Gandalf - Frodo was just as useless as I imagined. Reading how the story was meant to be told was beautiful. Seeing Strider (Aaragon) sitting tenebrously in the corner, hood up, awaiting his cue to approach was a powerful image. The influence of the first encounter - the significance it (will hold) holds on the future of middle earth makes the reader appreciate the smaller words Toilken used to describe such a pivotal character, "Lean, dark, and tall" with a "pale stern face a pair of keen grey eyes". These small, somewhat insignificant characteristics described create a image of hope for middle earth, and Frodo.

There are many parts of this book that create a lovely sense of community among the hobbits - some whānauatanga. Like when Frodo and his band come across an old farmer; one that feud with the family line of Pippin'. There is anger and retribution in the feelings the farmer holds; but non the less he takes them in. The farmer, unaware of the dire state and future of Middle Earth. I wonder, when shit hits the fan, if he'll be worried about family feuds.

All in all, a slow, boring read (from a non-bias view), but a brilliant, familiar, and inspiring read for those that love the films.

Had wanted to read this book for a long time - and it took me a long time to finish! - but I found it to be hard work.

I can fully appreciate that Tolkien is a good writer. He litters the book with poems, songs, and plenty of detailed descriptions which show off his ability.

However, I found that there were large chunks of the book where there simply wasn’t enough happening to keep me interested. The first third is particularly guilty of this. And whilst detailed descriptions are great, they are often excessive. There comes a point where it doesn’t add anything else to the mental imagery, but he keeps going.

I’ve seen the films and think they’re excellent. For comparison, the rough halfway point in the film (Council of Elrond) comes at about 70% of the way through the book. It is a VERY sluggish start to the trilogy.

I do admire the lengths Tolkien went to to create such a detailed world and lore, and I think it’s that care and effort that carried me through. But, alas, I think I’m going to have a long break from middle earth.

3.5/5. I wish I hadn’t seen the movies before I read the books, or I wish at least that I didn’t remember the movies as well as I do. I knew most of what was going to happen, and I knew all of the important things that were going to happen. I knew that wraiths would attack the Shire and the group of four hobbits would flee, only to find Strider. I knew that he wasn’t a bad guy like the tension hinted towards, but that he was actually secretly a good guy. I knew they would get to Rivendell and council with Elrond, and the fellowship of the ring would be formed. I knew they would get into Moria through the gate next to the water, and inside Moria Gandalf would “die” (though I also know he doesn’t truly die, or at the very least he comes back) due to the balrog on the bridge. I knew Boromir would want the ring and get a bit vicious, and I also know he’ll die next book. All of the big plot points were spoiled to me, and most of the stuff in between. I wonder whether I would have liked the book a lot more had I not known what would happen. None of the tension or worry sticks to me, and it made an already slightly boring book far more boring. I still liked the parts of the book where things happened; the events, the dialogue, the characters, etc, but I was incredibly bored and brain-fogged by the descriptions of weather, the travel sequences, the even the detailing of the landscapes and Middle Earth history to some degree. I imagine if I didn’t know what would happen that those boring parts would be far easier to get through, but alas, I’ll likely never know. I listened to it narrated by Andy Serkis, and I thought he did a good job of making the book, and especially the dialogue, fun to listen to. The character voices were awesome and I loved it whenever someone spoke (unless they were singing; in which case, I didn’t understand have the words due to the flowery language, names of places and people I could barely hear and spell out in my mind, and the fact that understanding all the words notwithstanding the aforementioned is already difficult). I really liked all of the times when things were actually happening or people were actually speaking. Also I didn’t give this review any thought beforehand, so I probably wrote very confusingly and rambling-y.

I am not a fantasy person, which makes me struggle reading this book. I can appreciate that it is well written, and the genius behind the worldbuilding is remarkable. Just not my favorite read.

If there’s a book that doesn’t need an introduction, it’s probably this one: It established fantasy as a mainstream genre of fiction, and there is no way to overstate its influence on modern epic fantasy; Tolkien pretty much single-handedly popularized the notion of creating original worlds with their own detailed history, geography, and even language systems, as well as populating them with different fictional races and strange, often mythology-inspired creatures.

My earliest memory of Lord of the Rings is the yellowed, massively oversized poster of the 1978 animated movie that hung in my uncle’s study, nicked from the cinema where he used to work at as a teen. I found the poster to be scary, but was also fascinated by it, so when Peter Jackson’s adaptation eventually hit theaters, he took me to see it. I got obsessed, and he gifted me my first copy of the book for my birthday that same year; I have a vivid memory of my grandmother gasping at the size of the single volume, and of me checking the edition notice, realizing that this story was older than both my parents, which seemed unfathomable. I was eleven; a century younger than Bilbo Baggins, whose eleventy-first birthday party the story opens with.

“Don’t adventures ever have an end? I suppose not. Someone else always has to carry on the story.”


During events related in the more child-friendly prequel The Hobbit, Bilbo had stumbled upon a ring while lost in a cave, and took it back to his home in the Shire. All he knows about it is that it turns him invisible when he puts it on, yet he is strangely attached to it, and reluctant to leave it to his heir Frodo. He only gives it up, grudgingly, at the urging of his friend Gandalf, a wizard who has been harboring a suspicion: That Bilbo’s ring is the One Ring of legend, thought lost.

“One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them,
One Ring to bring them all, and in the darkness bind them”


All the while, in the distant, evil land of Mordor, the Dark Lord Sauron, Ruler of the One Ring which contains most of his power, is gathering strength, and means to reclaim what was taken from him in order to enslave all of Middle-Earth. Gandalf insists that the Ring must leave the Shire, and so Frodo sets out with three of his friends, with Sauron’s servants hot on their heels, meeting many dangers but also many friends on their way to Rivendell, a realm of the Elves, where a Council is held to discuss what to do about the Ring. Frodo accepts the burden of taking it to the only place where it can be destroyed—the Cracks of Mount Doom, the place where it was forged, in the heart of Sauron’s realm. To help Frodo in his quest, a Fellowship of Nine is created, consisting of the four Hobbits that set out from the Shire, Gandalf, Aragorn and Boromir, two men, the Elf Legolas, and Gimli the Dwarf. The Fellowship of the Ring tells the first part of the quest to destroy the One Ring, up to the eventual and inevitable breaking of the fellowship.

“The world is indeed full of peril, and in it there are many dark places; but still there is much that is fair, and though in all lands love is now mingled with grief, it grows perhaps the greater.”


The prose is pretty, but rather old-fashioned, and as such an acquired taste, and there are many rhymed poems, songs, and riddles that expand on the lore of Middle-Earth sprinkled throughout—too many, for my taste. In that way, this volume is a bit of an outlier, as well as with its somewhat repetitive, episodic structure: Frodo and his fellow travelers make their way from one safe haven to the next, encountering dangers in between these cozy refuges. The volumes are really just parts of one story deemed too long to be published in one piece, but if forced to choose, this would be my least favorite—I can intellectually appreciate the depth of the world-building, but I have read the series three or four times throughout my life now, and the Tom Bombadil part has never felt like anything but a chore to get through. It may be an exceptionally slow-burning narrative, but Tolkien undeniably weaves an impressively rich tapestry to tell an immersive story about the corrupting influence of power in a classic tale about the struggle between good and evil, and about how the integrity of character and selfless courage needed to step up for what may seem like a hopeless task can often be found where it is least expected.

It’s so sad that I’m giving a beloved book a low rating. Don’t get me wrong 3 stars isn’t bad but I thought I would enjoy it way more than I actually did. The writing is very boring and dull at various points and it was so hard to get through it. It usually takes me a few days or at least a week to read a book. This took me almost A MONTH!! The wordy descriptions of every little thing made it hard for me to read a lot in one sitting. I already have a bad attention span and this book made it so much worse. I’m not trying to compare this to the movies but the movies were so much better. All the action scenes were amazing. All of those same scenes in the book were very dull and unexciting. Like Gandalf’s death. In the movie it was so sad and everyone was heartbroken. In the book it was like, “He fell and people looked in horror. Then they moved on.” I understand they had to move on with their quest but the scene was very dull. It’s like when a book tries to hype you up and we’re getting to the climax point and then we get to the scene and… it was so boring and uneventful that you just wanna cry. That’s kinda how some scenes in this book were. There was rising action and then the climax wasn’t really a climax and it was just plain boring.

Characters: I feel like all the characters kinda talked the same and there’s no real unique personality to any of the characters. Which makes me like the movies more because everyone has a clear unique personality. Pippin and Merry are the funny ones and love to goof off. Aragorn is that lost kingly dude and he’s wise and kind and kingly. Gimli is a dwarf and I think that describes him enough. He’s brave and protective. Legolas is sassy and sarcastic and he’s my favorite. Sam the gardener and the protector of Frodo. And finally Frodo the ring bearer. We can all see unique personalities for each person in the movie. In the book I don’t think we have that.

Plot: I loved it! Aside from the long descriptions of every little thing, it was great. I enjoyed reading about the Shire and Tom Bombadil and obviously the main plot. This is great literature. Just because I say the book was a little boring doesn’t mean this isn’t a great book to read. I already knew the main plot so it wasn’t really a surprise when I was reading it. There are so many differences between the book and the movie and I quite enjoyed comparing the events that happened it each.

Writing: You already know how I feel about the writing. Most parts were boring and I had to put the book down several times. But I did enjoy it a lot and when the dialogue came or where it was a faster pace I enjoyed it more.

Don’t let any of the reviews get you down. Yes the book was dull at some points but this is still a great read and I think it’s very worth it. If you’re looking for great literature this is it. Please read it and just push through. I swear it’ll be worth your time.

I struggled to fully connect with this one. There were quite a few sections that felt overly drawn out, and the sheer number of fantasy names and references often left me confused about who or what was being talked about. Some of the descriptions I can appreciate, yes—but there were so many of them that I often found myself zoning out or skimming through. It’s incredibly descriptive to the point that it became a bit of a slog, even though I can appreciate the craftsmanship behind it. So dense and heavy with detail.

There’s also a surprising amount of singing, which I personally didn’t enjoy. I ended up skipping most of the song breaks because they didn’t add much for me and often broke whatever momentum the story was starting to build. The Tom Bombadil section especially felt totally out of place and, honestly, I still don’t really understand the point of it.

Despite all this, there were moments I genuinely enjoyed—particularly when the writing felt more focused. The final chapter, for instance, was fantastic. It flowed so much better and felt like the kind of storytelling I had hoped the whole book would offer. That chapter alone was a 5-star experience for me, and it left me with a bittersweet sense of what could’ve been.

I have to admit, I liked the movie adaptation more. I really wanted to love this book the way so many others do, and I’m honestly sad to be giving such a low rating to such a classic. I was prepared for the old-fashioned prose and the slow pace, but I still found the book incredibly boring at times. Everything unfolded so slowly, and there was rarely a moment where the pacing picked up or any real suspense kicked in.

That said, I do plan to finish the trilogy—I want to see where the journey goes—but I’ll definitely be mixing in some more modern reads along the way. I completely understand why this book is beloved and seen as a masterpiece. It deserves that recognition. But for me, personally, in terms of enjoyment, this was a 3-star read.

As much as I want to give this book 5 stars, I can’t find many reasons Fellowship of the Ring deserves more than three. The writing is excellent, don’t get me wrong, but the plot could not be less enticing.

Coming off the heels of reading the first three books in the Red Rising series where the characters contain multitudes and differing interests, I could not believe how one-dimensional the characters seemed in Lord of the Rings. Frodo feels as if he has no progression. After numerous life or death incidents he feels as flat as ever, trudging forward without any self reliance. I feel as though Frodo cannot handle a single scenario in this book without a “big brother” swooping in to save him at the last moment.

As I mentioned earlier the writing is a high point. Tolkien is very descriptive, almost to a fault. Every detail of the landscape, weather, creatures, and companions is represented in these expansive walls of text, which may be off putting to some but I found rather charming.

In any other book with a relatively developed plot I believe the writing would shine, however the combination of the dull journey from the Shire and the flooding of information Tolkien shares creates a real slog of a book where I just kept finding myself wondering when the book would really start to pick up.

Gut geschrieben aber mir persönlich viel zu langweilig und die Hälfte der Charaktere haben gar keine richtige Persönlichkeit und für mich somit auch keinen mehrwert. Aragorn carried die ganze Geschichte auf seinen Schultern. Wenn man es als Reisebericht ansieht, ist es solide.

My review is not a rebuke of this book or what role it plays in the history of fantasy. Undoubtedly the author changes the genre and builds something beyond him. Perhaps he even builds on the ideas in this book in the next ones which I will read and see. However, I found as a single text it was lacking for me.

It is oddly paced with little detail devoted to big moments and considerable detail to people talking and singing in what feel like less important points. It feels rushed and also overly long. I don’t like saying it but I felt cold as I read it and once I finished it. It took energy for me to read it, something other defining pieces of fiction have not.

I still regard it as an important piece, but it is not one I will rush back to or think about as a book beyond its place in history and the fantasy movement.

I finally finished The Fellowship of the Ring, and I have to admit—it was a bit of a drag. While I appreciate Tolkien’s incredible world-building and the impact he’s had on fantasy literature, this book felt long-winded and slow at times. He has a way of turning what could be one page of action into twenty, and that made the pacing drag for me.

There were moments I genuinely enjoyed, especially once the fellowship began to take shape and the bigger picture came into view. Still, the overall journey felt more tedious than exciting.

I know everyone likes their own thing, and that’s totally valid—but because this series is so widely loved and iconic, I can’t help but feel that some of the 4- and 5-star reviews might be a bit obligatory, more about the legacy than the reading experience itself.

I really enjoy the second movie, so I'm hopeful that the next two books will offer more energy and emotional depth. Looking forward to continuing the story, even if this one didn’t fully click for me.

2) all this random Lord of the Rings lore in my brain can finally be put to use 📜🧠
3) ITS TRUELY THE GREATEST ADVENTURE STORY EVER TOLD 🗺️🌋⚔️

At this point in my life I do not posses the literary analysis skill to proper write a review that will do this book justice, but regardless, I will attempt anyway.

✏️𝓣𝓱𝓮 𝔀𝓻𝓲𝓽𝓲𝓷𝓰:

The way that Tolkien wrote this book is just genius. I mean, the descriptions are so rich and so lavish but just sparse enough to leave some to your imagination. The writing flows so well and it's so easy to get swept away into another world. Speaking of another world, Tolkien did a fantastic job building such an elaborate and imaginative world. It's world building like nothing before and I truly believe that most High Fantasy rides on the back of Tolkien's genius work. At times it can be a bit wordy but I think that's part of the books charm and I wouldn't have it any other way.

🧝🏻‍♂️𝓣𝓱𝓮 𝓬𝓱𝓪𝓻𝓪𝓬𝓽𝓮𝓻𝓼:

I'd like to touch on the characters because they are truly the star of the show. Especially Aragorn. 🥵 I admit, when I was 12, I thought him a bit chopped and I constantly thought that he should probably wash his hair. But now. Now that I'm older I finally see the light. 💡ARAGORN THE MAN THAT YOU ARE.

Now let's move on to my other husband: Legolas Greenleaf. 🧝🏻‍♀️ My preteen obsession with him was probably very unhealthy. I mean, I thought I was going to marry this man, but of course Im fully a Aragorn girl now but that past will never be erased. The hundreds of photos I had of him in my camera roll will forever haunt me.

Anyway let's move on to our main protagonist: Frodo Baggins. He's a bit hard to like at first, I found him a bit bland and I was really like "we have to endure THIS GUY for three books??" But by the end I was fully sold on him.

📜𝓣𝓱𝓮 𝓹𝓵𝓸𝓽:

Yes it does move a lot slower than the movies. But it captures so much more than the movies could ever encapsulate. There's whole sections that are cut out because they had to keep the fast pace nature of the movie so a lot of magically moments were cut out. I see why this was necessary but it saddens be nonetheless.

Not much can be said about the plot, its perfection and that's all you need to know.

It's honestly a difficult task to enjoy a novel at this level of perfectly balanced style. I don't disrespect the great balance, but it doesn't intrigue me either. Look at Tolkien's contemporaries, like Evelyn Waugh, Graham Greene, Stella Gibbons, Iris Murdoch, etc. Their works all had their charm in having been unbalanced in writing - this book didn't, to my perception.

It's certainly an achievement of literary realism and its style. However, I should say that it is a realistic novel which is devoid of both "modern-novel excitement" or "medieval-literature grotesqueness."

It's unthinkable to let Pippin or Frodo having something unethical with a wife of a random peasant, for example, but that is what Medieval literature mostly has. Lancelot, various character from Medieval comedies, Celtish fairies, and even Renaissance Dante Alighieri were certainly illicit, and their immorality is one of the essential themes of European Medieval literature.

As a person who's written a BA thesis on Shakespeare (he understood Medieval thinking very well. cf. Falstaff), it's more than exhausting to read this novel, because I'm always interrupted by my (more updated to the scientific version than Tolkien, for anyway we had decades of studies) knowledge of Medievalism. Every three page, I say to myself "when will the grotesqueness come...," which is a bleak reading of this colossus of realistic style.

Short review: Great, albeit slow plot, intricate and detailed worldbuilding, and fleshed out characters. Recommended for people who like to fall into new and complex worlds, but for the crowd that fancies the plot more than the journey, I'll recommend the abridged version.

Long Review:
I'll just say this is a classic for a reason. The world is carefully & intricately carved with so much attention to detail. This book has a deep care for description and setting of the atmosphere, so much so that every time I put this down and picked it again I felt like I was stepping through a portal into a land that was foreign yet so familiar to me. There were vivid, enchanting descriptions of nature, of forests, of mountains and of rivers. It was exhilarating.

The politics and the relations between different races are described in great detail and the all the characters, including side characters we meet only once are given distinct personalities, voices and vices. Left me in awe of the author's mind.

But like all great books this had it's shortcomings.

First off there were too many songs. I grew tired.

Second off all too many times did we go on a tangent and I almost forgot what we were doing in the first place. Every single time the characters sat down to rest from their journey they'd certainly go on a tangent and we'd get to know more about the world, which is fine and dandy but the monologues often went on for like 5-10 pages straight. Strangely it wasn't even info-dump as most fantasy books tend to have them in certain capacity, but it was just useless information that seldom came handy, except for teaching us about some weird custom of the elves. Fried my brain.

Thirdly, the characters made bad decisions ALL the time. Imagine you're on some journey with the threat of death hanging over your head would you not tell your companions that

Fourth, It was too long. This did not need to be 500+ pages. I wish I had read the abridged version and would advise you to do so.

Anyways i'm happy to have read this, however long it was drawn because it is a valuable piece to literature in the fantasy genre. There are few fantasy books today that can do what Tolkien does so effortlessly: lead you into another world that would stay with you for a long, long time.
Not a huge fantasy fan, but this was such a cute book

The first installment of one of the most renowned fantasy trilogies ever created was honestly a lot slower than I would have imagined. I was surprised to find myself struggling to get into the first half of this book (Book 1).

Tolkien drags on the journey of the Hobbits to immerse us in the world of Middle Earth better through his thorough descriptions, but it feels almost too slow and at points repetitive. As soon as the Hobbits reach Rivendell (Book 2), the story picks up and really becomes addicting. I feel, however, that while Tolkien has a master sense of world-building with his vivid descriptions of the paths and sights, he lacks character-building. Aside from Gandalf and Aragorn, the characters feel rather dull and unmoving in this, especially the Hobbits and Legolas. I think the films do a much better job of fleshing out distinct personalities in this regard for each member of the Fellowship.

There was a ton to like in this great novel, too, however. As I mentioned before, the world-building Tolkien creates is extremely vivid. I found myself memorising the map in the back of the book to keep up with the path of the Fellowship. The entire section in Moria and the bridge had me on the edge of my seat. Gandalf's sacrifice was really hard-hitting, and his final words were so well done: "Fly, you fools."

I rarely ever say this, but I think Peter Jackson's adaptation for this first installment is actually an upgrade from the novel (not that the novel is bad by any means). By cutting down a bit of the Hobbit's solo journey to Rivendell and giving more personality to the Fellowship, he is able to keep the main story intact and deepen the emotional stakes.

Overall, I thought this was a solid starting entry to the trilogy, but it fell a bit short of the nostalgia and quintessentialism of its predecessor, The Hobbit, or There and Back Again.
