Not to be confused with the BBC radio play. I only recently found this version and I'm glad to have listened to it! I'd put it at 3.5/5.

Here's my silly little brain-dump list of differences/similarities between the NPR (1979) and BBC (1981, revised 2002) radio plays--I see them compared very often.

Abridged/"Cut" Sections:

NPR version does cover two key events in the first half of the Fellowship (Tom Bombadil and the barrow-wights) and has more Crickhollow scenes. The NPR version also concludes not too long after the company departs from Lothlórien, which makes sense considering the shorter runtime. Meanwhile, BBC (2002) closely, and I mean closely, follows the events of PJ's films in both overall content, pacing, and events.

Duration: NPR (3 hrs and 24 mins) | BBC (4 hrs and 35 mins)

Instrumentation/Poetry/Songs:

Both have instrumentation, however, BBC (2002) incorporates music into the radio play to a greater extent (poetry sections are also accompanied by music). The NPR version also noticeably leans less into sound effects and production, and relies more heavily on narration.

- - -

If anyone were to ask which radio play to listen to, I'd recommend listening to samples of both and going from there. My 3.5/5 rating = an enjoyable listen, but not the version I would find myself returning to out of personal preference. Great performances from the cast and overall production.

El máximo exponente de la fantasía épica o alta fantasía, y se entiende el por qué.

Reconozco varios elementos que han influenciado a algunos autores del género de la época actual: personajes heroicos, travesías peligrosas, presencia fuerte de la magia, descripciones minuciosas del clima y del ambiente, etc.

Como catalizador de gran diversidad de historias, comprendo la razón por la que Tolkien es EL REFERENTE. Cumple con los requisitos de una buena fantasía y sabe muy bien cuál es el trayecto de su trama, hacía dónde va y los detalles minuciosos de su mundo, controla perfectamente la psicología de sus personajes y deja en claro el papel de cada uno de ellos.

Pero vayamos punto por punto, no es que pretenda proponer una opinión innovadora, seguro que ya habrá más de un argumento que comparta mis ideas con respecto a la historia, pero quiero aportar con mis propias palabras un granito de arena al ice berg de comentarios.

Personajes: diversos y definidos. Me caería bien la mayoría de estos, sino fuera por tres cosas: 1) Algunos me parecieron insulsos o poco interesantes, por no decir que no tenían nada qué aportar para la cantidad de escenas que se les dedicó. Bien podían haber muerto y la historia seguiría su curso. 2) Los diálogos eternos de redundacias, sobre todo cuando hablaban los elfos. Se comprende que es parte de su naturaleza ser tan elocuentes y refinados al hablar, pero por el amor de todos los cielos, me llegaron a cansar. 3) Conozco spoilers de algunos personajes con los que sé que debería simpatizar, pero que no lo logré por culpa de estos mismos. En fin, no es culpa del libro, pero así es.

Y me gustó el personaje de Sam.

Trama: Bien establecida. Con algunos capítulos aburridos, pero que se ven claramente por qué el autor los consideró necesarios (Tom Bobaldil fue de los que más me aburrió).

Mundo: el tesoro del libro. La historia de la Tierra Media es muy compleja y bien hecha. Aun desconozco cosas que ignoro si se revelarán en el resto de los libros (estoy tan acostumbrada a las explicaciones de los sistemas s de magia de Sanderson que dudo que Tolkien me ofrezca algo parecido. Puedo pecar de inculta, pero es lo que pienso).

Narración: A veces da vueltas en un mismo punto, pero está bien hecha y es elegante. La parte de las canciones fue de lo más tedioso, pero eso le aumenta la riqueza a la fantasía. SIN EMBARGO, las descripciones de batalla dejan mucho que desear. Tolkien es bueno con las descripciones del ambiente, pero con la acción... Supongo que prefiero otro estilo, uno menos genérico. Y... Puede que esté mal, pero muchas veces encontré similitudes entre su estilo de escritura y las que se pueden encontrar en algunas historias bíblicas. Fue un detalle interesante.

Conclusión: Buen libro, pero no es el que más emoción me ha generado a la hora de leer fantasía, y eso pesa mucho en mi calificación y opiniones. Admito que es, por excelencia, el mejor ejemplo de mundo de fantasía de todos los tiempos, y supongo que lo será por mucho más. Leeré el resto de los libros para cumplir con el requisito de consumidora del género.

"Gredzenu pavēlnieks" ir pasaulē slavenākais fantāzijas darbs. Pirmā daļa "Gredzena brālība" tika izdota tālajā 1954.gadā. Šis fantāzijas darbs ir pasaules literatūras klasika, kuru zina vai ikkatrs pasaules iedzīvotājs.
Lasītājs nonāk jaunā pasaulē - Viduszemē, kur mīt hobiti, elfi, rūķi, burvji, orki, pūķi. Arī cilvēki.
Hobits Bilbo Baginss kādā no saviem ceļojumiem atrod gredzenu, kuram piemīt samaitāta vara, kas uz karstām pēdām iedarbojas uz tā valkātāju. Pēc šī gredzena tīko daudzi, bet nonākot sliktās rokās, gredzens var nodarīt neatgriezenisku postu.
Ar šo gredzenu saistās lielākās cerības un briesmīgākās izbailes.
Frodo, kas ir Bilbo tuvākais radinieks, saņem šo gredzenu mantojumā, un kļūst par gredzena glabātāju. Frodo uzdevums ir nogādāt šo Varas gredzenu vietā, kur to var iznīcināt. Kopā ar saviem uzticamākajiem ceļabiedriem Frodo dodas tālajā ceļā, kas ir piedzīvojumu un briesmu pilns, aiz katra stūra viņiem uzglūn tumšie spēki un gredzena tīkotāji.
Šis stāsts nes sevī svarīgāko vēstījumu, ka tikai visi kopā, ticot un darot, mēs varam uzveikt ļauno. Tas ir stāsts par drosmi, draudzību, uzticēšanos un ticību saviem spēkiem.
Līdz kādai 300.lpp. man lasījās ļoti grūti. Autora valoda ir poētiska, teksts ietver ārkārtīgi daudz un dažādu Viduszemes vietu nosaukumus, tiek pieminēti ļoti daudzi ķēniņi un ķēniņu dēli. Tā visa bija tik daudz, ka es jau saputrojos un vairs nespēju izsekot līdzi. Arī daudzās dziesmas bija gan par daudz, gan par sarežģītu. Pēc 300.lpp., kad Gendalfs visus notikumus saistībā ar gredzenu salika pa plauktiņiem, tad arī tālāk lasījās daudz raitāk un interesantāk. Kopumā notikumi noris ļoti lēni un gausi, daudz resursu tiek patērēts uz varoņu gulēšanu un ēšanu. Interesantākie notikumi sākās jau tuvāk grāmatas beigām.

Šis ir jaunākais grāmatas izdevums, ar tiešām ļoti pievilcīgu grāmatas vizuālo dizainu, kā arī grāmatas beigās ir Viduszemes kartes, ko ir interesanti papētīt.

Cuando pienso en las razones del por qué me costo tanto terminar esta lectura, se me viene de inmediato a la cabeza la forma en la que está narrada la novela, ya que sentí desde el comienzo que se trataba de condensar demasiados detalles de la historia en un libro de solo 500 páginas, esto provoca un sentimiento de hostigamiento hacía el lector que obviamente tratará de entender y comprender cada detalle que Tolkien entrega sobre los lugares que se visitan, sobre los personajes y sobre grandes héroes que existieron en el pasado.

Otro problema para mi, es el tono del libro, puesto que a momentos se dan indicios de que es un libro épico y adulto en donde sus personajes pasan por peligros reales, todo esto para después mostrarme a los personajes cantando felizmente. Esto me dificultava tormame en serio todo lo que estaba sucediendo en la historia, para mí nunca se sintió la gran amenaza del señor oscuro, por lo tanto nunca me preocupe tanto del destino de los personajes.

Para finalizar, no todo es malo y aburrido. Tolkien construye un mundo único y mágico para el lector, se da el trabajo de crear e introducir diversas clases de personajes, teniendo elfos, horcos, hobbits, enanos, entre otros. Gracias a las cosas que este autor se atrevió a proponer en esta novela, hoy existen grandes historias como las de Geralt de Rivia y las de juego de tronos, eso siempre hará que uno respete el trabajo del autor.

Es una lectura densa que tiene grandes momentos, sin embargo por el tono de la historia y por contener taaantos detalles sobre el diverso contexto que rodea a los personajes me dificultó disfrutar de la novela.

It almost felt like Tolkien was saying a lot, without saying anything at all at the same time, if that makes sense. It’s as if he was trying to convey the story in a meeting, when it really should’ve just been in an email 😂 I need to look on Sparknotes to understand what the heck was actually going on. I definitely want to continue on with the series because it’s so iconic and I want to read it just to say that I’ve read it, but I’m realizing that fantasy is just not my thing, for the most part.

I can get behind fantasy books that have the right amount of world building, while also really developing the plot and the characters. I’m finding, though, that a lot of fantasy books are either one extreme or the other: they either really emphasize the world building, and forsake the plot and characters, or they really emphasize the plot and characters, but forsake the world building. There needs to be a balance! That’s why I really enjoy Harry Potter because J. K. Rowling does such a great job at all three: world building, the characters, and the plot. Why can’t every fantasy author be like her?

Why do fantasy authors feel like they need to go on tangents as if to prove that their ideas for world building need to be validated? You don’t need to rant & rave about insignificant world building points just to let people know that you have an imagination. Keep it simple and relevant.

My dear fans,

I know this review may come as a surprise to some, as this is a well known and well loved set of books. There are bits and pieces of this book that I really enjoyed, such as I meeting these interesting characters and seeing how they impact the crew we’ve been following: Tom Bombadil & Aragorn (Strider) namely.

This may be a hot take, but my main issue with this book is that the pages just blend together so much. If Tolkien wanted to spent this amount of pages on the journey from The Shire to Rivendell, I wish he used these pages to help built the relationship of reader to protagonists by learning more about them through dialogue or actions, instead of literally talking about the directions the Hobbits used in intricate detail.

I plan to finish the other two books, as I know so many people who are deeply fond of the series. I hope that the other two books pick up the pace a little bit.

The Fellowship of the Ring is an undeniably captivating book that draws readers into an epic journey through Middle-earth. The vivid descriptions of landscapes, the sense of adventure, and the deep bonds of friendship forged among the members of the Fellowship make it a memorable and engaging read. Tolkien masterfully explores themes of loyalty, courage, and the weight of responsibility, which continue to resonate with readers today.
However, one aspect that stood out to me was the limited inclusion of female characters. The story is heavily centered around male perspectives, and the few women who do appear—like Galadriel and Arwen—play relatively passive or supporting roles in the broader narrative. While their presence is significant in certain moments, it’s hard to ignore how their contributions are overshadowed by the male-dominated journey.
Despite this, the book remains a cornerstone of fantasy literature, offering rich world-building and timeless themes. Still, it invites reflection on how the genre—and storytelling in general—has evolved (and continues to evolve) toward more inclusive narratives.

My overall sentiment toward this book is similar to the Hobbit. I'm not sure why this book/story is claimed to be the pinnacle of all fantasy books. And really, most people I speak to about this can't even use it's release date as an argument to justify their reasoning because they didn't read it back then during a time when 99% of fantasy books were only written as children's stories. If you stop here and read nothing else of the review, the star rating tells it all. It's average. Not bad by any means, but far from incredible.

Okay, strap in.

As I completed the monstrous Prologue (seriously, what book has a 27 page long prologue) and a couple chapters, I immediately realized the tone of this book was different from The Hobbit. To confirm my suspicion, I went to Tolkien's website and learned a couple things. First, The Hobbit was a children's book. Tolkien said (and I quote) "I had the habit, while my children were still young, of inventing and telling children's stories for their private amusement. The Hobbit was one of them." Secondly, the Tolkien website describes the author's original intentions was for Lord of the Rings to be for a different audience, an adult audience. This makes sense because everything about the writing style and word usage was more advanced (albeit, slightly). The website categorizes The Lord of the Rings as YA for nowadays readers, but it would have been considered an adult book when it was published.

Oh, backtracking for a moment. Something I forgot to mention in my review on the Hobbit was that another disappointing part of it was there are zero female characters. I re-remembered that during The Fellowship of the Ring when the first female character was introduced (after over 15 male characters already existed). It made me so sad and upset and irritated. By the end of the book, there were a total of 3 females out of 35+ characters in this book. Kinda ridiculous. And the second female you meet says literally nothing. You're just told that she in the room with a group of people who are talking. What a pile of nothing. I actually stopped reading for 2 days because every time I picked up the book, I got annoyed with it to the point where I couldn't focus on the story. Eventually, I got over it enough that I could continue. But I'm still bitter to this day and you can probably tell since I'm still ranting about it...moving on.

During the Forward (written by the author, for the readers), Tolkien mentions that many Critics have many issues with the book. But 1 criticism of the book that he, and everyone apparently agrees with, is that the book was not long enough. I whole-heartedly disagree. Though there are moments/characters/lore which could have been fleshed out, there are far too many sections that go on forever - the Prologue, as one example. But it continues further into the book too. Each major segment that was designed to move the plot forward was clever and comprehensive (aka: there were no plot holes, scape goats, etc). However, each of these segments had so many menial/mundane moments - irrelevant or repetitive conversations, walking/travelling only to describe the same environment we already know about or songs about nonsense - sometimes back to back songs (yes, the multitude of full length songs are back). I know everyone says (and I mostly agree) that "the book is always better than the movie" but this is an example where a movie would (probably) streamline these part to build better flow for the audience. A movie often loses atmosphere or context or sometimes entire characters, and it has to make up for it with a spectacular visual experience. I'll be watching the movies for the first time after this to see how well they do.

Speaking of songs, there are way too many. The Hobbit (which had about 10, I think) was already too much for my taste. The Fellowship of the Ring was even more crazy with like 20 songs (some of which are re-sung at a later time for "reasons"). And these are not short verses. I copy/pasted a few songs and compared the length with Taylor Swift songs. These are longer than hers. To be clear, songs are fine in books, even long songs. If there's a purpose and they help elaborate on learning what kinda person they are "they like singing" or "lets gather around a campfire and tell a story through a song" - but this book has songs and singing just for the sake of it. Almost like the author simply wanted to change up the story telling method.

I think what makes this story (at least book 1 so far) so good and people desiring more (aka: a longer book) is how comprehensive the backstory is for every place, person, location and thing. However, the currently length is not flattering due to how much menial elaboration there is. The lore and politic moments often go down long tangents referencing places, battles, people, etc. that you've never heard about before or will hear about again. It's like there's a companion book that should have existed to give you context to all this backstory. It does make you want to learn more about these unknown things, but having them in the book like this kinda feels like filler.

The main story is hit and miss. The overall concept is great and unique compared to most fantasy books. But it does suffers from pacing issues as well as random side quests that are long and add nothing of value. The motivation for the main character to continue the quest at the midpoint of the story is kinda dumb and actually makes no sense. It's like they purposefully made it over-complicated and convoluted to hide the fact that there's no point to any decisions being made. Additionally, there is just lore dump, after lore dump. Backstory upon backstory. Mostly unfamiliar references to past battles, people etc. The only meaningful discussion was the history of the ring. Ultimately, the problem with this presentation is the importance everyone speaking puts on these moments and characters they talk about. But there's no meaning to the reader. Its like, hmm...it's like if an author kills off a character in chapter one. You don't have any connection to them so you basically shrug your shoulders like, oh well, I didn't really know them. As opposed to a character getting killed off at the end of the story that you got to know for 500 pages

There's a bunch of tie-ins to the Hobbit, which were really well done compared to how most author's handle prequels. It's not simply a repeat. They mention the prequel's quest in very brief terms, so that if you haven't read the Hobbit, you'll wanna go read it at that moment. Then to compliment that, you get a lot of extra context from recent characters which fill in the gaps that existed in The Hobbit. This whole integration was awesome.

Even though most of what I wrote here seems negative, the book isn't "bad" - I just wanted to highlight all my criticisms (and mention a few good things). I had my doubts before I started reading this. And though I'm not surprised I didn't fall in love with it, the only "actual" disappointment is the lack of character diversity (aka: 3 bland female characters).

Good luck book 2. I hope you can do better

My first time reading Lord of the Rings and I know it is sacrilege to give it such a middling rating. There are parts of the book that I enjoyed far more than the rating suggests. I will not waste any time on a plot summary; even I knew it before reading, thanks to the films. As is usually the case, the book provides a deeper experience. I enjoyed the lengthier treatment of life in the Shire provided in the book. My anticipation for the story built as the first chapters covered decades of the lives of Frodo and Bilbo before the quest truly began. Even the extended version of the film doesn’t have this scope. Additionally, I loved the descriptions of the addictive, overpowering effects the ring has on all around it. It is not surprising to have a “good” character like Saruman corrupted by the ring’s influence, but watching even unquestionable heroes like Bilbo suffer under its intoxication is powerful.

So, why only 3 stars? The balance between worldbuilding and plot advancement went out of balance for me mid-book. I appreciate some level of background support, but I can also get impatient as a reader. The formation of the fellowship in Rivendell stretched on for me and pushing through a section that I anticipated as building momentum and interest had the opposite effect. Some aspects of the book’s worldbuilding are fascinating. Sauron’s disruption to the middle earth status quo gives an opportunity to contrast the worldviews of dwarves, elves, hobbits, and men, and their inclinations on issues like isolationism, immigration, and prejudice. I have less interest in the tales of historic lineages and ancient history of the world. I like the idea of representing this content in song, but in practice, I did not find reading them to be much fun. I would have much preferred to spend more time on Fellowship members Gimli the dwarf and Legolas the elf, who get much less attention than Gandalf, Aragorn and Boromir, and the Hobbits.

Thankfully, I felt my interest levels growing again as the Fellowship made its way through Moria and particularly at the climax of the book, where we’re teased with Gollum’s introduction to the story and the havoc the ring plays with Boromir’s commitment to the Fellowship. I will definitely continue on to the next book in the trilogy.

Going into LOTR I had very high expectations for Tolkien's magnum opus, however these expectations were not at all met in the Fellowship of the Ring. The book was far from bad, but the first half was quite the slog to get through due to the writing style. Once the story found its footing in the second half and fell into a rhythm, I found myself much more excited to continue reading. All in all, Tolkien's writing was not my favorite style, but the story being told is great and I can see the opportunity for it to continue to improve throughout the trilogy. I'm excited to complete the trilogy and see where Tolkien takes his story.

Undeniably a monumental work of fantasy—a richly imagined world with profound depth and scope. While I appreciated the incredible detail and the thought Tolkien put into every corner of Middle-earth, I found myself struggling at times to stay fully immersed in the story.

The strength of this book lies in its world-building. Tolkien’s descriptions of places like Rivendell, Lothlórien, and even the Shire are so vivid, they feel alive. The history, languages, and cultures he created are astonishing, adding layers of authenticity to the narrative. I could sense the weight of Middle-earth’s history in every passage. However, it’s this same level of detail that, at times, felt overwhelming. There were moments when I wanted the story to move forward more quickly, especially in the early chapters and some of the long travel sequences.

That said, I absolutely loved the camaraderie among the members of the Fellowship. Watching their relationships evolve, particularly the friendship between Legolas and Gimli, was a highlight. Frodo’s quiet bravery and Aragorn’s steady leadership were compelling, and Sam’s loyalty made my heart ache. These characters are the beating heart of the story, and they kept me engaged even when the pacing felt slow.

Certain scenes stood out as unforgettable, such as the harrowing flight from the Black Riders, the haunting beauty of Lothlórien, and, of course, the dramatic confrontation on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm. These moments were gripping, emotional, and masterfully written, making the slower stretches worth pushing through.

While I struggled with the density of the detail at times, I recognize that it’s part of what makes Tolkien’s work so enduring. The Fellowship of the Ring isn’t a book to rush through; it’s one to savour and absorb, even if it requires patience. It’s a remarkable foundation for an epic story, and despite the challenges, I’m glad I embarked on the journey.

The charm of the LOTR world is its diverse cast of characters. There are dwarves, elves, humans, and most importantly, hobbits. Exploring the values and oddities of each group made the characters compelling and realistic, even though they were magical creatures.

It's evident from Tolkien’s writing that he felt very connected to the LOTR world. Each location in the book is unique and the descriptions are vivid, albeit repetitive at times. He could write pages describing the same forest, so while masterful writing is always a good quality for a book to have, I thought it was overdone just a little in this one. Naturally, I had high expectations for The Fellowship of the Ring. Arguably, it’s the most influential fantasy novel of all time. Tolkien’s ability to create a world so rich and full of detail is undeniably impressive.

Hobbits make for likable heroes. Despite their stature and simple outlook on life, they have a lot of fight in them. Gandalf, Saruman, and Aragorn are great too.

However, I cannot say I particularly enjoyed Tolkien’s prose. He has a habit of repeating himself and apart from the Mines of Moria, which was easily the most riveting section, there’s a lack of haste for the majority of the story.

I think I might like fantasy that’s a little darker with plenty of moral ambiguity. Nevertheless, I really enjoyed The Hobbit. Is it sacrilegious to say I preferred it?

Despite being little dull, I can appreciate it in many ways, and I hope to find the next instalments a little more thrilling.

P.s. It makes me appreciate Peter Jackson even more.

By the end I think I finally starting to get used to the whimsy and weirdness of Tolkien's world. Tolkien será su guía y las llevará caminando, a veces a caballo y a veces en bote, por un largo recorrido por los elementos más fascinantes de su mitología, ya que con El Hobbit no se profundizaba lo suficiente, al parecer.

Prepárense para caminar mucho, como les digo, subiendo lomas, bajando barrancos, torciendo a la derecha y a la izquierda en un camino que les llevará a las secciones de El Bosque Viejo, donde está la curiosa escultura de Tom Bombadil, la sala de Rivendell, donde la efigie de Elrond dirá muchas cosas, luego a Moria, con sus altas columnas y un raro ejemplar de Balrog, y después a Lorien, con más elfos, como los de Rivendell, pero diferentes, entre ellos la hermosa Dama Galadriel, que es un regalo para la vista.

Durante el camino, que es largo y detallado, se nos unirá una compañía curiosa, y espero de corazón que de tanto andar a su lado no dejen de apreciar lo fascinantes que son. Y es que, ¿les he dicho ya que el camino es largo?

Mantengan el ánimo alto, pues les aseguro que las secciones que he mencionado merecen la pena, pero hay mucho que caminar, muchas torceduras en el camino, claros en el bosque y ríos con los que tropezar, y por todos ellos debemos pasar, pues el mapa de las tierras que pisamos también es extenso y cuidadosamente trazado. ¡No decaigan, damas y caballeros!

No decaigan, porque esta es solo la primera parte del Museo. No decaigan.

This falls under the category of books I wish I loved but just don’t. I obviously adore the movies, so I was pretty predisposed to liking this, but I really don’t vibe with Tolkien’s writing and pacing. I won’t chalk my feelings up to it being “old” writing because I’ve recently read “old” books (pre-70s) that riveted me. Look, this book moves very slow.
The attention to detail is nice. The characters and landscape are well realized. The story is great. When we are in sections of the book where dialogue dominates the page or any kind of action dominates the page, we are in a good place. What really drags this down is Tolkein's description of the geography and where we are in relation to other things. He names like 8 different things to describe where 1 thing is. Very often, the characters are giving each other directions like they're living in the 1990s without gps.
I understand this is part of the world building. But this method often feels more like a textbook than part of a story. And in some ways Tolkein's style comes across as though this is a history book, not a novel.
This is afterall a relatively old book, being one of the first to establish such rich world building. Can you blame it that it isn't as refined as its counterparts in the 21st century? I suppose you have to a little bit.
There's also one chapter, that runs about 50 pages, that is just brutal. The members of the council recount stories of how they got to Rivendell, by just orating what happened (like a history textbook). We don't live out those scenes with those characters, we just hear them tell us what happened. It is dreadfully boring.
The movie actually does a great job of taking us into those scenes (biggest example is the turn of Saruman).
Overall, I respect this book's place in history. I love the story and the world and the characters. That's worth something. The dialogue and action sequences are really strong. But some of what amounts to world building is often dull.

I recently read The Hobbit for the first time and absolutely adored it, so I thought I would jump into The Fellowship of The Ring and finally give the LOTR series a go.

I found this book difficult to rate, because on one hand I think the main story is incredible, and obviously this series is much beloved. However, on the other hand, I did have to struggle through reading this book, and at points I felt like it was becoming a chore and pushing me towards a reading slump.

It's really clear why Tolkien is renowned for his world-building. He's packed so much fictional history into this book, that this does feel like you're stepping into a vast new universe. However, this world-building that Tolkien is known for is the thing I struggled with the most throughout the book. There were some chapters I just struggled to get through due to the sheer amount of references to places, languages, songs and characters. For a lot of the time, these things are completely irrelevant and inconsequential to the main story which feels frustrating at times. I personally found it difficult to keep track of all of the information I was been given, and while it does help to create this world, I'm not sure if we needed quite so much of it.

I would recommend this book as it is a staple of the fantasy genre and has shaped a lot of modern-day story telling. However, I would say to be prepared for a long, and at times, boring read. The main plot and characters are wonderful, but it is extremely slow-paced.

Some people say life is too short to read books you don’t enjoy. I mostly disagree. Learning to read books that are difficult, unpleasant, or otherwise frustrating teaches you a lot about what you value as a consumer of art and of the world, and it helps you build the stamina and confidence necessary to work on your own big projects, which now can be informed by research that, while not fun in the doing, is gratifying in the application. At least, that’s what pushing through books I don’t fully enjoy has taught me. There are many different ways to build the same muscle.

If I were to assign the first installment of LOTR a star rating based purely on my enjoyment, I’d give it a two. I didn’t have a great time reading it, as I found the journey sequences slow, repetitive, and boring. I felt like I was watching the director’s cut of a movie by a director whose taste does not align with mine. IMHO, The Fellowship of the Ring could have been a hundred pages shorter with no negative impact on the plot whatsoever. (Literally just nix every cardinal direction. I do not care what’s westerly or southward. Ever.)

But our unaligned tastes (mine and Tolkien’s) don’t really matter. LOTR’s impact on the high fantasy genre is ubiquitous, and for that alone I’m glad I read it. I loved being able to contextualize other series I grew up with (Harry Potter, The Chronicles of Narnia) as inspired by Middle-earth. Tolkien built one of the first truly immersive fantasy worlds, and—more impressive to me—he could really turn a phrase (when that was his priority, of course—I fear it often wasn’t).

I preferred reading The Hobbit because I prefer the Shire to any other Middle-earth setting, even Lothlórien. But I still give Fellowship a three. When all is said and done, I might not have liked my experience reading it, but I liked what it was doing, and I liked what it taught me.

Oh, and I loved Sam Gamgee. That right there is my guy.

Ritorno nella Terra di Mezzo

Dopo averlo letto per la prima volta a quindici anni, per la seconda a trenta, ora che lo affronto per la terza volta (e questa volta non dirò a quanti anni!), e nella nuova (e discussa) traduzione, sono forse pronto a riconciliarmi con Tolkien?
E uso il nome dell'autore, e non dell'opera, perché che lui stesso lo voglia o no, che lo neghi pure nell'introduzione alla seconda edizione, dove afferma che Il signore degli anelli non è né vuole essere un'allegoria, è inevitabile che la visione, le idee, il sentire dell'autore (la cui origine religiosa, e di una religione ben determinata) filtrino nell'opera, è inevitabile che ci siano dei motivi per cui ha scritto una cosa invece che un'altra.
E quest'opera, poi, non lascia scampo, perché è un'opera totale non solo nel dettaglio del Mondo creato, dagli ornamenti minuti di armi e vesti, sino alle singole foglie degli alberi delle sue grandi foreste, ma anche nella visione, nelle idee, nel sentire. Il signore degli anelli, più che un'opera totale, è un'opera totalitaria, in più di un senso del termine, perché ogni singolo evento che viene raccontato, ogni gesto, ogni parola, rientrano inevitabilmente in un disegno più grande, a cui vengono sottomessi, e questo disegno è quello di una lotta implacabile tra il bene e il male, concepiti in termini davvero assoluti.
Il bene e il male, in Tolkien, sono due entità, due sostanze, due realtà che vanno a innervare la materia stessa del suo Mondo, ogni sua particella, prima ancora che le menti e le azioni dei personaggi. Ed è una dicotomia fortemente improntata all'opposizione tra purezza e contaminazione: le creature malvagie che dilagano nella Terra di Mezzo non si limitano a compiere cattive azioni, ma minacciano di corrompere la sostanza delle cose, di guastarla, e sono costantamente definite con sintomatici aggettivi, come "immonde", "spregevoli",
"ignobili". Non c'è possibilità di tregua né di comprensione per ciò che, nel Mondo di Tolkien, si trova al di fuori della cerchia del bene, ma solo una battaglia inesausta che deve concludersi con l'annientamento del Nemico, nominato con una ben chiara maiuscola (e quanto maiuscole si trovano in Tolkien, a rimarcare la sostanzialità, la personificazione dei concetti).
Nelle lunghe discussioni che ho avuto con seguaci tolkieniani mi sa fa notare che, no, Il signore degli anelli non è così manicheo, perché ci sono personaggi che possono passare dal bene al male, e poi c'è Gollum, così ambiguo, sempre là sul crinale che separa le due dimensioni. Ma io ho ogni volta risposto che se esistono certo personaggi che vacillano tra il bene o il male, o che cascano direttamente dal primo al secondo, resta il fatto che a noi lettori è comunque mostrato con chiarezza quale sia il bene e quale sia il male, abbiamo costantemente la voce dell'autore all'orecchio a rammentarci come dobbiamo giudicare le azioni di questo o quel personaggio, lasciando poco spazio per i dubbî. C'è poi chi mi dice che Il signore degli anelli sarebbe un inno alla tolleranza e all'apertura, perché dipinge la capacità di popoli diversi di unirsi oltre le proprie divergenze. Sì, ma per cosa si uniscono? Si uniscono per sterminare senza porsi alcun dubbio al riguardo quelle creature, orchi in primis, che ci vengono mostrate come irrimediabilmente malvagie, brutte, sporche, ributtanti, creature viventi senza le quali (è questa la conclusione) il Mondo sarebbe un posto migliore.
Il rigido manicheismo, quasi esasperato, de Il signore degli anelli è anche ciò che mina le ambizioni stilistiche del suo autore. Le cui capacità sono sicuramente superiori a quelle di tanti suoi successivi epigoni (cosa comunque non difficile, ma per i demeriti di questi ultimi!), ma che stentano ad ascendere verso l'alto quando sarebbe necessario, ovvero nel dar forma convincente alla luce e ai suoni della sua fazione del bene, in particolar modo agli spazî in cui si muovono gli elfi, che risultano così convenzionali e deboli quando non va troppo male, ma stucchevoli quando va peggio. Ma questo è forse lo scotto da pagare per un autore che, nella forma (e non solo nella forma!) preferisce guardare indietro, a un tempo in cui scrivere non significava sperimentare o quantomeno sorprendere, bensì seguire una norma e una tradizione, scolpire parole ed eventi lungo linee consolidate, e questo anche nella costruzione dei personaggi, che nel Signore degli anelli sono di rado figure psicologiche, ma soprattutto simboli, emblemi.
L'inattualità de Il signore degli anelli è il suo grande pregio e la sua grande tara. Pregio, perché nel suo intento e accettata nei suoi termini l'operazione di inventare una nuova epica talmente rivolta al passato risulta in gran parte riuscita, laddove hanno invece fallito gli imitatori che sono venuti dopo. Ma è una tara perché l'opera non accetta di uscire dalle premesse intransigenti che la informano. E rende quindi difficile averne un'opinione, o anche solo una reazione emotiva, che non sia netta, di amore o di rigetto.
Per me il caso fu il secondo, quando a quindici anni misi per la prima volta mano a un'edizione che riportava la prima, vecchia traduzione (quella famosa, tra il resto, per gli "orchetti"). Allora avevo idee e visioni forse forti quanto quelle di Tolkien, ma dal lato diametralmente opposto al suo (negli anni dell'adolescenza ero un fervente seguace di Lovecraft, tanto per capirci). Ne seguirono, nel corso degli anni, le già citate lunghe discussioni con quanti invece considerano Il signore degli anelli quasi un testo sacro. Ora che a questo testo ci sto ritornando, che lo sto rileggendo, mi scopro ad esperirlo con più distacco. Affronto un'opera che ha segnato, anzi, quasi fondato il suo genere, e che si è imposta (tra le poche fortunate) anche fuori dal suo stesso genere, che è diventata un classico a prescindere. Che è sicuramente superiore, come già detto, ai successori. Che ha il merito di aver costruito un Mondo robusto, solido spesso, la cui realtà immaginaria può essere quasi toccata con mano, pagina dopo pagina. Che piaccia o non piaccia.
E poi c'è la questione della nuova traduzione italiana, su cui sono state spese parole infinite. Al di là del fanatismo di molti adepti della Terra di Mezzo, pronti a contestare anche la posizione delle singole virgole, da profano posso dire che, certo, la nuova resa di alcuni termini specifici può lasciar perplessi, ma le frasi scorrono molto meglio, l'italiano sa farsi alto e basso alla bisogna, e il vocabolario è ricco quanto serve. E poi ricordo un'intervista al traduttore, sicuramente competente in merito, dove affermava che la vecchia versione era infestata da due o tre errori per pagina. E credo (spero) di potermi fidare.

TLDR: read it for the significance but know it has its problems.

After many attempts, I finally finished the first installment in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. Despite my lack of initial engagement, I prioritized this book because it is an iconic work of high fantasy. Published in the 50s, this book is challenging for a modern reader, and is ultimately less engaging than either The Hobbit or the films.
Nevertheless, I recommend it because it is foundational to the genre.

I’m writing this long post because I want to be able to articulate (mainly to my fandom friends) why I appreciate butt don’t connect with LOTR.

Nature Writing

Tolkien’s commitment to describing every inch of Middle-earth comes at a cost—momentum.

Tolkien excels at constructing a vivid, mythic universe filled with deep lore and a sense of timelessness. His love for nature shines through in his long, (sometimes gratuitous) detailed descriptions of landscapes, forests, and mountains. Every leaf, every winding path is given weight. The juxtaposition of the scenes is immense - Tolkien takes us on a journey from the bucolic peace of the Shire to the dangerous and foreboding mines of Moria, and then to the ethereal beauty of Lothlórien.

However, Tolkien’s descriptive prose often verges on the excessive, slowing the narrative’s pace considerably. This nature-heavy focus is where I begin to struggle. While the landscapes and settings are undeniably beautiful, they can become overwhelming in their length and repetition, causing my mind to drift.

Unlike the lighter, brisker adventure of The Hobbit (which I adore) where the focus is squarely on Bilbo’s growth and the events that propel him forward, The Fellowship of the Ring feels weighed down by its own grandeur, and the action often takes a backseat to elaborate depictions of hills, rivers, and forests.

Lack of Psychological Depth

Tolkien keeps his characters at arm’s length, more interested in their roles and archetypes within the mythic story than in their individual, nuanced motivations.

Tolkien introduces a wide array of characters who represent the different races of Middle-earth. While this diversity enriches the story’s scope, the actual character development suffers.

Tolkien’s characters are often archetypal: Frodo is the reluctant hero, Aragorn the noble unwilling king, Sam the loyal companion, and Gandalf the wise mentor. Their growth is minimal, and their inner worlds are barely explored. There is very little psychological complexity. Frodo bears the Ring with an increasing sense of weariness, but the internal struggle of this burden isn’t explored—it’s more about his physical decline and a vague sense of looming despair.

Where a character like Boromir is concerned, we do see a hint of complexity: his desire to use the Ring to save his people. But even here, Tolkien chooses not to delve deeply into his motivations or moral struggles.

The temptation of the Ring is presented in almost simple biblical terms—good versus evil. This is the biggest barrier to connecting with the story on an emotional level.

In contrast, authors like Dostoyevsky (one of my favorites) who also often writes from a third-person and detached narrative style, immerse readers in the minds of their characters. The exploration of fear, guilt, pride, and moral conflict is central. This is what I want to read - work that creates an intimate portrait of flawed human beings.

Male-Dominated Narratives and Limited Female Representation

Women’s roles are secondary and mostly passive, leaving much to be desired for readers, especially women, who look for strong, active female protagonists.

There is an overwhelming male presence in the story. The Fellowship itself is composed entirely of men, and the few female characters present in the story—such as Galadriel and Arwen—are primarily defined by their beauty, grace, or ethereal wisdom. The movies attempted to address this by expanding Arwen’s role, giving her more action and agency, but the book remains firmly within a male-dominated perspective.

Religion, Allegory, and the Subtle Christian Influence

Many readers interpret The Lord of the Rings as a Christian fantasy novel, given Tolkien’s strong Catholic faith. While Christian themes are certainly present—self-sacrifice, redemption, and the struggle against evil and temptation—the book lacks the direct allegory one might expect if you are for instance familiar with Tolkien’s friend CS Lewis. Tolkien clearly prefers christian themes. Although Frodo’s journey can be seen as a Christ-like burden - carrying the sins of the world at great personal cost. There is a sense of providence throughout the story, suggesting a guiding hand akin to divine will - interestingly there seems to be both divine and evil will something I ponder on frequently.

This subtlety of reference is good in my mind, but it may leave some readers searching for a deeper meaning. It also is incredibly annoying to listen to theories of a deeper meaning that just isn’t there.

Backstory: The Challenges of The Silmarillion and Inaccessible Mythology

One of the more frustrating aspects of The Fellowship of the Ring is how much of the crucial backstory is left unexplained, relegated to The Silmarillion.

The cosmic creation story of Middle-earth is arguably more engaging than the relatively straightforward “good versus evil” struggle presented in The Fellowship of the Ring. The fact that this information is often missing from The Fellowship of the Ring itself can leave readers feeling like they are missing a vital piece of the puzzle or can lead them down a google rabbit hole.

Frodo and Sam- Master and Servant

The relationship between Frodo and Sam makes me uneasy - which at times resembles a master-servant dynamic. Sam is deeply loyal to Frodo, but his loyalty is often portrayed through subservience that can feel uncomfortably imbalanced. He consistently refers to Frodo as "Master," which he was as his precious employer and his unwavering devotion borders on self-erasure, with Sam’s identity and sense of purpose almost entirely defined by his service.

Sam’s loyalty is presented as noble and endearing, this dynamic can feel well not very friendly in modern terms.
This dynamic brings to mind a relationship like that in Driving Miss Daisy, where the bond between the two characters is genuine but fundamentally shaped by a hierarchical imbalance of power.

Comparisons with Other Moder Fantasy Works

Compared to modern fantasy works, The Fellowship feels archaic in its lack of character complexity and representation. Authors like George R.R. Martin have taken the foundation that Tolkien laid and expanded upon it with a greater focus on character psychology, moral ambiguity, and political intrigue. Martin’s characters are full of conflicting motivations, flaws, and unpredictable choices, making them feel far more real and human.

Final Thoughts

Tolkien’s ability to create an entire world, complete with languages, cultures, and a profound sense of history, is unmatched. This deserves its status as a cornerstone of modern fantasy.

This book is not for readers who seek intimate character exploration, a faster-paced narrative, or diverse representation.

The films by Peter Jackson, in many ways, address some of these limitations - richer character dynamics, and an emotional resonance that Tolkien’s text lacks. They condense the sprawling journey and imbue it with a level of immediacy and action that the book’s more measured pace doesn’t quite achieve.

I wanted to like this book; I wanted to be OBSESSED with this book. I’ve been trying to get more into fantasy, and so far all of my efforts have been successful. And I can’t bring myself to say I disliked The Fellowship of the Ring, but…I was ARMY CRAWLING my way through this—for four months. I think the two major hindrances for me were the exorbitant amount of world building and the lack of character building. The minute details of geography and genealogy of peoples and ancestry and the thousands of different names for one person or place or thing truly made the reading experience—and I hate to say this—miserable. This is not to take away credit from the world building, I just wish it had been used productively and efficiently rather than just providing details to provide them. I understand that irrelevant details can help flesh out a world that needs nuance, but by God was it a chore to get through.

That being said, I wish some of the energy that had gone into the world building had gone into the characters. Now, I have found that older books tend to approach characterization differently from contemporary fiction, but I couldn’t help but be disappointed in the main character—or, indeed, most of the characters (apart from Sam). I find that most of the characterization I associate with any of the cast in this book is derived from my own imagination of what I want them to be like. You could argue that this is the sign of a great storyteller, to create characters that take on lives of their own in the minds of readers, but for me it was just one less thing to latch onto as a life ring in the sea of plot and world building.

With all of this being said, I will wrap up the negativity with this: I just felt kind of dumb while reading. I normally love to follow along with maps, and I strive to make sense of the web of plot details and character relationships in denser books like these, but I was forced to give up on that quickly, otherwise I never would have finished. My confusion wasn’t helped by the fact that I dragged the reading experience on for months, but part of the reason for that dragging out is because I never knew what was going on! Rather, I didn’t know why what was going on was going on. The moments where I was more clear on where they were going at any given time and why, I loved! Indeed, for much of the reading experience I told myself I didn’t have to read the next book in the series, I just needed to finish this one so I didn’t waste those months spent on it. However, the last few pages made me reluctantly rethink. Maybe I will continue the series? I am still unsure. To hastily wrap this review up—overall, The Fellowship of the Ring is well-crafted but not necessarily an enjoyable read.

Hoy vamos con la reseña del primer libro de la trilogía de «El Señor de los Anillos», de J.R.R. Tolkien: «La comunidad del anillo». ✅️ Lo bueno

✨ El inicio me resultó mucho menos denso de lo que recordaba. ¿Será que yo maduré como lector?
✨ La narración es impecable y tiene buen ritmo. Es un libro de aventuras, así que, en cierto modo, tiene sentido que pase una cosa detrás de otra.
✨ Gollum. La escena en la que aparece por primera vez es de lo mejor del libro. La competencia de acertijos que mantiene con Bilbo es superinteresante,
✨ Tolkien describe todo con precisión y construye muy bien las escenas. Todo el episodio en el Bosque Negro, especialmente con las arañas, me resultó muy inquietante.

❗️ Lo malo

🔸️ La parte final me desconcertó un poco, porque (spoiler alert) no esperaba que al dragón lo derrotara un hombre salido de la nada y que hubiera una batalla final contra los trasgos.
🔸️ Llegó un punto en el que, pese a que todo está muy bien escrito y es entretenido, solo quería que el libro acabase de una vez.

Es una gran lectura, aunque probablemente no un libro que leería dos veces.

Finally getting to this 20+ years after reading The Hobbit. Someone stole my Fellowship copy in sixth grade, keeping me from reading on. Undeniably, this series paved the way for Fantasy as a genre, so respect is due. When you consider the complexity of the world, JRR Tolkien had such an imaginative mind and ability to tell a compelling tale. Listening to this while hiking through an old growth Olympic rainforest and then the alpine was an experience unparalleled, my real world mirroring the novel. I was actually so creeped out being in a forest by myself reading the forest scene leading up to Tom Bombadil, that I kept looking over my shoulder, which in hindsight is hilarious.

There were some minor things that missed the mark for me as well as some more grating choices Tolkien made. First, why was anything related to Tom Bombadil necessary for the plot? My biggest critique is the damn songs. After the fifth one early on, I began audibly groaning simply because they weren’t particularly good nor did the majority of them add much to the story. It was like Tolkien decided every scene transition needed a damn bard. It was so bad by the end that I fear any Englishman who sings a Medieval style song IRL to me may irrationally trigger me. Another minor letdown was me being ready to slam my trekking poles into the ground for Gandalf’s famous line, “You shall not pass!” only to feel deflated realizing the line is “You cannot pass!” in the book, which didn’t hit quite as hard. Overall, glad I read it and acknowledge it’s historical importance, but it wasn’t any more than I’d expected and some parts were worse than I’d been warned by friends.

After 25 years, I decided to reread The Fellowship of the Ring with my son. While there were standout moments, such as the journey through Moria and the Council of Elrond, I found that much of the book was bogged down by lengthy and seemingly irrelevant histories of families and other background details. These passages really disrupted the pacing of the story. On the plus side, it turned out to be a great book to help my son fall asleep! Three stars might even be generous.

My problem with road trip literature (like On the Road) is that it can boil down to “this happened, then this happened, then this happened” at times. I like the first half of this a lot when it’s mostly in the shire or nearby and people are talking. The stories people tell and the little bits of expositional narration about the wider lore of the world are intriguing

The travels are not as interesting. There’s still some good stuff buried in there, but not all of it is captivating. Also a few too many songs. Tolkien obviously is a guy that focused a lot on European mythology and culture and creating his own distillation of it requires a few songs but if you’re going to go out of your way and create your own language for this world, why not give the songs a tempo at the very least? They’re all pretty basic rhymes that if I wanted to could read in the same speed and voice

Even though he didn’t set out to make an allegory for the world wars (and the introduction is him saying what he would’ve done had he wanted to), the peoples and lands of the book do have real world correlations so you can see how people read into it as such. I like the European-ness and would like to see how the rest of the books follow up on it. This review of the first book is already too long but just some initial thoughts that will likely change when I finish the other 2…. Whenever that may be

Für viele ist Der Herr der Ringe das eine Buch. Aus diesem Grund habe ich das Gefühl, mich direkt für meine Bewertung rechtfertigen zu müssen.

Ich mag die Peter-Jackson-Filme sehr gerne und finde auch die LotR-Fans generell sympathisch. Es gibt kaum Welten, in die man so eintauchen und so viel Wissen ansammeln kann wie Mittelerde. Fan-Formate und Trivia auf YouTube sind schon das ein oder andere Mal in meiner Watchlist gelandet. Daher dachte ich mir dann 2021, nachdem regelmäßiges Lesen in meinen Alltag Einzug gefunden hatte, dass ich ja auch mal das Source-Material lesen könnte.

Zwar habe ich das Buch dann nicht auf Englisch und nicht in der „guten“ deutschen Übersetzung gekauft, sondern in der aktuellsten Variante, aber das soll mir verziehen sein.

Am Anfang war ich noch belustigt über die ausschweifenden Erklärungen zur Welt und die gemächliche Erzählweise, dann wurde es aber immer schwerer für mich, das Buch in die Hand zu nehmen. Ich hatte einfach keinen Spaß beim Lesen. Teilweise ist das bestimmt auch dem Fakt geschuldet, dass ich die Geschichte (von den Filmen her) schon kenne. Bei Harry Potter oder Game of Thrones stört mich das aber auch nicht. Auch dort habe ich Teile der Geschichte bereits vorher als Film/Serie gesehen und danach voller Freude die Bücher nachgeholt (bzw. bin ich noch dabei, das zu tun).

Vielleicht ist es die märchenhafte Welt, vielleicht die Gesangs- und Gedichteinlagen, vielleicht der Fakt, dass die Gefährten erst nach ca. 450 Seiten aufbrechen.

Insgesamt wurde ich einfach nicht warm mit dem Buch und ich habe 3,5 Jahre (!!!) gebraucht um es zu beenden.

Leider ist LotR in seiner Buchform (zumindest momentan) nicht mit meinen Lesegewohnheiten kompatibel.

Hey there! So, I just finished reading "The Fellowship of the Ring" by J.R.R. Tolkien, and I thought I'd jot down my thoughts. Keep in mind, I'm not usually into fantasy books, but I decided to give this a shot since it's such a classic.

First off, this was my introduction to proper fantasy literature, and I've got to say, it kind of confirmed my suspicions that fantasy might not be my cup of tea. Don't get me wrong, the book wasn't bad – it just didn't blow me away.

The story follows Frodo, a hobbit who inherits a powerful ring and sets off on a journey to destroy it. Sounds exciting, right? Well, it kind of is, but also kind of isn't. The whole book felt like one long walking tour through Middle-earth. We meet new characters, visit different kingdoms, and face some dangers along the way. It's definitely an adventure, but sometimes I found myself thinking, "Okay, but when is something really going to happen?"

I will say that I enjoyed the characters and their interactions. Tolkien does a great job of making you feel like you're part of the fellowship. The friendships, the bravery, the scary moments – it all feels very real. But for me, the plot itself was a bit thin. It's basically "hobbit finds ring, hobbit must destroy ring" stretched out over hundreds of pages.

The writing style is pretty easy to follow, which I appreciated. However, I did struggle with remembering all the names of people and places. Seriously, does every character and location need such a complicated name?

By the end of the book, I wasn't super excited to pick up the next one in the series. I mean, I can see why people love it – the world-building is impressive, and there's a sense of epic scale to everything. But for me, it just didn't click in a way that made me want to invest more time in the story.

I'd give it 3 out of 5 stars. It's well-written and I can appreciate why it's a classic, but it didn't quite hit the mark for me personally. If you're into fantasy or want to check out a cornerstone of the genre, go for it! But if you're like me and prefer books with more straightforward plots, maybe think twice before diving in.

Remember, this is just my take as a casual reader. Millions of people absolutely love this book, so don't let my opinion stop you if you're curious about it!​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Tolkien stworzył niesamowicie szczegółowy świat, który, choć nie jest najprostszy do zrozumienia, fascynuje na każdym kroku. Trzeba przyznać, że autor włożył ogromny kunszt w budowę Śródziemia, od jego historii, przez mitologię, aż po różnorodne rasy zamieszkujące ten świat.

Jednak, mimo że świat Tolkiena jest imponujący, sama książka nie jest pozbawiona wad. Przede wszystkim, tempo akcji jest bardzo rozwleczone. Zdarza się, że wciągające fragmenty przygód bohaterów są przerywane przez długie opisy, które nie zawsze dodają coś wartościowego do fabuły. Zamiast pędzić przez wydarzenia, czytelnik często zostaje zmuszony do przebrnięcia przez zbędne szczegóły, które mogą spowalniać i zniechęcać.

Kolejną wadą jest zauważalny brak kobiecych postaci. O ile świat Tolkiena jest pełen różnorodnych ras i kultur, to niestety rola kobiet w tej części trylogii jest bardzo ograniczona. Brakuje silnych, wyrazistych bohaterek, które mogłyby dodać książce więcej dynamiki i różnorodności.

Podsumowując, „Drużyna Pierścienia” to książka, która potrafi zachwycić swoim światem i szczegółami, ale wymaga od czytelnika sporo cierpliwości. Choć warto ją poznać, to dla niektórych może być ona zbyt rozwlekła i zbyt uboga w różnorodność postaci.

My god this was so long, especially considering how it is written. The stories in the book are interesting but they drag on for so so so long that I was more looking forward to finishing the book than actually reading it or finding out what happens.

The book starts with Bilbo leaving the shire and leaving the 💍 with Frodo, his illegitimate son 😆, some long years after the original adventures of The Hobbit. Some more long years later, Frodo sets on on an adventure on his own to take the 💍 out of the shire and to Rivendell, where on the way he meets his fellow hobbits Sam, Merry, and Pippin, as well as a traveling ranger called Strider, or Aragorn as he is known to others.

On the way with Sam, Merry and Pippin, they happen to fall into the land of the seemingly magical and ancient Tom Bombadil, which makes for good reading until it started dragging on and on and on.

After that adventure they make it to a place called Bree where they end up meeting Strider and make a lot of noise. Strider then becomes their guide to Rivendell which ends in a fight with the Ringwraiths who had been following them since the start of the journey.

In Rivendell they finally find Gandalf, and find also surprisingly the long time missing Bilbo, who Frodo spends a lot of time with. Also in Rivendell they meet the leader Elrond, who had scheduled a conference called "The Council of Elrond" which happens to be one of the more entertaining chapters of the book.

In this council they go over the history of the 💍 and other items and meet up with Legolas, Gimli, and Boromir who join on the mission to take the ring to Morodor in attempt to destroy it.

Following the meeting they make their journey to Mordor, with stops in places such as Moria and Lothlorien in order to get to their destination. This results in the fall and loss of the wizard and leader Gandalf.

The book ends with a strong chapter where the "Company", what the group called themselves split to go in different ways, with Boromir finally turning evil which had been hinted at for multiple chapters prior. The book ends with Sam joining Frodo to go alone to Mordor and leave the rest to go to the home of Boromir, Minas Tirith.
Bastante introductorio. Me sobraron un par de canciones pero la narración es muy bella, el final es emotivo y te deja con ganas de continuar la historia!

It took me quite a while to get through this book, but by the end, I really enjoyed it.
I will say that Tolkien’s writing style is a bit tedious for me. He does lore dumps in big blocks of dialogue rather than simply explaining in narration, which would be more understandable and significantly shorter. He describes in detail some overly minute and often unnecessary details. Although this attention to detail can at times make the world more immersive, it also can be exhausting to read.
The other things that I’d prefer to see slowly exposed, such as character and relationship development are, on the other hand, overly simply stated. He’ll just state, “these two characters are friends now” without any interactions for the readers to understand why the relationship was altered.
Ultimately, the lore is great and the plot is intriguing, but all of Tolkien’s plot reinforcement came at the expense of multi-faceted characters.
Overall I very much enjoyed! I felt like some of the time I was absolutely enthralled and enchanted with the story and other times I was very bored. I can’t wait to watch the movie though!!

Now that I’ve had time to digest this fully, I will explain my 3 stars.

First of all, I know, I KNOW… I’m offending generations or nerds world-wide. I’m sorry. Please don’t take my nerd card away.

Second of all, this is the first book in maybe a year that has taken me longer than 2 weeks to finish. I have read entire series in less time than this book took me. I had to use Audible, which I generally hate, to guide me through this book.

Tolkien LOVES adjectives. I thought there were only so many ways a person could describe things. I was wrong. The plot takes a back-burner to descriptions of places and people and animals so frequently that I ended up ultimately forgetting what was going on.

I hate Frodo. I wish Aragorn or someone else at least a little more likable was the main character. A whiny and petulant little brat as the protagonist of this story? Really? And he’s mean to his friends! Booooooooo!!!

Now, the saving grace of this story is obviously the world building and the painstaking detail with which he built entire languages and peoples and it all feels real. Nobody does it like Tolkien. That is worth 2 stars alone. It is an incredible story; I just hate the main character and the run-on sentences are SO distracting. I had a really hard time with this. And maybe it’s just the difference in time periods with the writing style, I’ll admit that I’m maybe not smart enough to read it the way it was intended to be read.

Anyway, fellow readers, please forgive me for this.

En 2024, je m'y mets finalement. Je ne pensais pas lire Le seigneur des anneaux un jour, n'ayant jamais accroché aux films et donc été attirée par les livres. Mais, il ne faut jamais dire jamais, particulièrement (dans mon cas) lorsqu'il s'agit de lecture. 

Je suis entourée de grands fans et de personnes qui n'ont pas apprécié leur lecture, voire abandonné, trouvant le tout "indigeste".  Je comprends les deux groupes. Pour ma part, je n'ai pas du tout trouvé ça trop long ou lent. C'est un univers dense, mais la lecture reste simple, le style étant très abordable. J'ai aimé la description de l'univers qui donne assez de détails pour parfaitement visualiser chaque décor, tout en laissant assez de place à l'imagination de chacun. On voyage réellement et les lieux visités ne sont pas juste des noms, sans réelle identité. J'ai vraiment apprécié mon début d'aventure qui m'a permis de m'évader loin de mes nuits blanches et de mes migraines. 

Cependant, si ce qui m'impressionne le plus est l'univers incroyable, riche et dense, car ça demande un travail monstre, un investissement exceptionnel et bien évidemment du talent, je comprends aussi qu'à certains moments, ça puisse être trop pour certaines personnes. Il y a des passages dans lesquels les informations données sur l'univers ou le lore, alourdissent le récit, selon moi. Particulièrement au début, ce qui peut en décourager certain.e.s. 

En ce qui concerne les personnages, étrangement, je n'ai pas l'impression de les connaître. Je n'ai pas de défaut particulier à souligner par rapport à leur écriture ou comportement, mais j'ai le sentiment d'avoir observé toute leur aventure d'assez loin, plus emportée par l'univers en lui-même que réellement concernée par leur quête. Mais ça viendra peut-être avec la suite que je compte bien lire bientôt.

Ho finalmente terminato il primo libro della trilogia del Signore degli anelli, dopo essermelo trascinata in lettura per mesi. Purtroppo infatti non è stato un libro che mi ha coinvolta e appassionata tanto quanto avevo immaginato e in alcuni punti la noia mi ha impedito di procedere spedita. I read this book years ago, before the movies came out, and couldn't see what the fuss was about. Now, decades later, I re-read the first book, wondering how my perception will have changed. Well, having read the book twice now, I strongly believe that the movie did this book a great favor in making it widely accessible to the world, because the book itself is not accessible at all.

Yes, the books are 70 years old at this point, so I shouldn't expect modern conventions when it comes to plot, language, and pacing. And yet - the movies are 20 years old and are able to deliver on these concepts. I respect the amount of thought and work that went into creating the world of Middle Earth and the setting for the War of the Ring, but it feels like far too much. The background, ancestry, history, and geography of the land are explained in far greater detail than is necessary for the reader to understand. The first 10% or so of the book is just talking about hobbits and their history, and Peter Jackson was able to give us the same idea in just a few minutes of screentime. The fellowship that this book is named after is formed about 2/3rd of the way through the book, and then is dissolved relatively shortly thereafter. Contrary to how it's portrayed in the movie, it seems that this dissolution was always the intention of the group, as Aragorn mentions that he always intended to follow Boromir to Minas Tirith, rather than go on to Mordor.

Anyways, it almost every instance where the movie deviates from the book, it feels like it's to the movie's credit.

Jeez, what a difficult work to review. I want to say at the start: I recognize and endorse Tolkien's place in the English literary canon. The Lord of the Rings has had an incredible impact on fantasy writing and literature in general. It would be ludicrous to deny Tolkien's genius. However, book reviews are not merely about the literary quality of a work, but also the enjoyment one had reading the work. This second part is, shall we say, the rub.

The truth is I just did not enjoy the reading experience. Even with the amount of incredible world building, and a couple of fun set-piece moments, I still found the majority of the work (dare I say) a little boring. I believe this is primarily because of the way Tolkien writes his story. Tolkien was a professor of Old English and he was very much a linguist. As a result, The Lord of the Rings is written as an old Anglo-Saxon epic. The writing is archaic and makes it a bit difficult, at least for me, to fully enjoy. The other point of criticism is that all the characters speak in long drawn out sentences that result in paragraphs of information regarding some lore related point. It simply got exhausting after awhile.

There are, however, some bright spots. I really liked the design and build up of the Black Riders. The Mines of Moria was also the best part of the book for me. I also liked any focus on the Ring of Power itself. This is because of the moral message that Tolkien is conveying through these discussions. His warning against absolute power is very well received through these discussions.

Look, maybe I'm just not a Tolkien fan. I wish I would have enjoyed the read a lot more than I did, but I can't lie about my experience. I do plan to read the rest of the trilogy, but I have no idea when I will get around to doing that. I do recommend everyone to, at the very least, give The Lord of the Rings a chance because I think it is a classic work. But, of course, your milage may vary.

I have a lot of mixed feelings about this book, but overall, for the most part, I loved it. There were places that I didn't quite understand what Tolkien was trying to say but overall a very strong plot and story line. Of course, I had known the plot and story from the get go but seeing things that had not happened in the movie take place in the book was lovely and made me wish they had been put in to the movie, even for a short while, Tom Bombadil, for example, was a fantastic addition to the story (in my opinion) as he sort of shaped out the hobbits on their journey and encouraged them to be brave and continue with their quest.

Our introduction to Aragorn is brilliant. I really loved that. Aragorn is such a strong character, and he really is important to the story line.

Borormir is a much more preferable character in the book than he is portrayed to be in the movie. A lot more caring and understanding and I very much enjoyed his story line.

Legolas and Gimli, of course, are exceptional. Even if they don't get many lines. Gimli is a very strong character, much like Aragorn, and is as lovable as he always was. Legolas is much the same, not much "screen time" if you will but a very likable character in his ways and actions.

Pippin and Merry are very light hearted characters that bring a humour to the book. And we all know about Sam and Frodo who have not much changed in the movie adaptation savve for Sam's cheekiness and Frodo isn't so much of a wuss in the book.

As someone who grew up with the films, it felt quite nostalgic reading this book, but I found I got lost in the detail as Tolkien really builds this world so meticulously and magically. As an English teacher, I really appreciate it, and I am in awe of what he was able to create. But as a fantasy reader, I found I got lost in the detail of the world, the influx of characters that I almost felt stupid at times and felt I was really missing important details.

What did help was that I listened to Mary Clay Watts' podcast 'That's What I'm Tolkien About' on Spotify in between each chapter and I listened to the audiobook on Audible, read by Andy Serkis. Mary Clay based her podcast off of Michael Schubert's podcast 'Potterless', which I also listened to while I was reading the Harry Potter series, so I was familiar with the formate and I enjoyed reading the books almost as a novice like Mary Clay was, and going on this journey with her. It's not the most thought provoking podcast of all times, but it helped me see things in the chapters that I would have possibly missed and it was interesting to her people engage in interesting and lighthearted conversation about it.

I wouldn't recommend this book to an on and off reader as you really need to get into the book to enjoy it, but if you are a fantasy reader, and someone who enjoys the movies, it is definitely worth the read. I don't think I would have enjoyed reading the physical book as much as I enjoyed listening to Serkis' reading, and I think it would have taken me a lot longer to get through it, as the chapters are incredibly long, but the audiobook was great.

As a LOTR fan, it hurts my feelings to only give this 3 stars. I loved The Hobbit with everything i have, and i was so excited to start this triology. But why only 3 stars?

• The songs
Throughout the book, there a lot of details explained, about world building, timelines, characters etc. All of those are important to understand the plot and what not. What i found unnecessary however, were all the songs and poems. If you've read this book physically, it's easy to skip over them. But for me, as an audio listener, it was annoying. The first few songs were nice, set the mood, gave atmosphere. But right around the time they visit Tom Bombadil (which for the keen eyed readers, is just in the beginning of the book), it was already getting on my nerves. I understand in said time, songs and poems were relevant to tell stories. But did i need to listen to all of those? What was the point exactly?

• The pace
I'll admit that i'm not a big fan of slow or fast timelines. The sweet spot is somewhere i don't even know, but this wasn't it. It felt dreaded, even in the parts where something actually happened, i wasn't on the tip of my seat. Everything felt slow and stretched. It was also difficult to understand the timeline this way.

• The timeline
Tolkien made sure to drop hints here and there of how long the journey had been taking place, but it felt almost surreal? Like what do you mean a month passed already? It was hard to understand from time to time. If you'd ask me now, i have no clue how long it's been since they left the Shire. Not all too important, but something id like to know.

So, as far as the negative comments, this'll be it. I did enjoy the story overall. As a big fan of the movies, you get to know different stories and explanations about certain things i hadn't heard before, which makes it all the more understandable. It's still a difficult story, after all. The reason why i love Tolkien is his world building. Even without seeing the movies, you can perfectly understand how the setting around is supposed to look and feel (my boyfriend was the judge of this). So 3 stars feels sufficient for my experience.

For most of this book, I was ready to give it 2 stars. It is clear to me that Tolkien wrote this book as an excuse to create a language and write songs. In general, I don't mind slower stories that are more about the journey than the destination, but I found much of this book terribly boring. There is lots of explaining and description. Just a bunch of people standing around talking to each other and not much else going on.

But then, post-Council of Elrond, I started to really enjoy the story as the Fellowship got on its way finally. I found the second half much better than the first. I was much more engrossed. The journey through the Misty Mountains was by far my favorite part of the book. I debated for a long time about whether or not this deserved an extra star just because I started to actually enjoy it in the last third or so. But I decided on 2.5 stars (rounded up).

Reading this actually made me realize just how good a job the movie-makers did when they adapted it. This might be an unpopular opinion, but I definitely prefer the movies over the book. They did a good job streamlining it and editing out the parts and characters that weren't as important or interesting for the overall narrative (Tom Bombadil anyone?).

Perhaps the fact that I listened to the audiobook played into my experience a bit. The narrator sings all the songs in full. But on the other hand, I have to give credit to Andy Serkis for the great variety of distinct voices he was able to do for each of the characters. And even singing in different voices. As much as I disliked the songs being included in the book at all, the narrator did a good job with them. (And FYI, if you plan to listen to the audiobook, there are two versions, and Andy Serkis is definitely a better narrator than Rob Inglis, in my opinion.)

I recognize that Tolkien is a master, and I do not dispute the influence his work has had on fantasy and culture in general. Perhaps the print version would have been better for me, but I don't see myself ever picking this book back up. But because I actually did enjoy the last half of the book, I'll give the next book in the series a shot.

Maybe the next one won't take me a year to finish.
