From the literary perspective, this is a no-brainer 5-star achievement. Every word is carefully chosen, there are no holes/inconsistencies in the storyline, events and reactions do not feel forced or unjustified, the characters are complex and whole... it is art without a doubt.

However, from a personal taste perspective, LOTR FOTR didn't quite do it for me, hence the lower rating. While I felt gripped at times, it was not maintained throughout the book.

That said, I loved the psychological side of the book - Frodo and, in particular, Gollum's addiction to the ring, obsession, self-hatred, and much more. I also appreciated Frodo and Sam's relationship as a vehicle for exploring the power of friendship and platonic (or not?) love.

It's valuable to compare this book to my experience of reading Tolstoy's Anna Karenina, which boasts a similar literary artistry. With Anna Karenina, the characters were similarly multifaceted, with complex and authentic dimensions, and the plot was consistent and psychologically-fuelled. Both books had contextual descriptions that felt somewhat laborious. However, Tolstoy's focus on the female protagonist, and the grounding of his story in the real world, allowed me to feel more connected and curious about the book than I did about Tolkien's LOTR.

I hope to continue to books 2 and 3, as Tolkien's literary craft is truly remarkable. However, I will probably leave this for a later time.

This was just a very average reading experience for me. I have seen the movies several times and just recently watched them all again, which is what motivated me to finally read these. And I gotta say, I think I enjoyed at least the first movie more. While watching Fellowship, I keep thinking that while it was very good and entertaining there just seemed to be so much context missing. The book gives...some more of it, but honestly not that much. I think Tolkien had a lot of great ideas and concepts and his world building is very thorough and detailed. However, a lot of this isn't translated into the actual narrative well, you get a lot of songs, and surface level mentioning of events and places, but most the details appear to be in the appendices or in the Silmarillion. The narrative itself doesn't have that much more meat on the bones. A lot of it reads as some dudes out backpacking and focusing on very very detailed mundane things like the road or river their on, the road or river their going to, the landscape, where they should go next, and when they will eat. It doesn't feel like some epic quest. The urgency also just lacking, which feeds into it. The movie feels rushed, but by god, the book practically makes it feel like destroying the ring hardly matters from a timing perspective. Gandalf is gone for 17 years in between Bilbos farewell and when he comes back. Frodo then takes several months to sell his house. The party stops in several places for weeks at a time...the tension is just not there. At all. So a lot of the structure is mundane backpacking with some occasionally interesting places and lore sprinkled in and then just huge unnatural exposition dumps to actually further the story. Also, most of the characters just feel a lot more wooden and in the background than they do in the movies (not everyone tho, but most).

Some things I did like, while the additional world building and context isn't as detailed as I wanted it, it is still there. I really did enjoy the books discussing the other rings of power and in general I think it handled the back half better. Moria is about the same but Lorien and the breaking of the fellowship felt..."better" in the books (Rivendell was probably a bit better too). I also think this book had better connecting tissue to The Hobbit and Bilbo in general (which makes sense), but Bilbo feels so tacked on in the movies and everything just flows so much better in the book, which lead me to enjoying the very beginning quite a bit too.

Ultimately I'm glad I did finally getting around to reading it and I can of course appreciate this for what it is, but I feel like it has a great foundation and bones and could have been better, but it feels very clunky in a lot of areas.

I really really wanted to give this book a 4 star rating but I just couldn’t do it. I can tell you exactly the point where I fell out of love with this book and didn’t pick it up for two weeks - about 35 pages into ‘The Council of Elrond’.

The Council of Elrond.

In this one, specific chapter, we have to go through the *entire* story of The Ring again, from it’s very creation to the present, even though we read 90% of that in the first few chapters of the book. It was incredibly repetitive and could have been skipped.

Gandalf also gives a play by play of *literally everything that ever happened to him since leaving Bilbo’s birthday, and even before that(!)* in one long monologue that lasted at least 15 pages. This book was written in a third person perspective, why could Gandalf’s journey not have been sprinkled between chapters of the Hobbit’s journey to Rivendell? Why must it all be crammed into one chapter of the book where we get:

- The full history of The Ring (again!)
- Introductions for the whole Fellowship (but no character descriptions?!)
- Gandalf’s whole life story, research and adventure
- And a bunch more stuff that I completely blanked out because it was going on for. so. damn. long.


——


Another big gripe for me was the lack of descriptions. The most description we get for any of the Hobbits (main characters!!) is that they have brown curly hair? And even that is only if you have an edition of the book with the History of the Hobbits BEFORE the prologue. From this book, I couldn’t accurately tell you what Frodo, Bilbo, Sam, Merry, Pippin, Boromir, Gimli, Legolas, any of the Elves (save Galadriel), any of the Orcs or what a Balrog looks like.

——

And oh my god don’t get me started on Tom Bombadil. Cool character, cool concept, but it was like I was just reading a fever dream for a few chapters.


——

There were times that I could really really get into it, though. I enjoyed Aragon’s character a lot, the setting of the Shire and Gandalf’s dialogue really did make me laugh out loud. The way the men are written is so refreshing and non-toxic. I love the interactions and the relationships between all of the Hobbits.

(Let’s ignore the fact that I think only three women speak in the entire book? One of the Sackville-Bagginses, Arwen (and she’s only talking to sing) and then Galadriel.)

And obviously the world building is incredibly impressive. But it comes at the detriment of: descriptions, plot and the overall construction of the story. If I had not watched the film prior to reading, I genuinely feel like I would have been lost.

Book: LOTR – the Fellowship of the Ring book 1
Author: J.R.R. Tolkien

One Ring to rule them all

“One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them, One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them In the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.”(Tolkien 95). Frodo lives in a world full of life and sudden death A world ruled by rings. The One Ring is what gives someone the power to rule the world such as Sauron did to middle earth. Frodo A young hobbit who lives in the Shire lives a peaceful life until he is greeted with A quest to destroy the One Ring by casting it in Mount Doom. Frodo and friends go on to form a fellowship to fulfill this quest and destroy the ring so Sauron may never gain power again.

The main character of the Fellowship of the Ring is very likable and relatable even though he lives in a fantasy world. Frodo enjoys doing similar things that people do in the real world such as family, singing, and reading. Unlike the previous protagonist from the Hobbit Frodo is unlike his uncle Bilbo as he does not long for treacherous adventures or heroism. Other characters in the story such as Aragorn, Sam, Gandalf, etc were fun and likable as well as they all had their own unique roles and attributes that made the story engaging. What I believe to be one of J.R.R. Tolkien's best skills in writing are the world building and settings that he brings to life. The Shire feels alive with the children running about as Gandalf lights fireworks into the sky that are in the shapes of dragons and light up the whole village. When the group was resting on the hills near Bombadil’s home you could visualize and feel the area “the warm sun and the scent of turf”(Tolkien 179).

The story took some time to start up completely but once it did around chapter five the pacing carried me throughout the story where I was never bored there forward. Constantly feeling hunted by the Black Riders made the story feel constantly intense as “Frodo stared at the fire and did not speak. ‘You would have been, too, if you had been chased for two days by Black Riders.”(162). The Black Riders always enforced this impending feeling of doom that never left throughout the story even just the sound of hoofs made the characters on edge. Where I left off at the end of book one was an excellent cliffhanger to bridge between the two books. Just before the book ends Tolkien leaves the reader with an aftertaste of dread and defeat as it seems like it is the end for Frodo as the Dark Riders catch up with them. This would be the last outcome I would’ve expected as just before this you felt like Frodo would be brought to safety and healed of his wounds yet he isn’t given the smallest break.
Frodo is different from Bilbo in the sense that he changes in a different way than just becoming more brave. Whilst Bilbo grows to enjoy his adventure and the dangers with it Frodo never really enjoys his adventure but pursues it out of responsibility and determination for his own friends and the Shire. Frodo at the end of the Fellowship of the Ring is much different from him at the end of the series as instead of setting the ring aside to destroy he almost embraces it in the Fellowship. Once the hardships become more difficult for him to endure with his injuries he finds no other way to cope with it than the ring. This is huge for his character development from the start where he swore that he would never use it or become addicted to its power. I enjoyed Tolkien's writing style as far as the use of old English to suit the fantasy world but I grew tired of his other traits in writing. Tolkien commonly incorporates songs into his writing which some may like but I found it to be quickly repetitive and unrealistic with moments in the story.

My most favorite part of the story was when Gandalf explained the story of the ring and its old bearers. I find the ring to be the most interesting part of the story because it has almost controlled the whole world in the LOTR. The way it manipulated Smeagol into murdering his brother out of greed for the ring. The ring is the only reason Sauron is so powerful and that there was a major power imbalance in the world. There are so many examples of the ring being the reason for so many downfalls throughout the world of LOTR. Now if I did have to choose a least favorite part of the book it would definitely be the portion of the book that was spent at Bombadil’s home. This specific part of the book was just so slow because of the lack of action for pages and pages straight. In my opinion there is not much that really stands out with Bombadil’s character other than him being around for years. This part plainly just had bad pacing and very low plot significance leaving me to think it could have been cut out of the story.

As much as I would recommend the movies more, the Fellowship of the Ring is a pretty interesting and enjoyable fantasy story at times. If you already watched the movies and want to go more in depth to the story and small details you will find a lot in this book. To follow the complex story I would recommend this book to anyone over the age of 13-15 because there are a lot of plot elements and characters you have to remember.

The Intro in something bigger
The Hobbits are very peaceful folk who's culture affects the story. A hobbit, named Frodo, that lives in a cozy and peaceful land, called the shire, has been wrapped into a journey that is said to be very long and dangerous. All because of one ring that holds a dark secret. He and his friends leave the shire to begin their journey. Frodo is a hobbit, who was taken in by Biblo, another hobbit, that has many secrets. The story is focused on Frodo and his journey. The struggle for the main character is traveling without getting caught by the dark things that follow him. There seems to be no end to this fear. He stops in many places and fears every moment.
Frodo has become more fearful since the beginning where he thought that peace would last forever inside the Shire. The “Hobbits of the Shire, with whom these tales are concerned, in the days of their peace and prosperity they were a merry folk.” (prologue). The theme of the first book is adventure, friendship, and care shown by the culture of the hobbits, but that still doesn't give the book enough interest.
The author through the book gives more context and background using character interactions. Gandalf says “that is a very long story. The beginnings lie back in the Black Years, which only the lore-masters now remember. If I were to tell you all that tale, we should still be sitting here when Spring had passed into Winter.”. The readers get the background of the story over time through character interactions with one another.
Warning this book is nothing like the movie and is a lot longer and more in depth than the movie. There are many new characters that are displayed inside the story. The first book is only about walking so not for those who hate long books. The book elongates the events and gives many different challenges making it much longer than needed. While character-work is not one of the many things Tolkien is known for, I also found myself relating to and growing fond of the cast.

Overall, The Fellowship of The Ring is a well-written, if at times dreadfully paced novel, that hooks you into the world of Middle Earth with a few magical moments that leave you wanting more.

“The Fellowship of the Rings”, by J.R.R Tolkien, is an elaborate, plot-driven story with compelling characters and stunningly detailed settings. This sequel to the well-beloved “The Hobbit”, follows the tale of a hobbit named Frodo Baggins- the ward of the protagonist, Bilbo from the aforementioned novel- in a quest to destroy a fated ring in order to save his world. It’s a classic tale of adventure and bravery, with beautiful characterizations, and a prototypal message of good versus evil. Despite this, it cannot be said that it is an easily enjoyed book. With its lavish scenery and intricate characters, “The Fellowship of the Rings”, is so detailed it’s difficult to understand. There is no doubt that the plot of this book is highly intriguing, and while detail is an essential element in building compelling stories, “The Fellowship of the Rings” takes that detail to such an extreme level that it takes away from the plot. There are several sections within the book that are practically impossible to read through given their agonizingly slow pace- something that could have undoubtedly been avoided had the author held off on the several pages worth of description about a forest. Overall, “The Fellowship of the Rings”, is a good book, it’s well-written, elaborate, and an undeniably well-thought-out piece of literature; but all of those traits are washed away by unnecessary detail, and ruthlessly slow pacing.

Frodo didn't have much character himself until the final chapters. Gandalf and Aragorn are the real stars of the show, and pretty much every character (except Legolas, who tbh barely had any personality) was more interesting than Frodo. I don't have a problem with it, though. Without the movies in my head, maybe I would have thought Frodo was boring and not fully appreciated his steadiness and introspection until the end of the book. But now that the Fellowship is off in separate directions, Frodo will have more space to shine, while the other members of the Company will have enough backstory/character building from book 1 to make us invested in their portion of the journey.

Strider is my favorite character, hands down, and not because of the movies. His depth shines in every action he takes and word he speaks. Similar with Gandalf, who comes in second place. Sam holds the trophy for third.

The world and story itself don't stand out amidst the past couple decades of fantasy literature, in my opinion. But I have no doubt it helped revolutionize the genre during its time.

Sci-fi/fantasy stories since the ~1980s heavily rely on the idea of a Chosen One who is a prodigy with abilities and powers beyond anyone of their generation. I love that Frodo is just a regular fellow, odd by Hobbit standards, but just a guy who wants to do the right thing with the tools he has.

I am a new Tolkien-head, so you know, take everything said here as someone reading the books for the first time at 29 years old.

The world building, beautiful. The descriptions, also great! It is interesting reading it from a perspective of someone who has really only interacted with modern fantasy, as so much of fantasy is based on these works.

However, to lay it all out there if you’re someone like me that does not know much about Lord of The Rings and is gonna take on the trilogy, I suspect that the first book is more of a hurdle than the others.

You will find there is a lot of walking through the woods. They walk through the woods, they stop for maybe 10-20 pages, and then right back into those woods.

The tension is a little uneven. Sometimes you feel it there, feel the intensity of the situation, sometimes not so much.

Not a lot of ladies in this book. There are some hot elves, and Mommy Bombadil, but other than acting as cool magical ladies, they’re really not a focal point in anything I’ve read so far. They exist to be magical, beautiful, and nothing else (from what I’ve seen).

A popular point I’ve seen recently about these books, and that I’m sure I’m only noticing because I’m reading now and paying attention to discourse on it, is that evil is just evil in these books. There is no nuance, the orks are not redeemable “people”, they’re evil and that is that.

I have started the second book, and I have enjoyed it! It starts a lot more action packed than the first, and I’m finding myself more excited to get back to it than the first. I’m sure there will be plenty of woods walking, but that is okay!

Después de finalizar satisfecho tras mi lectura de El Hobbit, inicié motivado y con mucha curiosidad de seguir explorando y conociendo sobre la saga más famosa de Tolkien. Desafortunadamente, mi experiencia con La comunidad del anillo no fue tan gratificante como lo imaginaba. No es que no haya disfrutado de este libro, sino que el contraste entre lo que disfruté con lo que me pareció aburrido me deja en un punto medio del que no puedo salir. Naturalmente, continuaré con la saga, pero por lo menos ya estaré prevenido de que puede ocurrirme algo similar en la siguiente lectura debido a la similitud de las obras de Tolkien.

El libro estuvo compuesto de tres partes: Prólogo, libro primero y libro segundo.



El prólogo fue una muy mala manera de comenzar el libro. Fue muy aburrido conocer un montón de nombres, familias y datos relacionados a los hobbits que sinceramente no me interesan. Estuvo bien hacer una recapitulación sobre la historia de Bilbo para quienes no recordaban el libro anterior, pero por lo demás, sobran muchas páginas aquí. El primer día que comencé la lectura me pareció tediosa y agobiante.

En cambio, el libro primero sí me gustó mucho. De hecho, creo que fue mi parte favorita del libro. Fue una parte llena de cambios, aventuras, huidas y peligros que en verdad me encantaron: Eso era lo que quería encontrar en esta obra. Acompañar a Frodo en su aventura fue cambiar la imagen negativa que tenía de este personaje debido a las películas. Recuerdo que en las adaptaciones solo verlo me daba fastidio, pero aquí conocí otros aspectos del personaje que incluso produjeron mi simpatía hacia él. De igual manera, conocer a Aragorn (Trancos) fue genial y casi que de inmediato se convirtió en uno de mis personajes favoritos de esta historia: Su valentía, inteligencia y experiencia en verdad que logran atrapar tu atención, eso me gusta de un personaje.

Si el libro hubiera finalizado en esta parte mi calificación sería de cuatro estrellas. Hasta aquí estaba mayormente satisfecho. Sin embargo, el declive comenzó cuando llegué al libro segundo. La magia que sentí la perdí completamente. Que un personaje tan indefenso como Frodo este desprotegido o con poca protección hace que la lectura sea atractiva, pero cuando ya lo protegen demasiados personajes poderosos eso lo vuelve aburrido. Desde ahí no me volví a emocionar, las páginas se me hicieron largas y rápidamente concluí que no pasarían más situaciones interesantes. Y justamente eso fue lo que ocurrió, excepto por el final que estuvo increíble: Eso no lo niego. Pero de resto fue una aventura al estilo Narnia cuando están con Caspian en La travesía del Viajero del Alba: Un viaje protegido donde los problemas no llegan nunca a ser tan drásticos.

Si por un lado, la percepción que tenía de Frodo mejoró considerablemente, por otro lado, la que tenía de Gandalf se desmoronó como arena en el desierto. Que desilusión que el mago poderoso, sí, con experiencia y muchas habilidades resultara ser tan torpe. Muchas de las situaciones que ocurrieron técnicamente fueron por culpa de Gandalf. En serio que sus errores e imprudencia me sacaron de quicio. Por ejemplo, aparentemente nadie podía conocer sobre “el gran viaje”, pero Gandalf era quien se lo comunicaba a todo el mundo. ¿O sea qué? Puede que sus acciones quizás fueran necesarias, pero en serio que son un poco contradictorios los comportamientos de Gandalf. O por lo menos, así me pareció a mí.

Pero no todo es malo. Un detalle que me gustó mucho, por ejemplo, fueron los poemas. Cada uno está compuesto con una dedicación envidiable, y ayudan bastante para que la lectura no se vuelva monótona. En este tipo de libros de fantasía normalmente se repite el mismo patrón: Recorrido, llegada a un lugar, peligro, batalla o huida, otro recorrido. Pero gracias a estas canciones o poemas, el lector puede conocer alguna historia extra sobre un reino, un personaje o la trama principal. Este tipo de elementos son como un descanso para que el lector tome aire y después ya pueda soportar lo más denso del libro: Los recorridos.

Recorridos que para ser sincero me parecen infinitos. Todos los autores tienen un estilo diferente de narración pero aquellos que son tan descriptivos con los lugares pueden llegar a hartarme si el día de la lectura no tengo la disposición mental para soportar la mención de tantos árboles, senderos o montañas. En El hobbit, por ejemplo, si tuve una buena actitud con las descripciones e incluso las disfruté, pero aquí no ocurrió porque la trama principal estaba muy interesante y quería conocer más sobre ella. ¡No puedo tener tanta paciencia para leer sobre un recorrido cuando solo quiero saber sobre el dichoso anillo!



Dichoso anillo, que claramente y por mucho, es el mejor elemento de la historia. Su historia, las consecuencias de llevarlo puesto, sus habilidades... todo sobre el anillo es genial en la historia. No por nada la saga se llama «El señor de los anillos». El anillo es la mejor creación de Tolkien. Es lo que le da vida a esta historia, lo que genera intriga y lo que hace que más y más lectores sigan leyendo su historia más aclamada hoy en día. No quiero ni imaginarme esa misma atmósfera, con los mismos personajes, pero batallando por un fin diferente al anillo. Sería rarísimo.

En resumen, un libro con una buena trama pero que me deja un poco insatisfecho por ciertos elementos que me producen pereza y aburrimiento. Es un libro que no repetiría, pero que tampoco me arrepiento de leer porque conocer sobre la historia del anillo sí ha valido la pena. Eso sí, a pesar de mis conflictos internos, es un libro que recomiendo para los amantes de la fantasía. Quizás no sea perfecto, pero es una buena elección para aprender más sobre el género de la literatura fantástica y conocer el estilo de uno de sus máximos exponentes.

الكتاب الأول كان ممل أوي ومليان بالأوصاف المتعلقة بشكل السكة بتاعتهم واللي كانت بالنسبالي غير مبررة، خلاص يا معلم عرفنا إنهم ماشيين في مروج وسهول وإن فيه سديم في السما، أي وصف كانت دماغي تلقائيًا بتجرده إلى صخور وحشائش وأشجار وتلال وشكرًا على كدا، إنما الوصف المغرق ده كان ممل جدًا وكان واخد حيز كبير من الكتاب الأول ومكانش بيضيف للقصة حاجة.

أما الكتاب التاني فكان تحفة، لأنه بدأت فيه الأحداث تتصاعد، وجوانب الشخصيات تظهر، وبقت الأوصاف بتاعت طريق الرحلة بتاعتهم مهم إن القارئ يعرفها عشان تساعده على التخيل، مش مجرد سهول ومروج وحشائش وبلاه بلاه بلاه، لأ في الكتاب التاني دخلنا جوا مجموعة جبال موريا وكان مهم إنك توصف عشان القارئ يتصور دهاليزها وقد إيه هي ملغزة ومخيفة، ودخلنا جوا غابة للإلفيين، وجوا نهر محاط بمرتفعات وفيه جزيرة في الوسط، وكمان حصل كذا هجوم للأوركس، واتقدمت شخصيات جديدة، كان الرتم أعلى ومناسب أكتر بكتير من الكتاب الأول، وهنا بس حسيت بعظمة تولكين وخياله الغني والواسع جدًا، بس لما كان التخيل والوصف ده له توظيف حقيقي شدني كقارئ، وآه صحيح الخرايط اللي في آخر الكتاب ساعدتني كتير في التخيل وتتبع مسار رحلتهم، من غيرها مستحيل كنت أعرف لوحدي، الراجل ده فعلًا عبقري وخياله في منتهى الخصوبة.

قعدت حوالي 10 شهور بقرأ في الرواية دي (اللي الفيلم بتاعها أحلى بكتير من الرواية نفسها على عكس المعتاد) خلينا نقول إني قعدت 80% من الفترة دي بقرأ في الكتاب الأول بس من كتر ما هو ممل، لكن الكتاب التاني كان بيشدني أقرأه صفحة ورا التانية، الترجمة معقولة، محستش بأزمة وأنا بقرأ، وكدا كدا القصة تقاطعها مع الحياة الواقعية قليل أوي فصنعة نقل المعنى من لغة للغة ومن ثقافة لثقافة مكانتش مطلوبة أوي، كدا كدا هو بيتخيل عالم وبيخلقه من الصفر.

3 من 5 لأن حلاوة الكتاب التاني خليتني أغفر للكتاب الأول ملله، كان ممكن يكون 5 من 5 لو كان الكتاب الأول والتاني بنفس حلاوة بعض =D

J.R.R. Tolkien's Fellowship of the Ring is the first installment in the Lord of the Rings Saga starring Frodo Baggins. This novel is often acclaimed for its fatherhood of the fantasy genre, however, I felt it to be quite a drag. While the premise is interesting and the story itself has a good direction, the pacing of the book can feel atrocious at times. It took almost the entire book just to reach and occupy its namesake, the fellowship, when in retrospect it feels like it should have taken only a few chapters. Likely due to Tolkien’s meandering writing style, I could see how it could appeal to some but it simply bored me. If shortened, I feel this work could be incredibly enjoyable as the base aspects such as world building and imagery are immaculate, but the manner in which the story is told leaves much to be desired.

It hurts to rate this so low.

Growing up with the films put such a firm image of this story in my head and I’d be lying if I said it was possible for me to ignore that. So, it’s clear to me now that my appreciation for the series is tied to the passion and love that others felt for these books that was translated into film. For that, and for my own love of those films, I’m obviously going to keep reading. But if I’d never had the experience of the movies through my childhood, I doubt that I would continue.

It ultimately comes down to large swaths of the book being dull, and nothing more. From my copy that has about 500 pages, there’s potential for perhaps 200 to be cut with no grievance to the story. So much of it is banal descriptions of the Fellowship climbing this hill and moving under those trees and traveling too far south and having to move back north and running into characters that have no bearing on the narrative other than to tell the Fellowship where next to go and days spent walking, resting, walking, resting, walking, resting, and walking in an egregiously repetitive cycle (if you thought that sentence was long, you should try reading everything I just described with it). It also irks me that things with great importance to the story are recalled through dialogue instead of being given properly to readers. The characters themselves are also lackluster, save for Sam and Gandalf.

There’s also far too much worldbuilding for worldbuilding’s sake. I don’t need to know the name of this hill and that river and those lands and these legends if they don’t carry any relevance.

Tolkein is seemingly unparalleled in his world building, but the growth of his characters lacked realism. I had to read this for my fantasy course but if it had been character driven, all for Frodo’s development, i would have found it much more compelling. Sauron seems to me to be a flat villain, in the same way that Satan is a flat villain in the story of the bible.
The relation of dark and ugly to innately evil is also disheartening to read, knowing the influence Tolkein’s work has on the fantasy genre. The tall and fair are written as innately beautiful and as having innate goodness (and wisdom) that can be turned but (to my knowledge) mostly if not only by contact with the dark and evil.
This segment of Lord of the Rings seems to me to have much to answer for in reproducing the connotations of black and white and dark and light. Not a hot take, but this feels so closely related to racialised views on the colours, and that leads me to read this as reproducing racist values; the darker, the more ugly and evil, the lighter, the more beautiful, and therefore more likely to be good.

Tolkien’s LotR books are, next to Robert E. Howard’s Conan stories, among first in which protagonists are entirely in the imaginary world. Unlike Lord Dunsany’s, E.R. Eddison’s or C.S. Lewis’ works in which our beloved characters are transported from the real world through portals, or they travel to another planets or their setting is in the fictional lookalike England, Spain etc, something that was pretty much a norm until that point.
Some could even argue that Howard’s inclusion of Atlantis and Valhalla (although mythical places themselves) during Hyborian age excludes him from that honorary company and leaves J.R.R. Tolkien alone as a sole contributing factor in shaping the genre in this completely off-the-real-world setting.
All I know is that Conan, who shaped today’s “Northern Barbarian” trope, drew his first breath before Bilbo did, so I wouldn’t discount him just because Atlantis was mentioned as an afterthought in early stages of developing of the world while author’s originality was shy to come through.
Where was I…
While rereading this series, specifically first book, I rediscovered appreciation I had for amazingly detailed worldbuilding, its history and lore. The academic approach to it. The seriousness of it. (Something that was much more evident in Silmarillion and many of Tolkien’s works that his son Christian assembled from his father notes.)
If aliens came to our planet and said: ok, let’s get to know each other, tell us what you’ve been up to so far; I’d give them Tolkien’s works and said that’s our history. We we’re Orcs. Look how much we’ve evolved and how far we’ve come. We’d leave better impression as such, than to give them our real history.
But that’s the thing. History is rich and complicated. Tolkien through all these rich and complicated stories told in this book made the history of Middle Earth believable.
He also because of that history seriously crippled the pacing of the book. And I dislike using the argument of pacing, because most of the time it is something you can adapt to and not have an issue with.
But here, with dense and descriptive prose Tolkien uses, it is a contributing factor. While it is a treasure for someone like me who adores imaginary history and lore and detailed worldbuilding, to explore it within a book, when we are in the middle of developing current storyline, it would be best to focus on that until it is finished, before we start the stories of old. Not in the middle of it. Something that worked with Silmarillion doesn’t mean it will work here.

Also, whomever makes a remake of movies should make a musical of it, because I swear, every once and awhile characters get this sudden urge to sing very long songs.

Vi primero la película, varias veces. Como siempre, hay diferencias importantes entre ésta y el libro en que se inspiró, pero es la primera vez que tengo varios puntos a favor de la película.
Considero que la energía de Tolkien se concentró demasiado en la complicada descripción geográfica e histórica de su mundo; si bien agradezco los mapas que dibujó, me perdía completamente cuando algún personaje empezaba a hablar de fronteras, cimas, ríos, montañas, bosques y demases, todas con nombres largos e impronunciables (porque creó varios idiomas para cada especie) en un mismo diálogo, en el que además añadía pedazos de historia antigua de la Tierra Media, trazando de paso lazos sanguíneos difíciles de recordar, por secundario que fuese el personaje que hablaba.
Quizá me faltó haber ido leyendo con un cuaderno a la mano, para no perderme en tantos detalles, nombres y lugares. Quizá la culpa recae en mí, por ser un poco dispersa.

Sin embargo, hay otro punto que no me gustó del libro, o más bien, que sentí que pudo hacerse mejor, y es la construcción de los personajes. Hay una cantidad absurda de personajes, pero la mayoría de ellos sólo son nombrados un puñado de veces, y luego, desaparecen de la trama. El problema con esto es que, en lugar de profundizar en los personajes "principales", a saber, aquellos que conforman la Comunidad del Anillo y con los que viajamos por cerca de 300 páginas, estamos constantemente siendo introducidos a más y más personajes de forma superficial. Me habría gustado saber más de Aragorn, de Gimli, de Legolas, incluso de Boromir. Sé que todo está narrado desde el punto de vista de Frodo, desde lo que él conoce, piensa y percibe, pero incluso así, creo que pudo haber incluido más conversaciones con estos personajes que lo acompañan en su viaje. No sabemos mucho tampoco de Merry y Pippin, siendo que ellos están presentes desde casi el principio del libro, al igual que Sam, que me atrevería a decir es el único personaje, además de Frodo, del que sí sabemos bastante más que su nombre y su especie, pues su personalidad se va trazando en cada diálogo, en cada acción, e incluso de acuerdo a su historia personal.
En este aspecto de profundizar a los personajes, los fanfics que he leído (sólo respecto a este primer libro) hacen un trabajo con creces superior.

Esas son mis quejas principales.
Dejando eso de lado, el libro me gustó. Es claramente la piedra angular de la fantasía épica. Me saco el sombrero ante Tolkien por su tremenda creatividad a la hora de crear este mundo de 0. Diría que es una lectura obligatoria para todos aquellos que disfrutamos del género.
Seguiré leyendo los dos libros restantes de la trilogía, e incluso, quizá, el resto de los libros que componen este universo cautivante.

Thankfully, this was actually much better than The Hobbit, but Tolkien’s writing still is not enjoyable for me and, at this point, probably never will be.

Something that I think is lost in Tolkien is how academic his work actually is; he approaches Middle Earth as a researcher and creates a world inspired by centuries of epic poems & allegories & mythology. I noticed this came through w/ his commitment to verse, to telling histories, and w/ the awkward flow of the narrative. His writing is blocky & feels more informative than expressive. The only thing his writing is very good at is creating a feeling of longing within you. I always find whenever I read his work or the work of C.S. Lewis (whom I’d clumped in the same category for obvious reasons) that I find myself desiring a more intimate picturesque relationship w/ rivers & hills & good food & alcohol, that I want to shake off the excess of modernity & enjoy a simple and quiet life. Since Tolkien & Lewis both approached fiction as something intertwined w/ their religious faith, I think that’s purposeful and also a bit dangerous. Of course, it’s nice to read something that can help us escape from the terrors of our technological reality & return to a more holistic portrait of humanity, but I think there’s a possibility that too much of longing can reinforce ideas about an imaginary “old-world” that fuels movements like MAGA & Christian Nationalism.

I can respect The Lord of the Rings as an academic experiment, and I’m looking forward to eventually reading the remainder of this trilogy, but I wouldn’t call myself a Tolkien fan by any means.

I struggle to pull myself away from the Peter Jackson film, but having recently re-read The Hobbit, and loving it but not the movies, I find myself with an interesting observation. Everything about the Jackson Hobbit films that do a disservice to the book (bloat, wishy-washy characters, characters that add little value, etc.) are things that the Jackson LotR film improves upon from this book. It is so slow, repetitive, and circuitous. The stakes are high in the grand scheme, but from moment-to-moment, the tension is surprisingly low. I do appreciate that Tolkien bothers to emphasize how long and hard the journey is, and therefore how many times and for how long the party must stop; I feel that, if anything, is missing from the film. But I cannot properly rate or critique a book on what it doesn't do or how it compares to a derivative property. So, I'll look at it in relative isolation.

I've come to the conclusion that Tolkien is not a great writer but rather a great conceptualizer. The world is deep and full of lore. The introduction gives some context that makes the Shire feel lived in. But is it necessary? Does that make it a good story? In my opinion, "no," to both questions. He is inconsistent with his characters. Sam is clearly defined, Aragorn is not (he reads almost goofy at times, especially in Bree). Almost every conversation should and could be half as long, if not shorter, without sacrificing any realism or artistry (or whatever Tolkien was trying to capture). And while no decisions or actions happen uncompelled, many fall flat (here I risk going back on my word about speaking to what didn't happen) because of relatively low stakes--foreshadowing or exposition that could pay off here as well as later, but saved only for later. The action is seriously lacking in detail and brief, which is frustrating considering how much time is spent discussing geography and taking breaks. The big item left on the table is the pursuit of evil. The Fellowship spends a huge amount of time in Rivendell waiting to hear if the Ringwraiths are still afoot and have retreated so they can travel in peace. I suppose this is sensible, but not interesting if not countered with a stiff dose of situational irony. Later, not only does Gollum get literally within an arm's reach on the river (with no more consequence than a "queer" feeling), but as the orcs are supposedly chasing from Moria they seem to simply get farther away. The report at Lorien suggests that they are near (and some are killed, if I remember, off-page), but then the Fellowship stays a month before moving on, providing plenty of time for a Black Army regroup. When Aragorn and Frodo notice Sting glowing a pale blue in the final chapter, one might expect an attack. Here there is no payoff as well (again, I assume this is for later). Other than Gandalf's fall (and Sam turning Bill loose), it seems as though Tolkien was afraid to punish or torture our heroes. However, he has no issue punishing the reader.

I'm torn about how to rate this.

I appreciate Tolkein's landmark work. I appreciate how he influenced an entire genre for decades to come.

But I absolutely did not enjoy the singing (which I could not for the life of me absorb without knowing a tune to sing it to), and the first half (at least) of the book was a great chore to slog through. By the time Strider/Aragorn joined the party, things started to pick up. However, I am continually frustrated by the flat dialogue and the lack of character depth for a lot of the men of the fellowship; most of my characterization was projected from the film depictions, and not by the written word.

I think, in truth, I simply prefer more character-driven, nuanced stories that aren't straight black-and-white, evil-and-good. I like it best when I read about a study in grays, about the human condition and the reasons why people might strive to do (sometimes) terrible things in desperate situations.

So I am glad I read this book, but it's not something I would revisit time and again. I'll likely finish the trilogy someday, but I'm thoroughly glad to put Tolkein down for awhile and give the slow long slogs a rest before I pick him up again.

Whenever I read a massively iconic and influential work, I approach the reading experience with such trepidation. The Lord of the Rings series is one of those works I always categorized as reading 'one of these days.' I watched and enjoyed the Peter Jackson film trilogy and it only reinforced my opinion that the Lord of the Rings book series would be a daunting read. Well, I just finished Fellowship and I think I deserve a prize for reading such an intimidating book.

And I thought the book was fine. Although calling the book fine and rating it 3.5 starts doesn't really capture my full feelings on the book.

This is not the action-packed epic fantasy that the readers of today would expect, nor is it an intense character study. The films primed me to expect something a bit more action-packed. This is a slow-moving book, but that doesn't mean it was a boring ride. This book is (and I assume the rest of the series is as well) primarily focused on the world of Middle Earth. What surprised me is that the world of Middle Earth is the main character. It seems I made an amateur mistake in thinking Frodo would be the protagonist.

I've seen Tolkien described as a master world-builder, and I will hold off on my final verdict until I have completed the series, but it seems to me that he's interested in sterilized lore rather than building a fantasy world from the ground up. We get glimpses of old ancient history as well as the poetry and songs, both ancient and new, of Middle Earth. But Tolkien doesn't show much interest in other aspects of world-building, such as the economic or religious factors and forces that can shape a world.

One thing that surprised me when reading this book is the amount of time that passes in the book. For example, between Bilbo's birthday party and Frodo leaving the Shire, 17 years have passed. This book was slower moving than I anticipated, but this is one of those books that asks the reader to immerse themselves into its world.

FotR is my comfort movie but this book isn’t it. The first two thirds is important for worldbuilding I know but damn is it boring. Let us not read of hobbits walking through the countryside ever again.

Look I'm gonna have a controversial opinion about this book. And before anyone is like "you didn't get it" or "you missed the point" you have to understand this book is at a highschool reading level, this is not difficult to read. I was also taught to read critically and examine the way people write, and that's what I did here too.
This book was fine, it's a classic fantasy that was pretty much the genesis for most modern fantasy. But I don't think it's the masterpiece people say it is. This is all MY OPINION okay?? I think Tolkien does an amazing job world building here, the only author I've seen get close is GRRM. Tolkien wrote languages, drew maps, and made all kinds of lore. But I think the actual writing of the story and how the characters relate to one another kind of falls by the wayside in this book.
First of all I'm gonna say that the main character of this book is Gandalf. Yes Frodo is the ring bearer but he barely has anything to say for most of the book. Even going so far as to tell people "no I won't say!" When people ask his opinion or his thoughts on things. Gandalf on the other hand does the MAJORITY of the talking in this book, there are full scenes where no one else even gets a word in edgewise. He's also....kinda mean? Like he calls several of the characters stupid and disregards what others have to say.
Which brings me to my next point: Tolkien is bad at including characters in a scene. For the majority of the trip through Moria, most of "The Company" don't get mentioned. When they first enter the mountain this tentacle monster grabs Frodo and they all run into the doorway, but the way it's written you don't even know if Aragorn or the other hobbits make it in! You can assume they do but most of the people talking throughout Moria are Gandalf, Gimli and Frodo. Boromir speaks ONE time while in Moria and you just forget most of the characters are even present. It would take nothing to mention them sleeping or sitting but they are either forgotten about or mentioned collectively as The company. For a long time in this book Legolas has nothing to say unless someone needs to be picked off with an arrow. I just found it odd.

Another thing is hobbits are supposedly very hungry and value food all the time. While several times they wish they could have a good meal, food and what they're eating is very rarely mentioned. There are two elven feasts and no description of what is being eaten. Which is whatever, but Tolkien spends SO MUCH TIME describing fucking landscape and rock faces and grass and never details what the hobbits are eating.

I also (and this is just my personal peeve) fucking hate the use of poems and songs. This book is honestly probably 30% poems. Elrond even tells Bilbo he can't come to the feast until he finishes a song. Then at the council, Bilbo has something to say and is basically like "sorry Elrond, I didn't put this in song form yet, do I have your permission to just SAY it plainly?" And Elrond is like "if you must!!"

I didn't hate the book but I did have some stuff I didn't like about it. This is all my opinion and I will indeed read all three books.

كما هو معتاد، تتميز الرواية بتفاصيل أكثر في عدد الشخصيات والأحداث مقارنة بالفيلم. هنا بعض النقاط:

1. في الفيلم كان "فرودو" شخصًا صغير السن ولطيفًا، عكس المذكور في الرواية بل كان كبيرًا في السن وسريع الغضب.
2. كان "جندلف" يعلم مسبقاً بأن الخاتم مع "بيلبو" من خلال تعذيب "جولام" ولكنه لم يكن متاكداً بأنه الخاتم الاوحد.
3. تأخرت الرحلة وبدأت في الشتاء، وليس في الصيف كما في الفيلم، بسبب تردد فرودو واصراره على الانتظار حتى حفلة عيد الميلاد.
4. بدأت الرحلة بـ "فرودو" و"سام" و"بيبن" فقط، دون "جانداف".
5. الفيلم لم يذكر بعض لقاءات فرودو مع شخصيات مثل "جيلدور" وعائلة "ماجوت" و"توم بومباديل".
6. "ميري" و"بيبين" كانوا على علم بأمر الخاتم قبل بداية الرحلة.
7. الشخص الذي أنقذ فرودو من طعنة الخيال الأسود كان "جلورفنديل"، وليست "أروين أبنة إلروند" كما في الفيلم والتي لم يكن لها دور يذكر في الرواية عكس ما كان في احداث الفيلم.
8. حضور "بيلبو" اجتماع مجلس إلروند وأعرضه بحمل الخاتم وإتمام المهمة.
9. الرواية توضح علم "سام" بمكان فرودو بعد قرار ترك الصحبة.
10. المشهد‎ الاخير في الفيلم، قتالهم مع الاورك ومقتل "اراجورن" واختطاف ميري و بيبين لم يكون مذكور في الرواية، من الممكن ان المخرج اراد التخلص من شخصية اراجورن قبل البدء في الجزء الثاني.

I have mixed feelings about this book. Initially, I never intended to read it, but a ton of my friends recommended it and always raved about it, so you can imagine just how disappointed I was after reading this book. The story started out promising and developed a vast, rich story with dynamic characters, interesting lore, and a very cool main antagonist but as I read on, the story got more and more boring. The book is famously known for having a "slow start" but I'd like to argue that the entire book is just slow. When Frodo is trying to leave the shire, there is lots of anticipation built up and as the bad people begin to be introduced it gets very exciting, but the second Frodo gets to Rivendell the story feels to have stopped. When they finally leave, the book falls into the typical fantasy book trope, where every 5 chapters or so there is a bad guy, they nearly escape and then go on. This began to feel very repetitive and it almost felt like the author didn't want to introduce any more new interesting plot, so he just spent 50-100 pages or so with the same repetitive behavior. This felt very distasteful to me and in conclusion, the story sort of fell flat. I will DEFINITELY not be reading the second.

For being the cornerstone of modern western fantasy it's a damn good read all around.

So they just look like gibberish with a lot of vowels to everyone whose not you? and to question the inclusion Tom Bombidill (spelling? idk I give up) bc who was he. The magic mushroom man? Well I’ve finally done it - started and finished the Lord of the Rings and I enjoyed it. Not sure if I will read the rest of the books but I might. The story telling has to be admired and I understand why there is an almost fanatical following of this crew. If your like me and scoffed at the thought of reading this give it a go, not what I expected in a good way.

I read the Lord of the Rings when I was maybe ten, and as I recall, I enjoyed it enough to finish the series and Sam Gamgee was my favorite character. I have kind of aspired that to be one of those people that loves J. R. R. Tolkien, but not having read him for a quarter of a century at this point, I didn't really have the street cred for it, right? So I was happy to re-read it in audiobook form on a looong roadtrip just now with the husband.

Sadly, I did not quite love it. There are some beautiful passages that I want to revisit on paper (e.g. the elves sailing away from Lothlorien), but in general it's kind of a boring read isn't it? The council of Elrond goes on forevvvver. And real talk, does anybody actually read the poems and songs? Don't lie, you skipped right through them like we did. Also, the husband, as a big fan of the movies, was shocked by how long it took them to get to the Prancing Pony. 😂 I think I remember liking Tom Bombadil as a kid, but now? He is freaking annoying. Fight me. I think the Barrow-wight section was the part I ended up remembering best from my first reading, and I still enjoyed it. Also, the moment when Golem climbs up into their treehouse thing in the middle of the night, and when Merry and Pippin get stuck in the willow. Oh, of course the escape from Moria is epic too. Basically, the moments when exciting things are happening, rather than characters just sitting around telling stories. I guess I'm saying, Tolkien is good for action and suspense...it's just all those in between parts...😅

I still want to finish re-reading the series and eventually try Silmarillion too. But I also feel kind of like, how can it take them another two whole books to get it done?

Lord of the Rings is something that I grew up with, I played the old PS2 games, I watched the movies, I read the hobbit, I did it all…except for read the books of the Lord Of the Rings Trilogy. It has been praised as the best fantasy ever by so many people, and unless the series gets drastically better, I would have to disagree. I felt that this first book in the trilogy was slow, somewhat boring, and the writing was not easy to follow in my opinion. I would read a paragraph, have no idea what was said, and have to reread multiple times. To me the writing seemed to have no flow. I really thought that I would love this series, I was planning on reading as much classic fantasy literature that I could, but now I am questioning that plan. If the early fantasy writers had similar writing styles to this, then I can’t say I would see myself enjoying it. With that being said, the world, the plot, that characters, are all great. I love the world of Middle-Earth, and I think my faults and disappointments may be in the writing style of Tolkien…which is weird because I remember loving The Hobbit, as a little kid. As much as I thought I would love reading, I hope that when reading The Two Towers my mindset drastically changes, or Tolkiens pacing and writing changes from book 1

So then why 3 stars?
First, 60% of the book is effectively entirely setup. There's so much stuff that should be condensed pretty harshly. Too many songs, too.
There is also too much tell and too little show. I'll read an entire 10 pages, and then at the end of it it'll say "they felt fear" and that's pretty much all that needed to be said.
This book gets credit for being the first pioneer of the genre, and for being well thought out, but it's an absolute struggle to read in today's day and age.

This was a huge mixed bag for me. I’m a long-time fan of the movies, and read “The Hobbit” years ago. I had an enjoyable experience reading that, so why was this read such an absolute uphill battle? I figure it’s because Tolkien spends a LOT of time instructing the reader on what’s happening rather than storytelling. However, he eventually breaks into this epic, fast-paced flow for the Mines of Moria sequence, which honestly was standout fantasy writing for me (the Balrog heating up the main hall like a furnace isn’t as clear in the movie as it is in the book, a delightful detail).

I also spent a lot of time casting Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen, Viggo Mortensen etc into the dialogue and scenery. Which helped somewhat, but then also ruined the flow for me because I was comparing it TOO much to what I consider a very solid film.

Overall I have to give this three stars because of the Moria sequence, and because it’s genuinely fantastic source material for what are no doubt fantastic films. I just wish that instead of Biblically dictating us on every move the characters make, and bombarding us with monologues, he would let the natural splendor of his universe take more center stage. Sigh.

Ahh. The Lord of the Rings. Arguably one of the most famous book series of all time, and in all my years as a voracious reader, I have not yet managed to start my journey with Frodo in the Shire. Here's how my story with Middle-Earth starts: I read The Hobbit in high school with no intention of committing myself to the LOTR trilogy, because I wanted to pace myself and see how I would like Tolkien's infamous descriptive and sometimes dense writing. I surprised myself in really enjoying the Hobbit, but I just never got around to LOTR.

Flash forward 4 or 5 years later, and having read many fantasy books in that time, I felt I was finally prepared to take on Tolkien's famous trilogy. I honestly do not know exactly how I feel about The Fellowship of the Ring.

I will admit, I found the story hard to follow along in many parts and found myself constantly rereading parts or googling summaries of chapters. Part of it is definitely my difficulty to focus when I read (generally speaking, not just with fantasy) and also the writing style Tolkien employs. I loved seeing Bilbo again and Frodo was an easy character to become invested in.

But once we started going down the rabbit hole of the lore behind the ring and other Middle-Earth related histories, I found myself becoming disengaged and wanting the pace of the story to pick up. I will admit, by the last 100 pages or so, the story really got quicker and more engaging that I finally felt the adventure narrative Tolkien had so cleverly and masterfully created for us to enjoy. I still found myself getting lost in the names of all the different side characters and trying to piece things together, but I think by now I got the big picture.

It was a solid read overall and I am excited to continue my journey! Adventure awaits!

I finished the first book in the Lord of the Rings trilogy the other day and I’m excited to read the next one! It took me a while to get into this book. I’m not sure if it’s because I enjoyed The Hobbit so much that I compared the two of them. Although the first half of the book moved a bit slowly for me, I loved the rest. I’ve liked getting to know the history of the one ring and how many hands it’s passed through as well as finding out more about Gollum. I’ve also enjoyed the new characters we’ve met such as Aragorn, Sam Gamgee, and Tom Bombadil. Remembering some of the places and people mentioned in The Hobbit has also been fun for me!

It’s a great story, but it drags. It’s REALLY slow. There are so many different descriptions of places, and food, and walking, and the dialogue is so difficult to understand. There are also scenes in the book that are like 10 pages long, and in the movie they’re a few minutes. The council of Elrond is over fifty pages, and it really shouldn’t be that long. I personally think that the movies are better. That being said however, what’s impressive about this book is the world-building. It always impresses me when an author is able to create his or her own fictional world, with different languages and people. That must be very creative. It must have taken a lot of work to write these books. Tolkien’s story is very interesting as well, and there are scenes in the books that reference his times in WW1. The story is in some ways about war and it’s effects. It is also about fellowship and hope. You can see many other kinds of commentaries on the state of the world as well, like the conservation of nature. It’s a very good book that I would highly recommend. However, some people cannot get through the long descriptions and the writing style, but I would suggest that you pay more attention to the story, so that you can have a better reading experience. Sure, it’s not the best writing I have ever read, but the story is what matters.

When this book is good, it’s great. But when it’s bad, it’s kinda terrible…

To start with the bad, the lack of immediate focus muddies the narrative and leaves the plot clumsily structured. Sure, the overabundance of histories, songs, family trees, and all the landscape imagery make for a vast and vivid world, but half of it is shoehorned in and it diminishes Frodo’s adventure. There is no sense of urgency, either. We get to see the threat of the Enemy only at the very end of the book. Meanwhile, any plot elements bigger than a hobbit are told (and sometimes repeated) almost exclusively through info dumps.

At times, these issues made me feel like I was reading the first draft—a manuscript perhaps edited to do away with continuity errors, yet with little attention paid to pacing, suspense, and most importantly: the characters. Most of the cast barely have any personalities beyond their designated roles. This is especially unfortunate because the epic moments which might’ve balanced out the flat characters are few and mostly reserved for the end of the book.

Bilbo, from The Hobbit, is also needlessly mentioned so many times in The Fellowship of the Ring that it came across as fan service. Some of Tolkien’s other works and stories (at the time of the Fellowship’s release not even published) are also referenced, but most of those mentions felt out of place and did little to enhance the story of the Ring. Now, I love the world Tolkien has created and I’ve enjoyed many of his other works (The Hobbit included), but the form of storytelling presented in The Fellowship left me rather disappointed.

As for the good stuff, the book did get me attached to Middle-earth. The long-winded descriptions of Frodo’s journey might be tiresome, but they do a great job of letting you feel the footsteps taken, envision the sights absorbed, and share in on the experience gained, such as it is. Tolkien’s world of this age is a land of decaying beauty, with no hope of days returning to their past glories, and the silent grief that follows such sentiment resonates throughout the book. A sense of comradery, courage, and love for all things simple and fair are all also present and weaved into Tolkien’s writing.

Besides the heartfelt themes, the book also holds many memorable quotes—some simple, some thought-provoking, and some both. My favorite one being from Gimli the Dwarf! Memory is not what the heart desires…

Anyway, I wish there were more such subtle moments in the book, instead of constant talks of food and supplies, but oh well… Overall, the good and the bad balance themselves out for me, and I did find value in this reading experience. Though, a good round of editing would’ve done this story wonders! Just sayin’…

Yo creo que este libro no necesita presentación. Desde el primer momento en que abrí sus páginas, quedé cautivada por la trama épica y emocionante que se desarrolla en un mundo lleno de magia y peligros.

Pero lo que realmente me enamoró de este libro fueron los personajes, en especial Gimli. El autor, J.R.R. Tolkien, ha creado una raza fascinante y única, con una cultura y una historia propias que hacen que cada uno de ellos sea un personaje inolvidable. A mí es que de este mundo creado por el autor tengo predilección por los enanos. Me pirran 😍 y Gimli es la caña.

Este personaje es valiente, leal y lleno de humor, y su amistad con Legolas es uno de los puntos más destacados de la trama. Además, su habilidad con el hacha y su amor por las joyas lo hacen aún más interesante y carismático. Y es que adoro a los personajes gruñoncitos pero con fondo tierno 🤷🏻‍♀️. Me encantan.

Pero "La comunidad del anillo" no es solo un libro sobre enanos, sino sobre la lucha del bien contra el mal, la amistad, la lealtad y el sacrificio. La trama es compleja y emocionante, con giros inesperados y momentos de tensión que te mantienen pegado a las páginas hasta el final.

Tenía miedo por la forma en que estaba escrito ya que muchos me habían dicho que es complejo de leer; y debo decir que lo noté más al principio y luego se me pasó en un suspiro 🤣 A mí lo que me parece que dificulta la lectura es que se describe con bastante detalle; pero como está escrito de forma muy bonita solo se hace un poco denso al principio.

Sin embargo, reconozco que yo siempre he sido más de El hobbit que de El señor de los anillos. Sigo manteniéndome en la línea; pero Gimli hace que me encante esta historia jajaj

En resumen, concuerdo con los fans de estos libros en que es un libro imprescindible para cualquier amante de la literatura fantástica. Y si eres fanático de los enanos y de mi querido Gimli 💛 en particular, no puedes perderte esta obra maestra de J.R.R. Tolkien.

After hearing about Lord of the Rings too frequently at my summer internship I felt obligated to read/ watch the series. I will say it is definitely not something I would’ve picked for myself as the book tended to drag out certain parts of the quest and had a ridiculously long prequel.

The Fellowship started off strong with Bilbo and Frodo’s birthday party and ended on a high note with Sam and Frodo continuing the quest. Without giving too much away I thought the book had great sensory details making it clear to imagine where the characters were on their quest. Tolkien’s character descriptions and dialogue was something I thoroughly enjoyed throughout the chapters but… I wonder if I would’ve preferred some chapters to be in only one characters perspective. I think that having only one character’s perspective written in the first person would have provided more insight and inner monologue on how that character was feeling on certain parts of the quest which would’ve benefitted the story.

Would I recommend this book to everyone? No. Will I be finishing this series? Probably not. But… I do think the book does not deserve as much hate as it received when I was sharing with my friends what I was currently reading. It is definitely a book for true fantasy and war lovers that are searching for a new series to start.

It’s just that Tolkien’s writing style is about as interesting as reading the phone book. The craziest shit happens in this book and Tolkien is just straight up like, “Sad!! Oh well, there’s strange anglo-saxon inspired poetry to get to. Moving on.”

Now tbf I didn’t really expect to like this book. I’m not a massive fantasy reader and I avoided this for quite a bit. I only caved because my favourite history podcast did an episode on Tolkien and also it’s possible that I wanted to do a deep dive into GRRM’s inspiration before my next ASOIAF reread. Maybe not the best of intentions to find enjoyment in a book, but on the other hand I usually very much do find enjoyment in tearing into a lame book to dissect the author’s biases and opinions. In that regard, this wasn’t a total failure, though I’m guessing the last book especially will be the most promising (hopefully. If I make it that far). Still, I didn’t find a whole lot of other things I liked about this book. Was it technically well-written? I guess so. Was there an intriguing plot? Sure. A fascinating setting? Lots of cool lore to discover? A loveable group of misfits on their way to accomplish an impossible task? It’s all there. And yet. Mostly it was just like reading about a group of people you don’t really know going on a long walk. And Tolkien’s detached way of telling the story didn’t exactly manage to endear me to any of the main characters. I liked all of them, but I didn’t really care about any of them yet. And I definitely think that this book suffers from the fact that it’s not really a book, but the first part of one really, reeeeally long book. It just feels like the beginning of something for 500 pages, and I don’t know but I kinda feel like that’s just too damn long for a beginning.

Fundamentally this was really just okay to me. Not bad enough to stop my quest to find proof for Tolkien’s personal opinions in his writing and explore GRRM’s inspirations while I’m at it, but really? I didn’t get the hype. I remain ignorant to whatever it is that makes the girlies go crazy over this.

OVERARCHING COMMENTS FOR THE FULL LOTR AND WHY IT TODAY GETS JUST 3 STARS

Had you asked me to rate LOTR 20 years ago, a certain 5 stars. A decade or bit more ago, ago, a 4-plus for sure. An even 4 in all likelihood, if not a bit more, just 6 or 7 years ago. But today? Three stars, maybe 3.5 if on Storygraph.

First, the background. I’ve read all of LOTR at least half a dozen times, The Hobbit the same, and The Silmarillion at least three times. I read most of the earlier ancillary short stories that reportedly flowed from J.R.R. Tolkien’s pen, though in all likelihood, even the shorter stuff flowed from the pen of son Christopher as writer as much as editor. Hold on to that thought.

Several things, in constellation, have led to my gradual disenchantment with LOTR.

One is that, per Anaximander, I’m not the same person who read it 30-plus years ago, or even 20. (I could throw off “A Elbereth githoniel” and a few other lines eons ago.) I’m not a person to play “gotcha” on JRR (or even Chris) getting some detail of chronology, ancestry or something else wrong across decades of writing and editing. So, that is not a leading complaint.

Rather, with age, I have not become disenchanted by our present world, but I have become disenchanted by JRR’s Middle Earth. One element in that disenchantment was a critical essay on Tolkien “versus” technology that I read several years ago. I’m not a neoliberal who thinks there’s a price on everything, including nature, but I’m also not a Luddite. I also know that the British Empire in which Tolkien was comfortable grew to power leveraging technology to expand its colonial dominions. So, yes, he might be a bit of a hypocrite.

The essay was, I believe, in a book of biographical essays about JRR, including his brother’s death in WWI and his reaction to that as a formative experience. As I recall, seeing that plus his university career lead to how he framed the different Elven and Human peoples I found interesting. And also Western imperialist in some ways. And “narrow.”

Then, there’s the issue of LOTR being an allegory or not. As fans know, JRR reacted vociferously against this. Now, it would be easy to say that Gandalf = Churchill, Sauron = Hitler and Saurman = Mussolini, though that leaves no room for Stalin, or Roosevelt. But, that’s not the only analogy issue at question.

Is LOTR an allegory of Christianity? Does the Pope shit in the woods? Is a bear a Presbyterian? This is a different allegory, and per my snarky mangling of metaphors, it should be clear where I stand. If not specifically an allegory of Christianity, it’s a parallel religious world to Christianity, with a creator who is (implicitly in both religious worlds’ first documents by chronology of the authors) both omnipotent and omnibenevolent, and in both cases trying to deal with Ye Olde Problem of Evil in both scenarios. And, per this Wiki piece on his cosmology, ultimately by a sort of default falling on, or into, a Manichean stance. I think that, rather, Tolkien boxed himself in and couldn't get out. I do accept, per that, there's ROUGH parallels to the Divine Comedy.

And failing in both, whether in LOTR, or more clearly in the Silmarillion, which, as I have aged and changed, strikes me as antique, with a drapery of sadness I’ve always seen, and also … wooden!

But, since that’s the raison d’etre of the whole trilogy and the Silmarillion, and the “children’s tale” of The Hobbit, I have to say it as it is. Most of my readings of LOTR were before I became a confirmed secularist, and all but one whole or partial readings of the Silmarillion were. Here I contrast Tolkien with Ursula LeGuin and her Earthsea trilogy, with its quasi-Jungian “shadows” and no explicit dual-omni monotheistic creator background.

I also said “hold on to that thought” up above. The disenchantment deepened those 6-7 years ago or so as I realized just how much all the new rounds of short stories were really Christopher Tolkien, not his dad. Like Jon Lovitz playing Picasso on an old Saturday Night Live and scribbling on a napkin to pay a waiter with what would allegedly be millionaire value artistic genius, so I see Chris as picking up scribblings and notes from his dad, writing stories off them that were 90 percent or more his own, but passing them under his dad’s name, with his own “subtitled” beneath. And, I had no desire to read any more. This happened about the same time as I read the various essays about JRR. Either one probably would have disenchanted me somewhat, but the two combined did a pretty full trick.

One final note about LOTR as allegory. Tolkien talks about how Elves who get bored of Middle Earth can go Over the Sea. Wouldn’t they eventually be bored there? Per people finding Dante’s Inferno exciting but Paradiso boring, or who are familiar with Mark Twain’s Captain Stormfield, isn’t this a reflection on the problem with eternity in general?

"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is an epic fantasy novel that has achieved legendary status in the world of literature. While it undeniably has its merits, I find myself giving it a three-star review due to a few aspects that, in my opinion, prevent it from reaching its full potential.

Firstly, the novel's pacing is a significant issue. The story takes its time to build momentum, and at times, it can feel slow-moving, especially in the initial chapters. While some readers may appreciate the level of detail and world-building, others might find it tedious and wish for a more brisk narrative.

Additionally, the extensive cast of characters can be overwhelming and challenging to keep track of, especially for readers new to the fantasy genre. While each character brings something unique to the story, I felt that some of them lacked the development necessary to make a stronger emotional connection with the audience.

Furthermore, the prose, while beautifully descriptive, can also be overly verbose and intricate, making the reading experience demanding at times. Tolkien's elaborate writing style may not be everyone's cup of tea, and some readers might prefer a more straightforward and concise narrative.

That being said, "The Fellowship of the Ring" undoubtedly excels in its imaginative world-building, creating a vast and immersive realm that has become a benchmark for fantasy literature. Tolkien's ability to craft a rich mythology and vivid landscapes is commendable and has influenced countless authors in the genre.

The novel also boasts moments of profound emotion and high-stakes drama, especially in the latter part of the story. The journey of the Fellowship and the challenges they face evoke a sense of epic adventure that leaves a lasting impact on readers.

In conclusion, "The Fellowship of the Ring" is a classic and beloved work of fantasy, but it does have its flaws that might hinder the enjoyment for some readers. While the world-building and epic scale are commendable, the pacing, extensive cast of characters, and dense prose might be less appealing to certain audiences. Nevertheless, it remains an essential read for those seeking a grand and immersive fantasy tale.

My dad has been pushing me to read “The Lord of the Rings” since I was 12 years old, but I’ve never been able to get through the dense writing and the sometimes pointless plot devices (Tom Bombadil, anyone?). But after reading “The Hobbit,” I thought I should give one more go to these books that are so important to my dad.

And what do you know — turns out, “The Fellowship of the Ring” is a lot more palatable when I can essentially tune out during long passages about elven lore or the landscape or Bilbo’s latest song. It is with great trepidation that I write this review, knowing that the great majority of readers will likely not agree with me. I consider myself a fairly well-read individual, and I am well aware of Tolkien’s legacy as the “Father of Fantasy Fiction”, however, I struggled through this novel.

In no way am I minimizing his contribution to English literature, as I realize that his imagination is above reproach, his rhetoric, impressive. However, I truly detest monotony, and this novel is laden with it. I trudged through the overly-detailed descriptions of the geography. The characters seemed to languish during the prolonged events, and very little progress was made through the entire novel. Also, the ever-growing list of names for the same character or location was exhausting! I just can’t understand why so many aliases were necessary, other than to create complete confusion.

To some degree, I truly feel that the same effect could have been accomplished (even to adequately set the elaborate scene), in ¾ or less of its current length.

When all is said and done, I cannot, in good conscience, rate this novel less than 3 stars; the impact of his work on literature, and as previously mentioned, his extraordinary imagination, are priceless.

Tolkien had an incredible mind that this trilogy immortalises as the ultimate testament to his legacy. His world creation is exceptional, leaning on expansive deep-rooted history, mythology, law, and legend alongside the sense of transience and lost grandeur that pervades the narrative. The attention to detail is so meticulous it brings a shocking sense of realism to this visionary fantasy.

His skills as an architect are unparalleled however I felt that his skills as a writer did not begin to measure up. The story adopts a quest structure that unfortunately fell victim to a repetitive obstacle solution, obstacle solution format. The opportunity to breathe life into the journey narrative that is so rife within the fantasy genre was lost in my opinion. On top of this, the major objection I had to his storytelling was the prevalence of unnecessarily strung-out minutia that did nothing to progress the plot or develop the characters; I really can't overstate quite how much walking and eating goes on throughout the trilogy. All the action was drowned in a constant barrage of irrelevant details which made the pace unbelievably slow such that getting to the end felt like the mental equivalent of delivering the ring to Mordor.

The characterisation left much to be desired. I felt that the characters lacked individual voices. Much of the dialogue sounded the same regardless of who was saying it. I would have liked to have delved a lot further into what separated the fellowship, their different backgrounds, customs, and outlooks.

The prose itself was purely descriptive with simple straightforward vocabulary. He says what he means and doesn't stray far from his comfort zone. The stark lack of literary technique meant that the only thing to engage the reader was the story itself.

Despite these criticisms the story is a beautiful one with incredibly touching themes. Tolkein redefines the definition of heroism with Frodo as his protagonist. Frodo relies on strength of character rather than strength of arms to endure the hardships he faces. He has no ability to fight, or to use magic, he does not feel the thrill of adventure, and does not yearn for glory or recognition. His humility and integrity make him the hero of this story.

The overarching theme of The Lord of the Rings is centered around the corrupting influence of power.
The full extent and nature of the Ring’s power never becomes entirely clear to us, but we get the sense that the Ring symbolizes a power almost without limits, and which is utterly corrupting. Regardless of the wearer’s initial intentions, good or evil, the Ring’s power always turns the wearer to evil. For many, the great power offered by the Ring overrides all rational thought. Tolkien warns us of the dangers of power hunger, and instead glorifies the simple life. His philosophies stand the test of time and have the same impact on modern society as they did after publication.

It truly is remarkable how every adaptation he made feels like a near-perfect decision (turning Mary and Pippin into lovable pranksters from the outset; turning the Balrog from large to enormous; adding in Boromir's death to Fellowship for an extra-emotional ending), and it's one of the few cases in which, yes, I actually do believe the movie is better than the book.
