I understand why Tolkien's work is so revered. He created a vast, rich world with its own history. He basically spawned a new genre from which everything from D&D to video games draws inspiration. So much of today's culture is indebted to his creative brilliance.

The problem? He just didn't write this book very well.

There's no questioning the amount of work he put into Middle Earth, but far more of that creativity felt made up in the moment - that is to say, without much forethought - than I expected. The highs of the story didn't feel like highs, and the lows didn't feel like lows. Tones are weak and unbesetting of the magnitude of many key events. His words are far too meandering, lazy, and without any sense of urgency; he uses 50 words when 30 would suffice. He spends far too much time making the readers feel like they're in a geography class. Many of his choices to use third-person narration instead of character dialogue completely baffled me. The Fellowship of the Ring may have been captivating in the 1950s, but it was a hard book for me to read and get into today. It needs better structure, crisper transitions, and quicker pacing (and shorter chapters!).

Fans of the LotR books always warned me that a lot was left out of the movie, but even still, I was surprised at how much. Tom Bombadil, many more scenes at Rivendell and Lothlorien, the lack of the battle at the end (Tolkien handles endings really poorly) and even, to some extent, how the scope of the entire Rings storyline was presented. Several key lines were accurate, at least ("One ring to rule them all...," "You shall not pass," and one of my favorites, "May it be a light for you in dark places..."). I prefer the movie to the book by far. If ever there was a time for someone to create the first true "remaster" of a book in the same way way they do for movies and video games, this would be the perfect candidate for such a project.

La adaptación ha sido una de mis películas favoritas, sobre todo en el género de fantasía, por años. Estaba muy emocionada por al fin leer con madurez esta historia de Tolkie, pero, lamentablemente, la experiencia no fue la que esperaba.

Así como a Frodo le tomó 17 años abandonar la Comarca para iniciar el viaje que irremediablemente lo llevará al Monte del Destino, parece que recorrí igual cantidad de tiempo intentando terminar este libro. En muchas partes sentí que había escenas innecesarias y que no tenían sentido dentro de la trama (¡que alguien me explique por favor todas esas páginas dedicadas a Tom Bombadil!) ni los diálogos parecían tan exquisitos para lo genial que fue Tolkien.

Entiendo la importancia del Señor de los Anillos para la literatura fantástica y si necesito seguir leyendo los demás libros para tener una opinión mejor formada, pero por ahora me quedo con el sabor amargo de debatirme entre una calefacción de 2 o 3 estrellas.

3.5 estrellas la verdad c:
Me siento muy feliz por haberle dado una segunda oportunidad a este libro, ya que la primera vez que lo leí me pareció bastante aburrido.
Aunque todavía estoy de acuerdo con lo que dice Jack Edwards sobre que el libro es "Simplemente un montón de criaturas caminando" me ha logrado atrapar en la 2da parte de la historia donde ya comienzan a suceder varias cosas interesantes.
Aprecio mucho el libro por lo que es y lo que representa para la literatura de fantasía y me encanta que tuve la oportunidad de detallar perfectamente cada espacio que descubrían los Hobbits a través de su viaje por el mundo del Señor de los Anillos pero también, comprendo que tanta descripción y poco diálogo puede convertirse en un tema un poco aburrido con lo que pasa el tiempo y la narración.
El libro me pareció bastante tedioso en la primera parte, y la verdad no creo que fuera necesario que fuera tan largo. Considero que la historia del pasado es un poco difícil de comprender, ya que se cuenta en forma de canciones o poemas que me parecieron bastante aburridos y sin ningún sentido, como si solo los hubieran escrito porque si y ya, lo que hace que el pasado del mundo del Señor de los Anillos se convierta en un tema tedioso y poco interesante de descubrir, porque de seguro te van a poner una canción de 3 páginas para explicarte algo que en realidad no necesitas. El libro también se enfoca en describir temas bastante mundanos cómo la comida que tuvieron en el viaje, el tiempo que se demoraron en desayunar o comer y luego descansar que son temas que en realidad a lo largo de la historia no tienen mucha importancia y creo que pudieron haber sido omitidos.
Me hubiera gustado tener la oportunidad de conocer más a fondo a los personajes de la comunidad del anillo ya que se conoce bastante de algunos (Como Aragorn, Gandalf, Boromir y obviamente Frodo) pero hay otros personajes que siento que solo los pusieron ahí porque tenían que haber 7 personas en el viaje y no porque necesariamente sean importantes para el desarrollo de la historia. La necesidad de personajes como Gimli y Legolas es que simplemente son fuertes y ya, como que no se les da otro motivo o característica a pesar, de que en mi parecer, son personajes bastante interesantes de los que espero conocer más sobre su personalidad en el 2do libro. Creo que no era necesario agregar tantos personajes sino se iba a ahondar un poco más en su carácter (Todavía no veo la necesidad de tener a Pippin y Merry en el viaje ya que literalmente no hacen nada, y tampoco es que se mencionen mucho y solo se les califica como los amigos de Frodo y ya) Espero que en el 2do libro también tengan más protagonismo porque me gustaría conocerlos mejor.
Al final, me gustaría mucho leer el 2do libro porque me atrapó la historia y en lo personal me emociona mucho que se vea una interacción con Gollum, porque es mi personaje favorito y me parece una criatura interesante que trabaja muy bien el tema de la unión del bien y del mal.

Mutter der Fantasyepen, wunderbare "Ergänzung" für Fans der Filme.
Man kann einfach noch tiefer in den Hintergrund der Welt eintauchen, der im Buch einfach viel komplexer dargestellt wird, Mittelerde wirkt ungemein lebendiger als auf der Leinwand.
Viele Szenen und Charaktere haben ein deutlich anderes Gefühl als in den Filmen, meistens zum Positiven, aber durchaus nicht immer! Mehr als einmal habe ich mich dabei ertappt zu denken "Irgendwas fehlt hier" - Ich denke es war der geniale Soundtrack und die, dem Ohr wohlbekannte Sprachgewalt der Schauspieler, was man als Leser natürlich nicht auf die selbe Art liest.
Oft machen die Szenen im Buch aber auch mehr Sinn, und kleine Plotholes aus dem Film werden hier bereitwilliger aus dem Weg geräumt. Man merkt dann schon dass die Filme "Action Abenteuer" für junge Erwachsene sind, das Buch bringt eine ungemein vielschichtigere Erzählung.

Insgesamt aber eine Spur zu viel Landschaftsbeschreibungen für meinen Geschmack, die dadurch gerettet wird, dass man die Landschaft "live" auf der Karte mitverfolgen kann. Wer darauf keine Lust hat, muss sich damit abfinden, oftmals im Dunkeln zu tappen wie die geographischen Zusammenhänge jetzt wirklich sind, die für die Charaktere des Buches aber eine wichtige Rolle spielen und viel Platz einnehmen. Die Prosa ist auch nicht überwältigend - vor allem bei der Lyrik (die alle paar Seiten vorkommt) musste ich mich dann manchmal durchkämpfen und das als Lyrikliebhaber. Es passt gut als Charakterisierung der Völker und Individuen, aber um ihrer selbst Willen ist die Lyrik einfach suboptimal. Ich denke Tolkien hat hier als Sprachschmied seinen Spaß gehabt, die einzelnen Rassen in ihrer Sprachkultur auszubauen, aber ob sich das 1:1 aufs Lesevergnügen übertragen lässt, halte ich für fragwürdig... It was inevitable that after my exceptional experience with The Hobbit that I’d want to at least try to read what some denote as the ‘greatest story ever told.’ Tolkien’s imagery and descriptions, particularly of the environment, was still dreamy and remained my favourite part of his writing. However, I didn’t feel the connection that I had with The Hobbit as Fellowship of the Ring was exhaustingly dense and difficult to get through, and I found myself losing interest more frequently than expected. That isn’t to say I didn’t enjoy the book, I just know there are multiple chapters I may have dozed off while reading…

Much like The Hobbit, I was captivated by every chapter involving the elven realms since I adore the descriptions. The chapters that included Tom Bombadill also had my heart.

However, I stumbled across a review that said each character didn’t appear to have an original voice, and that if you removed the name of the speaker, it would hardly have an effect. Unfortunately, I have to wholeheartedly agree. Besides their defining races, all characters essentially (with the exception of a few, namely Gandalf) had the same voice and personality. While it can be argued that this book is largely plot-driven, I still think that having unique and compelling characters is essential to any fantasy story. This may have been why I was frequently bored.

Of course, The Hobbit was written for a much younger audience that was intended for The Lord of the Rings so comparison can only go so far. But I am glad that I still gave Fellowship of the Ring a shot, even if I didn’t connect with it. After a break, I know I’ll come back to finish the series.

I think it took me so long because you really need to get used to Tolkien's writing. Simply put, he is a linguist and wants to show off his academic work. This, and the fact he has to write almost every time they eat and sleep, make the first book seem like filler. He definetly nailed the they-are-on-a-long-journey part, but a book with this much 'filler' would probably not be published now.

When it was good, it was great. But for every compelling scene and genius piece of world building, there is a dying Frodo requesting a song while they try to escape the Nazgûl.

- Aragorn being all 'ach, too bad you died Gandalf, I was so right tho advising not to come here, that was quite smart of me'

Ah, the routine catching up on reviews- now that's a classic!

Now, I will admit picking up Tolkien's much loved trilogy was only brought about by a very recent LotR film marathon (that stands for Lord of the Rings, if you've only just emerged fully formed into the world yesterday). It's safe to say whole scenes of Peter Jackson's adaptation live rent-free in my head, as well as being able to mostly recite all the lines off by heart from the amount of times I've watched them (and yes, of course the extended versions, how could you even ask me that?). It might, in light of all this, come as somewhat of a surprise to learn I had never actually read the books, with the exception of The Hobbit, a long time ago. I did try- but I was an impatient, easily distracted and bored teenager, and Frodo's aversion to even the remotest excitement in his life seemed practically alien to my feverish adolescent imagination of what being grown up and free to do anything would be like (ah, to be young and painfully unprepared for the crash course in the disappointments of adulthood!)- in any case, it's safe to say I didn't enjoy them, and indeed hardly went further than Bilbo's party to my recollection.

Having grown up now, and feeling at this stage of my life sufficiently jaded with it all (thanks, poor mental health- this is not a cheerful review, huh?), I found I had a lot more patience for the characters, and was very willing not to judge them against their film adaptation counterparts at every moment. Again, this seems pretty intuitive, but it's surprisingly easy to paint their faces in the same way as the actors you know and associate with those characters, especially when the films are sort of my version of the canon (what sacrilege! As a huge book-over-movie sort of gal, this is very painful to think about. I would appreciate your thoughts at this difficult time.).

Having said all that, I found I just couldn't really love the books. I scored all of them the same, as they each at various points seemed to drag. Although I didn't find the writing anywhere near as dry and difficult as I remembered it from my previous failed attempt at reading it, it certainly didn't stop me short with particularly vivid descriptions or clever turns of phrase. That it paved the way for other writers to do so is something I can appreciate, certainly at an abstract level- but the fact that we have sprawling fantasy epics with much more engaging writing now means I can't completely strip those away and review this as if those didn't exist.

There's nothing particularly I can say about this, the first of the three. I didn't much care for Tom Bombadil, but I also didn't despise those chapters. Honestly, what grated the most (and it's again a criticism I level at all three books) were all the goddamn songs. If these really did it for you, I'm sorry, but they were mostly not that good and maybe I am not musical enough to be able to conjure a melody to fit them in my head, so they just read like slightly shit poetry. I mean, have you ever googled lyrics for a song you've not heard? If you're just reading the words with no concept of a melody to string them together, well most lyrics you'll find would hardly qualify as mediocre poetry, and this was sort of the feeling I was left with. And there are not an insignificant number of these songs Tolkien is so keen to share with us! Just... groaaaaaan.

All in all though it's worth pointing out that even without a bias, you would be hard-pressed to argue that the films don't do the source material justice- whole lines lifted verbatim and used in the movie, some given different settings but hitting hard all the same, and very little changed or trimmed (unless it made no real difference and slowed down the pacing). What I'm trying to say is, I am not convinced you would be missing a ton of context if you never had a desire to check out the books for yourself. Ok ok I'll grant it we are spared the whole "Arwen's fate is tied to the ring" nonsense, but having said that it's hardly like Tolkien's world is populated with many memorable women having anything to do in the first place so you know... Again, a project of its time, sadly, for all the innovation it is otherwise credited with.

Reading this book so many years after the first time (back when I was far too young to have even a chance of enjoying it), I thought I'd grown enough as a reader to like it at the very least. It seems that hypothesis was incorrect, however, since finishing this book took me a whopping FIVE MONTHS. Shocked and appalled, gasps throughout the audience.

I swear, if I spiral into an identity crisis because of this book (too late), I'll become the most obnoxious sci-fi reader and pretend I've never heard of fantasy.

My issues are these: Tolkien is what polite circles call loquacious, and others call excessive. If he was going to spend paragraphs detailing the geographical location of the party (whose path we already know), then WHY did he include MAPS in the FIRST PLACE?!?!
...
...
...
FURTHERMORE: What on earth (or middle-earth) was the pacing of this thing?? I feel like nothing happened, then a brief glimmer of something happened, then nothing again. Why should I keep reading if no characters are compelling enough to drag me through this non-plot?!

On a positive note, I did experience moments of genuine engagement and interest in this story (you're a real one, Gandalf), but they were so few and far between they couldn't possibly make up for all the times I was bored.

I wholeheartedly acknowledge the impact and importance Tolkien's work in LOTR had on the genre I love, but it's still disappointing to read something so well beloved and feel like the odd one out because it felt like a chore.

Whereas The Hobbit had so much action that it became borderline unbelievable, The Fellowship of the Ring felt like a chore to get through. Sure, there were chapters that were a 5/5, but the majority of the book consisted of walking, talking, and singing. At this point I’m invested in the series and will see it through, but I’m a little disappointed so far.

La primera vez que leí está historia me encantó, pero en esta segunda relectura encontré detalles que no me agradaron del todo y sentí que no avanzaba nada por lo lenta que es la historia, y eso que lo escuché en audiolibro.

Debo aclarar que la voz del narrador es perfecta y muy buena. No tengo nada malo que decir a eso. Mi calificación es por las innumerables descripciones de paisajes, sentimientos o cuando los personajes relataban los acontecimientos.

Hay muchas partes que son innecesarias, además que a través de la descripción me recalcaba sin descanso la maldad que está avanzando, ejemplo: su capucha negra se confundía con la noche fría y aterradora. O como: en sus ojos vacíos no se reflejaba la bondad de antaño en los días donde los bosques eran verdes y frondosos, etc. Y como es a lo largo de cada capítulo si fastidia bastante.

Otra cosa que deteste fue el prólogo, que pretensioso fue el autor. Es cierto que la novela es muy buena, independiente de si uno disfruta o no la historia, pero eso no implica que el autor quiera enaltecer la historia. Solamente a una persona que quiera publicar un ensayo analizando la obra le podría interesar, al resto del mundo no le va a cambiar la vida si sabe o no que tanto tardo el autor en escribir.

Ahora, en comparación con la película, hay escenas que son mejor logradas en el libro, y otras en la película. Por ejemplo, la famosa escena del puente, dónde Gandalf grita esa frase de: "¡Tú no pasarás!" Está muchísimo mejor en la película por la música de fondo, los efectos especiales y por la actuación del actor. Pero cuando Boromir intenta quitarle el anillo a Frodo ya cerca del final, es mil veces mejor en el libro, el diálogo de Boromir en su codicia por apoderarse del anillo refleja lo mucho que ya está controlado sin darse cuenta.

En general si tengo un buen sabor de boca y deseo continuar con el siguiente. De algo si estoy segura, disfruto más las películas que los libros.

This isn’t for everyone. If you are someone who can become completely engrossed in a fictional world to the point where it becomes a second home, you’ll probably like this. However, if you’re someone who can’t stand slow pacing then it probably isn’t for you.

Personally, I’m giving this 3 stars. Overall, I liked it, especially towards the end as the cast of characters grows more interesting and the adventure becomes more perilous, however due to it taking so long for the plot to completely catch my interest, I can see myself liking the other entries in the series far more.

As I mentioned, the pacing is very slow to start. The main characters for almost the entire first third are very similar in personality and we only really get a much more diverse cast of characters in the last third. The action scenes are also very brief and lacking towards the beginning. They’re really small, which granted does make the later action feel much larger, but that didn’t help motivate me to keep reading.

There were a few things which did keep me interested though. For one, Middle-earth must be the most well-developed fictional world of all time. It is sometimes overwhelming how much of this place’s history is referenced. Though sometimes I felt overloaded with proper nouns, I think the good far outweighs the bad. There were occasions I was so engrossed in the setting that I felt as if I was there. The descriptions of nature also fed into this escapism for me.

And, although this is about a quest to save the world, sometimes there’s just a very nice subtlety to it. I think Frodo, Sam, and Aragorn have some very subtle character arcs in this that really lend to the narrative. Also, the magic has some subtlety to it as well: almost every time Gandalf used magic, it never felt too unrealistic, as if sometimes Gandalf just had a greater understanding of science than the other characters… which I really love.

I think when this book is at its best is when the Fellowship is all together (or mostly together). After they finally unite, there are so many fun character quirks and interactions that breathe life into the party (particularly between Gandalf and Aragorn as well as Legolas and Gimli). I will say, Merry and Pippin were definitely not used enough after the whole Fellowship came together. To me, it felt like they served their purpose in the first half and then just tagged along for the second. Sometimes it felt like they would just disappear completely until one needed to say something so I wish they got a little more to do.

Overall, if you can put up with the slow start, I think it’s worth your time. The writing—especially towards the end—is really good.

There's no doubt that Tolkien is a master of world building, but he's very detail orientated, and at times I just got bored, and felt ready to DNF it, but then at times it would pick up, and I just wanted to stay for Gandalf, Sam, and Aragorn.

Merry is another personal favourite of mine, he carries the party of Hobbits through the first part of their journey. He's very resourceful, and strong headed, confident and optimistic, where the others are more inclined towards pessimism and easily frustrated when their progress is halted or slow moving. Frodo is insufferable, I find him really ridiculous and annoying, he's very quick to want to abandon his friends the second there's danger. Like many protagonists, they're always the easiest ones to despise, purely because they cause so much excess trouble for those around them, and most often they're selfish and stubborn, and Frodo is no exception to this rule. All he ever seems to do is pass out and have to be carried (physically and figuratively) by everyone else, who in turn have to pick up his slack, he's exasperating. I definitely would've liked more Sam interactions, he's a sassy little king, and deserved more speaking time.

Honestly just wrote this review to add a Aragorn Gif, because what a dreamy king. One of the few people who brings the Hobbits out of their shells.

I think Tolkien was more of a linguist than a writer. It almost seems like he wrote these books just to create songs and languages. I mean seriously there is soooo much singing. I do find his style of writing charming.. but it just got pretty dull after a while.

The first half of the book was basically just the hobbits wandering around the shire doing fuck all. Eating, singing, walking. Eating, singing, walking. You could probably space out for 5-10 minutes and not miss a thing. And there were too many where instances of things happening that had absolutely no bearing on the plot or character development. Just random fodder. Like the farmer and Tom Bombadil.. why are there pages on pages devoted to these useless characters. We don’t even meet them in the movies and I think that was for the better. I mean seriously they don’t even get to the prancing pony until almost half way through the book. The pacing was just a bit off to me.

Another thing that bothered me is the timeline of when Frodo actually leaves the shire. Bilbo leaves Frodo his ring after his birthday party. Gandalf leaves to investigate the nature of the ring and eventually finds Gollum. He doesn’t return to Frodo for another 17 years. Quite a long time but okay. Gandalf warns Frodo that he’s in grave danger.. the Wraiths know his name and the shire and they’re searching for him. Quite a grave situation… you’d think Frodo would leave almost immediately (as he does in the movie). But wait then he would miss his beloved Summer in the shire and also his birthday party. Better to leave in the fall after his party. So on Tolkien goes explain how wonderful summers in the shire are and the details of frodos birthday.

What?? Why wouldn’t he leave right away. I mean he learns the wraiths are actively hunting him yet he decides he can’t leave before a proper birthday send off! Nonsense.

Another thing I didn’t love and hesitate to mention since it could have been a result of my consuming medium (audible) but the characters dialogue was a little off putting to me. Everyone was so preachy and sing-songy. Like there weren’t many normal conversations.. it was a lot of grand soliloquies and proclamations. It was hard for me to fall in love with the characters the same way I did with the movies.

To be fair, most of my gripes are isolated to the first half of the book before the story really picks up. Again I absolutely love the world and characters that Tolkien created in this book.. it was just a tough read for me.

This was a good story all in all, and I enjoyed a fair bit of it. The story itself just felt bogged down by repetitive and wordy dialog (the story of the ring is repeated three times in just the first half, as an example) and a lackadaisical approach to the journey.

Everytime someone brought up the fact that they needed to leave a place as soon as possible they all then in turn decided to take a nap and leave in 10 hours, even though every single time they did that before it led to more trouble. None of their difficulties would have happened had they just sucked it up and picked up the pace a bit instead of dawdling for a month at a time. It was very frustrating to read that every hardship was caused by the main characters just procrastinating.

While this series set the bedrock for the fantasy genre in general, it hasn't aged the best unfortunately and makes me really want to re-read the Hobbit again with it's better pacing and fun story.

On one hand, the Lord of the Rings is undoubtedly a masterpiece. I have no idea how Tolkien managed to create such a detailed world, invent multiple languages, write a billion little songs, AND tell such an epic tale all while being a professor at Oxford, but it's truly something to behold.

On the other hand, Fellowship can be so, so dry. I was both amazed yet unsurprised when I looked at the map and realized that Frodo and Sam make it more than 3/4 of the way to their destination in this first book, because as the reader you feel like you have taken every single step of their travels with them, for better and for worse. I understand that there was a lot of ground to cover (both literally and figuratively), but it wasn't exactly thrilling to go through so many pages of ekphrasis and textbook-like imparting of lore.

What surprised me most, though, was that I found a lot that was relatable and comforting as a young adult reading today: Frodo's grappling with unwanted responsibility but finding strength and support in community is something I think a lot of people go through as they grow up, and I think that many readers today can relate to the general sense of anxiety caused by living in uncertain, difficult times. There is indeed danger in such dualistic morals as those presented by this story, and the construction of the Other in Tolkien's work presents..... a lot to unpack, but I can see how so many people have resonated with this story in spite of its flaws. Tolkien may not have been the first, only, or best fantasy writer of his time, but his stories clearly stick because of their timeless ability to connect with people. So while this first book may be dry, it's an experience worth having and I'm excited to read the rest of the trilogy at long last.

“Now at last we must take a hard road, a road unforeseen. There lies our hope, if hope it be. To walk into peril- to Mordor. We must send the Ring to the Fire.” pg. 280

I am certain that the fondness of familiarity will creep over me when I eventually reread it with the benefit of foreknowledge of its comings and goings. I appreciate Tolkien’s skill. However; goodness, John, I know what a tree is! Vivid, regardless. I have been trying to read the darn thing for coming on 9 years and am glad to have finally achieved it. He writes like an academic, which should appeal to me, however his work can be daunting. The Hobbit is one of my favourite pieces of literature of all time, and I hope the remainder of the series grips me in that same way; the way in which this book unfortunately failed. It will, I’m sure, pull together well in companionship with its sister tomes, but it struggles alone.

One glowing compliment I will give The Fellowship: it balances mirth with peril very well. There is enough goodwill to balance out the stakes that the protagonists must ultimately face. Power that is wielded for good is accompanied by kindness and freely given smiles. That may be the only thing the film adaptations fail to capture adequately.

I enjoyed the world and the setting. The descriptions of the scenery really brought it to life and at times it felt like the land was its own character.
Frodo was a little delight, I love regular people (or hobbits!) showing fear and vulnerability but being brave anyway. In the fellowship, Frodo, Sam and Strider were the characters that I enjoyed spending time with the most as they had more of their own personality.
The main issue I have is that the writing was the same tone throughout. So during tense moments there wasn't suspense or atmosphere that matched what was happening. This made the book feel long as I didn't feel the climaxes and anti-climaxes.
I would have also liked to know more about Gandalf and his powers. It seems sometimes he has the power to do something and sometimes he doesn't. It was never really explained what the rules around his magic are.
Still looking forward to reading the next two 💪

I can't remember a time when I was unaware of Lord of the Rings. It was one of the first books I've read, and Middle-Earth was further stamped into me by the endless array of spin-offs, video games, cartoons, and films that followed, saying nothing of the entire genre of high fantasy that owes much to this one book. Yet at the same time I hardly remembered the book itself; I knew the ins and outs of the plot in the same way I know Roman history -- a general outline of events, rather than a particular tale told by a particular author. So coming back to Tolkien after almost thirty years, I was curious to see what I'd find.

I tried to recreate the experience of someone reading the book for the first time, but of course it was impossible. I knew every scene. Indeed, it felt like the author knew I knew every scene, like I was reading a story about LotR from someone who assumes I'm familiar with the source material, rather than LotR itself. Initially, I can't say I liked it. The dialogue was stilted, the songs terrible, and the plot filled with needless twists and turns that resolved too quickly to ever feel threatening. As the book went on, however, Middle-Earth drew me in, and I latched on to every snippet about the setting as I did in the yesteryears. But is it because of the richness of the setting itself, or just because it's so familiar to me? I don't know. I can't shake the feeling that if the book came out today, I'd read it and forget it.

Possibly, the most overrated book of the Twentieth Century.
Not as innovative as the Tolkien dogma states nowadays. Most elements are to be found in previous or coeve works of fantasy.
Not believable in the way characters (do not) develop. "In nomine omen" raised to the status of psychological trait, for cardboard people moving against a stark background of reactionary manicheism.
Indeed, not subtle at all in its racism. Little England at its worst, with every class (race!) at their place, tall fair haired and skinned rulers, stout farmers happy to serve, dark southern-easterners ready to betray and conquer; more than anything else, evil as external to US, and ethical choices guided by valour. For fuck sake, how old was the guy when he wrote this thing, twelve?
(About Tolkien being a forever-twelve-year-old male with superiority complex and megalomaniac fantasies, has anybody else noticed how every tall and handsome character keeps being progressively revealed in ever increasing glory at every stage of the narrative, amidst gasps of recognition and adoration from the onlooking crowds? It reminds me of the passage, in Ulysses, where the Hungarian father of Mr Bloom is celebrated in triumph by the whole Dublin gathered at the docks, in a (voluntarily) hilarious flight of fantasy. Minus the irony. The second-hand embarrassment flows mighty in this book.)
Not surprising that Tolkien became a source of inspiration for the Italian far right scum. Where else will you find racism, xenophobia, reactionary classism, and white male megalomania wrapped in a SUCCESSFUL MODERN MAINSTREAM CLASSIC???
I still cannot fathom how this thing has been voted best book of the Twentieth Century. Or, maybe, I dare not investigate why.

This said, I am thoroughly enjoying my experience listening to the audiobook narrated by Andy Serkis. He does not even try to dissimulate the pompous tone of Tolkien's prose On the contrary: with a master stroke of great class, Serkis goes full Beowulf and manages to serve this half-boiled fanta-linguistic treaty disguised as fantasy novel, as if it were some ancient epic. Also, I happen to not share many readers' distaste for hobbits, and I am affectioned to Gandalf for personal reasons. How right was Terry Pratchett though, taking the piss...

And I tried but wow - was this series hella boring. I think I got as far as three quarters of the way in the second book and I gave it up.

I decided to give this book another shot this year and man, was it a struggle.

The exposition and information dumps are way, way too much. Tolkein gave a lot of thought and effort into his world - his head canon is immense - but this book needed an editor who would not be afraid to cut and splice this material (there is always room in the Appendices!). The pace is like a brambling path that branches off this way and that (what was the bloody point of Tom Bombadil and his wife!? What was with all this singing interjected randomly?! Why all these references to ye olde lore that ultimately has no impact on the plot?) with several starts and stops. After Frodo initially receives The Ring he doesn’t properly leave on his journey for nearly three years! And he is technically around 50 years old, no young, cute Elijah Wood. I guess there is no real rush, it is just a world-ending nuke hung around a chain that the literal embodiment of Satan is searching for - take your time, Frodo.

There are also several things, large and small, that get under my skin. The fact that the elites - kings and descendants of kings - are considered Good and True while the peasant class are happy to work in the fields. The fact that certain people - those who are extremely fair - are described as good while the others - who are almost described as dark-skinned or black - are unequivocally evil. People and creatures are the same on the inside as they are on the outside. The immense work and attention on humans, elves, and hobbits but next to nothing on orcs and goblins. Surely, they have their own society and culture as well? Where do all these orcs, uruk-hai, and goblins come from? Do these warriors have wives and lil’ babies? Do they keep pets? Do they have holidays? Do they sing and produce art?

On the other hand, it is comforting to know that the good guys are the good guys and the bad guys are the bad guys. I am all for “gray” characters and for complex, twisty protagonists and antagonists. But knowing that the good guys are truly good - and demonstrating that throughout the entire series through words and actions big and small - is just so pleasant. The characters go through literal hell - especially Frodo and Sam - and yet through it all they retain their essence, their essential goodness.

I also love the male-to-male friendships and relationships. I will admit I do read much in the way of fantasy or even science fiction, but I cannot think of another series that has so many examples of characters displaying positive, strong masculinity. Aragorn is a true badass, a literal Ranger and action hero and yet he is also tender, kind, intelligent, and an amazing friend. The quartet of the four hobbits is one of the bright spots in this series, especially Sam looking after Frodo - feels unique in both literature and in film (the actor who played Sam, Sean Astin, mentioned in interviews and in the DVD commentary that fans wrote in expressing their sincere appreciation and gratitude for the tenderness between Frodo and Sam). Boromir, Legolas, and Gimli - all different “races” of beings - also display courage along with fear, frustration along with gladness, weaknesses along with courage.

There are several unintentionally funny moments - Frodo mentions that geese squeal and squawk at Nazgul. I did find some fanart of some geese squawking at Nazgul months and months ago and now I cannot find it 😣 - but I do imagine that every time the Nazgul were hunting the hobbits they were trailed by waddling geese hissing and squawking at them. The singing would throw off the pace so much that it balanced between annoying and funny. Gandalf struggling to figure out the way through the mines of Moria is a true dad moment and it tickles me.

I truly, really wanted to love this book. I wanted to hop into reading it and find another all-time favorite series. Unfortunately, having struggled to finish it for months, giving it 3 stars is a generous rating.
Somehow, despite the unfathomable popularity of this story, over the years I had kept myself mostly spoiler free, with the intention of finishing the books first before watching the Peter Jackson movies. However, when I excitedly picked up the Fellowship of the Ring, I didn't expect to sign up for what feels like over 300 pages of dragged-out, excruciatingly slow exposition. It reads like a folklore tale, which is kind of the idea, but it is personally not the kind of literature I am interested in at this stage of my life. And I understand the purpose of the slow parts, I get the point of the lengthy descriptions, detailed retellings of past events and the name-dropping of the entire family tree of any and every character, but seriously... it's so boring to read. I suppose it would be quite interesting to those already invested in the mythos of Middle-earth, but as someone who stepped into this with very basic knowledge of what I'm getting into, I found it incredibly difficult not to dnf this book. I'm going to finish the series more out of principle rather than keen passion. I would say that after "The Council of Elrond" (an insufferably long string of monologues) the book picks up pace and the exciting part of the journey begins. The entire tone shifts to a much more adventurous, intriguing tale that makes you want to read more.
I understand this would probably sound like blasphemy to the people that worship this series, but that's the great thing about opinions, everyone gets to have their own.

Frodo reads like an overprivileged middle aged man rather than a hero we can empathise with. It cannot be denied that the bones of the plot are exceptional, but once the hobbits reached Rivendell I was riven by boredom. I thought the Council of Elrond would be the pinnace of all my LOTR fan-girling but it's one of the worst chapters I've read in years. Don't get me wrong, there were parts I loved and I finished eager to read the next volume. However, the second half of the Fellowship of the Ring simply did not slap until Moria and the breaking of the fellowship.

📖 Reseña: La comunidad del anillo – J.R.R. Tolkien

La comunidad del anillo es el inicio de una de las sagas más icónicas de la literatura fantástica. En este primer tomo, Tolkien nos introduce al vasto mundo de la Tierra Media y nos cuenta cómo un joven hobbit llamado Frodo hereda un anillo que guarda un poder oscuro y ancestral. A partir de ahí, comienza una travesía épica junto a una compañía de personajes inolvidables —magos, elfos, enanos y hombres— con el propósito de destruir el Anillo Único y evitar que caiga en manos de Sauron.

La historia es grandiosa en su escala y ambición: Tolkien no solo cuenta una aventura, sino que construye todo un universo con lenguas, mitologías y culturas propias. Sin embargo, esa misma profundidad puede hacer que la lectura sea difícil. A mí, sinceramente, me costó mucho avanzar. Tardé meses en terminarlo, y hubo momentos en que la narración se me hizo densa y excesivamente descriptiva.

Aun así, reconozco el enorme valor literario y la influencia de esta obra. Hay capítulos que logran transmitir una sensación mágica y melancólica que pocos libros consiguen. Los paisajes, las canciones, la camaradería entre los personajes… todo tiene una belleza muy particular que se aprecia más con paciencia que con prisa.

En lo personal, me alegra haberlo leído, aunque no se convirtió en una de mis lecturas favoritas. Lo disfruté más como una experiencia que como una historia que me atrapara de principio a fin.

⭐ Puntuación personal: 3/5

With HBO’s new series, Power of the Rings, debuting, I felt it was a good time to knock off another Great American Read book from my list and to start J.R.R. Tolkien’s original series, Lord of the Rings with his first book, Fellowship of the Rings. Even though the series made the GAR’s top five, I’ve postponed reading it to the end of my GAR reading adventure for fear that it wouldn’t live up to the cinematic extravaganza of the movies. What I discovered in listening to the audiobook was that the movies actually helped me fully visualize the events of the book and the characters felt like long lost friends from my younger years. So the question is… would I have enjoyed the storyline if I hadn’t seen the movies? The answer… sadly, probably not. So I am thankful for the movies in that they introduced me to the brave Bilbo Baggins and his motley crew as they wandered through Middle Earth on their quest. I also discovered that in reading The Fellowship of the Rings while watching The Power of the Rings it gave me a unique perspective of speculating how the events that propelled Baggins’ onto his quest may have started. And so while I only give the book a three-star rating, if I wrap the book up with the movies, then the whole enterprise would jump to 5 stars. Now, I must leave you and get lost in the next episode of Power of the Rings as I contemplate Baggins’ future words that “Not all who wander are lost”.

wow really took my time with this one. i loved the world-building of "lord of the rings", even with all of those dumps of information that were thrown throughtout the entirety of the novel. for a fantasy book from 1950's, i can certainly say that lotr set some "rules" for the world of fantasy literature, and obviously is one of the reasons this genre grew in popularity throughout the years - and in all fairness, you can understand why once you read the series.

i don't consider it a book that everybody can easily love, but one that regular readers (not a really good idea to get into the whole reading scene with this one, especially if you don't like to test your memory with lots of details) should try.

the characters were interesting, with Sam, Tom Bombadil and Aragorn as my absolute favourites, but some of them clearly lacked some personality, with their whole purpose being to make Frodo happy and literally nothing else.

as far as i'm concerned, sometimes I couldn't stop myself from perceiving Frodo as the stereotypical fantasy male main character, who unfortunately, as much as he tries, keeps putting himself and the people around him in great danger, but still, despite it all, everybody loves him deeply and can't contain their appreciation for him, whenever he goes. still liked him, though. But of course I see it this way, in 2022, although considering how old this piece of literature is, I would say Frodo was an unquestionable example, maybe even the blueprint, for next-generation fantasy male main-characters, almost like he set the scene for them all; Frodo - the OG.
*special mention: all the damn time, every single creature insisted that Frodo should stay away from the ring, never hesitating from trying to convince him of the bad influence it could possibly have on him if he starts wearing it. what is the next thing Frodo does as an act of clownery at a party, after making a whole-ass deal of making a promise with himself that he's not ever gonna wear the Ring? that's right, he puts on the ring. like wtf?? that's what i mean by the "stereotypical-gets-himself-in-the-middle-of-trouble-male-main-character" thing.

and do i even need to mention the so-called iconic "friendship" of Frodo and Sam's? 'cause all i need to say in order to sum it all up is: "historians will call them close friends, besties, roomates, colleagues, anything but lovers, history hates loverssss!!".

A Ring was created by the Dark Lord Sauron who inhabited Mordor, several years before, bent on taking over Middle Earth. This Ring was never seen again when Sauron was defeated and Isildur took the Ring for himself. This Ring holds immense power, being passed from person to person only to corrupt them with greed. Frodo never expected to find the Ring himself, and is paid a visit by Gandalf, warning him of the immense power in his grasp. So Frodo, Merry, Pippin, and Sam travel away from their beloved Shire. Along the way, they meet Aragorn, a ranger with more to him than meets the eye, Gimli, a dwarf of strength and stature, and Legolas, a skilled and poetic elf. Aided by Gandalf, a powerful wizard, they begin a Fellowship to destroy the Ring with the Dark Lords disciples on their trail.

The Lord of the Rings is objectively one of the greatest fantasies of all time. I had dnf'ed this before because I just couldn't get interested in it. I decided to try it again. My main problem was I couldn't stop comparing it to the movie (I had no idea Aragorn would have grey hair, or that Frodo would be fifty). However, once I struck those comparisons aside, I was able to evaluate and enjoy The Lord of the Rings a lot more.

The world-building is spectacular if overwhelming at points. It had a way of explaining family trees all of a sudden, if it gave the reader information that wasn't necessary but only strengthened the world. Imagining Middle Earth, if it feels so rich, complicated, and big. I enjoyed paying attention to every single detail that Tolkien threw into the plot.

Tolkien harnesses the unexpected hero to its fullest potential. This story isn't the fastest-paced. Yet once you get interested, it's easy to speed through. And I finished this book in one day. The characters aren't particularly complex, nor do they go through character growth. They are still good characters to lead the story. I enjoyed watching this journey.

Tolkien's writing pays attention to detail. He writes with confidence and fluency. The Fellowship is my favorite part of the story. Although I enjoyed seeing the journey rather more than reading, I appreciated seeing where The Lord of the Rings first started.

In the Fellowship of the Ring, I can see a more refined and put-together overall story than what came in the Hobbit.

Many details that happened in the Hobbit were left unexplained or had random McGuffins occurring that allowed the main character to get out of situations that I wasn't too big of a fan of. The prologue and the first chapter of the Fellowship of the Ring seemed to dedicate the majority of their time to not only setting up the journey to come but also trying to connect it to the Hobbit and explain certain details that were left out in the Hobbit, like for example how Gollum got the ring in the first place.

The lore behind the ring went from a plot device in the hobbit to the most important item in the entire series having its lore connected with the entirety of the series and everything that came with it was very interesting. In regards to the journey though I did feel the double-edged sword of the overwhelming amount of explanation in detail that JRRT goes into when it comes to explaining every single thing especially when it comes to the locations to be a blessing and a curse. A blessing because the amount of detail he goes into if you pay attention you can vividly picture what he's trying to portray to you but also a curse because this by far more than anything else in the story hurts the overall pacing of the story.

Many times I was impressed by the detail and dedication he put into but at the same time I felt like I just wanted the story to continue I've read enough about how this location looks and I just want the plot to continue. The number of characters that come along with the journey was once again a bit bloated. Sam, Aragorn, and Legolas were fine. Everyone else was more or less forgettable to me, and I did not care for them. The conflict and battle scenes also felt were actually kind of short and disappointing when it came to explaining how a fight plays out. It left a lot to be desired from me, especially when it goes into such long and heavy detail when it comes to other things. I wish that energy was more in the fight scenes as well, and the ending to the first book, although alright, was just alright. It wasn't amazing or great, just alright. It felt like an end of a chapter (which it was sure) instead of an ending to a book, I guess it was just a tad anticlimactic to me.

J.R.R Tolkien's Prose
I'm glad that within the 17-year release gap between The Hobbit and The Fellowship of the Ring, that his prose are more refined. Still quite unorthodox but it didn't seem like he has that "casually talking to a friend" type of attitude when it came to writing this one. I understand The Hobbit was written for children and this was not. I'm more so also talking about his transitions into different scenes and feel were more smooth and organic as well.

Verdict
Nonetheless, I liked this entry, and I'm looking forward to the next one as I feel I'll probably like that one more. (Update, I do)

Again, I would have skipped over the songs, ngl, if I was reading them because 90% have no bearing on the plot. But it was nice listening to Andy singing. It was also MIGHTY IMPRESSIVE that he sang most of them in the relevant accent to the character doing the singing. Like, wow, mate. Gimili's was my favourite.

Overall Rating 6/10
Spoiler Free Section
Reasoning
I have mixed feelings for this book mainly because coming into the book I had already watched the movies. As a result, I already had prior knowledge of the book which I felt really hindered my ability to enjoy the book. The reason I believe this is because the book is mostly about a long meandering journey in which obstacles both environmental and physical are present and the main appeal (in my opinion) is not knowing what will occur. However, this is negated if you have watched the movies and know most of what the characters will encounter. Although, I must say, even if I had not known about what would occur though the book, I doubt I would have enjoyed the book seeing as how I read the first book in the Wheel of Time Series and did not enjoy it much. This is relevant to the discussion of The Fellowship of the Ring due to how similar the two are in plot and especially in regards to how both have the characters go on a long journey.
With that being said, I thought the writing was great with the imagery being fantastic and that the characters were compelling and fun to hear about and listen to. Furthermore, I really enjoyed how the plot was (in my opinion) well set into a wider world. What I mean by this, is how locations the characters would pass through would often have their own histories attached to them and stories. This trend continues with many events and people being mentioned in the book with their own detailed histories. This idea also extends to some characters being attached to a wider world. The effect of this is that it makes the world in the Lord of The Rings seem relatively more "real" compared to worlds of other fantasy books I have read in which only people and locations relevant or to be relevant in the plot are mentioned in some degree of detail. To be more specific, I feel that this applies much to the "Percy Jackson" books and fantasy books by Brandon Sanderson (granted I do love Sanderson's books).
Moving back to its effect in LOTR, it makes the journey of the Fellowship of the Ring seem like just another story in a long line of stories within the world of Middle Earth (albeit one of incredible importance) which is an interesting feeling to have in a book.

Spoiler Free Summary
The story centers around a young near human named Frodo Baggins who has a beloved uncle who has had his share of adventures in his youth. However, upon receiving an incredibly dangerous and important gift from his uncle from a previous adventure, Frodo's life is upturned forcing him to leave his lifelong home and embark on a quest with some companions of his. This quest leads him on a long journey in which his view of the world is widened and his desire for home grows as he encounters many different peoples, environments, and obstacles (both environmental and living). Despite these challenges, he continues on with the goal of accomplishing his quest despite the setbacks and tragedies that come of his journey partially due to the companionship he has following him.

Spoiler Section

Spoiler Summary
Frodo Baggins, a young hobbit, comes into possession of a magical ring, which is the key to its creator, Sauron, an ancient evil spirit, to take over Middle Earth. Moving onward, this gift eventually comes to the notice of a wizard and friend of Frodo by the name of Gandalf who learns of its true nature. Out of grave concern, Gandalf spurs Bilbo to leave before the forces of the dark lord catch him which sparks Bilbo on a long journey at first with three other hobbit companions. However, as they journey farther from home they attract the attention of a human ranger, elves, and the ringwraiths while encountering pieces of history and other supernatural forces from a carefree immortal to barrow wights along the way. These struggles do take their toll eventually leaving Frodo gravely injured by a weapon of a ringwraith and ever more longing for home. However, his spirits and health are restored for he was able to reach an enchanted realm of the elves in time in which a fellowship is created to aid Frodo in destroying the ring in the realm of Mordor where it was created, and thus his journey continues. Despite the addition of a talented elf, dwarf, and prince to his retinue, Frodo and the newly created fellowship continue to encounter obstacles (from magically spurred elements to creatures of the enemy). As a result, and out of desperation the fellowship choose to enter Khazad Dum (and thus the Mines of Moria), a once prosperous underground city of dwarves where they are harangued by, a kraken, orcs, trolls, and a fire demon (Balrog) which leads to the untimely death of Gandalf. Shaken by these events, the remaining members of the fellowship leave the mines and continue on their way, but the continued presence of orcs and the rings ability to tantalize the hearts of men with power prove too much for the fellowship resulting in them separating, leaving Frodo and his friend Sam alone to continue on their way.

Things I Enjoyed that Was Not in The Fellowship of the Ring Movie
I really enjoyed Tom Bombadil due to the relative mystery of him and how he is said to be incredibly ancient yet is not terribly concerned with the wider world and seems relatively carefree. I also enjoyed him due to his appearance being something I had not seen in the movie and thus there was novelty in his showing.
I like how the powers of the ring are more directly stated and explained. What I mean by this is how Galadrial states that "the rings give power according to the measure of each possessor" (Tolkein, 432) when Frodo asks about why he has limited abilities with the ring. To continue, it is also stated that Frodo does have some passive abilities with the ring with enhanced senses and a sharper mind. I find this to be beneficial because while I am fine with soft magic systems I think something like the ring (that is incredibly important to the story) should have some clear boundaries set on it even if they are ones I could infer even from the movie. By that, I mean about the power according to the possessor, not the enhanced abilities Frodo receives.
This is a kinda obvious divergence between a movie and a book, but I really enjoyed the writing style of the book in the detailed descriptions of actions and scenery as something about the writing really sat well with me. I cannot really describe this but the sentences and the words allowed me to read fast while still coming up with a very detailed image in my head as I was reading which was a nice combination especially as I did find the book to be just a hair too slow for my taste at times.

Review of Theme(s)
I think the theme I found most prominent and engaging was that of loss of what once was. This theme I found in how Frodo loses his innocence of the world as he experiences more of it. This can also be seen in how while the beauty of the elven lands are described it is also mentioned that this is but a winter another spring or summer will not come to the lands again. Finally, I found this theme prominent in how it is mentioned that many of the elves will leave Middle Earth entirely, meaning their generally cheery ways go with them. What I found/find engaging about these themes is just how when something ends you often can't get those same experiences back nor can other people. What is more, I find this to be relevant in my life for my last day of high school tennis for the school was yesterday (Thursday) and how this is my last year of high school meaning some situations of mine will soon end. However, the theme of loss is also engaging within the confines of the book given how well Frodo's life is, the lands of the elves, and the elves' culture is described in such a great manner that gives me some emotional connection to them making it somewhat sad that those things were lost or will soon end in the book.
Moving onto the theme of good vs evil, I really enjoyed it in this book. A big part of that is due to how the few books I have been reading recently are a bit more nuanced when it comes to good and evil, so it was nice to have a change in pace. Furthermore, Tolkein's use of imagery is really helpful to this themes because I'm sure he uses environment to help convey good and evil. This can especially be seen in the description of the elvish lands (which are lacking in evil) and the landscape becoming more stark as the story nears its close and the Fellowship breaks up, the orcs close in, and Boromir is tempted by the ring.



Review of the Magics (Spoilers for A Song of Ice and Fire (Game of Thrones)
I am giving the magic of The Lord of The Rings its own "little" review section due to how I find the magic in fantasy books to be a big part of their appeal and find them to be very interesting (abnormally so in my opinion).
Before I begin, the aspects of magic systems in fantasy books I find to be appealing mainly revolve around their mystery (even if their mystery is eventually diminished or solved), their effects, and how they relate to the plot.
The Lord of the Rings has a soft magic system without clearly defined rules, limitations, or explanations. I think this works well with the book as a long winded explanation of the powers would take away some of the mystery and not fit well with the book. However at the same time, I am still a little disappointed that there is little to no explanation of the magic such as in how there is no focus put onto why there are wights, why Gandalf has his abilities (I know he is a spirit sent by Eru, basically God, but that is not stated in the book), or why there are wargs beyond just. Furthemore, the effects of the magic are decent with a wide variety of effects. I particularly enjoy the magic of the elves related to their lands being supernaturally wonderful and the corrupting effect of the ring. Then in regards to how the magic is relevant to the plot, I find it to be good with the ring being the main driver, with the magic of Gandalf being in reaction to threats, and with the elve's magic just adding to scenes and themes. However, I do wish the magics could take on a flashier role in combat beyond summoning a flood or breaking some stone.
However as opposed to the magics in Game of Thrones, The Stormlight Archive and Mistborn (all series of books I really enjoy) I think it falls short due to a lack of a distinctive amount of any of the factors I find that makes magics appealing. What I mean by this is that most of magic in Mistborn is clearly defined in their effect, but at the same time some of the broader magics have a huge amount of intrigue that is relevant to the plot and will eventually be answered in an extremely satisfying way. In addition to that there are some great fight scenes involving magic that result in some great mental images.
Furthermore, The Stormlight Archive revolves around a world in which magic is deeply ingrained in the world (it's economy, fauna, warfare, religion, etc) in a way that the Lord of the Rings lacks; however, I think The Stormlight Archive is a rare occurrence in this regard to any fantasy book.
Moving onto the magic system which I think is the most similar in use in plot to The Lord of the Rings is A Game of Thrones. In regards to relevance to plot and mystery. I do think Game of Thrones blows The Lord of the Rings out of the water due to the presence of really distinctive scenes of magic in the A Song Of Ice and Fire series. Specific examples are mainly the time jump near the Bridge of Dreams with the stone men after Tyrion discusses a characters supposed true identity and the resurrection of Beric Dondarrion (the one in the cave). What I find appealing is the lack of full answers, yet there is room to speculate, combined with how magic is not a driving force behind the plot, but it still plays a supporting role that can interact with a main plot (In my opinion there are several main plots going on in the book series). A specific example of what I am describing is Euron Greyjoy acquiring magical items helping him to become the king of the ironborn which puts stress on the Iron Throne (yeah I know its complicated). This is contrast to The Fellowship of the Ring where it seems the magical lands of the Elves are only present and to show the theme of loss and Gandalf only uses his magic in reaction to threats which is not as an exciting mix, but still enjoyable.


Summary (Yeah I bet you want a summary after reading this mouthful, but hey if you want reviews that are in a conversational tone like that example this is what you will get from me).

To quickly summarize my feelings and thoughts for the book, I would not likely read this book again due to the appeal of the unknown factors in a journey long since been discovered by me even before reading the book. However, I am glad I read it as I did enjoy the writing, the theme of loss, the decent magical system, and the environment.

As a reader, I have a complex relationship with J.R.R. Tolkein's "The Lord of the Rings". On one hand, the historical significance of the novel and its impact on the fantasy genre can't be ignored. Tolkein essentially created the fantasy genre and for that, all fantasy fans should be grateful. I was particularly impressed with Tolkein's definition of heroism, which focuses on inner qualities rather than external abilities. This idea has had a profound impact on popular culture.

However, I did find Tolkein's writing style to be a bit of a challenge. The meticulous descriptions of even the most trivial details could be a bit tedious. Additionally, some parts of the book, such as the Ent poetry, were just not enjoyable to read.

Despite these struggles, the characters in the book are what kept me invested. I was enamored with almost every character, with Gandalf being my absolute favorite. The age-old tale of good vs evil is still one of my favorite themes for any novel. The setting in Middle-Earth was also a highlight for me, and I often daydreamed about living among hobbits, elves, and dwarves. The quotes in the book are memorable and have set the bar high for great writing.

However, the slow pace of the plot, with excessive descriptions of nature, did test my patience at times. The writing style is straightforward, making it easy to understand, but I found it to be rather simple.

In conclusion, "The Lord of the Rings" is both a mixed bag and an important book for me as a reader. Despite its flaws, the world, the characterization of Sam and Frodo, Gandalf, and the action make it a worthwhile read for fans of the fantasy genre. The elven info dumps and political maneuvering got tiring, making reading the book feel like a chore at times, but the memorable quotes and impact on the literary world make it a classic that cannot be overlooked.

In the early 2010's I knew nothing specific about the Lord of The Rings, besides the vague understanding of its legendary status and that the films had been a huge part of nerd and pop culture despite having mostly passed me by. Around this time the (terrible) Hobbit trilogy had just released its first installment in theatres, so general interest in this work had once again reached an all time high. My wife, then girlfriend, and I decided to rectify that. On a whim I bought the 3 films and watched them all.

They were... alright.

I was on a bit of a reading kick at this time in my life, so thinking that the books might be much better than the movies we both agreed to read the books together.

Flash forward to today, and just a few weeks ago I finished the first volume in the series, "The Fellowship of the Ring" on audiobook, narrated by Andy Serkis. To my eyes this is easily the superior way to experience this story that I've attempted so far.

There is something about this story that suits spoken delivery, be it the frequent songs and historical asides. In the text it struck me as an annoying diversion, but spoken it feels as natural as a campfire or bed time story. The songs are definitely more tolerable when you can hear them, though Serkis is a far worse singer than he is a general performer and voice actor.

Speaking of Serkis, his performance is so stellar that I almost always could tell which character was speaking based on the delivery of the words alone, especially early on. This becomes somewhat more difficult and inconsistent when the Fellowship gathers -- Boromir, Gimli, and Aragorn and Merry and Pippin sometimes bleed together. Considering that voices as unique as what Serkis delivers here are generally a luxury reserved for full cast recordings, this is worthy of praise.

There's not much I have to say worthwhile about the story overall. Tolkien's world is often more fascinating and intriguing than the course of the story or its characters themselves, likely in part due to how iconic this tale is and has been in the public consciousness. The written tale does add a greater depth and breadth that is lacking from the films, and that alone is worth some reccomendation. If you struggled to read this work in the past I'd definitely reccomend giving this or another recording of this story a try.

As an avid fantasy fan, this could be my downfall! I am in the minority here among fellow fantasy readers, but I really do not think this book is all that good. Let me start by saying though, I did not hate it, though the review I’m about to write may make it seem like I did.

Firstly, if you are a fan of this book or even about to read it for the first time ever, I recommend listening to the new audio production of it narrated by Andy Serkis, who does a phenomenal job! Truly, his narration made much of this book bearable when perhaps it would not have been.

I think, for me, the easiest way for me to sum up what I didn’t like about this book is that it lacked heart. It is a history book plain and simple. Tolkien wrote a history of his world, disguised as an adventure. The fellowship, is put together by one individual deciding. They are assigned the duty. In turn, sucking all the depth and beauty out of the narrative. If they had chosen to go, if they had understood the danger and yet dedicated their service and lives to the task of destroying the ring, this would have created such a wonderful tale full of the heart I mentioned just now. Yet, that is not the case. Elrond tells them to go and they do. I wanted their to be so much more depth to their quest. Themes of courage, friendship and loyalty were so absent for me. None of them were loyal to the quest, they were obligated. In fact many of them had plans to leave Frodo before they even reached danger.

Another huge piece missing for me is character depth. Outside of Frodo and Sam, there is very very little character depth or growth to be found. Most of the characters are interchangeable to me based on how they are presented in the narrative. Gimli and Legolas barely say two words between them. Their “friendship” so underdeveloped it literally happens off the pages and we get one line that says “they were now the best of friends.” Lazy writing, that lets me know instantly they are in the story as plot devices only and not fleshed out characters with purpose.
To me, each character felt as if they were in the narrative so that when the party arrived at a new location, the appropriate person was available to give us a history lesson. Why not just have Gandalf and Frodo and Sam go on the quest together since Gandalf has been everywhere? Why throw in characters that have so little to add to the narrative? It was confusing and ultimately extremely disappointing.

My third and final gripe with the narrative is that there was no, zero, zilch, sense of urgency around the quest. In fact plenty of times when they were in “danger” they would stop to take a break, sing a song, and talk about the long history of the place they were in. Gandalf just died, Orcs are chasing us, but let’s stop at this river and sing a song. That’s not me exaggerating, that literally happened. Because of the pacing of this, the danger felt non existent. There were no stakes. They would spend days in one place while this supposed evil was after them. It felt inconsequential and to be Frank boring. There was no adventure. No urgency. No excitement.

So what kept this from being a two star read? Sam and the world building.
Sam as a character was brilliant. His loyalty and charm were contagious. He had all the heart of the entire story laying on his shoulders. He was kind, and naive and wide eyed. His curiosity of the wide world was a treat and a great distraction from the other one dimensional characters he was surrounded by.

The world building and lore of Tolkien’s world is undeniably brilliant. The amount of depth he put into his world and history is impressive and unmatched by nearly any other writer. So much information is presented to us about Middle Earth and the people who inhabit it, that you have no choice but to tip your hat to Tolkien in this regard. Had we gotten this information along side well developed characters, grand themes, and an exciting adventure, well then this book might have been worthy of all the praise it receives.

Unfortunately, anyone, myself included, reading this after seeing the movies, will be unable to do so without comparing them. It is inevitable. And while there were one or two instances where I felt the book did a better job, overall, to me, the movies far exceeded the books in nearly every way. (Please don’t come at me with pitchforks and torches!)

This is a classic, and I feel almost sacrilegious to leave such a scathing review. However, I’m grateful, as a fantasy fan to have this under my belt. Will I read the other two books, yes, because it would be even more sacrilegious of me not to.

The Fellowship of the Ring is a good book. It’s honestly an excellent book. The writing is beautiful, the setting is throughly expanded upon, the characters are well developed and the world building is amazing. It literally paved the way for the fantasy genre in mainstream media.

So why on earth would I rate it 3 stars?

Well that’s complicated. I love fantasy. But I also love a specific type of fantasy. I’m not sure how to exactly describe it but I like a more fast paced, female centric, modernized style, diverse, female written stories. That’s not to say Lord of the Rings does not have those characteristics, because it does in small doses, I just like those characteristics to be a focal point in the stories I read.

For me, the story itself wasn’t easy to connect with. I felt the pacing to be quite slow, which is probably a product of its time, but for me it was a challenge. The repetitive descriptions and singing were not easy to continuously read through. The characters took awhile to connect with as the story doesn’t start to pick up until more than halfway through the story.

I’ve always wanted to read or at least try reading the Fellowship of the Ring, and I’m just happy I gave it a shot and got to experience Tolkien’s fantastically creative world. I think as a reader it’s my duty to try and expand my reading ability through different genres and broaden my reading zone in terms of comfortability.

Maybe in the future, as I become a more nuanced reader, I will try and give the Fellowship of the Ring a read-read. Maybe I’ll fall in love with it and continue on in the series. You never know. This is just a personal review of a book I greatly respect but didn’t identify with.

I’m not going to spend much time on a review because Tolkien is the freaking father of fantasy. Even if I don’t find my very first read-through to be a perfect experience, he’s still the GOAT. All my favorite authors have been directly inspired by his work. So my slightly less enthusiastic review in an ocean of opinions won’t change anything. I’ll just give some rapid bullet points.


What I liked:

• Gandalf. I always viewed him as a less cool Dumbledore. I still like D better, but G really gained my respect in this first book. He’s quite a lovely and wise mentor, and a decent wizard too.

• The scenes under the mountain are peak suspense. Yes I did write this just for the pun.

• The tone & setting. It’s a good tonal balance between whimsical and dire, with a lush world unfolding around every bend in the road. I always feel like I’m in Middle Earth when I open these pages.

• Most of the nine walkers were great. They all had their distinct personalities and purposes. One exception was …wait for it…

What I didn’t like:

• Frodo. That might be harsh. He’s certainly not terrible, but he lacks much of a personality. He just kind of existed, often mumbling about the burden and then in the next breath singing songs

• Too much singing

• The lack of female characters. Galadriel is basically the only one who even speaks in this book. Arwen was present, but I don’t recall her saying anything. It’s a constant nagging irritation.

• Pacing. This is actually one that if I were to factor it into my rating, it would drop it to 3 stars. The ebbs and flows of this book are awkward. The climactic action happens too soon. Too much time is spent on doing nothing. But I understand that The Lord of the Rings is not a true trilogy; it’s one book and this is just the first volume. Therefore, I can’t necessarily penalize pacing until I see the full scope of the story. So far, though, it’s pretty slow…


There you have it. I’ve finally started LOTR. I feel like I’ve got a long journey still ahead…

The Lord of the Rings is one of my favorite movies, so when the new TV show was released I decided to give a chance to the books. While, it was good and I can understand why people love it, it wasn't what I was expecting.

Plot

Young Frodo Baggins is given a monumental duty in a peaceful Shire town when his elderly cousin Bilbo entrusts him with looking after the Ring. To destroy the Ring and stop the Dark Lord from carrying out his terrible plan, Frodo must leave his home and embark on a perilous journey across Middle-earth to the Cracks of Doom.

The plot was simple. However, I really hated the pace of the book. The book was super slow and for the most, this book was basically the hobbits walking for different places. Also, the author pauses the story in order to explain the history of Middle-earth and even with songs, which makes the pace even more slower than it is. I hope the next book is better in this particularly aspect.

Characters

Frodo

Frodo was trusted with the ring. He was a good character. He doesn't have any special ability or powers, but he really wants to help bring peace to Middle-earth by destroying the ring.

Sam

Honestly, I think Sam was one of the best character of this book. I really loved him and his loyalty and friendship with Frodo. Probably, the best part of this book was definitely the friendship between him and Frodo.

Gandalf

Gandalf is a very wise and intelligent wizard. He accompanies Frodo in his journey and helps him when he needs.

Merry and Pippin

For me, these two ere definitely the comic relief characters. They were so funny, I really loved them, especially Pippin. I love their dynamic and the dynamic Pippin has with Gandalf.

Aragorn

Aragorn is a man that help Frodo in his quest. He seems good, but I don't think he was very developed in this book. I hope I can see more of him.

Boromir, Legolas and Gimli

These three also belong to the Fellowship of the Ring. I don't think I have an opinion about them. They didn't have much time in this book, but I'm certain I'll see more of them in The Two Towers.

Writing

Again, Tolkien's writing is good, but it's not for everyone and I can see why so people don't like it. Sometimes it can drag a bit, especially the dialogues.

World-Building

The world-building is really good. I really like the Middle-earth and I think it's where Tolkien really shines.

Audiobook

The audiobook was good and kept me interesting in the story. I really like how the author narrated the story.

Final Thoughts

This trilogy is a very important piece of literature. Most of our fantasy novels are inspired by Tolkien's. And the novel itself wasn't bad, but some parts dragged a bit, especially the middle of the book, which I found particularly boring.

The book was pretty lengthy, and a lot of the excess information could be cut, like the random legends, songs, and stories that have no relation to the plot. I did like the plot as we neared the end, but it was only through the audiobook that I could make it through.

The ending was good, but I don’t think it made up for the 300+ pages before it (especially the torture of reading through Tom Bombadil). I’ve heard that Lord of the Rings books only improve as we go on, so I’ll definitely try and finish the series.

I think it's obvious that this book and series need no introduction. Many fantasy readers, like myself, have started their reading journeys with this particular story.
