“All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us.”

Maybe partly because of my familiarity with this story, I couldn't really enjoy reading it for the first time. Fellowship has always been my least favourite entry from the series, so naturally, it was a bit of a slog to get through. But that's not to say that I don't have other problems with this book.

“The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.”

Firstly and most importantly, it was boring. The Lord of The Rings is a quest fantasy, so usually, the beginnings of such books are slow and repetitive. Yet despite this, some authors manage to somehow keep the reader on the edge of their seat. Sadly, Tolkien is not that kind of author. A lot of the book chapters were needlessly long, filled with songs and poems that took me completely out of the story.

“Even the smallest person can change the course of the future”

Another thing that bothers me is how unnecessarily complicated everything is. Almost in every chapter, you get a history lesson filled with dozens of the same-sounding but different names of people or places. I found it impossible to keep track of all this information that's dumped quite gracelessly onto my head. And that's coming from a person who is somewhat familiar with Tolkien's lore, world and history. Imagine someone completely new to his creations read it.

“One Ring to rule them all,
One Ring to find them,
One Ring to bring them all
and in the darkness bind them.”

My last problem, I think, is quite controversial. I do not care for any of the characters. Maybe Aragorn and Eowyn are the exceptions, but I'm just thinking of how they were portrayed in the movies since I haven't read all the books yet. Frodo, Sam, Gandalf and Co are so one-dimensional and dull to read about that I don't particularly care if anything happens to them. Perhaps, I'm used to modern fantasy exploring the morality of people. In Tolkien's world, everything is black or white, evil and good. There is a clear line drawn between those two, and not one of our heroes can meddle in that grey area that is the in-between. The closest we get is Boromir, but even that is played off as the ring's corruption and not his actual thoughts or wishes.

“Deserves it! I daresay he does. Many that live deserve death. And some that die deserve life. Can you give it to them? Then do not be too eager to deal out death in judgement. For even the very wise cannot see all ends.”

Nonetheless, Tolkien has created something so vast and loved that the title of The Lord of The Rings is known almost everywhere. Despite all the aforementioned things, this book remains a monument in all literature. I pray that I'll get to share the many things I love about this series and world in the next two books.

# ⛰ What It's About

Who doesn’t know the classic fantasy adventure of Frodo and his companions in the journey to destroy the one ring? In any case, this epic adventure full of rich culture, magic, and friendship is a tale told so cleverly with high levels of vocabulary, creating an immersive experience. The first book in the series explains the origins of Frodo & Bilbo Baggins, how they came to obtain the ring, and the decision for Frodo to leave the Shire on a quest to prevent the enemy from reuniting with it.

# 🔍 How I Discovered It

My dad used to read the trilogy every few years as it was his favourite series due to its complex and academic writing and vocabulary. The movies came out near when I was born and dad would watch them with us as kids critiquing the inaccuracies throughout. Finally, as an adult in love with fantasy and old English, I decided to try my hand at reading the books and then re-watching the movies to critique them myself. So far I’m enjoying the process. I just watched the first movie again for the first time in many years after I finished this book. I’m impressed how many things were quite accurate, although there were definitely things missing that would have given the story more depth, I am impressed how well the director did in keeping the characters and overall adventure true to literature.

# 🧠 Thoughts

Loved it. It really filled in so many blanks I had in the movie on concepts that were a bit confusing or lacked depth. I really loved that Tolkien wrote all the languages in full for the book - as a philologist it makes sense.

## What I Liked About It

I admired all the poetry and the music that was incorporated into the book. It had so much more culture and realism of races, times, and history than any other book I’ve ever experienced. I loved the complex vocabulary used as it improves my own language structure and vocabulary. I also feel that complex language gives you more specific descriptions of situations as you have the knowledge to portray a scene with vocabulary

## What I Didn't Like About It

While I love how culture-rich the story was, I found the endless talks about the history of a family line with many long names and titles to be difficult to get through, as well as confusing. While I believe it did add to the story, I also feel that sometimes it took away from the story due to the tangents from the main storyline. Although I found this difficult, I appreciate the effort, time, and thought that was used to create such depth of story history.

# 🥰 Who Would Like It?

The Fellowship of the Ring picks up where the Hobbit left off: Bilbo Baggins still bears the ring (taken from Gollum) that has the power to make him invisible. According to legend, the Lord of the Rings is the Dark Lord Sauron. He has been missing the One Ring for a very long time, and he desires to reclaim it so he can enslave all of Middle-earth. As suspected by the wizard Gandalf, this is the exact ring that Bilbo possesses.

At the beginning of this book, Bilbo gives the One Ring to his heir and cousin Frodo at his 111th birthday party. Gandalf tells Frodo that the Ring must be taken out of the Shire since Sauron's power is rising. Frodo leaves the Shire with the Ring at the age of 50. After a series of toils with the Black Riders who work for the Enemy, Frodo reaches Rivendell with a few of his companions. It is there that Elrond, master of Rivendell, initiates a council to decide what to do with the ring. During the Council of Elrond, Frodo agrees to carry the Ring to the only place it can be destroyed: Mount Doom, in the very center of Sauron's realm of Mordor.

The Fellowship of the Ring includes Frodo and the eight others who will accompany him on his quest: Sam, Merry, Pippin, Aragorn, Gandalf, Legolas, Gimli, and Boromir. Unfortunately, the group loses Gandalf along the way when fighting a demon. The pivotal point in the book comes when the Fellowship must decide whether to head toward Mordor (east), or toward safety in the city of Minas Tirith (west). Ultimately, Frodo decides to sneak away from his comrades and head east towards Mordor alone. This breaks the Fellowship. However, Sam eventually reunites with Frodo so the two of them set off on the remainder of the quest together. This is how Lord of the Rings #1 ends.

I thought that the plot of this book was a bit confusing, and parts of the quest tended to drag on while I was reading it. Perhaps this is just because I am new to fantasy, but I definitely enjoyed the Hobbit more than the Fellowship of the Ring. I am not sure if I will read the rest of the Lord of the Rings series yet. I did find the power of the Ring to be an interesting concept though. It seems like whoever has the Ring doesn't want to let go of it, yet this also comes with an overwhelming sense of responsibility. Furthermore, there is a strange phenomenon when one places the Ring on his finger. While the invisibility provided by the Ring offers a source of protection, the Ring also alters the mind in troubling ways, bringing one closer to the Enemy.

The Fellowship of the Ring (The Lord of the Rings #1) by J.R.R. Tolkien- Novel- The Fellowship of the Ring is the first of three volumes in The Lord of the Rings, an epic set in the fictional world of Middle-earth. The Lord of the Rings is an entity named Sauron, the Dark Lord, who long ago lost the One Ring that contains much of his power. His overriding desire is to reclaim the Ring and use it to enslave all of Middle-earth. The story of The Lord of the Rings begins with several events that take place in The Hobbit. While wandering lost in a deep cave, Bilbo Baggins, a Hobbit, one of a small, kindly race about half the size of Men stumbles upon a ring and takes it back with him to the Shire, the part of Middle-earth that is the Hobbits’ home. All Bilbo knows of his ring is that wearing it causes him to become invisible. He is unaware that it is the One Ring, and is therefore oblivious to its significance and to the fact that Sauron has been searching for it. The Fellowship of the Ring opens with a party for Bilbo’s 111th birthday. Bilbo gives his ring to his heir, his cousin Frodo Baggins. When the time comes to part with the ring, however, Bilbo becomes strangely reluctant to do so. He gives up the ring only at the determined urging of his friend, Gandalf the Grey, a great Wizard. Gandalf suspects that the ring is indeed the One Ring of legend. After confirming his suspicions, he tells Frodo that the Ring must be taken away from the Shire, as Sauron’s power is growing once again. Frodo sets out from the Shire with three of his Hobbit friends—Sam, Merry, and Pippin. Along the way, they are pursued by the nine Ringwraiths, servants of Sauron who take the form of terrifying Black Riders. The hobbits spend a night in the company of wandering Elves, who promise to send word ahead to friends who will protect the hobbits. Barely out of the Shire, the hobbits get lost in the Old Forest, where they have to be rescued from a malevolent willow tree, which swallows up Merry and Pippin, and then from an evil tomb ghost. The hobbits’ rescuer is Tom Bombadil, a strange, jovial entity with great powers who is the oldest creature in Middle-earth. The hobbits make it to the town of Bree, where they meet Aragorn, a Ranger who roams the wilderness and who is the heir of the Kings of the ancient Men of Westernesse. Those who do not know Aragorn’s true name call him Strider. Frodo tries to keep a low profile at the inn in Bree, but he ends up causing a scene when while taking part in a rollicking rendition of a song he falls, accidentally slips the Ring onto his finger, and vanishes. That night, Aragorn advises the hobbits not to sleep in their rooms at the inn. In doing so, he saves their lives—for the first of many times. A letter Gandalf left at the inn months before advises the group to head for Rivendell, a realm of the Elves. Aragorn sets out with the hobbits the next day, and with his help they avoid the Black Riders for some time. However, at the top of the hill Weathertop, the Company is forced to defend itself against the attacking Riders. Frodo is wounded during the skirmish. Frodo’s wound, made by a weapon of a servant of Sauron, plagues the hobbit as the Company makes its way eastward. Aragorn is greatly concerned about the power the wound might exert over Frodo. Near Rivendell they meet the Elf-lord Glorfindel, who has been out looking for them. At the last ford before Rivendell, Frodo, riding Glorfindel’s horse, outruns the ambushing Black Riders, who are swept away in a flood created by Elrond, the master of Rivendell. El nd heals Frodo and then holds a meeting to discuss what to do about the Ring. During this Council, Frodo learns the full history of the Ring. Frodo accepts the burden of taking the Ring to the only place it can be destroyed—the place where it was forged. It promises to be a long, nearly impossible journey, as the Ring was forged in the Cracks of Doom, part of the fiery mountain Orodruin in the very heart of Sauron’s realm of Mordor. At the end of the meeting, the Council creates a group to help Frodo in his quest. In addition to Frodo, the Fellowship of the Ring includes Sam, Merry, Pippin, Aragorn, Gandalf, an Elf named Legolas, a Dwarf named Gimli, and a Man from the south named Boromir. The Fellowship heads south and attempts to pass over the Misty Mountains via the pass of Caradhras. Their way is blocked by snow and rock slides, and they are forced to divert their path through the Mines of Moria—the ancient, underground realm of the Dwarves. During the journey through Moria, Gandalf falls into the chasm of Khazad-dûm while protecting the Company from a Balrog, a terrible demon. The rest of the party continues on to Lórien, the forest of the Galadrim Elves, where the Lady Galadriel tests their hearts and gives them gifts to help them on the quest. Frodo, spellbound by Galadriel’s power and wisdom, offers her the Ring. She refuses, however, saying that, despite her intentions, the Ring would corrupt her; ultimately, she would only replace Sauron. Leaving Lórien, the Fellowship travels by boat down the Great River, Anduin. At night, they spot Gollum—a deformed creature that had once owned the Ring but then lost it to Bilbo Baggins in The Hobbit—following them. When they reach the Falls of Rauros, the Fellowship must decide whether to head toward Mordor on the east or toward the safety of the city of Minas Tirith to the west. Boromir, overcome by the Ring’s power and desiring the Ring for himself, confronts Frodo. Frodo fends off Boromir and decides that he must go on to Mordor rather than to the safety of Minas Tirith. However, Frodo cannot bear the thought of imperiling his friends on the dangerous journey or allowing the Ring to corrupt them, so he attempts to leave secretly and continue the quest alone. Frodo does not, however, manage to elude Sam, so the two of them set out together for Mordor. I am eager to read the second part of this novel.

I think it was kind of a dull read. I had a pretty tough time paying attention to what I was reading for the first half. I also had a bit of a tough time comprehending and following along in that first half. During the Tom Bombadill section I particularly was confused and struggled with it. I felt like some weird stuff was going on and that Tom was secretly inhibiting them or something but nothing came of it, at least not yet I supposed. There were a couple other times where I was just not on the same wavelength as the book where I expected it to take a turn into something and it didn’t at all. I think I just struggled with how different the writing and story telling is, especially in that first half.

In the second half I came to enjoy the writing style more. I started listening to the audiobook while reading which at least helped me move through the story faster. I think the characters’ voices and hearing how some of these crazy words are pronounced helped immerse me and kept me more engaged as well. All in all, I started to find the writing style almost relaxing and calm with the slower pace and flowery language. I still had some issues at times in the second half but I’m finding it charming and I’m excited to keep reading.

It didn’t seem like we got a ton of characters moments for them all but the ones we did get were really defining and efficiently gave us information about who they are. Merry and Pipping seemed less fleshed out for me. I think I had a good grasp on everyone else’s character, but I only really knew them as a pair and didn’t have any defining traits to separate them. I particularly like the Gimli and Legolas dynamic and how their friendship grew. I also really liked Gandalf and his sacrifice was one of my favorite scenes in the book. J.R.R. Tolkien's classic tale is regarded as a foundational piece for modern fantasy writing, and whilst it is easy to see why the book is so highly regarded, it is not without some distinct flaws. Don't fret Lord of the Rings fans, I do accede that The Fellowship of the Ring is a great and gripping tale... about 70 percent of the time. The other 30 percent was a trial of endurance; I will admit I am not the hugest fan of poetry in general, but have never taken issue with it when included in an authors writing style. However, the poetry in The Fellowship of the Rings is often imposing and feels unnatural. Perhaps my negative experience was due to listening to the Audiobook, but I found that Andy Serkis did an exceptional job of Narrating the tale otherwise.

The second issue I take with this book is that the story arc is absent, there is certainly a beginning to this tale, but, the final pages left me unsatisfied as there was no ending in sight. However, I will be reading the second book in the series because most of the time the world building and storytelling in this novel was incredible. It was gripping to follow our heroes on the start of their journey and Tolkien's renown for constructing an immersive and epic fantasy world is certainly deserved. Potential readers should be prepared to read all 3 novels in the series when they begin this book.

So I finally decided to read the Lord of the Rings trilogy. I've long since seen the movies and I love all of them very much. But, I've always been intimidated by the books. I've heard mixed things about them -- that people either love them or that the books are really long and dry. But, I finally decided to take the leap and see for myself.

This book took me for-freakin-ever to finish -- about a month from start to finish. That's terrible for me and the primary reason is that it kept putting me to sleep! I couldn't read for more than an hour or so before I had to put the book down and take a nap. So, I resolved to only reading it before bed. Even then, I put it off for days because of dreading reading it. I know, this is like one of the most loved books ever, but I didn't like it that much, it was way too dry and drawn out. So why three stars, instead of two? I'll explain below.

First off, I was really shocked with how long things took in this book as opposed to in the movie. For example, in the movie between the party and Frodo setting off on his journey, it appeared to be just a few days. Well, in the book the time between the party and the beginning of the journey is 32 years! That's right, just a bit of a difference in time-frame there. In addition, they were in Rivendell for months before setting off again, and there were other things too. This marked the biggest differences between the book and the movie. But, I suppose it's more realistic given the way they're traveling and such.

Some other differences between the book and the movie:
1) Merry and Pippin are not as mischievous and playful in the book. They act more like adults than teenagers. I kind of missed this because I enjoyed that about them in the movies.
2) There is a whole journey before they even get to the Prancing Pony -- about 150 pages worth of journey. Including Tom Bombadil, who wasn't even in the movie. It was pretty boring and I could see why it was left out of the movie though.
3) Gandalf never told them to go to the Prancing Pony, they just assumed they might meet him there.
4) The story of how Gollum first obtained The Ring was told by Gandalf in the very beginning of this book, not in the 3rd book.
5) They run into the Trolls that are still stone (from The Hobbit) -- that was cool.
6) The romance between Aragorn and Arwan is non-existent in this book. Although he stands by her at one party, that is all that happens between them. The necklace she gives him in the movie isn't even given to him by her in the book. It's given to him by the Lady of the Wood on behalf of Arwen.
7) The people in the fellowship do not volunteer to help Frodo in the meeting, they are chosen some time after the meeting and not really given a choice either way.
8) The breaking of the fellowship was being discussed before Frodo even takes off. They are all apparently deciding that they've had enough of helping Frodo and want to do other things. I thought this was very weird and pretty selfish of them.
9) Boromir is really annoying and I don't like him at all in the book. I get he's struggling with falling under The Ring's spell, but in the book he's just really negative and an asshole all the time.

The other primary difference is that the book is extremely drawn out. As I've said earlier, everything takes longer than in the movie. But, this is not the only thing. Conversations and walks seem to take forever. It just doesn't seem like too much editing happened. There was just too many unnecessary words that caused the book to be overly dry. However, despite all the words, I thought the book wasn't nearly descriptive enough when it comes to the surroundings and things around them. I'm not really sure if I would have enjoyed this book more or less, had I read it before the movie. I think I may have enjoyed it a little less because I used visuals from the movie to fill in places that were lacking descriptions in the book. However, I might have enjoyed the book more had not known -- generally -- what was going to happen. It's hard to say.

Overall though, the reason I gave this three stars, instead of my usual two stars if I don't like a book, is because of the world J.R.R. Tolkien built. The world is so full and huge -- with the Elvin language, maps, races, history, places, etc. I cannot in good conscious belittle that. I'm sure the world building took an extreme amount of time and effort to accomplish and I'm truly impressed by that. However, I wish the book was written a little better in description, less dialog, and more action. Even the action that was in this book didn't get my blood pumping and me turning the page. So that is a huge downfall of this book. I will continue reading them, but I think I'm going to take a little break from LOTR for now.

3.5/5: Having watched the films first I can’t review this book in isolation. All in all I enjoyed it, I found a real thrill at being back in middle earth, and I enjoyed the extra detail I was given about events and people I love. BUT, the detail often came at the expense of pacing and I found the story dragged in places.

General thoughts aside, the key thing that really struck (dare I say disappointed) me when I was reading this and comparing it to the trilogy was the differences in the Fellowship’s characterisations.

Be it a consequence his social setting or religious views, I really get the impression that Tolkien was a man with a firm belief in predetermination. This idea that everyone is born into a specific role/ position that’s reflected in their nature. Aragon is a man born to be king, therefore he is a good courageous leader with confidence in his abilities. Sam, as the son of Frodo’s gardener, is the epitome of a good and loyal servant to his master etc. For Tolkien being true of heart (a big theme for the book) involves performing the role you were born to play.

That’s the sense I get, and I’m not the biggest fan.

Part of it comes from my self-made, capitalist-girly brain reading classism into the whole thing. But beyond that it just makes everyone so much less interesting.

Aragon isn’t a reluctant hero who worries about his ability to lead, he’s the heir to the throne and he knows it. He’s been waiting in the north for the stars to align or whatever, and now he’s back for the throne. Peter Jackson’s ‘the same blood runs through my veins, the same weakness’ becomes an eager ‘the time is near when [my sword] shall be forged anew.’

Boromir is not a man raised to be king, challenging why he should surrender the fate of this people to the power of previously absent stranger. Instead he’s a self-aware placeholder who’s happy listen to Aragon, the man he has a ‘natural’ fealty to.

In a wider sense, Legolas and Gimli lose a lot of their individual characterisation and become basically reflections of the races they’re there to represent. The hobbits keep a personality, but honestly a cynical part of me whispers that it’s simply because there’s four of them and the reader needs to be able to differentiate.

I could go on, but I think I’ve illustrated my point. I get the impression that for Tolkien there is only ever a singular path; all a person can be is who they were born to be. Conflict in the book stems from the question, do I have the courage to follow the path I’ve been set, or do I give in? It is not, do I take the path appointed for me or do I follow another? Therefore, whilst the storyline and world building are strong, a lot of the characters lack nuance, and they lack the likability that nuance and individuality can breed.

In hindsight, Peter Jackson’s greatest achievement wasn’t groundbreaking cinematography, but taking the members of the Fellowship and turning them into people you’d actually like to spend time with.

*SPOILER ALERT* - If you’ve never read the book or seen the movie for J.R.R. Tolkien’s THE LORD OF THE RINGS: THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING, you might not want to read further since this review includes information related to the conclusion of the book. 💍
.
It was quite the stir a couple months ago when Amazon Prime Video announced that they would be releasing a series with the origin story of J.R.R Tolkien’s #LordOfTheRings universe, complete with a cast of characters that are not all white. I was already part of the way through this new Middle-Earth journey, and honestly, I’m here for it; excited for that premiere in September. In the meantime, though, THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING, upon my May 2022 listening, is getting a 3-star rating. It’s just one of those that was so improved by the film that the original material simply doesn’t hold up as well.
⭐️⭐️⭐️
.
FAVORITE SCENE THAT DOESN’T APPEAR IN THE MOVIE: When Frodo and Sam meet Gildor of Lorien (their first elf; Sam fangirls hardcore) at the beginning and learn a bit more about the world of the book and the current tensions. (Honestly, when you watch the #ExtendedEdition, there really aren’t a lot of scenes that don’t appear in the movie to choose from.)
FAVORITE NEW MOMENT OR DISCOVERY IN THE MOVIE: All the humor, particularly those moments that show hobbits’ distinction from the rest of their world (“Second breakfast,” etc, “Great. Where are we going?”) and “Nobody tosses a dwarf!”
HONORABLE MENTIONS: Expanding Aragorn and Arwen’s interactions and love story; “You - shall not - pass!”
CHARACTER MOST WRONGED BY THE FILM ADAPTATION: Glorfindel, an elf from Rivendell: in the original book, he is the one who rescues Frodo from the Ringwraiths and brings him across the river to safety. He gets completely written out of the movie.
HONORABLE MENTIONS: Tom Bombadil (but honestly having such an all-powerful character introduced so early in the story does create some plot holes - kind of like the eagles), Gildor, Boromir (there’s just so little about him that’s likable, but then when we meet Denethor in the 3rd film it all makes sense).
CHARACTER THAT THE FILM TREATED THE BEST: Arwen. The book barely mentions her, and it certainly doesn’t give her the chance to be the hero who saves the day and rescues Frodo from the chase the way that the movie with its budding 21st century feminist sensitivity does (remember that this movie came out in 2001 - but just for comparison, #Mulan was 1998).
HONORABLE MENTIONS: The Ringwraiths - the ethereal scream and one- to two-word communication is much scarier than the complete sentences that the Nazgûl use in the book (“I come from yonder, have you seen Baggins?” / “Open in the name of Mordor” / “Come back! Come back! To Mordor we will take you!”); Pippin - for the above-mentioned humor reasons; finally, Aragorn, whose internal journey to step into his destiny as Heir of Isildur and King of Gondor comes through much clearer in the Extended Edition - and shows Boromir’s death to be one of its greatest catalysts. 🗡
RANDOM FUN FACT ABOUT THIS BOOK: Sir Christopher Lee, who played Saruman, was the only member of the cast or crew to have met J.R.R. Tolkien personally.
ANOTHER FUN FACT: Every single actor in the movie - besides the director’s son who makes a cameo as a small hobbit - wore a wig.
ANOTHER FUN FACT: Extreme heat with 100-plus degree temperatures on the day of shooting for the final battle meant that many of the actors playing Uruk-Hai had to be carried off the set due to heat exhaustion.
ANOTHER FUN FACT: The moth to which Gandalf whispers was born shortly before filming that day, and died soon after the scene was finished. 🦋
BONUS FUN FACT: THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING was my first-ever PG-13 movie! I was in 4th grade when it came out, and to convince my dad to take me to see it, I had to first read the whole book, then research online why it was rated PG-13, and explain how I knew that all the scary parts weren’t real. It was a lot for a 10-year-old, but so worth it in the end!
.
This series, like #HarryPotter, is much more familiar to me as the film version, and this is one of the most faithfully adapted film series - which might explain why it was so successful. (They also made sure to get the two most prolific series illustrators, Alan Lee and John Howe, on board for art direction.) Of course, there are a few gems in the book that didn’t make the cut, such as Bilbo being an absolute SAVAGE in the gifts and bequests to his relations: “There were several labels of this sort: [...] / For LOBELIA SACKVILLE-BAGGINS, as a PRESENT; on a case of silver spoons. Bilbo believed that she had acquired a good many of his spoons, while he was away on his former journey. Lobelia knew that quite well. When she arrived later in the day, she took the point at once, but she also took the spoons.” 🥄
.
Of course, with the additional humor of manners and the day-to-day goings-on, a THIRD of the book passes before the hobbits arrive in Bree, so it feels really slow. Plus, why did Tolkien feel the need to write and include so many songs? 🎶 (It seems that was kind of “the thing” in British literature for centuries: texts with songs interspersed. Our guy Shakespeare did it too.) And in this book, there is so. much. camping. 🏕 It stressed me out just wanting Frodo and all of them to find a decent bed to sleep in. 🛏
.
Interesting, the difference that simple word choice can make. In the chapter where Gandalf is defending the Fellowship on the bridge from the monster, he never even says his now-trademark phrase “You shall not pass!” Instead, it is only “You cannot pass.” 🧙🏻‍♂️Doesn’t pack quite the same punch, does it? (And don’t forget the true filmmaking mastery of the blend of music, slow-motion, and muted dialogue that immediately follows Gandalf’s fall. It’s even more impressive when one considers that, because of the shooting schedule, the actors filmed those scenes with their mourning reactions before any of them had even met Sir Ian McKellen or seen him dressed up as Gandalf.) 🍂
.
One great detail from the book that didn’t manage to make it into the film: an answer to the question of HOW the One Ring rules the others and “in the darkness bind[s] them.” At the end of “The Mirror of Galadriel” chapter, we discover that because Frodo possesses the One Ring, and Galadriel is wearing her 1 of the 3 elven rings, he can hear her thoughts and see her plans. 🧠 This is how Sauron managed to take down the kingdoms of men, and helps explain why Boromir believes that possessing the ring will allow Gondor to triumph over Mordor. It gets brushed over in the movie, though, because of Galadriel’s ability to speak directly into people’s brains. (WOW this is so nerdy.) 🤓
.
Finally, in the afterword, J.R.R. Tolkien explains exactly why his work is NOT an allegory for World War II, and offers a pretty grim explanation that if it were, “the Ring would have been seized and used against Sauron; he would not have been annihilated but slaved, and Brad-dûr would not have been destroyed but occupied. Saruman, failing to get possession of the ring, would in the confusion and treacheries of the time have found in Mordor the missing links in his own research is into Ring-lore, and before long he would have made a Great Ring of his own with which to challenge the self-styled Ruler of Middle-earth. And that conflict both sides would have held hobbits in hatred in contempt: they would not long have survived even as slaves.” 😔 Luckily for us, though, Tolkien “cordially dislike[s]” allegory, and so we get a much more optimistic story.
.

El Senyor dels Anells ja era conegut arreu del món abans que se'n fessin les pel•lícules ara fa uns anys però gràcies a aquestes el món de J.R.R. Tolkien arribà encara a més públic.

Al primer llibre de El Senyor dels Anells en Frodo Saquet es veurà immers en un gran repte: destruir l'anell únic i acabar així amb la malvestat d'en Sauron. Fou en Bilbo, però, qui recollí primer l'anell durant la seva gran aventura, temps enrere, a El Hòbbit. Aleshores, aquest mitgerol encara no havia descobert el gran secret que amagava aquest anell. Els anys passaren sense que en Bilbo hagués aixecat cap sospita sobre el seu misteriós anell fins que al final, ja vell, el deixà en herència al seu nebot Frodo Saquet.

En Frodo, amb l'ajuda de tres hòbbits més, rep l'encàrrec del mag Gàndalf el Gris de portar-lo d'amagat fins a Rivendell, un indret erigit pels elfs. Allí es crearà la Germandat de l'Anell que dóna sentit al títol d'aquest llibre. A partir d'aquí en Frodo, acompanyat de 8 persones més de totes les races que poblen la Terra Mitjana, es veurà immers en la missió de llençar l'anell al Mont del Fat, el volcà on va ser creat i l'únic lloc on pot ser destruït.

Si comparem aquest llibre amb la primera pel•lícula trobarem alguns canvis, frases en boques d'altres o dites en moments molt diferents però el personatge més rellevant que trobarem al llibre i que no apareix a la pel•lícula és en Tom Bombadil un senyor enigmàtic i alegre que ajudarà als hòbbits poc després que aquests sortissin de les seves llars.

Aquesta obra té un desenllaç obert ja que es tracta d'una trilogia. El protagonista haurà recorregut un llarg camí però encara haurà de passar per moltes més vicissituds que descobrireu en els següents llibres. Aquest és sens dubte un clàssic de la literatura fantàstica i d'aventures per a joves.

Tolkien is one of the things I’ve been most passionate about for the past six months and I was more than excited to start the fellowship of the ring which was a good but slightly *slightly* disappointing start to the Lord of the Rings trilogy.

The problems start in the first half of the book. Set in the shire, we spend around the first 100 pages dicking around in Hobbiton before Frodo even sets out on his journey. And I enjoyed the first 40 pages of this like yeah it was fun dilly dallying in the shire - charming, sure - but FUCK ME, after 100 pages of Sackville Baggins slander I literally could not give a single rats arse. All I can say is thank god I was somewhere where I was doing a lot of waiting for three days because I ploughed through all this shit rigorously and with diligence and without having this explosive start I do not know how long this book would’ve taken me. The next 150 pages dragged almost just as much. It was literally just stupid hobbits fumbling along paths they didn’t know, country they couldn’t cross, dangerous situations they almost died in way too much. Tom Bombadils house was ok? i enjoyed the respite from just relentless misery and weathering the hobbits seemed to be enduring the entire journey so far but there was too much singing for me personally. I debated skipping some of the songs but couldn’t bring myself to do so and looking back I’m glad I didn’t because now I know for a fact they weren’t that good rather than just being able to suspect it and I can validly slate them.

However, the light at the end of the tunnel was soon to appear, STRIDER (!!!). This rascally little scoundrel made reading so much more bearable and as soon as we got to Bree the book became a lot more palatable as it felt like real progress with an aim was being made by the characters. Tolkein really did a good job of establishing fear and general discomfort throughout the book. Typical Tolkien-core use of pathetic fallacy worked wonders on Mount Cadharas, truly I did feel like a downtrodden snowlogged hobbit whilst reading this and wanted them to just turn back at all times and felt relief when they did. Felt like when I go walking with my dad and he finally says we can turn back; success for the little people! Same again in Moria (MORIA!!!!) during the Balrog fight. The subtle boom boom every now and again did wonders for sending chills up and down my spine and bringing sultry lip bite-smile to my face which felt like I was the centre of a fan fiction. ‘She smiled, her hands shaking gripping the fellowship of the ring with full force, biting her lip as the dark shadow of legend appeared and struck fear in her heart’

Writing style was on the whole enjoyable, more complex than the Hobbit but definitely more than manageable for a smooth brain like myself. LOTS of pathetic fallacy and descriptions of environments which was gr8 at first and I enjoyed throughout in small doses but did get to be quite overwhelming at some points like yes Tolkien for the sixth time I’m already assuming that the cliffs which are literally just cliffs are steep, jagged, and grey in colour you don’t need to tell me again.

I liked the characters but I think it’s entirely possible I only enjoyed them because of the film, at times there was literally no non-essential dialogue which would’ve definitely lubed up the reading process by a lot. Borimir gets an honourable mention, as far as characters go as he actually offered up a lot of dialogue and he had some pretty solid character development, I enjoyed seeing him slowly be tempted by and descend into madness on account of the ring and I enjoyed seeing how his betrayal of frodo pained him as it did actually offer some evidence that the members of the fellowship are actually friends.
Despite all the previous hobbit slander I will also say that the friendship between the hobbits is a great aspect of the book, I enjoyed seeing merry and pippin relentlessly assert that they would go where their friends would go, I kinda liked Sam and Frodo’s dynamic, Sam certainly was loyal which is admirable, however he’s more an employee of Frodo which makes the dynamic feel a lot different to how it did in the films and I definitely prefer the films. Calling Frodo ‘master’ sorry Sam that doesn’t work for me. However I felt like by the end of the book their relationship had become more friendly and I’m excited to explore it in Two Towers.

Overall I was let down slightly by this book but enjoyed it nonetheless, it’s definitely overrated but was still certainly worth a read.

Okay, so I preferred The Fellowship of the Ring to The Hobbit . I previously read this book over a decade ago, when I was somewhat enamoured by Peter Jackson's film adaptations and watched them regularly. I found this impacted my enjoyment of the book significantly, and back then I really struggled reading through the trilogy. I think I was averaging about a page a day. In my memory, the reasoning I had for this was that I found whenever the book was in alignment with the film, I had very little interest, but I found any deviation (Tom Bombadil being the stand-out in my memory) really intriguing and enjoyable to experience.

I was therefore very surprised whilst reading The Fellowship of the Ring now just how often this book does deviate from the film. I have no idea why I struggled all those years ago, but it can't have been for that reason. Now, whilst I do still adore the films, I don't watch them quite so regularly because I'm old and I don't have the time. I found this reading of the book interesting to note where certain elements of the book had been adapted to the film, how certain moments were combined or shifted, and just how much content there is in this book that is absent from the film. For the most part, I quite enjoyed reading this book.

For the most part. After reading The Fellowship of the Ring, and previously The Hobbit , and a couple of years before that Lord Foul's Bane , I've come to the realisation that I'm not a huge fan of fantasy books that feature a lot of travelling. I'm sorry, I just don't found reading a bunch of characters moving from one oddly named place to another oddly named place particularly interesting. I need Joe Abercrombie's excellent character work from The Blade Itself (and particularly the sequels) to sustain my interest in any travelling shenanigans. Whilst I can appreciate that Tolkien has created a highly detailed world here, I struggle mentally plotting the journey due to the way the travelling is described (even with the aid of the maps).

Still, when The Fellowship of the Ring works, it really works some magic. The highlight chapter for me that really emphasises the elements of Tolkien's writing that I most enjoy is easily The Bridge of Khazad-dûm - so expertly crafted and so thrilling. There is plenty here that I liked. I don't think all of the members of the Fellowship were given their opportunity to shine (and I'll admit I struggle separating the book depictions of the characters from the movie depictions/cast in my head) but I think enough is done that each is distinct. This is more of an issue with the four hobbits than the rest of the Fellowship.

Anyway, I enjoyed this book more than I was expecting to, and I'm looking forward to tackling the sequel. I do have a couple of outstanding minor gripes (being directed via certain footnotes to trawl through a huge appendix in a whole other book, and all the introductory Note on the Text, Note on the Revised Text stuff I found rather tedious), but, I enjoyed more of this book than I tolerated.

First printed in 1954. This is the 50th anniversary edition. The publishers of Lord of the Rings split it into three volumes, much against the wishes of the author J.R.R. Tolkien. The first volume eventually got released as ‘The Fellowship of the Ring’, which, in my Kindle edition, spans 450 pages. The one I own physically is a combined edition.
An epic high fantasy novel that follows the lives of characters originally introduced in its predecessor ‘The Hobbit’, LOTR has often been the source of inspiration for fantasy authors over the past five decades, notably those of ‘Eragon’ and ‘The Wheel of Time’.
In volume one, Frodo Baggins—a hobbit—takes over the magical ring from his uncle Bilbo Baggins and embarks on a quest with his fellowship that includes three hobbits, two men, an elf, an old wizard and a dwarf. What follows is an adventure that transcends realms within the fictional continent of Middle-earth.
I’ll start with the positives:
The biggest achievement, here, is the world building. There's a feeling that even outside the pages of the book there is a world yet to be explored within the legendarium. Tolkien’s writing makes you believe in the bigger world, like a universe slowly unfolding. I was also surprised by the choice of words. The language in ‘Fellowship’ is simple and digestible without compromising on its beauty. The poems interspersed throughout the book do not always contribute to the plot, but they are perfectly rhymed and make you feel they belong to discovered tomes. The history and culture in the book are believable.
Reading familiar quotes from the book brought a smile to my face. Notable mentions are: “All that is gold does not glitter” and “Not all those who wander are lost.” I have been living these quotes. The placements in the story couldn’t have been more apt.
Frodo is the only well-developed character in Volume 1. Sam Gamgee is adorable as his loyal friend.
And yet… there are reasons why I can’t call ‘The Fellowship of the Ring’ a favourite book of mine. My views on it are mixed. At 450 pages, it could have offered more.
The writing is lengthy but not necessarily vivid or evocative. I found it hard to distinguish the hobbits from each other and ended up Googling the movie actors playing Pippin, Merry, and Sam to help build up mental images of their faces. Else, they were interchangeable. Voices and dialogues are not distinct. The chubby one. The cousin. Even Gimli, the dwarf, was vaguely mentioned. Removing him from Volume 1 wouldn’t have altered the course of the story; he was more of a token dwarf character. When the first human, Aragon, was introduced, he was referred to as ‘the tall one’, from a hobbit’s perspective, but as another human, Boromir, got introduced, the latter didn’t have much of a role until the end of Volume 1.
The description of a monster ‘Balrog' was so vague, and when I Googled how it looked like in the movie and fanarts, I was left wanting for more. With 450 pages of descriptions, in my opinion, the author could have fleshed out the details where they really mattered because you see tons of filler descriptions and poems throughout the book.
Many fantasy readers call this book poetic, but I choose to disagree.
As a lover of lyrical prose, I didn't find ‘Fellowship’ lyrical or poetic. Even contemporary writers have managed to write decent lyrical prose.
I read more on Kindle instead of the collector’s edition that I own thanks to the info dumping in the book. The advantage of reading on Kindle is that I get to use the X-Ray and Wikipedia add-on features—just at the touch of a keyword—and for a book like LOTR, this is the fastest way to gain additional knowledge instead of flipping to the appendices toward the end of the book.
While the plot and character development are above average, the camaraderie between the characters, nostalgia, and great worldbuilding did the heavy lifting for ‘Fellowship of the Ring’.
I’d recommend it to those readers looking for a case-study on world-building or those new to fantasy.

The focus is on characters who aren't relatable and it's just another boring battle of good versus evil, a tired trope that authors use because they don't have the capacity to create real people.

I finished "The Fellowship of the Ring" ('Fellowship' after this) yesterday afternoon, and I've been trying to figure out how to express my feelings towards it ever since. I went in wanting to love this book, I love the movies and The Lord of the Rings is my dad's favorite series, but I just didn't. On balance I thought that it was somewhere between average and slightly above average. I say 'on balance' because one of the issues I see in this book is that it is not uniform in quality.

The first half of 'Fellowship' is undeniably well written. I found it interesting and relatively engaging. The problems, in my mind, stem from it lacking variety and moving slower than a stationary bike being pedaled uphill. The lack of variety stems from the initial composition of our adventuring party: Frodo, Sam, Merry and Pippin. While they become unique characters with important roles later in the series, during the first book Frodo's companions feel indistinct. Sam, Merry and Pippin play off of Frodo in very similar ways, causing the book to feel very samey until Aragorn is introduced. The other problem I have with the first half of 'Fellowship' is that it takes a long time to get where it's going. As I just mentioned, the book picks up a lot when we are introduced to Aragorn and he is added to the party, but that is almost 150 pages into the book. Overall, I would probably rate the first half somewhere in the 2/5 to 2.5/5 range.

The second half of 'Fellowship' sharply contrasts with the first in terms of pacing. After the hobbits arrive at Rivendell, it is almost non-stop action. They move from Rivendell to the Mines of Moria to Lothlorien and it feels like there is hardly a dull moment, in spite of the fact that a very similar amount of walking takes place. While a lot of credit can be given to the uptick in the amount of action, I think that the addition of the other five members of the Company go a long way in making the book more interesting. In the second half of 'Fellowship,' the party actually has interesting personalities and character interactions. Boromir wants the Ring from Frodo, but he feels duty bound not to take it by force. Gimli and Legolas gradually get over their dislike for each other. Gandalf gets to make fun of the hobbits. Aragorn has to grow into his role as a leader. There is just a lot more going on with the characters, and that makes the journey much more enjoyable. I would give the second half of 'Fellowship' somewhere between a 4/5 and a 4.5/5.

Overall, I think that the book starts slow and ends strong. I'm looking forward to reading "The Two Towers" to see whether it keeps the momentum it builds through the end.

Lord of the Rings, by my estimation, really only has two things going for it.

1) Timing. It was the first high fantasy series to become popular and introduced a lot of tropes and themes to the genre that would be copied for decades afterwards. Nobody can deny the massive influence it’s had. I would argue we didn’t really start to meaningfully pull away from Tolkien’s influence on fantasy until the early 2000s. Even the grimdark of the 90s was consciously “anti-Tolkien,” and thus can’t be said to be free from his influence since it's a direct reaction against him.

2) World-Building. I personally don’t think Tolkien’s Middle-Earth is the most interesting fantasy world ever devised, but it’s inarguably constructed with more depth than any other. At least, I’m not aware of any other fantasy authors that have created fake languages for their fantasy worlds, or written anything on the level of The Silmarillion for backstory.

Unfortunately world-building is much less important to most readers than character and plot, and Tolkien’s plot is simplistic to a fault and his characters lack depth, at least by the standards set by modern fantasy novels.

The things I come to fantasy for, as a 31 year old man who got into the genre around 2010, are completely lacking here.

The environment is not actually fantastical and unique. It’s English countryside. Lots of forests and prairies. And despite not being very notable, he’ll spend a LOT of time describing it for you.

There are no intricate politics, in fact no real politics whatsoever. There’s Sauron, who is bad, and everyone else, who is good. There’s no discussion about what Sauron wants or what a land ruled by him would actually be like. Talk to me about Sauron’s policy positions. Maybe he’s not so bad?

There are no psychologically interesting characters/races/cultures. Elves, being long-lived, tend towards procrastination. That’s about all we get as far as psychological depth. Characters are paper thin and all the dialogue is stiff as a board. This is very jarring considering I'm reading through the Thomas Covenant series at the same time, which came out twenty years later but is still "old fantasy" by my standards but is absolutely drowning in a delicious ocean of psychological and moral depth.

I’ve already addressed the lack of a compelling plot. One of my favorite modern fantasy things is laying out the rules of how magic works and then using it in clever ways to solve problems that feel “fair” to the reader. Magic has no rules here, it just does stuff, which makes it not interesting at all from a plot perspective. This isn’t inherently bad, I like a sense of wonder sometimes too, which you lose when you over-explain magic, but there’s just nothing else here to latch onto. One of the reasons I like magical realism is the combination of massive character depth akin to literary fiction with unexplained magic that adds a sense of wonder and heightens the emotional themes of the story but doesn’t solve problems or involve itself in the plot in any real way. This is some weird middle ground where magic isn’t explained, doesn’t have defined rules, but still solves plot issues sometimes.

And finally, I’d like to present the most damning evidence against this book: Tom motherfucking Bombadil. Fuck this motherfucker. Why does he exist? Why does he sing so much? How can I make him shut up?

This is hard to rate because I respect Tolkien's writing but a personal preference of character development before world-building made this a little difficult to get through. This is my first time listening to an Audiobook (HP doesn't count because I read the physical books first so zoning out wasn't a big deal) and I enjoyed the experience. However, I knew immediately that I would need to re-read these in physical form.
Pros:
~THE WRITING!! My goodness, the lyrical way Tolkien writes made me think I was listening to music (and I'm not talking about just the songs interspersed in the story). There were multiple times where I had to pause and just sit in the amazing way a sentence or paragraph was written. I completely understand why Tolkien is a favorite of many. I also thought it was clever of Tolkien to sneak in some Scripture now and then, even though this is not a "Christian" book.
~Gandalf and Tom Bombadil were such awesome characters. Despite Tom only being on a few pages, he stole the story for me. I loved his cheeriness and that it's never fully explained just how powerful he is. Gandalf is also mysterious but is warm and interesting. Galadriel was another character that stood out to me and I wanted more of her.
~Rivendell. I wish I could live there! Between the descriptions of the elves, their melodious way of speaking, and the music in the audiobook, I was entranced.

Cons:
~Chapter 16 nearly made me give up. My husband is a huge Tolkien fan (like multiple copies of the same book kind of fan) and warned me about chapter 16 being incredibly dense. He was not lying! I barely remember anything from that chapter because there was so much information. This is where I would have rather read than listened so I could really absorb everything that was being explained.
~World-building vs character driven story. This again is a personal preference for me. I have only recently gotten into the fantasy/sci-fi genre so I'm used to more character driven plots. The need for the world-building, I understand. The issue I had, however, was I didn't feel connected to or invested in any of the characters. When my husband asked who my favorite character was so far, I couldn't come up with a favorite. Even though I enjoyed a few (as mentioned above), I didn't feel like I absolutely loved any of them. Again, I understand that Tolkien need to establish Middle Earth and its history/background so that everything made sense. I just don't prefer this type of storytelling.
~The songs. OMG, there was a lot of singing in this book. I mostly tuned out or skipped these parts since they mostly didn't seem to be necessary to the story as a whole. These seemed like little trinkets for hardcore fans to enjoy and since I'm new to LOTR, I didn't really appreciate or see the point to them.

All in all, I understand why Tolkien's works have lasted and are still enjoyed to this day. He was an incredibly skilled and creative writer. I am looking forward to finishing the series and seeing where the characters go. After finishing this book, I feel more prepared for the writing style of the next two.

J.R.R Tolkien’s “The Fellowship of the Ring” has a compelling plot and intriguing characters, but unfortunately did not live up to my expectations. The story is about a hobbit named Frodo Baggins who has to go on a journey to stop an evil force from destroying middle earth. Frodo has possession of an all powerful ring, and is destined to prevent evil from getting it. The journey he goes on is full of twists and turns; allowing the reader to become immersed in the story and its unpredictability. Even though I liked some elements of this book, I still had problems with it. The first issue I had with this book was the pacing. Although the story only covers about a year of time, it drags out a lot of unnecessary moments and shortens more important ones. The book felt extremely slow sometimes due to this. For example, there was a very long chapter called “The Council of Elrond” in which the company and many others gathered in Rivendell to discuss how to proceed next in their mission. The problem was that the chapter was far too long for what was going on, and dragged out a discussion that could have been covered in only 5 or 6 pages instead of 14. There were a lot of chapters like these that could have been a lot shorter to focus on more vital and engaging parts of the story. Another issue I had with this book was that there is way too much lore and detail for a reader to be expected to know. The book has extensive maps, history, legends and cities that a reader is supposed to fully understand after learning about it. The problem with this is that it pulled me away from what was actually happening in the story, and it was too complicated to remember the fine details when you might need to anyways. Reading about this lore, in my opinion, was also extremely boring as it felt repetitive and irrelevant. That said, a few of the elements of this book I really did love. The characters are unique and each one was created with scrupulous amounts of detail. Each one had specific histories, problems, backstories, and traits that made them stand out from each other. There was not a time when reading this book that I was disappointed with the way Tolkien designed these characters. I also loved the description Tolkien would give a reader, painting a vivid picture of what was going on. An example of this is, “The water rippled on either side of the white breast beneath its curving neck. Its beak shone like burnished gold, and its eyes glinted like a jet set in yellow stones” (Tolkien 363). These descriptions really brought the story to life. Overall, I had ambivalent feelings about this book. Therefore I will give it three stars for that reason. I would probably recommend this book to older teens who like fantasy novels and anyone who can handle reading slower paced books. The language of the story can be hard to understand and some of the plot is confusing.

¡Buenas tardes, lectores! Al fin he conseguido leer este libro, me ha costado más de 10 años y 3 intentos. Creo que es una historia conocida por prácticamente todos así que me voy a ahorrar haceros una sinopsis y voy a contaros directamente mi opinión.

Mi madre es muy fan de esta trilogía, tanto de los libros como de las películas (que por cierto he conseguido pasar todos estos años sin verlas ni saber cómo se desarrolla la historia) desde que los descubrió de adolescente. Siempre me había dicho que tenía que leerlos porque me iban a encantar. Spoiler... No. Lo comencé y lo abandoné dos veces, así que al fin me decidí a leerlo entero y no posponerlo más.

Lo he conseguido y no sabéis lo que me ha costado. Las mismas sensaciones que cuando lo empecé por primera vez, es una historia tremendamente lenta. ¿La promesa que nos hace el autor? Un viaje. Lo cumple de sobra pero se recrea demasiado en detalles de la ambientación que no aportan nada a la historia y la hacen, para mí, soporífera. La acción es prácticamente nula por lo que he tenido la sensación de que van de un lado a otro sin más. Desayunan, caminan, comen, caminan, cenan, a dormir y así en bucle.

Reconozco que Bilbo me ha caído bien pero no me ha pasado lo mismo con Frodo, es demasiado parado, tengo la sensación de que simplemente se arrastra a regañadientes pero en el fondo no quiere estar ahí. El resto de personajes... Les falta personalidad, supongo que habrá un avance en los siguientes libros pero en este son simplemente planos.

Mi nota es un 2.75/5 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐. Aprecio que esta trilogía dio pie a la fantasía épica, uno de mis géneros favoritos, y que ha sido fuente de inspiración para autores que le encantan (entre ellos Sanderson). Solo por eso leeré los otros dos libros aunque la realidad es que no lo he disfrutado.

Frodo's humble life in The Shire is upended when his eccentric uncle bequeaths him a relic from his adventuring days. Through his friend the wizard Gandalf, Frodo learns that though seemingly innocuous, it is a ring forged in darkness, and its creator is willing to destroy everything to get it back. Reluctantly, Frodo leaves his home accompanied by several friends, and they journey with Gandalf to seek the counsel of the elves of Rivendell and answer the question of what should be done with the ring.

I come away with insane respect and admiration for Tolkien's sheer imagination, but it could have been punctuated with a tad more excitement. It's clear that this series was a catalyst for a subsequent explosion of fantasy adventure fiction.

Similar to the galaxies of Star Wars, Middle-Earth is likely more enjoyable for you if you were exposed to it at a younger age. I respect Tolkien's writing style and humor, and I enjoyed the provocative descriptions of the natural world and banter between characters.

Not enough happens, though. The traveling company moves from one place to another, faces inescapable odds, and at the last minute, someone who Gandalf met in the months prior saves the day, feeds them, and then they set off to face more inescapable odds.

I personally don't find lists of locations or a minute-by-minute chronicle of Middle-Earth's history enjoyable, because it feels like there was no real payoff in these 500+ pages. It feels like I didn't get a complete story. And for my purposes, I didn't-there are two more books. I'll read them because I feel the need to finish what I started, and as a whole I'll probably enjoy the LotR series. But in this standalone story, Tolkien's style doesn't make up for a first half of wandering around nor a dissatisfying ending.

That, and the fact that Andy Serkis' performance of the book was absolutely wonderful and without his narration I'd never even have finished it.

The Fellowship of the Ring started out great. I loved the part of this book that took place within the Shire. But the moment they left, it got boring and some parts dragged on and on for what seemed to be an eternity. Though I appreciated the performance of Serkis' when it came to the songs, the songs themselves started to annoy me the moment they reached Tom Bombadil and that annoyance never faded. There are SO MANY SONGS in this book. If I hadn't been listening to this on audio, I'd probably have skipped over them, alongside many other paragraphs and pages that caused the story to drag.

In the end, I think I wasn't really paying attention to the book for at least 50% of the time I listened to it. I do really want to rewatch the movie(s) now though, so that's what I'm going to do!

I said this when I reviewed The Hobbit and I will say it again: Tolkien’s imagination and his creativity are staggering (considering the time this series was written and published), and I think every fantasy fan is eternally thankful to him for practically inventing the genre. With that being said, I really really really don’t like his writing style. It is episodic, unnecessarily descriptive and unbelievably dull. The interesting parts of the story are compressed into pages of mind-numbing exposition, while the boring parts are described in excruciating detail, down to the veins on the tree leaves.

The narrative focuses quite heavily on linguistics and the history of Middle-earth (understandable, seeing as it is written as a historical record), however, I found this type of world-building to be almost too practical and rooted in reality which, for me, defeated the purpose of reading escapist fantasy.

Something that kept me interested, though, is the characters and the relationships between them. I think this is the one aspect that will carry me through the rest of the trilogy.

I did enjoy this book, but not as much as I had hoped to. It's been sitting on my shelf for near a decade now, but it wasn't until my class in genre studies required me to read it, that I picked it up.

The way Tolkien writes can be a bit difficult for a modern reader. He seems to use an older sentence structure, and that can be a bit dry and clunky. But what inhibited my enjoyment the most was his endless streams of landscape descriptions. Who needs an entire page dedicated to describing a tree? (Much like the book Eragon in that way).

Because of these long winded poetic musings the tension of the plot is lost. Which is a shame because it is so well developed!

Needless to say I can see why this book has inspired an entire genre, and continues to be held at the forefront of High Fantasy; but its not a book I'll pick up again anytime soon.

A Sociedade do Anel é uma boa introdução para o mundo da terra média de Tolkien, tem grande foco na criação da mitologia por trás do Um Anel mas poucos momentos de grande ação, tornando-se uma leitura lenta e com excesso de descrição. Apesar disso, a forma como as histórias dos elfos e das personagens que são contadas pelo livro não deixam de ser interessantes: o conto de Gil-Galad, Beren e Lúthien, Isildur, Gollum, todos falam de personagens importantes para o enredo, mostrando sua significância nesse mundo.

A primeira parte do livro é excessivamente lenta, certos pontos podiam ser removidos que não afetariam tanto na narrativa, como os capítulos em que Tom Bombadill aparece. Assim, o começo do livro é apenas os passeios dos hobbits pelo condado e a lenta fuga deles dos Cavaleiros Negros.

Já a segunda parte torna-se mais interessante com a formação da Comitiva em Valfenda, a jornada que tomam até Moria e os perigos que enfrentam pelo caminho. Mas ainda assim é carregado de muito detalhe das paisagens, dos rios, das montanhas e cavernas que passam. Os momentos de luta são apenas alguns parágrafos, o que deixa a desejar.

No final, gostei mais do lado místico que o livro carrega, das histórias antigas que traz, da ideia de grandiosidade que é contada desses tempos longínquos. A história do momento presente que o livro relata vira apenas a introdução para o que acontece nos próximos volumes.

📌 Primul volum din Stăpânul inelelor îl are ca protagonist pe Frodo, moștenitorul lui Bilbo. Misiunea lui Frodo este să ascundă inelul furat de Bilbo în Hobbitul de Sauron, Seniorul Întunecimii. El pornește la drum cu câțiva prieteni buni care să-l ajute pe parcursul acestei misiunii.

📌Acest volum nu mi-a plăcut la fel ca Hobbitul. Aventura lui Frodo mi s-a părut un pic plictisitoare. Aventura lui Bilbo a fost mult mai interesantă. Din cauza asta și datorită scrisului mic, cartea a mers foarte greu. Mi-a luat o grămada de timp ca să o termin.

📌Frodo, ca personaj mi s-a părut mult mai interesant față de Bilbo. La început Bilbo a renunțat foarte greu la inel, în schimb Frodo nu l-a folosit aproape deloc și ar fi fost foarte bucuros să scape de el. Am simțit că Frodo a avut o voință de fier care l-a ajutat să nu cadă în mrejele inelului.

📌În acest volum ca noutate cu privire la ființe au fost cavaleri negri care erau spirite ale inelului și lebedele negre. Mereu mi-am dorit să văd o lebădă neagră. Finalul volumului s-a terminat într-un mod interesant. M-a făcut imediat curioasă de următorul volum. Sper că va fi mult mai interesant ca această carte.

I have thought a long time about this review. I am a huge fantasy fan and Lord of the Rings has been one of the true classics which I never read before. I started it, twice. Is it possible, I actually don't like this classic fantasy book? The book som many people love?

So, I decided to persist. Through all the mildly interesting takes of journey from the Shire to Rivendell. The more I persisted, the more became this book a definition of a "book which grows on you". Now, after I finished it, I really believe all the long descriptive pages of lands of Middle-earth, songs of Elves and history lessons of made up universe created a true atmosphere and rich setting for me. Now, after all 531 pages, I remember the book as rich, deep, fascinating and different from the typical run of the mill fantasy (although admittedly, I have not read by far as many fantasy books as many of readers of this review might have).

At the beginning I was unsure about it, then I got bored with it and at the end I feel very emotional, excited and enriched by it. So this book was by all means a journey for me ;) let's see what the second book has in store for me.

There are things that I loved about this book and things that I hated. The hobbits are adorable, the blossoming of a friendship between Legolas and Gimli endearing and I am interested in finding out where the story is headed, but the pace of the book is painfully slow. This is a personal opinion, but I don't like to many or extensive visual descriptions. While reading the book, I lost focus very easily and had to reread, sometimes more than once, several passages, because of how easily my mind wandered of.

The author was painting a picture with words and I can acknowledge that, but I did not enjoy the process of reading most descriptions. It was too detailed for me, every small path they crossed, every rock they saw was mentioned and described there with painful detail and I had to put in a lot of effort to visualize those things.

I also did not enjoy the songs that were added. I understand it was with the purpose of immersion, but without actual music they felt bland. Since I read the Portuguese translation, I cannot judge the original lyrics, but in the translation they did not rime and felt awkward for songs, like they would not fit in with a melody.

I'm giving this 3 stars because, despite all this, the book was very well written, engaging at times and the world building is amazing, but I cannot give it more, due to how hard it was for me to finish the book.

این نظر حاوی حجم زیادی مخالفت با جلد یک ارباب حلقه‌ها بوده و ممکن است برای علاقمندان این مجموعه مناسب نباشد! البته قبل از این‌که اخم‌هاتون توی هم بره باید بگم شاید منم که با قصه‌های ماجراجویانه خیلی راحت کنار نمیام. شایدم اشکال از اون‌جایی شروع می‌شه که من تماشای فیلم رو گذاشتم برای بعد از کتاب، و قدِ کتاب شاید به فیلم نمی‌رسه؛ البته من همچنان و هنوز فیلم رو ندیدم و این حرفم در حد حدسه، پس برمی‌گردم روی کتاب.
یاران حلقه رو هم دوست داشتم و هم دوست نداشتم. کتابی نبود که به وجد بیاردَم و درعین‌حال کتابی هم نبود که دلم بخواد نصفه رهاش کنم. یه کم ناامیدم کرد. من از هابیت توقع زیادی نداشتم، ولی توقعم از ارباب حلقه‌ها بیشتر بود. ماجرا خیلی یکنواخت پیش می‌رفت. به عنوان یک رمان ماجراجویانه، ماجراها کم نبودن اما سرسری بودن. انقدر زود شروع و تموم می‌شدن که اصلن فرصت درگیری به منِ مخاطب داده نمی‌شد. اتفاق‌ها متفاوت بودن، ولی بسترِ اتفاق‌ها به‌قدری یکسان بود که آدم رو شگفت‌زده نمی‌کرد. شاید فقط دو بخش از داستان بود که لذت بیشتری بهم داد؛ شورای الروند و سرزمین لوتلورین؛ دو قسمتِ متن که دیتای جالب توجهی به ماجرا اضافه می‌کرد. مابقی فقط جاده بود و اتفاق‌های نه‌چندان غیرمنتظره‌ای که سهل و ساده و زود هم سپری می‌شدن. حتا اتفاقی که شبیه فاجعه توی داستان رخ می‌ده هم سرسری ازش گذشته می‌شه. سه جلد ارباب حلقه‌ها بالای دوهزار صفحه کتابه، و دوهزار صفحه بستر وسیعیه برای بسط دادن موضوع، اما انگار کیفیت فدای کمیت شده. دلیل دوم احتمالن شخصیت‌پردازی قصه‌ست. کتاب از ضعف شخصیت‌پردازی رنج نمی‌بره، چون تقریبن می‌شه گفت اصلن شخصیت‌پردازی‌یی نداره. کاراکترها به‌شدت تیپ هستن، و به‌جرات مرگ یا در خطر قرار گرفتنِ هیچ کدومشون منِ مخاطب رو تحت‌تاثیر قرار نمی‌ده. برای منِ مخاطب هیچ فرقی نداره که به این سفرِ چندنفره‌ی یاران حلقه، فردی اضافه یا ازش کم بشه. جای هر کدوم از کاراکترها با هر کاراکتر دیگه‌ای قابل پر شدنه و نقش هیچ‌کس تو جای خودش محکم نیست. کاراکترها از جایگاه خودشون هیچ دفاعی نمی‌کنن. من زیاد کتاب فانتزی نخوندم و به این دلیل از مجموعه‌ی #هری_پاتر مثال می‌زنم، و نه لزومن برای این‌که به نظرم این دو اثر قابل مقایسه هستن. توی اون مجموعه هیچ کس نمی‌تونه جای شخص هری پاتر رو بگیره، فقط هری در جایگاه خودش معنی داره. این‌جا این‌طور نیست. حامل حلقه هرکسی می‌تونه باشه. توی اون مجموعه رونالد یار کله‌شق هریه که زیر و بم دنیای جادوگری رو به‌واسطه‌ی زندگی در یک خانواده‌ی «از بُنْ جادوگر» می‌دونه، و در کنارش هرمایونیِ درسخون و باهوش قرار داره که با همین هوش و دانشش خیلی مواقع به کارهایی که دارن انجام می‌دن کمک می‌کنه. توی این کتاب هیچ فرق خاصی نداره که کی کنار حامل حلقه باشه. تنها شخصیت‌هایی که شاید کمی آدم رو بیشتر درگیر کنن گندالف و آراگورن هستن، که حتا گندالف هم عظمت خاصی از خودش که جادوگره نشون نمی‌ده، و مجموعه‌ی این‌ها در کنار هم، این کتاب رو برای منِ مخاطب از ضربانی که لازمه‌ی انگیزه دادن برای خوندنِ یه مجموعه‌ی سه‌جلدیِ دوهزار و چند صفحه‌ایه می‌ندازه. این برای من نقطه‌ضعف بزرگیه، برای کس دیگه بنا بر توقعات خودش ممکنه اصلن مساله‌ی مهمی هم نباشه. برای من هست، و نمی‌تونم کتابی که چنین حفره‌ی بزرگی برام داره رو عالی و یا حتا خیلی خوب بدونم. از این‌ها که بگذریم، توصیف‌ها کافی، گویا، و به‌اندازه‌ان. بدون این‌که خسته‌کننده باشن تمام مناظر رو به چشم می‌کشن، و این رو منی می‌گم که از توصیف اضافی فراری‌ام. مترجم از پس متن براومده، هرچند «الوداع»های مکرر متن توی ذوقم می‌زدن اما ترجمه خوب و یک‌دسته و برخلاف شنیده‌هام که با متن سخت‌خوانی قراره روبه‌رو باشم، به‌نظرم اصلن این‌طور نبود؛ کتاب ساده و روونی بود و لذتِ حداقلی برای ادامه دادن ماجرا رو منتقل می‌کرد. توی دنیای گیم و بازی یه بازی نقش‌آفرینی به اسم D&D وجود داره که نمی‌دونم اون برگرفته از دنیای تالکینه یا دنیای تالکین برگرفته از اون، ولی درصورت وجودِ یه تخیلِ قوی، اون بازی و این کتاب به‌شدت تجربه‌ی مشابهی برای آدم دارن. وقتی سه جلد رو تموم کنم حتمن بررسی می‌کنم که قدمت کدوم یکی از این دوتا بیشتره، و اگر سرزمین میانه قبل از اون بازی خلق شده باشه به احترام تالکین که سال‌ها قبل چنین دنیایی رو خلق کرده کلاه از سر برمی‌دارم، هرچند که لذت بیشتری می‌بردم اگر این دنیا رو با قوام بیشتری خلق می‌کرد؛ و امیدوارم که این ماجرا برعکس نباشه...
در نهایت، اگر دنیای تالکین رو دوست دارید اون بازی رو پیشنهاد می‌کنم. اگر کتاب رو نخوندید برای اولین‌بار توی زندگیم فکر می‌کنم تماشای فیلمش و اختصاصِ زمانی که خوندنِ کتاب‌هاش لازم داره به کتاب‌های دیگه، ضرر خاصی بهتون نمی‌زنه و چیز زیادی هم از دست نمی‌دید. اگر این کتاب رو خوندید و نظرتون باهام مخالفه مشتاقم دلایلتون رو بشنوم و چیزهایی که تنهایی موفق به دیدنشون نشدم رو ببینم. و اگر کمکی از جایی بهم نرسید، امیدوارم جلدهای بعدی بتونن نظرم رو حسابی زیر و رو بکنن؛ چون مجموعه‌ی بزرگیه و من قصد دارم تا آخرش بخونم، و ترجیح می‌دم لذتی که می‌برم خیلی فراتر از الان، و در حد و اندازه‌ای باشه که داره ازش یاد می‌شه. تا این‌جا وسعت آسمون این کتاب برای من در حد سه‌ستاره‌ست.

I finally "read" this book with audible. As an aspiring fantasy author I Have to take in Tolkien's work. The movies inspired me about as a child.
Sadly what I feared most about picking up this book proved true. It was VERY self indulgent with details. So much of the plot was meandering and unnecessary. Even in audio book form getting through the Tom Bombadill stuff and the wandering in the wood was like "Lord you aren't at your destination yet!!"
But! All that being said I don't regret it and I will physically read Two Towers if I can. That was always my favorite movie and Fellowship was always my least favorite of the three.
This did not deminish my love for the world I was introduced to in a different medium and I do not think any less of Tolkien. Everything I heard about his writing style was just true.
The stuff I thought I would love I loved. Like the interaction between chargers being simple and strong, the characters being will defined, in the descriptions being rich and artistic.
And the stuff that I was worried would drag for me and be tedious with tedious. Like how everything was slow and meandering and so much that was in there I want to see tightened up, filler thrown out, and three chapters could have been three pages with Just enough of the rich details to make me breath in the flowers.

A few things I picked up on:
- I didn't realise that Aragorn was so driven in becoming King in the books, and actually has his sword reforged in this one. Makes the title for the third book much less of a spoiler than I thought
- I wish that there wasn't such heavily-handed foreshadowing for certain events, like Gandalf in Moria
- There are a lot of pages that's just hobbits and fellows trudging about Middle Earth
- There are a lot of songs as well. The longer ones didn't do much for me, but there were a couple - including Gilgalad was an Elvenking and All that is gold does not glitter - that I really liked
- The movie is definitely better-paced than the book, but that might be because I'm reading it as one novel rather than all three at once

All in all, I definitely liked it a lot more than when I read it many years ago. I think you need to be in the right state of mind to really enjoy these books - one where you really are in it for the journey, rather than the destination. You sort of need to be a fan of the work or universe already, almost.

My relationship with Tolkien and The Lord of the Rings began with the 2005 film Brick, directed by Rian Johnson. In one scene, two high school boys are reclining on a beach, watching the sun set. Apropos of nothing, one asks the other, “Have you ever read the Hobbit?” Upon reply (“No”) he sums up the reason for his interjection thus: “Tolkien is really good at describing things.” In the context of Brick, Tolkien is merely a symbol of the introspection and reserved, inarticulate wonder characteristic of adolescent boys. The reader of Tolkien, who up to this moment has been the perfect criminal mastermind, momentarily becomes the nerdy teenager, staring with wide-eyed curiosity at the setting sun. When Tolkien’s descriptive ability is applied to the natural world it is rich and comforting. By describing the world of middle earth with exacting yet poetic detail, from the deepest pits of Khazad-dûm to the sunny hobbit holes of the shire to the towering trees of Lothlorien, The Fellowship of the Ring implies that every bit of the natural world matters. Much as I would like to see how Tolkien develops his pastoral naturalism throughout the trilogy, I think it will be a long time before I complete the series.
Regrettably, I cannot help but compare Tolkien to his contemporaries. When The Fellowship was published in 1954, the postwar literary scene was buzzing with new, avante garde reactions to two global wars, the surging of capitalism (and Sovietism), and a nascent wave of decolonization (e.g. the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu occurred a couple of months before The Fellowship was published). In this turbulent era, Tolkien combed through English folklore, traditions, and songs in order to produce one of the most polished, expansive works of fantasy the English-speaking world has. Is Tolkien a reactionary? Is he limited by his genre? While it is certainly entertaining, Tolkien’s choice of genre also demonstrates the affective and philosophical potential of fantasy literature. His concern with power and the ways in which nostalgia is used to serve its purposes evince a timeliness which still resonates today. But like many readers, I am frustrated by his pacing, his (uncomplicated) morality, and his peculiar narrative devices (why must every foreshadowing dream or vision be consummated quite so explicitly, so regularly?). Like the very mythic texts and grand heroic narratives that Tolkien models his work after, The Fellowship of the Ring possesses a hieroglyphic quality to it, in which one scene after another seems to be propelled by nothing more than an esoteric, ancient necessity to narrate events. It is not quite clear why things must be recounted; but here they are, in all their magnificence and ordinariness. Hobbitlike, I will wait to finish The Lord of the Rings til my 33rd birthday, when I am more of age and better suited to Tolkien’s timescale.
