Los libros de fantasía son los que más aprecio en mi vida, no solo porque fueron los principales en adentrarme al mundo de la lectura, sino también porque considero que casi siempre son los mejores en transmitir diferentes tipos de mensajes en comparación a los libros de ficción "normales" por así decirlo; me han acompañado en varias etapas de mi vida desde los doce años y siempre los tengo cerca del corazón.

Sin embargo, tengo un dilema con este libro: no lo odié, pero tampoco me encantó.

La primera vez que intenté leer esto no pude pasar más allá de las doscientas páginas, me sentía bastante indiferente en cuanto a todo lo que ocurría en la historia y me pesaba seguir, en su momento creí que solo era una cuestión personal (sin embargo al leer diferentes reseñas me he dado cuenta que a varios les ocurrió lo mismo) y lo dejé. Hasta hace poco pude terminarlo por fin, mejoró mi percepción en cuanto a la historia, pero desafortunadamente no mucho.

Supongo que uno de los problemas que tengo es que se enfoca más en la historia en sí que en los personajes (sumándole que es bastante lenta), lo que sea de cada quien, pero a medida que mi hábito de lectura evoluciona parece ser que me interesan ligeramente más los libros que se enfocan en los personajes y su construcción, tal vez simplemente este tipo de narración de Tolkien no es para mí (aunque hasta eso su prosa bastante descriptiva no se me hizo pesada).

A eso le sigue mi siguiente punto: no me sentí conectada con ninguno de los personajes. No sé, siento que las acciones y la evolución que tuvieron en todo el libro se me hicieron muy secas y poco creíbles (?). De nuevo, el hecho de que la historia sea bastante lenta y este aspecto de los personajes tal vez empeoró mi disfrute de la lectura.

No niego el hecho de que Tolkien haya sido uno de los escritores más importantes de la literatura fantástica, pero no comprendo por qué no llegué a querer esta historia como la mayoría, tal vez no fue un buen momento para leer esto o simplemente pertenezco a la minoría que no le gusta El Señor de los Anillos jajajaja.

Pero, ahora me dirijo a ustedes requiriendo de su opinión sincera: ¿debería seguir leyendo El Señor de los Anillos? ¿debería dejar la historia hasta aquí? ¿otra oportunidad o me limito a ver las películas?

In all honesty, I was slightly underwhelmed by this. This may have been inevitable to some extent, given how shaped by expectations were by the intense and unyielding praise for these books.

I still really liked The Fellowship of the Ring. There are some undeniably great elements. Firstly, Tolkien's world building is top notch. It's not always integrated into the story in the most natural ways, but the well crafted depth and intricacies are immersive enough to make up for that lack of elegance.
Some of Tolkien's descriptions are also really nice. Every now and then he would bring to life a setting in the most whimsical and fantastical way. That's a must have when it comes to fantasy. Thanks to his well realized world building, it was really easy to place these gorgeous images in a trodden mental map.

But all that aside, I do think there are some flaws with how he executes his story and characters. Much like the Hobbit, I feel like three stars best suites this book, but purely because of how well loved it is, I find myself doubting my opinion (something that I very rarely do). So it will get a generous 4 stars until a re-read establishes my true feelings.
I continue to dislike how Tolkien writes his characters. While they are undoubtedly a step up from the vague and lifeless shells that populated The Hobbit, I still find they lack crucial depth to be interesting characters. I wouldn't call the fellowship leads bad necessarily, but just acceptable. Nothing more, nothing less. They work to fill the story but don't add anything to it. Although I do love Sam. It's also worth mentioning that in the final few chapters I did notice an improvement with the characters all around. Particularly in Boromir who finally started to offer something to the story. That's a promising sign for the next books.

I also don't think the structure is all that engaging. I love when authors aren't in a rush. When they let the reader soak in all the details and atmosphere of the world they have so carefully crafted. But I don't feel that was the case here. Especially early on, there are a lot of redundant events and meaningless detours that I don't think benefited the experience. They get lost in two or three forests in the first 100 pages. In that time nothing interesting happens for the characters, story, or atmosphere. I really think this story would have benefited from revisions to make the journey feel more pressing. Also, the singing? What is with all the singing. Why does everyone feel the need to break out into song EVERY. FIVE. MINUTES. I felt like Shrek when Donkey wouldn't stop making noise on their journey to Far Far Away.

Overall, the Fellowship of the Ring is good. There's enough great ideas and care put into the book to make that stand true. But Tolkien, as a writer, continues to not impress me.

It feels wrong to say this is a three star book for me but that’s only because I have tried to look at this from someone who knows nothing of The Lord of the Rings and it’s effect on the fantasy genre to try and not hold it against its reputation. But as someone who has seen the films that has been difficult.

So that being said, my main problem with the book is surprisingly, the world building in places. The huge chunks of text that seem to just flow along the page like a lazy river which do help to paint the image of Middle Earth but I don’t need to hear the backstory of everything. But I guess that’s my only major problem with it. The characters are likeable and fun to read about and you do want to learn more about them, yet to get to the backstory of the character you have to sift through so much world lore first. Though I did like it when it was a character giving the backstory of characters, Gandalf telling Gollum’s backstory for example something about that part really grabbed me.

And there are so many songs and poems, some just seem unnecessary others help to flesh out the world which is interesting (even though I could just skim over them all), which I’m guessing some readers do.

This is why I liked the action scenes more. They are paced well considering the amount of characters in the Fellowship but also hold a certain sense of chaos as well, almost like you’re in the battles with the characters. The Barrow-Wight scene in particular sticks out as a great set piece.

So while I am looking forward to reading the next two books, at least there I’ll have some better understanding as to what my problems with them could be.

I would have given this 4 stars if the book had finished about 100 pages earlier! But what a great read. Early on in starting this, I read a review on Goodreads where someone was basically saying they were really frustrated with how slow the plot unravels and how they were trying to burn through the pages just to reach an interesting, thrilling chapter. Someone had commented on it saying that that was the complete wrong way to approach LOTR and I couldn't agree more. The Fellowship is more about the journey than the destination, and taking the time to imagine myself on the adventure with Frodo, Merry, Pippin, Boromir and Aragorn, seeing the landscape in front of me, feeling the danger from the Black Riders, made the book so much more enjoyable and exciting that I couldn't put it down. However I stand by my one criticism that the story tended to go on and on, even after there was a seemingly quite natural end. I think the last 3 chapters could have easily been part of the next book instead, and I found them really difficult to read.

Being a huuuuuuuuge Harry Potter fan, I found it super interesting to identify how many ideas Rowling has adapted (or maybe outright stolen lol) from Tolkein, for example; the relationship. between Gandalf and Saruman when the latter asks the former to join together to fight Men - Dumbledore and Grindelwald when the latter asks the former to join against muggles; the wall into Moria that Gandalf attempts to get through - reminded me very much of the cave in which Voldemort hides Slytherins locket in book 6; and perhaps the most obvious one, the Mirror of Galadriel which basically IS the Mirror of Erised.

Overall, I loved this book, but I was ready for it to end. I think for younger readers its definitely a challenge and I'm glad I've waited until now to read it. I also don't think I'll be reading the next two for a little while lol.

P.S. I LOVED Tom Bombadil, I don't understand how anyone wouldn't!! He was integral to the story and I think we should all be more like him lol

What to say of a classic novel that one admires more than one enjoys? Furthermore, what to say of book whose tale one has already experienced before, and whose films adaptations have been faintly etched in one's mind ad nauseam? The answers to these questions are unclear. What IS clear that I am pleased to have finally read J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Fellowship of the Ring," and thus begun the introductory journey into the epic story "The Lord of the Rings" in all its glory.

Having seen all the LORD OF THE RINGS and HOBBIT films, plus having previously read (and loved) Tolkien's 1937 classic "The Hobbit, or There and Back Again" novel, I approached "The Fellowship of the Ring" loaded up with history, information and prejudicial opinion (arguably too much so). "The Hobbit..." was such a beautiful, fun and gentle read, yet I heard that "The Lord of the Rings" books were more challenging (to read) and cut from a different cloth.

Having now read "The Fellowship of the Ring," I see that seventeen years after the "The Hobbit...," J.R.R. Tolkien's prose had changed somewhat, or at least his focus was different. Whereas "The Hobbit..." was essentially a tender children's tale filled with good, evil and adventure, "The Fellowship of the Ring" takes the good, evil and adventure aspects into a sophisticated, complicated and highly detailed overdrive catered towards young adults and up.

My fears were fully realized while reading "The Fellowship of the Ring," in that I got lost and confused sometimes as to which character was which, and who said and did what. On top of all that, I found myself consistently stymied by the immense amount of song found in the story. Even as a music lover, I found myself groaning every time a character broke into long, lyrical verses...which were boring. To make matters far more challenging, Tolkien spends an indecent amount of time diving deep into descriptions of mountains, grass, rivers, flowers, bushes, heathers, valleys, hills, rocks, trees, lakes, smoke, flames, hollows, stars, leaves, skies, clouds, streams and on and on and on. Though I did admire the author's commitment to the intricacies of the mapping of Middle Earth, it got to a point where the geography took over the story, with characters and the main plot of the One Ring being pushed into the background.

If there were not enough, there was another aspect of "The Fellowship of the Ring" that proved to be a challenge, and distraction, yet also a delight. So confusing! In a nutshell, as with "The Hobbit..." J.R.R. Tolkien's prose consistently contains rhyming couplets, on every single page of the book. On the one hand, it's a pleasure to read paragraphs filled with words and sentences that resolve themselves in rhyme. On the other hand, at a healthy 458-pages, I found myself handicapped by this particular style. The reason? Pacing. If one reads "The Fellowship of the Ring" at a regular or even fast pace, there is a strong chance you will miss the poetry and rhyming. If one reads "The Fellowship of the Ring" at a slower pace, one receives the beauty of the poetic rhyme...at the cost of a very slow pace on book that already dulls its pacing by the overabundance of descriptions of mountains, grass, rivers, flowers, bushes, heathers, valleys, etc...

Yet despite the pacing issues, and the complications involved with understanding the complex history and creatures offered up in "The Fellowship of the Ring," I still liked the book...even when I did not. In other words, I did not always enjoy what I was reading, and felt bored by the descriptions and repetitions. I mean, did there really need to be TWO Elf paradises with commanding kings and enchanting queens? Don't get me wrong, I loved Lorien, yet the effect of it was diminished by the fact the the gang already were awed with wonder during their stay in Rivendell.

Anyway, in the end, I may not have always agreed with Tolkien's choices, yet could not help but love his writing, as well as his characters. Okay, Pippin was annoying, yet I enjoyed reading about Frodo, Sam, Merry, Bilbo, Aragorn, Gandalf, Boromir, Gollum and Gimli. I liked reading about the Rings, and their creation, and experiencing our heroes fight their way through orcs, trolls and creatures of the unknown. Perhaps it's an enchantment I carried over from my love of "The Hobbit..."book, I am not sure.

What I am sure of, is that I liked "The Fellowship of the Ring" more than I expected to, and less than I wanted to. Despite its many challenges, I look forward to reading the next book in the series...even as I approach such a task with great trepidation. There are many roads, hills, hamlets and heathers to go before Frodo reaches Modor. Hope we all make it...

I think it's safe to assume everyone knows what this story is about. There's no point going into detail about the plot and characters here, so I'll rather focus on why this ended up with only three stars.

Starting with what I liked and was probably most surprised by was the quality of the prose. Having read my fair share of genre fiction from the mid-to-late nineties, I was expecting dense and clunky writing. So while the pacing might have been slow and the amount of detail excessive, the flow and beauty of every sentence took me by surprise. As an introduction to the story and its characters, this instalment did a great job of setting up what's at stake and why everyone is doing what they're doing. The world felt lived in and real, with everything from the various cultures, lore, and interactions between groups serving to immerse the reader deeper. From a technical standpoint, this did a lot right even by today's standards. It undoubtedly deserves the praise and recognition it garnered for making the fantasy genre what it is today.

Unfortunately, I also had a number of issues. The numerous infodumps were rather tedious with the majority of the information being irrelevant to the story. The slow pacing became glacial at times, making some sections feel like real slogs to get through. Tom Bombadil was beyond annoying with his contribution to the story only adding confusion and some unsatisfying plot points. I'm generally a fan of audiobooks, but being subjected to all those songs was unpleasant, to say the least. Finally, towards the end, I also started to get bored by the cast due to their moral righteousness within the narrative. All the good guys were unquestionably good, while all the bad guys were irredeemably evil. It's not necessarily an issue with the book considering when it was written, but for modern audiences, it can get a bit dull from a characterisation standpoint.

So hence the enjoyable 3 stars. I liked it for what it was and can see why people still recommend it to this day, but it's undoubtedly held back by the period it was written in, at least in terms of what I've come to enjoy. It's my favourite in the trilogy, mostly for how well it sets everything up and its a generally tighter focus on a small cast of characters as opposed to the multiple perspectives in the latter books.

I did it. The beast has been slain. The mountain has been conquered. I am unstoppable.

Quick thoughts
The audiobook for this was the right decision. This slow-burn of an epic fantasy had me giggling and smiling as much as it had be crying from boredom.

My experience reading LOTR (because it needs no introduction)
I made the bold decision to finally start my journey into the LOTR world and read the Fellowship (book 1 of 3, if you don't know). I decided the best way to do this would be to listen to the audiobook.
'All that is gold does not glitter, not all those who wander are lost.'
My short summation of my thoughts, was that the first third was really good and everything thereafter was a struggle. And that Sam is adorable.

I'm expecting that the next books will be epic, however, so I'm really excited about continuing. The story has been prepped and set SO well and I just love this world.
'All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us.'
So don't get me wrong, whilst 60% of this book really is as slow and uneventful as everyone says, it's also brilliant. When you imagine the world building Tolkien did back when he was writing this, it blows my mind.

My favourite character was by far Sam (which lines up with how I feel about the films), and my least favourite was Boromir. I mean, are we even supposed to like that wet fop of a character? He was so superfluous (but don't worry, I have watched the films and I do know he's ~actually~ quite important).
'Short cuts make long delays.'
My favourite thing about the audiobook was than Robert Inglis (narrator) sang every single song. This entertained me to no end.

My main complaint
Whilst I was genuinely surprised by how easy this was to listen to whilst multitasking, I found the hardest thing about the story was paying attention during the slow parts.
'He that breaks a thing to find out what it is has left the path of wisdom.'
I confess to frequently catching myself tuned out as an overly long backstory lulled my brain into white-noise mode.

Final thoughts
This was interesting to read and I feel very good about myself for finally having read the bloody thing. It was okay - it's clearly building up to the great story that is to come and I'm alright with that because it's Tolkien. Until then, I shall reserve my four and five star ratings until the battles scenes begin.

Here is hoping I get more from the remaining books of the series.

Pán Prstenů je literární klasika, která mě v dětství minula. Teprve před rokem jsem viděla všechny tři filmy v tom rozšířeném formátu s původně vynechanými scénami (takže jsem nedokázala rozlišit, jaké scény byly v původním filmu a jaké ne). Celá série mě opravdu zaujala, pro mě to je nádherný příběh plný velkého přátelství, dokonale vykreslených postav a oddanosti a u konce Návratu krále jsem si pořádně pobrečela. Přesto jsem se dlouho bránila si přečíst literární předlohu a až tyto prázdniny jsem se rozhodla, že to zkusím.

Velikou výzvou pro mě bylo už se prokousat prologem, kde si Tolkien libuje v mnoha historických a faktických podrobnostech. Užitečnou jsem však shledávala podkapitolu O nalezení prstenu, která stručně shrnuje putování Bilba z prequelu Hobit aneb Cesta tam a zase zpátky. Tuto knihu jsem nečetla a ani filmy mě příliš nezaujaly, avšak dle mého tento příběh čtenář Pána prstenů ani nepotřebuje příliš podrobně znát.

Začátek knihy mi ubíhal docela pomalu. Tolkien si libuje v dlouhých a barvitých popisech, což bylo určitě vhodným při převádění knihy na filmové plátno, ovšem mnohdy je to až příliš. Musím se přiznat, že sama prostě nejsem fanouškem dlouhých popisů, i když spisovatele obdivuji za nádherný fiktivní svět Středozemě, který ve svých dílech vybudoval. Zajímavějším a čtivějším se děj pro mě stal až v době, kdy se v příběhu objevilo více nových postav a začalo se formovat Společenstvo.

Myslím si, že knihu bych si určitě užila více, kdybych filmy neviděla, protože i ve spíše pozvolném prvním díle se objevuje několik dramatických scén a zvratů. Avšak i tak se mi zdálo, že jsem knihu četla takovým tím stylem, abych ji měla co nejdříve za sebou. Naštěstí se nejedná o rozsáhlé dílo, ovšem dle mého se musí svět dělit na dva tábory – na tábor, který miluje Tolkienovy popisné scény do sebemenšího detailu a na tábor, který to prostě nemusí.

Jak jsem filmy absolutně milovala, tak v dalších knihách trilogie knižní předlohy už pokračovat asi nebudu. Čerstvě si však chci znovu pustit ten skoro čtyřhodinový rozšířený první díl a připomenout si ho.

After the second time reading this, I feel I ought to leave a review. Some parts of this book are really great, but some parts are also immeasurably dull. I will admit that I did expect more from such a highly revered book, but that's not to say that it is bad. I shall leave my thoughts in list format as that is how my dysfunctional brain is feeling as I write this late at night:

- Gandalf is not a very great character. In my opinion, he's only seen as great because he has epic powers that no one else has, but he's really not all that nice. Prime example: "Throw yourself in next time, and then you will be no further nuisance. Now be quiet!" Sure, Pippin was being a bit idiotic in that moment, but that's seriously a jerk move on Gandalf's part.

- Elves are overrated. Seriously. What's so great about them being so fair? And don't any of them do anything practical? All they do is sing the best songs ever and look pretty. If they're going to make music they should at least like play a respectable instrument like euphonium or piano every once in a while, and maybe do something actually worthwhile like building things or farming sometimes. And they need to stop flaunting their superiority.

- Good thoughts: Sam is a pretty high quality character. I dunno what he sees in Frodo that makes him admire him so much, but I do admire Sam's unwavering loyalty. He is also the only character who was ever once semi-comedic in the entire book.

- Mixed feelings: There was a lot of scenery descriptions. Which sometimes were good, and sometimes totally unnecessary.

- There was no climax. I'm a fan of books with climaxes.

- The plot dragged on too long and Frodo had about zero character development. Maybe, I dunno, Frodo could have had more character development if Tolkien had focused less on the scenery and more on Frodo as a person? Just an idea.

- What is with all the unnecessary descriptions of which directions they are taking and all their different names and the things that happened in those places tons of years ago? It's not like I'm going to remember any of that information, and I don't think it's relevant to the plot or lack thereof.

- The plot as a whole is certainly not a bad concept. I just wish it had properly followed a traditional plot structure (a.k.a. had a climax) and had meandered less.


To close I shall leave you with two quotes that I did find amusing:
- "...he had put on his head a tall shapeless felt bag, which he called a hat."
- "There the white rind of the new moon could be seen glimmering in the remote lakes. Sam looked at it and puckered his brows."

Tolkien's writing has matured by a great margin since The Hobbit. The story is much more interesting and engaging, it's much more detailed and well thought through, and its target audience are not just children anymore.

In this book, Tolkien has completed the whole fantasy world of his stories and all its species and their different characteristics, he has even gone as far as to create a whole new language for the elves. That by itself is a remarkable aspect of this book, it takes the reader to a whole new world, created by an imaginative mind, a delightful experience.

All that being said, the story still suffers a little from anti-climactic scenes at crucial turning points.

Generally, I really enjoyed the story and am looking forward to read the rest.

Edit: I have been thinking more about this book and I might have realized the element which keeps me from enjoying this book as much as I expect. The problem is that the characters seem to be too good! They are almost always making the right choices, always being kind, and most annoyingly, so freaking courteous! To the point that the characters lose their human quality. It's true that most of them are not really "humans" but nevertheless, they cannot be sympathized with.

”’I wish it need not have happened in my time," said Frodo.
"So do I," said Gandalf, "and so do all who live to see such times. But that is not for them to decide. All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us.”’

(3.5) Not to be that guy, but the movie is much better. I found I liked this book solely for the fact that I love the story that the movies presented. As someone who often cites Fellowship as the best of the three films, I was overall disappointed as I continued on in this.

It’s enjoyable for sure. The world-building is second to none and the way in which Tolkien reveals information is stellar. Slowly developing the backstory of the environment and giving information from different perspectives was enjoyable, and never felt like an info dump. Tolkien’s writing, while dense, offers great insight and perspectives on life and offers up a multitude of themes to consider. He incorporates these into his narration and the characters thought processes. I liked that each character also has their own little quirks and jabs that you start to pick up on the more you read.

Although the wit is there, I couldn’t help but feel the prose was just dry. I found each character dull and uninteresting, once again only gravitating towards what I saw of them in the movies. Just about every statement is uttered with such lifelessness. Despite the enormity of the stakes, the urgency just isn’t there. No one, especially Frodo, seems to grasp the severity of what’s happening. All too often someone will say that Sauron is near, the Orcs are coming, etc. And then what do the characters do? “I see, now let me ponder this for several hours, or weeks, or until winter and then we can decide to leave.” I didn’t expect the high action that the film presents, but in doing this time and time again, we lose the sense of tension that we should be feeling. Not until Boromir turns on Frodo did I feel a sense of tension for anyone here.

What keeps me intrigued is knowing this story and the world that Tolkien places us into. It’s enthralling on its own merit. I hope my opinion lightens as I read the remainder of the series, and possibly as I re-read this somewhere down the road. To start off the journey though, this one was a solid 7/10.

I credit my ability to finish this book to the amazing audiobook I began listening to at the middle of the book. I was so incredibly bored by this book until the creators of the audiobook made it come alive for me. Their sound effects, music, and passionate reading were great.
The book itself was definitely a let-down for me. So many people encouraged me to read this series, but the writing style was not for me. There was so much unnecessary detail. There were a million stories that added nothing to the overall plot. I couldn’t stand when characters would go into a long-winded explanation for their reasoning behind a small, somewhat meaningless action they were taking. And the songs!!!! Why. On. Earth. Was. There. So. Much. Singing???? I definitely skipped them, but it was so excessive. In comparison with the movie, I could see the reasoning to why they cut a lot of the book out. I wished some plot points were left out or shortened the way the movie did. The fact that these characters waited literal months for no reason to start the quest or to continue their journey/leave a resting place was infuriating. Their enemy is gathering strength and planning for the future while they relax and write poems. And then they had the nerve to complain about traveling in winter when it was entirely their fault that they were out that late in the year! However, there was plenty of information the book provided that made the movie make more sense, such as Pippin and Merry joining the quest to begin with.
The story itself was interesting enough. The characters were okay, if a little one-dimensional. Frodo is a really dull character to have to follow, but I actually liked him a lot more in the book than I did in the movies. What bothered me most about the characters was the lack of positive female representation. I’m pretty sure about three or four women had any speaking lines at all. I couldn’t understand why no women were included in the fellowship. They were almost always beautiful and stationary characters, sidelined by a male character. The lack of diversity also permeated the choice to describe villainous characters as dark and/or black, which is very annoying. Although commenting on race was obviously not the intention, these descriptions are harmful and have not aged well. They speak to a more implicit view that black is evil rather than beautiful. One example is when a character says something to the effect of “I will not allow a black man to enter my establishment”. In the context, he is speaking of a black-hooded evil creature, but without context, it suggests something much worse. In terms of positive representation, I was pleasantly surprised by the range of emotions the male characters were allowed to express and the affection they extended towards each other. This book is a great model of normalized nonsexual male affection and unstigmatized displays of emotions, such as crying.
Overall, it was not my favorite book by a long shot, but it wasn’t horrible.

I've tried to read this book twice before and both times stopped reading somewhere around the Tom Bombadil sections. This time I practically forced myself to keep reading and persevered through his chapters to actually finish this first part in the trilogy.

Now that I've managed it, I can see why The Lord of the Rings is a classic (the world building alone is on another level). Yet, Tolkien is an overly descriptive writer and this kills the pace often. This book also made clear there is such a thing as too many songs/poems in a single novel, and here we crossed that line quite comfortably.

The Lord of the Rings being a classic that is beloved by many I expected a lot more from this book.
Right at the beginning you get hit with a lot of backstory for things and characters you don't yet have enough emotional investment in to care for. At least I didn't.

They cut the whole part where they meet Tom Bombadil from the movie and I get why, because it bore me so much that I put down the book and didn't pick it up again for another year.

Once the Hobbits arrive in Rivendell (which starts of "book two"), it gets better, as the focus shifts more to the interactions between the Fellowship the book is named after. Generally the book continues on in the same way as before (walking/riding horses, eating, sleeping and keeping watch, talking about and deciding where to go next, the occasional assault by the Black Riders or orcs, a stop in a town (probably elvish) where they'd like to stay bc it's so much safer and get unexpected or expected help in some form or other) but the interactions between the members of the fellowship finally gave me something I could get more invested in and by the end I did care about the main characters.

The last few pages were my favorite, where we see the corruption of the ring affecting more than just Frodo, which to me was the most interesting part of the book and I wish we had seen more of it earlier on, even though I understand to some extent why we didn't. The end also made me get a deeper appreciation for Sam, who is probably my favorite character now.

The worldbuilding is extensive and by all means seems to be the focus of the plot, but wasn't enough to keep me wanting to read this book. I hope there's more meaningful character interaction in the second book and more higher stakes conflicts and less worldbuilding purely for the sake of worldbuilding. Otherwise, I'm not sure if I'll manage to actually finish this series.

I know this is a well-loved book by many, but it seems like it's just not right for me. I do give it three stars though because it's readable once you get over the first block of backstory and worldbuilding, and it does have interesting bits that are worth exploring.

And I add the same thought I had after reading Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire: I think I would have enjoyed this a lot more if I had still been a child and could have gotten through the book by merely being enchanted with the worldbuilding instead of being exasperated because none of it struck me as being relevant to anything that is happening in the plot.
In which I may have to turn in my Nerd Card by admitting that I only found The Fellowship of the Rings to be merely "okay."

J.R.R. Tolkien is a literary wizard. The attention to detail in the geography, linguistics, and peoples he’s created for the Lord of the Rings books is awe-inspiring. Being addicted to fantasy and fiction writing, I can’t believe it finally took me this long to start the trilogy. While I’m inspired by Tolkien’s creativity, I did feel as if the Fellowship was slow-moving. It seemed to drag on and on, with very little action. I never truly had any “lost-in-the-book” moments—where you’re so engrossed in the story that it feels as if you’re actually living the pages rather than reading them. I was always very aware of the fact that I was reading. It was a struggle to get through, I’ll admit, when I usually can’t put a book down. But I still think Tolkien’s creativity (as described above) warrants the need to read this book. It’s why I’ll continue with the trilogy—because it’s definitely one of those classic series that any serious fantasy lover must experience.

I get how a lot of people do not finish this trilogy and get disheartened early in the reading. However, if you hang in there, you begin to pick up on the language, the complexity of Middle Earth, and you find what makes this one of the greatest fantasy novels of all time.

I want to first say that The Lord of the Rings is near and dear to my own heart, as I grew up watching the films, completely enthralled by the scope and grandeur of the story. I also want to say that if I was rating this book by the sheer genius of Tolkien's world-building, histories, and languages, it would have to be five stars. Tolkein is, without a doubt, the progenitor of the modern fantasy genre. I am intensely aware, at every moment in the story, that the lore of LOTR reaches thousands of years deep, with a complexity that can only be matched by our own, actual history.

However, I am not rating Tolkein. I am rating The Fellowship of the Ring.

It is hard to not compare this book with the movies, which is how I first knew this story, and because the movies are such a cultural juggernaut. In fact, I think the comparison, for me at least, is unavoidable. At times, the book barely ambles along at a slug's pace. I couldn't wait to get out of the Shire, just to fall into the Forbidden Forest, where I could feel myself aging by the moment. I spent about a month trying to read my way out of the Forbidden Forest, complete with Tom Bombadill and other random fluff -- an apt comparison: that's about how long it took the hobbits too. At times, I found myself anticipating a moment of dramatic tension or character development, just to have it jarringly glossed over in the most anticlimactic way. Every time the wraiths showed up, and the hobbits hid in a ditch, I had the most maddening sense of deja vu. I asked my husband once, "So do the hobbits ever, like, become actual characters orrr.... what?" At other times, it read more like a history textbook, or a cartography lesson, and I was distinctly reminded that Tolkein is more interested in creating histories or maps than he is in developing full, compelling characters or plot points. I felt that I was reading Beowulf, or the Odyssey, or the Canterbury Tales. (Which I also could not bring myself to fully enjoy).

Saying this, the book is undeniably well-written and compelling most(ish) of the time. I could imagine the scenery along the journey, even if, at times, I wanted less description of the ferns and hedges. Each new setting brought new characters, new cultures, new complexities to the world Tolkein creates. Once the company hit Rivendell, the pace was better, and each dramatic moment felt like it had more payoff.

If anything, this book has given me a new appreciation for Peter Jackson's reimagining of the LOTR. He stays incredibly loyal to the source material while managing to cut out or rework the portions that drag on and on in confusing circles. (Goodbye, Tom Bombadill!) He makes Frodo younger, more innocent and naive to the ways of the world. He makes Gandalf more sympathetic and friendly. We move straight from the Shire, to Bree, to Flattop in an actually reasonable amount of time. Yet we still have all the moments from the books that are written beautifully and translate beautifully to the film: Gandalf's fall into Moria, the beauty of Lothlorien, the corruption of Boromir, the stay in Rivendell.

So before I get into my feelings I do want to say that I was a bit intimidated thinking about filming this review. The next thing I'm going to say I don't want anybody taking as me saying I didn't like this book, or that this book was bad. Don't come for me. This applies to all classics and older books. I feel that it is important to allow people to make distinction between books that are historically important and books that are good. One does not mean the other one automatically. Many historically important books if you read them now suck. It is a rare book that is both, and just because a book WAS good, doesn't mean it STAYS good. I think a lot of people who gatekeep classics do so based on their appreciation of them, and there's quite a big "you didn't like this? let me tell you why you're wrong" and I do see that in the LOTR community. SO bear that in mind. I'm going to come back to that thought sort of at the very end.

This is an incredibly descriptive book. This is a book which contains a lot of trivia you may not care about unless you're invested in unravelling the Tolkien worldbuild. If you're the kind of person who IS constantly looking for context, then you won't mind that quite a lot of this book is infodumpy. I didn't mind it, because for me I was sort of taking in the stuff that gave more context to the parts of the film I enjoyed. I was learning history which was ok. But this is not a book that you dive into for action packed adventure. This book is about a quest. You are on the quest with the fellowship of the ring. Tolkien has written about a journey and he is taking you on it, describing to you everything you see ON that journey, so I think the enjoyment of this book comes really with a "sit back and enjoy the ride" attitude. I think you can infer a lot about Tolkien FROM that. That he's a person who appreciates the road to a place maybe more than the place itself.

In terms of infodump and context, you WILL appreciate this book more (if you're the curious type) if you can look stuff up, either on the lord of the rings wiki or referring to the appendices at the end of the return of the king. Which are pretty beefy and do contain oodles of extra info. But I do wonder, is it possible to appreciate and enjoy each piece of Tolkien's work in isolation, or do you have to take in every piece with the knowledge that it's part of a larger whole, to appreciate it?

Since I love the films so much, they're probably the best fantasy films ever made and some of my favourite movies ever, I'm going to be making a lot of comparisons to the movies through this review and how I feel they differ, how I think bits could have been done differently etc. BUT I think for me the biggest difference was the tone. The book is a lot more lighthearted and I don't know if that's because we don't have the graphic visual battles, the conflicts, which in the book are sort of two-lines then gone, whether the book is ACTUALLY more humorous, or whether the light-heartedness comes from spending so much time with characters in a comfortable setting before the conflict even begins. About a third of this book you're just relaxing with hobbits. But even the way the characters act seems much less serious in the book, one example that really stuck with me was that bit in the movie where you get that zoom in on frodo, and the compression of the holloway, and he's like GET OFF THE ROAD GET OFF THE ROAD. In the book they hear a horse and they're all like teehee let's all hide, and if it's Gandalf we can jump out and give him a start!

I was surprised though, genuinely, how many lines made it from book to film totally unchanged. The quotes which I had assumed were reworked to be more epic in a hollywood setting were actually just taken word for word from the book, and seeing those gave me an appreciate for how Tolkien writes and the fact that even if he couldn't get that grandeur across on paper, he certainly had these super intense emotional scenes playing out in his head.

---

So a lot of the criticism I hear about the movie in relation to the book was how much stuff was left out, and honestly yeah I was surprised how much was left out. There's such a focus on the shire and hobbit life to get you attached to the main characters, and the pacing of the whole thing is very different to the film. But I think personally, that's because Tolkien intends for LORD OF THE RINGS to be treated as one work. Rather than separate books. If you look at the amount of time in the shire as a part of book 1, yes it seems excessive but if you look at the focus on the shire as a whole next to focus on the rest of middle earth, the amount of time dedicated to it across the entire saga, it's pretty reasonable actually.

There are some things I was like mmhm ok I can understand why they cut this. The one I hear most people talk about is Tom Bombadil. How he's such a weird character, but firstly I get why he's in the book. He has the relationship with the world everybody wishes they had, he's the master of his domain, he exists as a reminder that there are things out there way weirder and more powerful than the hobbits can imagine. I don't think there would have been any way to put him in the film and make him match the tone of the rest without changing the essence of his character. I also get why they left out the wights of the barrow-downs, because they wanted the drama of weathertop to be the first conflict. They wanted THAT to be the moment where Frodo realises he's in over his head and I think having him face literal undead BEFORE that point would have totally diminished the insane impact the fight at weathertop HAD.

There was one thing that I really really disagree with them cutting, and to a lot of people I think it's going to seem like a minor thing. And that's Frodo's almost vision-like dream sequences. They're almost prophetic, they're rich in metaphor and almost foreshadow things to come and I really honestly think Peter Jackson could have done those artfully and beautifully and they would have enriched the films. I really believe that.

The last thing I'll say on the note of "bits left out" is if any of you haven't played The Fellowship of the Ring on ps2. It is literally a perfect chapter for chapter adaptation of the book, which honestly is super weird because it came out one year AFTER the movie. It has the shire, the old forest, old man willow, tom bombadil, the barrow wights, everything. It is a LOTR game based on the book. And it's honestly tragic that it never got proper sequel games. The other ps2 LOTR games were based on the movies and had movie cutscenes.

One thing that I thought was interesting was in this book there is a lot of hinting at a higher power "for good" being at play behind the scenes and there really wasn't any of that in the movie at all. I know that Tolkien was a devout Roman Catholic, so maybe it's his religious nature shining through into his work, I'm not sure honestly. The coincidences and how wild and essential they are, are acknowledged too. The most bonkers and obvious one was that, in the movie you have Elrond having summoned the council to Rivendell to discuss the ring, which he knew Frodo was bringing. So they're all called there and are waiting for the ring to come so they can hold a meeting. In the book they have all come to Rivendell for very different very personal reasons and all coincidentally happened to arrive at the same time. You have the main party of aragorn and hobbits, but you have legolas who has come I think because they were tracking Gollum, who escaped elf custody? then Gimli and his dad who turn up because they're here to ask for help from the elves to track down a bunch of other dwarves that went to try and cut a path through to retake Moria and haven't been heard from since. Then at the very last minute you have Boromir rock up because he's come to ask for help for Gondor and get elf counsel, and he didn't know where Rivendell was, he was searching for it for 110 days. That whole bit was just super weird.

Another thing that was really strange to me reading this was how little internal monologue or insight into the characters you get. You have Frodo's dream sequences and thoughts a few times, then Gandalf's once, and it's so out of place it's super noticeable and the first time I read it, I thought it was speech. And this does 2 things. Unfortunately the first thing it does is it makes the whole thing seem Frodo centric, which I guess was the intention but I could honestly have done without it. And the second thing is that it reads very much like a movie because you are a VISUAL observer you're a fly on the wall or you're one of the party, you're not a magical mind-reader, you're watching closely but that's it.

Something else that stood out to me in this book was the lack of female characters outside of Galadriel who is a fantastic character, but I know that Arwen is going to get fleshed out further down the line, and we're going to have Eowyn introduced in book 2, so I'm going to not comment on his female representation YET. I'm going to do that in my review of the third book once I have the big picture. I've read whole articles and essays on female representation in Tolkien's work while I was writing all these notes up. There's a lot of opinions. I highly recommend a google.

OK so. The main themes of Lord of the Rings, Fellowship of the Ring.

With the emphasis for so much of the book being on the shire, I think there's a big theme of normal everyday people being forced into conflict without much choice. I think there's the theme of whole legions of enemies arising, lands being put to the torch, forests being uprooted and entire cities being smashed to pieces ALL stemming from the greed of one person. There's the theme of doing what's right and potentially difficult and having to weigh that against doing something that's easy, will guarantee your survival but may not be altogether morally correct, sort of embodied by the whole thing with Saruman. With the elves leaving middle-earth to the undying lands I think also you have the idea, the theme that even if you win the war, something is going to be lost and you're never going to get it back. Maybe innocence. Maybe your ability to find beauty in the world once you've seen and now know what people are capable of.

One place I think the message of this book really shines is that you have this brilliant idea of heroism and what that clearly means to Tolkien. It clearly means standing up for what's right, it clearly means putting other people before yourself, but it doesn't mean aggression, it doesn't mean conflict or winning through strength. The heroes of this book are the ones in the party who are the absolute least able to fight and I think that's very deliberate. Maybe the thing that wins is an idea and determination.

Just tell me it will take 2 minutes. You can talk WHILE we're walking. I don't think it added anything to the book besides making some characters a bit more annoying, that he clearly didn't WANT to be annoying characters. Like Gandalf, he did it a lot. Yeah didn't like that.

While I really enjoyed the poetry, and the many many many many songs in this book, I think the way that they were introduced was bad. There's only ONE song for which I can believe the circumstances for it being sung, and that was the song in the tavern in Bree. Because it's a tavern. And because people are drunk and want to sing and dance and be dumb. But when they're all sitting around and talking, then one character just randomly starts singing under their breath and everyone else just stares at them and waits patiently for them to finish, then is like wooooow so gooood! I was like hmmmmmmm. Every time that happened.

I like Tolkien, but I'm a bit salty about what came after him. I think I resent the ripples this series made because I think a lot of fantasy stuff to a fantasy-outside feels so heavily Tolkien inspired that it's too similar to be original. I tried this book series before and didn't like it, and I think knowing or having the idea that so much fantasy came from this one thing I really didn't like very much, was something that pushed me away from high fantasy for a very long time.

Alright, before you get your pitchforks out, here me out on this one. If I was rating this book in 1970, I'd give it a 5. If I was rating it in 2000, a 4. Me in my 30's, in 2021? A 3. Here's why.

We have learned from the 10 books I DNF'd last month that this style of writing is not for me. Had I not been a fan of the movies (again, put your pitchforks away y'all), I probably would have DNF'd this as well. It meanders. A LOT. If this first book was written today, an editor would have EASILY told him to cut 60% of what we have here. And I daresay I agree. HOWEVER, that is with the caveat of, I've had the last 30 years to read these great sweeping fantasy tales. Something that the readers when this book was published did not have.

So yeah, I'd say that this book rated based off of when it was written would be much higher, but I have things I want to talk about.

First off, you know it's coming because I'm a woman in my 30's, WHERE MY GIRLS AT?!?! Really though. A quick internet search will tell you that in ALL of the Lord of The Rings (not just Fellowship) there are 11 women in the series AND THAT'S COUNTING A SPIDER Y'ALL! I couldn't find a list of ALL male characters but just a list of the "notable" male characters contained north of 50 men. The three women of note from this book (I'd say) are Arwen, Goldberry, and Galadriel. All of whom are described in various ways of saying 'beautiful' and 'perfect' and 'powerful'. Which is fine in and of itself but dang. Not only do we only get 3 women, but it's basically just the same woman three times over? Cool.

Now, further research on my end has informed me that the women of LoTR are all a sort of love-letter to Tolkien's wife (with the exception of Eowyn but we'll wait until book 2's review to talk about her as she hasn't hit the page yet), which I guess would make sense. Also, the time period in which he grew up, the war torn world he lived in. Like, I GET IT. This would have made sense for the 1960's. But it doesn't feel right for today. And I'm not reading it in 1970. Alright?

Second. Who the actual fuck is Tom Bombadil and what kind of drugs was Tolkien on when he wrote that entire section of the book? Wait, pitchforks down. I know you purists are all about Bombadil and how he represents this older magics of Middle Earth and in some forms he and Goldberry represent Adam and Eve (because Tolkien was so religious his wife had to convert to Catholicism before they could marry) and you feel that's all SUPER important to the plot of the next two books. I get it. But I honestly just don't care. It was clunky. It slowed down the pacing of the book and made me want to stop reading immediately. This whole section just reminds me of me trying to read Alice in Wonderland and if that wasn't an absolute shit-show, nothing ever will be.

The POEMS. There were a lot of them. Some of them completely in languages I don't understand. Again, I grasp the concept that Tolkien was actually more of a linguist first, author second so it would make sense for him to create a language and write a book using that language and have that super weird superiority flex over all of us. But y'all, I ain't here to learn another language. I'm here to read a kick ass fantasy tale. Did I get that? Maybe. Also, do you like my inclusion of the word "ain't" while talking about language?

Here's the real bit of honesty. I read this via audiobook (the 'ONLY unabridged version' according to the description) and if I'd read it physically I'd have skipped every single poem and song. I give zero fucks about them.

Lastly I think this story falters by being A) broken into three parts and B) so long it needed to be broken into three parts. Ya feel me? There's a lot to be said of story structure and how it makes a book enjoyable to read and when you chop that book into three parts, well, it's not quite as enjoyable. Again, modern day, a lot of this would have been edited out. And I wonder if this had been edited down and published in one book if it would have better served the reader.

All of that being said, I do plan to continue reading this series. I did enjoy reading the parts that actually moved the story forward. And I have heaps of respect and awe for both this author and his collected works and how they changed the fantasy publishing game forever. And from the research I have done I do think that Tolkien was one of those greats that will be hard to match in terms of his level of intelligence and the mark he's left on the world.

But none of that means this book is 2021 perfect. And I have to rate it based on that.

Review:
The Fellowship of the Ring was so slow. Just ... really slow. And throughout the entire book, hobbits, elves, and dwarves were walking. WALKING! They called their walk a quest because they strolled through a forest at night. But I pass some serious shadows when I take walks, and they don't become journeys. Even Frodo knew he was doing serious cardio when he started losing weight. And after all of that walking, they never made it to the Cracks of Doom (is that what they're called?). That's probably for the other books, but I don't know how much more walking I can take.

There were some good parts to the book, though. For example, one of my favorite parts that almost made me cry was when Sam and Bill were parting ways. I feel like it wasn't even that important, but at that point, we knew so much about Sam and his personality, and also how much he loved Bill. The scene also strengthened Sam and Frodo's relationship because after Sam had accepted that Bill couldn't come on the rest of the journey, Sam continued with Frodo.

Another part of the book that I enjoyed was when Gandalf died. That came out wrong, but I hope you understand. This part of the book gave off the same energy as the Sam/Bill scene, but considerably less so. Gandalf was such an amazing character, mainly because I knew he could solve almost any problem. So, when he was pulled down the cliff by the monster, my hopes for the journey’s success plummeted with him. However, Gandalf is giving me serious Dumbledore vibes, meaning he will make a reappearance. Someone as powerful as Gandalf can’t disappear without a trace.

Lastly, I want to mention the psychotic Boromir and how I knew he was a power-hungry, blood-sucking, no-good mongrel. There were times when he would look at the ring or think about the ring when it shouldn’t have been his concern, to begin with. Also, Sam realized Boromir’s suspicious behavior, showing how observant Sam is. Then, after Frodo escaped and Boromir went back to the others, he lied with disgusting expertise. I was afraid no one would realize his evil, but I think Aragorn is on to him.

Whew...I admit, it took some WORK to get through this one. I really wanted to love it and praise it and defend it like the die hard fans, but unfortunately I struggled to be captivated by this story. Though I appreciate the foundation Middle Earth and this tale have played in modern-day fantasy.

Thoughts:
I felt lost basically half of the book. I think the main reason for this is because they are traveling, and as someone who is very directionally challenged - Tolkien said "North, South, East, West" in about five hundred thousand different phrases, and I couldn't get my bearings. I am someone who reads very thoroughly so that I can soak it all in and picture the space, and trying to engrain these far out lands and cities (of which there're are about 7 million!) when really they have no importance was rather frustrating and tedious. The world building in this book is too extreme. I like a nice balance between plot, characters, and setting. Unfortunately the setting went over its allotted portion - I'd say a good 65% of this book is describing the color of the sky and elevation of the land - hills, mountains, sunshine, snow, you name it and they walk through it.

The other part I struggled with was the names. They didn't come naturally to me, so again, while reading I was trying to keep them in mind, but sometimes places and the histories of them were mentioned just for the sake of mentioning them. I'm all for developing some depth, but at least give the reader some pay off for knowing these people and places, or don't introduce them at all! ARGH :(

Also, why do single characters have multiple names?!! It is hard enough to remember one or two. Example: Strider, Aragorn, Dunadan, Ranger of the North, Ellesar are all the same person - I mean, COME ON!

Also, Tom Bombadil was quirky and all that, but we spent way too much time with him for him to be this unimportant *sigh*

So what did I enjoy?

- The opening scene was well paced and exciting after having read The Hobbit and already being familiar with the Shire and some of the characters.
- The characters, especially the hobbits! Sam Gamgee is quite entertaining. His loyalty is to be commended. I think he especially shone when he snuck into the Council of Elrond and when he knew his master so well that he was able to catch up with Frodo who was trying to leave them all behind. He was able to calm his panic of Frodo missing to think it all through, "'Whoa, Sam Gamgee!' he said aloud. 'Your legs are too short, so use your head! Le me see now! Boromir isn't lying, that's not his way; but he hasn't told us everything. Something scared Mr. Frodo badly. He screwed himself up to the point, sudden. He made up his mind at last - to go. Where? Off East. Not without Sam? Yes, without even his Sam. That's hard, cruel hard'" (pg 524). Aww, Sam is hurt but keeps on thinking and intercepts Frodo in time to join him. All is right in the world with their friendship.
- Boromir's slow corruption was well forshadowed and I think that's what made the last chapter so satisfying.
- I appreciate Frodo's introspection. I would have liked to spend a bit more time with him to learn of his character and musings more.
- I thought the fellowship's grieving of Gandalf to be very realistic. Frodo's song was touching.
- The bar scene at the Prancing Pony held some comic relief and action, and I admit the Black Riders were an ominous threat.
- The reveal that Gollum was following them was an exciting turn of events.

The best chapters: The first chapter was a good hook! The last one saved the pace of the story and makes me more optimistic about picking up the next novel. I also enjoyed "Strider" "The Council of Elrond" "The Bridge of Khazad-dum" and "The Mirror of Galadriel."

The chapters that could be shortened to one page: I'm looking at you, "The Old Forest" and "In the House of Tom Bombadil"

All in all, I think this book would be made all the better with some of the non-important setting descriptors edited out. That being said, I appreciate the great history of Middle Earth presented. I am intrigued by Frodo's story and mission and will continue to see him carry it out - hopefully we can focus in on this mission more. :)

The first book is unnecessarily long, boring and mostly irrelevant.

This book was slow, but I still enjoyed it.

The beginning was very long. I get that this is the setup for what is essentially a 1000 page book (as LOTR is meant to be read as a book, not a trilogy but I can't read all that in one go), but it didn't need to go on about some relatively unnecessary topics for as long as it did. Honestly, the first 200 pages had some major pacing issues, which makes the entire book difficult to get through. After the first half, however, the book definitely picked up and got pretty interesting and much more readable.

The characters were all over the place. Over the course of the book there are probably 9 main characters and I only really had a sense of 4/5 of them, the rest just kind of merged together in one way or another. The ones who I was able to separate from the rest of the characters were pretty interesting, and I think I got the most out of the characters through seeing them interact with each other as most of them felt pretty boring as individuals.

The worldbuilding was pretty good, although Tolkien tended to just dump it on the reader through occasional pages of in-depth, complex explanation, which was just really confusing. I did like what I could understand though.

Overall, this book could have done with less of everything: less pages (300 instead of 400 maybe), less characters, less paragraphs of pure worldbuilding- but the parts that didn't feel unnecessary were actually really good.

And all the song lyrics! They probably look quite nice in the physical book but having my audiobook narrator suddenly start to sing badly in the middle of a scene made me want to hurl my phone out the window. I’ll never get the name Tom Bombadil out of my subconscious.

*3.5* I love Tolkien and this book is definitely one of his greats. However, I had to take into account that most of the first half of the book I dreaded reading. Tom bombadil, how long it took to start on the main journey, and the journey of the three hobbits (Frodo, Sam, and Pippin) to the ferry were very, VERY dry. Everything from the hobbit’s meeting of strider on in the story were amazing, probably a 4.5 out of 5.

Oh okay, So that's Lord of the Rings. There were lots of songs like The Hobbit and for the most part I enjoyed the songs, especially reading the book while listening to the audiobook. I know this book was originally published in 1954, but I still didn't expect the not so subtle of the racism in the book. No need to try to read between the lines when characters are talking about the bad black men and not wanting to let them into the village. Also, there's definitely anti-semitism, but I would recommend to Google that than go off my lonely opinion.

Overall, the book was entertaining, but there were some slow, boring moments too. I  didn't care much for the long meeting and all the different histories the characters go into. May or may have not skimmed through that chapter, trying to get through it as quickly as possible. I can, of course, see how J.R.R. Tolkien impacted fantasy as a genre and I plan to finish the series. But if the series as is was released in today's day and age I would have probably not read the series.

Once I have finished the books, I'm curious to watch the movies and see the differences. I saw them many years ago, but I don't remember much at all.

Really quite boring, especially at the beginning, but I do see the appeal and of course understand the impact on all other fantasy/fiction. FINALLY I have been able to read this book and finish it. It was a long time coming. For ages, I couldn't tolerate Tolkien's writing long enough to make it past the first few chapters. Luckily, I've aged since my last attempt at reading this, and I've also slogged through far more massive, epic fantasy novels. I felt it was finally time, and I'm glad to say, I can finally appreciate it.

To be fair, my main complaint hasn't changed -- Tolkien's writing is still very flowy, descriptive, very winding and slow to get moving. It makes for a slow, rather dull read. Fellowship isn't a particularly long book by my standards, and it still felt like it took me forever. And at it's core, the book is 90% about people walking and 7% about people eating and making merry, and 3% of anything actionable that drives the plot meaningfully forward.

Still, since I went into it fully accepting that, and knowing what I was getting myself into, I was able to enjoy it. It was a pleasant read. Tolkien is a master at his craft, and he takes you on an epic journey, masterfully keeping track of a rather large cast of characters. The whole feel of the book is peaceful, meandering. Even the scenes were I was meant to feel afraid, where the danger was imminent, were pretty tame. That is perhaps my other complaint - this his writing is not exactly dynamic. And while he does well to convey peace and tranquility, grandiosity, splendor, even dread, doubt and urgency, nothing really makes me feel danger strongly. Not when Frodo got stabbed by the ringwraith, not while Gandalf struggled against the Balrog. The most exciting scenes were told in the same meandering, slow way as the rest of the book.

In fact, now that I've had some time to reflect on the book, I find myself having to downgrade it's rating from 4- to 3-stars. Again, it's not a bad book, per se. Just a little boring.

This book has a lot of potential, incredible depth and breadth of world, and is written in very classic, literary prose. The lore I found myself deeply drawn in by, and ravenous for more. That said, the actual adventure in this first volume falls very flat. Over half of the book is reading about the characters wandering through different environments and climate conditions, with very little happening that is actually of interest or even relevant to the overall plot. I was swept up deeply in the beginning of the story, of the history and the threat, but from the moment they actually set off on the adventure, my interest waned tremendously. The whole beginning of the adventure with Tom Bombadil and the hobbits meandering with difficulty through forests was a pointless waste of time, and set this adventure off from the start as a chore to get through. Worse, we were subjected to Frodo walking through forests for days just to reach his new home before setting off on his quest, when he could have just driven there and saved the walking for the actual quest so there’s not even more to read where nothing is happening. Had the entirety of this part been cut, the book would have been much improved. While the council, history, and decisions at Rivendell captivated me again for a time, the following trek into the mountains ventured back into monotonous territory of long and boring travels, and while the mines of Moria at least provided some plot, wars in the darkness are not of great interest to me. Lothlorien proved intriguing in the realm of elven magic, and the end was somewhat interesting at least, though never having been fond of splitting up the party and going alone unnecessarily as a plot point, I don’t think much of Frodo’s decision at this point. Overall, this first volume is way longer than it needs to be and gets way too bogged down in unimportant details, which detracts from the plot, so I’m giving it 3 stars.

When I first read The Hobbit by Tolkien, I fell in love with the story and it was wonderful to accompany Bilbo on his adventures and I couldn’t wait to finally start reading The Lord of the Rings series. This is the book series that has defined the genre of fantasy since its release and I was excited to find out why this story is so widely adored.

We are introduced to Frodo Baggins, a relation of Bilbo’s. Frodo has inherited the One Ring that Bilbo found on his previous adventure, which had been lost for centuries. Frodo has become the Ringbearer and must destroy the Ring before Sauron, the Dark Lord obtains it and enslaves the entirety of Middle-Earth.

I loved all of the characters and found myself becoming attached to young Frodo and Sam Gamgee instantly. The compelling danger of the One Ring intrigued me and I could feel its power through the pages. I also found myself in awe of the Elves and their world, much like Sam who absolutely loved them.

I appreciate what LOTR has done for literature because it has inspired many other classic stories throughout the years but I found myself getting bored and didn’t like how SLOW the pacing was. I’m not considered a fast reader by any means, but it’s taken me over a month to finish this book which is unlike me. When Frodo and the Company had reached Rivendell and attended the Council of Elrond, a lot was said about many different characters and Elven events that happened in the past but it felt like a huge information dump which was hard to keep up with and went over my head.

I’m an illustrator so imagining things in my head comes easy but when I’m distracted by descriptions of the trees and the appearance of the enemies aren’t well described, then someone simply shouts “Orcs are coming”, it was difficult to imagine what they were which in turn, took the emotional elements and suspense away.

Parts of this book were amazing but other parts just felt too lengthy. Tolkien has clearly succeeded in creating a world that many readers and fans of fantasy have loved for generations and I am glad to have finally read the first instalment of the series. I have never seen the films so Lord of the Rings is completely new to me. Maybe I shall give the films a watch before continuing the books...

Having just read 'The Hobbit', it only made sense to continue with the imaginative writings of Tolkien and try to expand my mind beyond my normal non-fiction tendencies into the world of good, clean fantasy and to slow down and enjoy the journey along the way. The point of the journey is not always clear to the reader, and I believe that to be a major contributor of the widespread public admiration of Tolkien's works. It is the journey itself, rather than the destination, that draws praise for this classic trilogy. The turn of events during these escapades is usually predictable. Hike into a thick, dark forest at night during a fog storm with a full moon and few provisions - and it is no surprise that danger lurks. Part of this predictability is perhaps what draws many readers in.

Like other readers, however, I grew frustrated with some of the plots. At the risk of sounding irreverent to what is deemed as one of the world's greatest pieces of literature, I had a hard time getting into this book. I wrestled to understand the point of some of the conversations, some of the characters, some of the places visited and people met. With these questions, my tendency was to go and try to find out more, to find out why. With this searching, however, came few answers.

After reading some of the reviews of the book, others have felt the same and are met with criticism encouraging them to "just slow down and enjoy". For those of us boring people in the world that want a reason for why things happen, sometimes that slowing-down-enjoyment is a self-inflicted struggle. Maybe we are just too logical and left-brained. Maybe I am too dense to follow so many plotlines - or are they really even plotlines at all? - I couldn't tell. Maybe the next two books will uncover the answers.

I can understand why this book fascinates. The vivid descriptions of the characters and settings, the imaginative stories and illustrations dreamed up by a clever mind - all of this makes at least this reader more of a fan of Tolkien's knack for creativity than the actual writings themselves. I found it hard to jump on the bandwagon.

La compagnia dell’anello è il primo libro della trilogia più famosa di Tolkien. Pubblicato nel 1954, narra la storia di Frodo che,venuto in possesso dell'Anello del Potere, è costretto ad andare a Mordor per distruggerlo. Un gruppo formato da Hobbit, Elfi, Nani e Uomini lo accompagna, la cosiddetta Compagnia dell’anello. Le tappe del cammino li conducono attraverso molte esperienze diverse, finché la scomparsa di Gandalf, trascinato negli abissi da un'orrenda creatura, li lascia senza guida. Così si scioglie la Compagnia dell'Anello e i suoi membri si disperdono, minacciati da forze tenebrose, mentre la meta sembra disperatamente allontanarsi.
Inizialmente sembrava noioso e lento da leggere, ma continuando sono riuscita a immergermi nella terra di mezzo con Frodo e i suoi compagni e ho iniziato ad emozionarmi, a provare gioia, tristezza e paura con loro. Alcune parti sono più veloci di altre, ma in sostanza tutte bellissime. L’unica cosa che non sopporto sono le canzoni presenti in quasi tutto il libro.

So I had a love/hate relationship with this book, to say the least.
The parts I loved were: the camaraderie between the members of the Fellowship, the beautiful descriptions of certain places and situations, and how much love and care clearly went into the book.

The parts I hated are a lot more extensive, hence why I gave it 3 stars. I felt that for the most part I was extremely bored whilst reading this. Yes, there were times when I thoroughly enjoyed reading about how certain places or trees or mountains or leaves or the sky were described, however it got very old after the first couple chapters. I'm not joking when I say this man really described every tree, every change in weather, every sight along the journey, every rock on every cliff, hill or mountain and every star in the sky. It genuinely got to the point where I had to laugh every time he described a tree or how the sky looked.
If you took a shot every time he unnecessarily describes something, you'd be dead before you finish the first chapter.
Another thing I hated was how slow paced this book was. There were so may entire chapters dedicated to just slow travel where almost nothing that important happens, and it's SO BORRRING!
And the exposition! Oh! the exposition... I mean we'd spend entire chapters on exposition dumps from gandalf and co. I almost stopped reading at several points because I had no idea wtf they were talking so much about. There are so many names and places with multiple names in different made-up languages that it gets incredibly confusing when they're all mentioned in a couple paragraphs with little to no context.
I understand that Tolkien built a whole ass world and wanted to cram a fat chunk of it into this story but it's a little too much at times. I appreciate the time and effort and craftsmanship of the world building but for me it was almost impossible to fully get a hold of and enjoy.
You'd think after all that I'd give it less than 3.5/5 but I just had to give it a decent score due to the sheer effort that was put into the world. Also, there were entire chapters that I enjoyed (granted only about 3 of them, but still). And the writing was very beautiful throughout.
I will be continuing with the books, but I think it might be a bit of a slog... alas, I have hope that I'll enjoy it.
In my opinion, Tolkien is great at world building, but can be a little droll in story telling, but definitely fascinating.
3.5* Love the characters and plot but there were so many parts that bored the life out of me.

Fantasy fiction is not my favorite genre. So I never really “got into” the book. I
read this book for cultural awareness, as I so often hear references made to the characters and locations. So now I’m glad I read it so I understand references to Gandalf, Frodo, Gollum, Mordor, etc.

My introduction to The Lord of the Rings is not through the books by J.R.R. Tolkien, but the film adaptations by Peter Jackson who for me created THE trilogy. During the early 2000s when the movies were a current phenomenon, I received the Tolkien trilogy as well as its prequel The Hobbit, together as a box-set. However, that sense of enjoyment I got from the movies was not there in the source material, which is absolutely a different beast that I felt had issues that might be addressed during my first read-through of the books in the past two decades.

So who is the Lord of the Rings? He is the Dark Lord Sauron, who had created the One Ring to rule the other Rings of Power as the ultimate weapon in his campaign to conquer and rule all of Middle-earth. During his adventure to the Lonely Mountain with the wizard Gandalf and thirteen dwarves, the hobbit Bilbo Baggins finds the One Ring, which had been in the possession of the creature Gollum. Years later, Gandalf realises what this ring is, which is then inherited to Bilbo’s cousin Frodo, who undertakes the quest to destroy it in the fires of Mount Doom in Mordor.

Having recently read The Hobbit – of which this book acknowledges some aspects – it is interesting to see how the author expanded from what was essentially a children’s book. Originally approached to write a sequel for The Hobbit, The Lord of the Rings was an excuse for Tolkien to delve deeper into the many cultures and languages within Middle-earth. This is definitely apparent in the prologue titled “Concerning Hobbits, and other matters”, which goes into great length about the Shire and pipe-weed, along with Bilbo’s recount of how he found the Ring.

Once we get to the main chapters, it starts off as a semi-sequel to The Hobbit with Bilbo celebrating his 111th birthday where he is reunited with Gandalf. However, once Bilbo departs from the Shire, the focus shifts towards Frodo, who now carries the heavy burden, which has many reasons from the internal-external forces associated with the Ring, to the quest to Mount Doom where he may not return. Sauron may be referred to as the Enemy, but the One Ring – carrying the life force of the Dark Lord – is the more interesting antagonist as it enforces the psychological motivation that a number of characters confront, whether it is Frodo, the human Boromir or even the royal elf Galadriel. Although you can see the story as a simple case of good versus evil, and yet there is an evil within even the most innocent of characters, certainly Gollum’s backstory is one of tragedy.

The story of The Lord of the Rings is a good one, conveying some interesting ideas, and yet Tolkien’s biggest crux is over-emphasising world-building over storytelling. This first book goes through cultures of hobbits, elves, dwarves and men, and with the eponymous Fellowship (or the Company as it’s often referred to), it is about a group formed of multi-culturism fighting one force that wants to rule all. However, you have to read through fourteen chapters so that you get to the Fellowship off on their quest. So much of the book feels like the hobbits spending way too much time on one place, such as the whole Tom Bombadil section that doesn’t advance the plot, while there are chapters like “The Council of Elrond” that are huge exposition dumps where we have to find out everything from history to current alliances.

As the first volume of a trilogy – of which Tolkien did not originally written as such, as evident in the way this book just ends – it does a lot of the heavy set-up which is the biggest problem. But there is enough in terms of character moments (like the dynamic between Legolas and Gimli) and epic set-pieces (the Mines of Moria is a highlight) that ultimately saves The Fellowship of the Ring.
