I have a lot of nostalgia for the characters and this story because I grew up on the films, but honestly, reading this just made me appreciate the films more. The writing is incredibly tedious, and to say the first half of this book was a slog is an understatement. The second half was significantly better and far more interesting, and it did make the writing slightly more tolerable. The audiobook also helped with this, though I admittedly zoned out for quite a bit of the book.

Sam, Merry, and Pippin absolutely carry this book on their backs, and I honestly think they are the best part about this book. I do also think the worldbuilding is quite incredible, and I can see why so many people love this book. That being said, I definitely do NOT think this is a must-read to be a fantasy fan, so the SFF gatekeepers can just sit down tbh.

I think it's also worth noting that there are definite racist and sexist undertones, as expected from a white male author in the 50s. I wouldn't say it's the worst I've ever read, especially given the publication date, but it's not great.

Overall, would not recommend. I may still continue on in this series eventually, but it's definitely not a priority.

This rating is more about a personal impression rather than an evaluation of the skillfulness of the author or the complexity of the book itself.

Completing the first part of the trilogy, I have to admit, that the world within the book is immensely complex and intricate. Maybe too much so for my personal taste, as I found myself drifting away from the plot on more occasions than one.

Whilst reading the Fellowship of the Ring, I struggled to make much progress in a single go or get immersed in the plotline. Lots of descriptions, more so the strange names of people long gone, who just did not leave any impression. I understand that it's a part of creating a complex world with a thorough history, yet it just didn't register as interesting to me personally. Maybe it just takes a certain type of person?

Even so, LOTR is a fantasy classic and I'll persist to complete the trilogy, however much effort it takes.

All in all, I am mightily impressed by J.R.R. Tolkien and his talented writing. Creating songs, inventing a language and putting in all kinds of little details in order to create this masterpiece. Surely it requires a lot of effort and talent.

So, as a book, I'd objectively give it 5 stars. Yet subjectively, I wouldn't find myself immersed, I resorted to perseverance and hoped for it to end sooner. The story so far didn't leave a strong personal impression, so I'll leave it at 3 stars for now.

The first of the epic trilogy in The Lord of the Rings.

The Fellowship of the Ring was J.R.R. Tolkien’s second novel. Published in 1954, it was an instant success, as fans had begged Tolkien for a sequel to The Hobbit since it was first released. Famous writers such as C.S. Lewis and W. H. Auden praised the work as the finest of their generation.

The first book in The Lord of the Rings series, but the second work in the Middle-Earth universe overall, it quickly became a bestseller. In 2001, Peter Jackson released the movie The Fellowship of the Ring, starring many famous actors such as Elijah Wood, Sean Bean, and Ian McKellen.

Finish reading this review and many others here!

I know The Lord of the Rings books are classics, and, for that reason, I believe everybody should read them. However, this wasn't my favorite book. Nothing seemed to be very urgent for the members of the fellowship. Frodo spends years in the shire after receiving the ring, they spend months in Rivendell, etc... You know the feeling of not wanting to put a book down? I didn't feel that.

*THIS REVIEW MIGHT CONTAIN SPOILERS*

This read was interesting. The world building and detail of this world was amazing. Tolkien must have spent an insane amount of time on developing languages, cultures and histories for his fantasy races. Many creatures, aspects and themes in the story originate from traditional folklore and mythology- especially Germanic mythology. The writing style was really descriptive and the poems/songs were really cute and nice to read.

The characters were alright. Bilbo is fun because his wealth, long-lasting youth and outside status made him eccentric and unique. His addiction to the ring and lack of willingness to give it up showed the craziness the ring causes. Frodo is the orphaned 'chosen one' who inherits the ring and is forced on this deadly adventure after he gets pursued by the Black Riders. Rather than Gandalf telling him when and how to leave, he leaves at his own accord with his hobbit companions, which gave him some agency. His hobbit companions are always whining or causing trouble while Strider/Aragorn is the unelected leader of the Company with a slightly creepy edge to him. Gandalf's death at the hands of the balrog was sad— his character is unique and quite well developed. However, I feel like he is going to get resurrected again. Boromir's turn to the dark side was interesting. Watching everyone fight over this one ring was funny and entertaining.

However, the main thing that was annoying was the lack of characterisation of the villains. It is unclear why Sauron and the Mordorians are evil and harmful for the world. Tolkien tells that they are evil but there are very few things that they do that can't be rationalised and explained. Sauron, the titular character (the true Lord of the Rings) receives no characterisation. He does not have a personality, family or personal motivation as to why he wants power and domination. It is unclear what he wants to do with his power once he achieves world domination. The ring was made by Sauron and therefore it should be rightfully his. Right??? Likewise, the characters of the Dark Riders were poorly developed and were given no characterisation whatsoever. The good vs evil narrative was annoying, especially because the concept of "evil" was poorly defined.

I feel like I should start with an apology. I really did want to like this book. And I definitely tried to. But it just wouldn't happen. And if you're a massive fan of this book, I would recommend not reading this review. I'd initially planned on being nice, but I don't do that with other books, and this should be no exception.

The synopsis, for those who've somehow evaded all knowledge of the series, is that Frodo, a hobbit, is given a magical ring by his uncle Bilbo. Frodo then finds out that the ring belongs to an evil (dark) lord, who has been searching for it. And that his goons are close to finding Frodo in his little town. And with advice from a wizard named Gandalf, Frodo and three of his friends set out on a journey to... make a plan?

See, we've already come to my first issue with the book: the lack of plot. Frodo, Sam, Pippin and Merry set out of their town, Hobbiton, to get to Rivendell. It's a very long and "perilous" trip. And they have no plan as to what they're actually going to do. They're just heading there and hoping that someone will tell them what to do. And I could be okay with that, except even in Rivendell, they don't make a definite plan. The book is 90% travel, and they don't get to deciding where they want to travel to until the end of the book.

Speaking of travel... there's so much of it. It's all walking/riding while they talk and occasionally stumble into other people. Oh, and world-building. And I emphasize that because I have opinions about it.

You know, I tried to read this book once before. I found it difficult to get into, and I've since heard that many people consider this book a heavy read. And it is, but not in a good way. There are just pages and pages of Tolkien giving detailed accounts of historical events, or telling us about someone's entire family history. And most of it has nothing to do with the events of the book!

If I were to take out the names of people and places, the book would be half as long as it is. And at one point, it was all just blah blah blah... And I'm sorry, but that's not my idea of good world-building.

There is a caveat, though. And that's that, after listening to why Tolkien wrote the book, I'm not mad about all the details. He wrote this book for himself, and these were the details that mattered to him. And I can definitely appreciate the amount of time and effort he put into constructing a world this vivid, with this much history. And I plan to reread the book after I've finished the series and watched the movies (finally!), hoping that I enjoy those efforts more.

And I think that's all my major complaints out of the way. Except maybe one about Frodo being a very dull protagonist. Of the side characters, Gandalf was interesting, and so was Strider. And Sam was my favourite. I've heard people talk about how much they love him, and I see why. He's so earnest and loyal that you can't help it.

I also enjoyed the politics involved with the various races, like the animosity between elves and dwarves. Or the opinions each race has of the others, and how that could affect their chances against the real evil, the Lord of the Rings.

Finally, the book is beautifully written. Prose is another thing that mattered to Tolkien, and he did a great job with it. His words weave an atmosphere and feelings that do more to let you see his world than the million different names. In regards to all the songs... all I'll say is that they weren't for me. Just like a lot of things in the novel weren't. Still, I'm curious to see where the series is headed.

I already have the second audiobook. Same narrator, which is good because Rob Inglis did a great job. There were a few occasions where I found the narration to be a tad inconsistent, but overall, I think he did his best with the number of characters the book has.

And... that's it for this review. It's already longer than I'd planned. I hope it didn't make you hate me.

Good but not great. The value of this book is cultural and historical and the precedent it set in the fantasy world. That doesn’t make it enjoyable to read now. There are really good elements here, it’s like a primordial hero’s journey that is present in our collective unconscious.

But, the writing has not aged well. The pacing is incredibly awkward. The climax of the book, in Moria, comes way too early in the book, and the remainder of the book seems aimless. Huge parts of the “plot” are described by characters during a meeting that lasts forever. Why could we not have seen these critical parts of the story first hand? There are also tons of “episodes” in the plot that are inconsequential to the plot and just feel like derailments from the main plot- Tom Bombadil, the wight barrows...

So, yes there are parts that are enjoyable. But there are a lot of parts that are unnecessary and uninteresting.

This is technically "unabridged" as per the cover, but only because it is an unabridged NPR radio drama. It's not an unabridged edition of The Fellowship of the Ring in its textual totality.

Now, that said. I appreciate that goodreads has connected works together for ease of discoverability, but it can be frustrating for this particular book --especially since it is not what they did for the similarly created BBC recordings. On the back-end, I can get the rda perspective for wanting to connect all of these things (like the library nerd I am), but I really think this should be a separate entry because it is so drastically different from the full text --even the full audio text. This is a drama, performed as audio theater and it is about 20% of the length of the full text (yes, that much is cut/compressed in this version).

It was enjoyable enough. The NPR version does a lot less hemming and hawing that listeners experienced in the BBC version. We don't have Bilbo or Frodo dawdling around at the beginning to set up a frame narrative for remembering the events. That can be a little frustrating when in the books, it was an action in the present and occurring over time naturally with a hinted frame through the books at the end. In this instance, NPR cuts right to it and they just do the drama. The voice work, however, is sub-par to the BBC's version of the drama. That's not too surprising given the popularity historically and continuously of radio dramas on the BBC, so they have much better, experienced voice actors (or maybe I'm biased to the unusual accents the American actors use).

I do always take an affront to any version that makes Sam seem silly or sound less serious and this recording did do that. On the bright side, the Treebeard and Merry & Pippin story is explored as evenly as Frodo & Sam's (which even on screen has not historically been the case). All of the hobbits are treated fairly and as a team. The way this drama is setup we see that hobbits are crucial to the future of Middle Earth just as they are in the original texts --all of them! and that is something other media take for granted (like Bakshi and even Peter Jackson's works to a degree).

With the time crunch, there are some sections squished together and sped up. We see the Arwen & Aragorn storyline cut for time and the re-forging/giving of Narsil/Anduril was very rushed. Aragorn does some exposition on it, but it is really crammed in at awkward places. Brightside, they did manage to wiggle in that meme about Aragorn forgetting Legolas's dad's name.

Overall it was a pleasant read, but I did not seem to be pulled into Tolkien's world as I was into the world of A Song of Ice and Fire.

Still, I'm happy I got to read it and I'm even a bit curious what Frodo will be up to (and up against) in the second book. Yes, I'm one of those people who haven't seen the movies oops.

Nikto nemôže poprieť fakt, že J. R. R. Tolkien a jeho knihy je akýmsi ,,základným kameňom“ fantasy tvorby. S týmto tvrdením sa aj ja stotožňujem ako milovník fantasy príbehov. Fantasy žáner zbožňujem už pomerne dlhú dobu, ale až teraz som sa dostala k tejto knihe, za ktorú ďakujem vydavateľstvu preškoly.sk.

Myslím, že každý fanúšik fantasy by si ju mal prečítať, aj keď nie každému sadne. Mne nesadla. Určite to nie je autorova chyba, ale tak úplne ani moja. Proste sme sa nezhodli.

Najprv som si myslela, že do knihy by som sa mohla zamilovať aj napriek tomu, že film ma veľmi neohúril – možno aj preto, lebo som ho videla hneď, ako vyšiel a potom som sa k nemu už nevrátila. Filmové spracovanie ma trošku nudilo a myslela som si, že makniha ohúri.

Tu musím vysvetliť fakt, že kniha ja rozdelená na dve kniha. V prvej knihe sú vlastne iba štyri postavy – štyria hobiti, ktorí putujú. A putujú a potom ešte ďalej putujú. Občas niekoho stretnú, alebo sa niekde zastavia, ale v podstate iba putujú. A konečne som sa po nekonečnom a úmornom čítaní... oprava, po nekonečnom a úmornom putovaní dostala k druhej knihe, kde sa objavia aj ďalšie postavy a hneď sa mi príbeh zdal zaujímavejší.

Autor dokáže neskutočne popísal prírodu, hory a vedela som si predstaviť, ako im pri putovaní musí šušťať lístie pod nohami, aj ako vonia vzduch. Tieto opisy boli vypiplané do dokonalosti. Na druhej strane mi chýbali opisy postáv, lebo ak by som nevidela film, nevedela by som si predstaviť ani jednu z nich. Musím voči autorovi vysloviť kritiku ešte na jednu vec, ktorá mi prekážala, a to že keď sa už popri všetkom tom putovaní objavila zaujímavá a bojová scéne, autor ju zhrnul na také tri riadky a postavy putovali ďalej. To fakt? Verím, že Frodove dobrodružstvá si zaslúžia detailnejší popis a trošku viac akcie a napätia. Napriek tomu na Pána prsteňov nezanevriem a mám v pláne prečítať celú sériu.

Na záver opäť ďakujem vydavateľstvu preškoly.sk za zaslanie knihy a túto a mnoho ďalších skvelých kníh nájdete na ich stránke.

1/21/21: Three Stars...but ONLY because I love the movie this book inspired

Well... At least I now can say I've read the first book of Lord of the Rings. And I can say with absolute and complete honesty: The Movie Was Better. MUCH Better. It was a great story. I mean, it inspired a truly EPIC film trilogy...and I DON'T mean that weird, and somewhat creepy, animated one from the 80s (still trying to erase the image of singing/dancing cartoon Orcs from my head). But the book... My overall reaction is "Meh" at best. And the only reason I gave it even three stars is because the movie that came from it.
What I Didn't Like
* Things took FAR too long to get going. The beginning was so much a Slow Burn that its barely-there simmer couldn't heat an area the size of a shoebox. Which leads into...

* Overly descriptive. I get that Tolkien wanted to establish a setting, but there are better to do so ways than describing every damn rock and tree and eyelash down to the atomic detail. Absolutely nothing was left to the imagination of the reader. Almost like J.R.R. didn't trust the reader to "get it right." As a reader with a vivid imagination who prefers a bit of leeway in picturing the world (and characters) about which I'm reading, I feel quite a bit insulted by this. This alone loses author cred with me.

* Too many scenes that could have been WAY shorter. The Counsel of Elrond, or example. I pretty much skipped this whole thing because so much of it was unnecessary and took away from the story.

* On the flipside, actions scenes that could have been fleshed out were glossed over.

* Two Words: Tom Bombadil. Not only was this whole bit irrelevant to the story, but the character was super annoying. Had he been put into the movies, it would have spoiled the whole thing. Unless the character was played by Jack Black, the only actor who could've pulled it off with any success.

* And lastly, but not leastly... Total Sausage Party. The entire book is populated by dudes and the only female characters, save for Galadriel (who is awesome, btw), are nothing more than outdated stereotypes. Goldberry waits on T.B. and the guests hand and foot, Lobelia Sackville-Baggens is a bitchy shrew, and Arwen is nothing more than a pretty decoration who doesn't even have a speaking part. If I wasn't insulted by the affront to my imagination (see overly descriptive), I certainly was by this! (aside: I know we get Eowyn and her "I Am No Man!" bit, but that's not until book 3...and we've got a LOT of Bromanceship to go before we get there) I could rant for pages about this, but Goodreads doesn't leave me enough space. And then my review would run the risk of becoming as long-winded as the book about which I'm ranting.

There isn't a lot to say about this book, for someone who read it like I did. I'm not one for books like this, usually; I am more of a fan of character-driven stories, and while sometimes the glimpses of large-scale politics we see in this book are interesting to me (e.g. the Council of Elrond), the long descriptions of the environment are not. However, I appreciated the detailed world building, the glimpses of the immense history of every character, location, or object. The scale of this universe is of a very rare caliber, and I applaud the effort. I imagine Tolkien's work is a situation where the more you put in, the more you get. Unfortunately, I don't think I'll be diving into the specifics of the Elven tongues, but I get the sense that there's a lot going on behind the scenes. The songs, for the most part, flew entirely over my head.

In terms of the glimpses into the vast lore, highlights for me were Galadriel and the history of the ring. That said, there are much better ways of conveying this information. If J.R.R Tolkien was writing today, he would have probably just made a wiki.

This isn't to say there aren't unique and vibrant characters in The Fellowship of the Ring. Each member of the Fellowship is charismatic and likable in their own right (yes, even Boromir), and their strengthening bonds and relationship with each other are fleshed out and endearing (Frodo and Sam; Legolas and Gimli; Aragorn and Gandalf; Frodo and Gandalf). This is why the second half of this book shines. It has just the right balance of questing and lore, and the journey through Middle Earth proper is compelling.

The first half, though, was definitely a slog, to the point that I took a multiple months-long break. There just wasn't a lot going on as Frodo and his friends stumbled through the woods, that is, unless you're an avid fan of the geographic features of the Shire and surrounding regions. I was just waiting for "the plot to start" --really, waiting for the immense world I've heard so much about to open up. The start of this book was unnecessarily slow, and the sections where Tolkien tries to invoke pastoral beauty and wonder generally fell flat for me (which is strange, because I think he absolutely nails it when the gang gets to Lothlorien; basically, everything that has to do with elves is great).

I probably won't read this again, and if I want to catch up to the story I'll probably watch the movie, although the movie is of course totally different, way more different than I could have imagined before finishing the book. But I think there's just enough here to keep me intrigued to continue on to next chapter of the saga, the next time I have a few dozens of hours to spare.

Note on the French translation: it's really good in my opinion, but my French isn't great, and it was a little difficult to understand at times. This isn't a flaw of the book. If anything it's a strength. Comparing a few of the more poetic sections to the original English, I found the translation really nailed it.

Other than that, The Fellowship of the Ring is a very good book filled with fantasy and I totally recommend!

Re-read Fellowship for a book club/podcast and was (mostly) pleasantly surprised! The prologue is still a hot mess, fight me, but there are some genuinely charming and nuanced moments throughout this book that I really enjoyed. And also there is a lot of walking, which I did not. Tolkien needed a better editor, and I'll stand by that to my dying day.

I wonder if anyone has ever done some kind of substantial study about the landscape of Middle Earth as described by Tolkien, because he puts a heck of a lot of time and effort into something that I apparently just blank out of my memory after every read. The pattern of walking for most of the chapter--with commentary about the plants, the lay of the land, the weather, and any animals seen--and then squeezing all the action into the last few pages was undeniable. It kind of amazes me that an editor let Tolkien publish this book as it stands, without substantially reducing Part I. In fact, in the synopsis of The Fellowship of the Ring at the front of The Two Towers, the entirety of Part I takes up two sentences in one of four paragraphs.

I wish Tolkien had taken the time to do a little bit more character establishment along the way. Because this book is epic in scope, I miss a lot of that witty internality from The Hobbit that gave us such insight into Bilbo's character, as well as minor characters along the way. Not that it needs to be witty, not in a SERIOUS book like The Lord of the Rings, but some of the character changes seemed abrupt, particularly Legolas and Gimli's sudden friendship. Much's of Boromir's behavior makes more sense in hindsight: the first time I read, this, I was surprised that an heir to a realm who (seemingly) impulsively took off on a journey of hundreds of miles to an unknown destination just to get advice about a dream then whined about any more experienced advice about what road to take home. It's almost certainly because he wants to keep the Ring as close to his homeland as possible, but we don't know that until the very end.

On this read-through, Legolas seemed very young and inexperienced to me, at least compared to many of the other elves, which surprised me for an elf from a place as full of potential danger as Mirkwood. Gimli is certainly interested in Moria--he knows that it's ruined but still wants to see and respect the work that his people created. Legolas, when the Fellowship approaches Lothlorien, is sad that he's seeing the forest in less-beautiful winter, and to Aragorn's reply that it's beautiful--and safe--enough as it is, Legolas just whines again that he isn't there in spring. Plus there's his protest that he alone of the Fellowship should be excepted from Aragorn's decision that all of them should go blindfolded in solidarity with Gimli. It's such a stark contrast with Pippin, definitely young (don't we find out in the Appendix that he's in his "tweens", his twenties?--who's brilliantly loyal enough to go against all of his own wishes in order to support Frodo.

I used to write such intelligent, English-major reviews. Now they're all just ramblings about my thoughts and feelings, even though I participated in an entire, semester-long class about Tolkien's world. Ugh.

Still, for all the characters don't have the kind of emotional depth and development and I enjoy in most books, they do open up to the reader over time--much more time than would be realistic for people forced into close proximity and cooperation for hundreds of miles, but we do get there.

I'll close with some thoughts about Aragorn, whose character is so different between the books and the films (which I also recent rewatched with Areg). In the latter, he has "turned from that [the kingship of Gondor] long ago [and] chosen exile." Sure, it fits with the generations that came before him, but it's also cowardly. In the book, though I do wonder why it took him so long in his very long life to face up to his heritage, Aragorn is grimly determined to take responsibility for his ancestors' mistakes and make them right: there is never any question that he will help Frodo and then go to take up the throne in Gondor, to the extent that he carries around a hundreds-of-years-old heirloom--the broken sword of Isildur--on his journeys in the wild. (Not exactly a small, lightweight item you can tuck in your pocket, but perhaps it's a symbolic reminder of the weight of history on his--well, waist, not shoulders.)

But to me, reading this now in 2020, I appreciate this unrealistic-feeling sense of responsibility. There are people today who aren't even willing to wear a mask in order to help save the lives of their own loved ones, not to mention facing a 400-year history of deeply-rooted racism in his country. Yet here we have a character who voluntarily comes out of obscurity to right the wrongs of his many-times-forefathers. Unrealistic? Probably, though I do think we see some of his reluctance manifest in his long delay to decide whether he goes with Frodo or to Gondor. Classist and rooted in Tolkien's British culture of centuries of divinely-ordained monarchy? Definitely. Boromir's eagerness to accept help for his country from an unknown claimant to the throne and his historically significant sword doesn't ring true. But in 2020, wouldn't it be nice to see some people who have no claim to fame step up to the plate to save their own worlds, if not the whole one?

Perhaps Sam, Merry, and Pippin are the better comparisons here. Be like them, whoever you are. The wide world may not know you exist, but don't let that stop you. Protect your loved ones, your homeland, and the strangers to whom you owe nothing. Wear a mask. Take the quest to restore justice even if you never committed (or knowingly committed) injustice yourself. For pete's sake, care about something other than yourselves. Goodness knows I need to be better at it.

I grew up on Lord of the Rings--I remember sneaking out of bed and down the stairs to watch the Fellowship of the Ring through the reflection of a painting when I was little. Gollum absolutely horrified me and the orcs frightened me, but I remember watching it all in awe.

Even though I've seen the films countless times, it took me until my freshman year of college to finally pick up any of Tolkien's books. I bought me a boxed set from Barnes and Noble with the trilogy and the Hobbit for Christmas that year. I read the Hobbit first, since a standalone seemed more approachable and the movies had all come out just a few years before. I was surprised to find it so hard to read--I honestly don't know that I would have continued it if not for an exceedingly long day at the airport.

I know, you're probably thinking that this review is for The Fellowship of the Ring, not the Hobbit. But my experience with the Hobbit is why I put off reading The Lord of the Rings for so long. I mean, I've had the books literally sitting right there for years and I never picked them up. So why did I ever pick up The Fellowship?

Perhaps I had a bit of guilt over having kept the poor books on the shelf for so long or maybe it was just because I was looking for a more classic book to read with my book club. In any case, I thought it would be better to have people to talk about it with and keep me accountable to finishing it (momma didn't raise no quitter, but she sure raised a heck of a procrastinator).

Reading The Fellowship of the Ring was a bit of a rollercoaster. I really didn't like the first half of the book. I was bored spitless and the worst part was that I felt bad that I felt bored. I wanted to like it, but it wasn't clicking. Quite honestly, I probably would have given up if I hadn't been reading it for my book club. But I'm glad I kept going. The second half was so much better than the first half. The pacing picked up, the scenery descriptions lessened (or maybe I became more immune to them), and the characters became more interesting.

So how was The Fellowship of the Ring? Good and bad, which is why I gave it an even 3 stars. Most of what I like also has parts of what I don't like. Here are my key takeaways:

As a linguist, I found the diversity and the evolution of the languages fascinating. But it did get to be a bit much in parts.

I liked the characters; however, I felt like we didn't get to know them very well. I kept wishing we had some stream of consciousness writing or even just some inner thoughts to see what the character was actually thinking instead of what they just said or did.

The descriptions were rather poetic and got my writer wheels turning, but goodness, Tolkien. Descriptions everywhere about everything. I got to the point where I'd kind of skim over them.

So how does one even rate The Fellowship of the Ring? It's a mixed bag for me, but ultimately, I'm glad I read it. I don't know if I'll continue with the series, but reading The Fellowship of the Ring at least once is worth it in my book.

Ironically, my first time reading The Fellowship of the Ring was at eight years old. I found it incredibly slow and unintelligible, and I haven't touched it since. Now, almost a decade later, after seeing the movies many times and fostering a deeper appreciation for the classics, I have finally revisited this novel. And may I say... I'm so glad I did. The movies really did not do this series justice. Because of the time constraints, the best parts of the story got cut out! Also, so much of the camaraderie between the Fellowship was lost, and the movies makes Frodo look like a whiny brat. Although the movies have their merit, particularly because of the visualization aspect, the book was (as books always are), on a completely different level. I absolutely loved the worldbuilding, Tolkien's writing style, the language, the description, the characters, etc etc etc. It was so fun to be a part of this world, and it makes me yearn to see the beauty of Lórien, the charm of the Shire, or meet the characters (especially Aragorn... what a man). Overall, I'm completely happy with this book, and, even though I know how the story goes, excited to continue the series!

Well, I finally did it. I have read 1/3 of The Lord of the Rings. This book has been sitting on my shelf since the beginning of summer last year, and I finally pushed through it.

The Fellowship of the Rings follows Frodo Baggins. He has inherited The One Ring from his uncle Bilbo Baggins ( who is our protagonist in The Hobbit ). He goes on a journey with companions to destroy the Ring in the fire of Mordor, before the enemy gets their hands on it, as it would cause great destruction and evil.

I thought that this book had both it's negatives and positives. I think I expected more from this book, but I'm glad I finally finished it. I loved the movies, and I'm looking forward to continuing on with the book.


The plot:

I thought this very much dragged. It took so long for something interesting to happen, that I didn't really care until after they left Rivendell and the real journey started, and only then did my reading experience become easier. Just so much walking and repetitive and unnecessary things happening. It took so long setting up. I liked the ending though. Sam and Frodo's friendship makes it all worth it.


The world-building:

Very interesting. I love the world that Tolkien has created. But what I don't like, is how we got a lot of the world-building through info dumps. But I'm excited to explore more of it.


The writing:

I don't think it's for me. It didn't capture my interest nor helped me become immersed into the story. It's not easy to get through and I am still not completely acoustomed with it especially considering I listened to The Hobbit.

Also I do not like the random song breaks, I skipped those.


The characters:

My favorite part of the book! I liked this cast of characters much more than the ones in The Hobbit. The friendships were wonderful. Sam, my cinnamon roll, I've adopted him in case you didn't know. He's too precious and was my favorite. I still do think we could have known a lot of them better, and that some did not have the same charm as in the adaptation, but overall I like following them and the bonds they are building.


Final Thoughts: Hopefully The Two Towers is better in the aspects I disliked. I mean the concept is interesting, but this was pretty boring. I expected better from this book and it took me so long to read, but it wasn't terrible. It was a middle tier book, so 3 stars makes sense.

I was inspired to read the LotR trilogy due to playing a video game from the universe. While I'm a huge fantasy reader, I had not been compelled at any point to read the series, though I have seen the movies multiple times.

Before I started reading this book, I decided to do some googling to see if the books are worth the read. I had, at one point, heard that the LotR books are rather boring to read through. After watching YouTube videos about the book & reading Reddit's opinion of it, I still felt compelled to read the trilogy after many years of disregarding it.

As I mentioned in a previous comment about the book, I can definitely see why some readers complain about the slow pacing and long, drawn out painting of the world. In the beginning chapters of the book, it's very off-putting. Tolkien definitely wanted readers to see the world of LotR as he saw it and so, took the time to draw out how the world appears using words and long descriptions of the landscapes.

However, one opinion that I have formed, where I seem to be alone in my thoughts on, is that he also did this with his expositions. This style of world building is incredibly evident in the chapter "The Council of Elrond". Particularly when Gandalf recounts his visit to Saruman and details his betrayal. This would have better worked as a prior chapter all on its own and would have stood much better to move the story along or grip the reader. Having Gandalf fully recount his tale of Saruman's betrayal during The Council did not even serve as a plot device established by Elrond in recounting how the Ring came to be with its present owner. It merely served as a long, drawn out explanation from Gandalf of why he did not come back to The Shire when Frodo was to set out on his journey.

There is one chapter near the end of the story that I felt was wholly and utterly useless. That chapter is "The Great River". It was nothing more than a chapter filled with the phrasing "The Company traveled and this is what the landscape looked like". It served no practical purpose to advance the plot. If you're going to read this book, skip this chapter.

While I will give Tolkien praise for his efforts in world building, I would also need to give criticism for the lack of character exposition and growth in his writing as there is little to no character development in any of the characters in Fellowship of the Ring. This makes being able to connect with any character in the story impossible since you know so little about most of them. Frodo is the worst of all, as on one page he's a character who seems thoughtful, knowledgeable and mature, but a few pages later, he's like a three year old child seeing something for the first time with no effort to hide his wonderment. It is this dichotomy in Frodo's behaviour and the lack of knowledge about the character's personality that makes you unable to speculate how he'll react to whatever situation the characters are in.

As for what made this book enjoyable, for me, it was the moments of peril and desperation, and also Tom Bombadil. There, I said it. I liked Tom Bombadil. I am convinced that without Tom having to save the hobbits not once but twice, the journey would have been over as soon as it began. Middle-Earth owes Tom Bombadil a nice bottle of elven wine. Moments such as on Weathertop, the Ford, the mines of Moria were all written in a way that just made me turn page after page and ultimately keep turning pages until the next moment of peril came when the writing would grip me once again and I'd keep going.

Is this book worth a read? Ask the elves for their advice.

As someone who grew up enjoying quite a few YA fantasy series and thought of herself as a fan of the genre, Lord of the Rings always remained a huge gap in my cultural knowledge. I had never read the books and never seen the movies.

Well, now I’m on my way to addressing the omission, but I’m not sure about my decision to consume the books before the movies. Tolkien is….a dry writer. Everyone warned me about this so I have no one to blame but myself.

Right from the prologue, I got a sense of where the man’s priorities lay. It’s quite bold of him to start with a brief, but detailed, history of the hobbits, a piece of expository worldbuilding that I think most authors would reserve for the end notes. (Even Hugo had the decency to place the infamous Waterloo section of Les Miserables at the beginning of Book Two.) I can’t speak for everyone, but I personally was not that curious to learn about the type of herb hobbits smoke when I hadn’t even encountered one in the story yet and I also don’t think I would have been too confused if I had read the book without understanding the structure of governance in the Shire. I actually didn’t realize until afterwards that the trilogy was a sequel to The Hobbit (I always thought The Hobbit was published afterwards as a prequel for some reason), so maybe Tolkien wrote this prologue in response to reader demand, but I’m not sure. The summary of The Hobbit itself was probably the most useful part, but various characters also cover that in the main book.

I’m sure something along this theme has been said by readers before me, but whatever Tolkien’s intentions, it doesn’t always feel like he set out to write a tale. It seems more like he created an immersive world and whipped up some characters with a mission that involved extensive travel so he could lure readers into a guided tour through the fancy maps he drew. Their other purpose seems to be to sing the numerous hobbit songs that he wrote, which are sprinkled liberally through the narrative. To Tolkien’s credit, when you read the book, the depth of the worldbuilding is apparent, but it seems like the story serves it more than it serves the story.

Despite all those gripes, I still plan on finishing the trilogy or at least on starting The Two Towers, mainly out of curiosity about where it’ll take me. As a protagonist, Frodo is relatively compelling and I appreciated the little moments that did resonate emotionally, particularly In many ways, I was reminded of the experience of reading an antiquated translation of some ancient epic. Often the language is stiff and you find yourself spending more time that you’d like on descriptions of places and gifts given, wondering how on earth this was cutting edge entertainment for its time, but, at the end of the day, there’s something august about reading something that has had such a long-lasting impact on Western fiction. At the very least, I’m becoming more familiar with the origin of several ubiquitous memes (though I imagine much credit goes to the movies) and who doesn’t enjoy that?

Antes de começar essa resenha, eu gostaria de dizer que eu realmente queria ter amado esse livro. De verdade. Essa é a quarta vez em que eu tentei ler A Sociedade do Anel - e a primeira vez que eu consegui prosseguir com a leitura até o final.
Um dos comentários que mais se ouve sobre O Senhor dos Anéis - e a obra do Tolkien em geral - é como o universo criado por ele é bem desenvolvido e detalhado. Infelizmente, o custo disso são intermináveis parágrafos abordando assuntos que, na maioria das vezes, não influenciam de forma alguma no enredo da história que está sendo contada. Ler a Sociedade do Anel é como ler um livro sobre as características da geografia física da Terra Média intercalado com algumas lições de história na forma de poema. Para ser sincera, eu nunca gostei muito nem de geografia física nem de poesia, então faz perfeito sentido que eu também não seja fã desse livro.
Outra coisa que me incomodou ao longo da história foi a falta de mais interações e diálogos significativos entre os membros da Comitiva, o que faz com que a amizade e lealdade incondicional de alguns deles pareça um pouco forçada. Uma das amizades que eu estava mais animada para ver, a do Legolas e do Gimli, foi desenvolvida com apenas algumas frases resumidas, sem nenhuma cena marcante que exemplificasse esse processo. (Eu preciso admitir que essa foi uma expectativa criada pelos filmes, mas ainda assim a falta de esforço direcionada para o desenvolvimento desses personagens me decepcionou.)
Apesar disso tudo, eu até que consegui aproveitar a leitura. Ela foi envolvente nas partes mais importantes (ou seja, aquelas que realmente tinham alguma coisa relevante acontecendo) e tem alguns trechos que tocam profundamente o coração do leitor. Eu gosto muito do povo dos elfos com sua sabedoria encantadora, dos personagens do Sam, do Gandalf e do Aragorn. Principalmente, eu gosto muito do fato de que o Frodo não é um personagem extremamente corajoso desde o início, mas que aprende ao longo do tempo a superar os seus medos em nome de um propósito maior. Ele representa bem a mensagem geral que é passada ao longo do livro: a necessidade de união entre os povos em momentos difíceis e de encontrar dentro de si forças para fazer aquilo que precisa ser feito.
Mas afinal de contas, eu recomendaria a leitura? Isso depende muito de quem estaria me perguntando. Para mim, o principal atrativo de O Senhor dos Anéis é a influência que ele teve dentro do gênero da fantasia (que é com certeza o meu gênero literário favorito) e é principalmente por isso que eu pretendo continuar a lendo os livros. No geral, o meu conselho seria: se você tiver curiosidade, dê uma chance a história, mas esteja preparado para um processo difícil.

I've heard that an occasional conversation starter among literary people is to admit that you've never read an acknowledged classic. Such applies to me and Lord of the Rings. (And many other books, too, of course.)

But I've long meant to. So I put The Hobbit plus The Lord of the Rings trilogy into my to-be-read system. I conquered The Hobbit a few years back. And a not-so-few number of weeks ago, my script said it was time to read The Fellowship of the Ring.

Now, my self-imposed rule is that once the "system" picks a book I must read it next, with exceptions only for newly-purchased books and library books; this can really depress my book-throughput for awhile if the chosen book is such that I keep finding other things to do besides read. And, regrettably, such was the case with The Fellowship of the Ring.

I've seen the movie, of course; it's very much the "good parts" version of the book. And, it's not to be denied that there are many, many, good parts. But (geez), there's a lot of walking, up and down hills, through forests, valleys, dales, caverns, and bodies of water. There's a lot of eating and drinking. A lot of singing, and detailed references to history, geography, and genealogy. All lovingly described, and not very likely to hold my interest, sorry.

All (of course) wrapped around a wonderful tale of an ordinary guy who's been plucked from his happy, normal surroundings and plunged into continual peril and terror, all because he's been chosen for a world-saving task that seems ludicrously hopeless. Fortunately, he has a few friends on his side.

But anyway, finished now. In a mark of how long this task has been hanging over me: the version of the book I read is not the one pictured above, but the first authorized version offered in paperback in the US, which I bought nearly 40 years ago.

No one can deny the impact of this trilogy. It single-handedly reinvented the fantasy genre and created so many tropes that fantasy stories now heavily rely on: the Dark Lord, the different races (ie. elves, trolls, intelligent dragons, dwarves, etc.), unlikely hero, etc. I feel weird rating this book, but I am just basing it off of my enjoyment this time around. I adore The Hobbit book. It's one of my favorites. The story is so endearing and engaging. While I adore the story of this book, the pacing made the book drag on SOOOOO LONG. It's the sole reason this book is not 5 stars. Since this volume is split into two separate "books," I decided to rate each individually and have my overall rating be in the middle of the two.

Book 1: 3 stars
Book one started off great with Bilbo's birthday party, but everything in between that and the introduction of Strider is so dull. Tom is such a random character and feels out-of-place in the LOTR world. I do adore how this portion in particular emphasized Tolkien's theme of preservation of nature. The whole story is basically about the natural world vs. industrialization. And how he goes about that with Sauron (the Dark who is using corrupted, manufactured magic) versus Gandalf and the Elves (the Light who use natural, elemental magic) is phenomenal.

Book 2: 4 stars
I read all of book two today and am so tired. Most of this portion is super engaging as we finally get to see the Fellowship's journey to Mordor. It did drag a bit, but was much better than the first book.

With all of that in mind, I do have to say that I much prefer the movies over the books. I am OBSESSED with the Lord of the Rings films. I can confidently state that they are the GREATEST piece of fantasy film/tv that I have ever seen. They fixed the pacing issues and engaged the viewer in a way that the book wasn't quite able to reach. The collaboration to visualize the world that Tolkien created turned out stunning and I will forever be in love with Middle-Earth partly because of it. Do I think these books are worth it? If you are a die-hard fantasy fan, you kinda have to check them out to see the roots of the genre. Nevertheless, if you're a casual fantasy fan, just watch the movies (extended editions of course).

Anni e anni fa, provai a leggere questo libro con scarsissimi risultati. Tentai quindi di dare una possibilità ai film, dividendo le infinite ore sullo schermo fra i vari impegni della giornata, e temo purtroppo di non aver neanche portato a termine la visione.
Lo scorso agosto, però, ho partecipato ad un gruppo di lettura che aveva come libro del mese proprio Lo Hobbit, altro romanzo di Tolkien che avevo provato a leggere, ma che non ero riuscita a finire. Questa volta, però, la lettura mi aveva presa completamente, tanto che ho portato a termine il libro in pochissimi giorni, e mi è piaciuto talmente tanto, nonostante lo stile di scrittura dell'autore che non rientra fra i miei preferiti, che ho deciso il primo di settembre di iniziare la lettura della Compagnia dell'Anello, primo libro nella serie effettiva del Signore degli Anelli. Ho letto un capitolo al giorno, e questa storia mi ha tenuto compagnia per gran parte del mese di settembre.

Questa volta, sono riuscita a portare a termine la lettura, che è stata sicuramente piacevole, ma purtroppo lo stile di Tolkien proprio non fa per me. Odio i romanzi così tanto descrittivi, odio la tematica del viaggio che prosegue per capitoli e capitoli e capitoli (in questo caso, tutto il libro) e non ho apprezzato il fatto che molto spesso questo libro mi abbia ricordato proprio Lo Hobbit, testo scritto prima della storia del Signore degli Anelli.
Con questo non voglio dire che non mi sia piaciuto o che non continuerò nella storia: si tratta di uno dei pilastri del fantasy, che rappresenta il mio genere di evasione per eccellenza, e sicuramente porterò avanti la lettura, e vi stupirò, ma cercherò anche di recuperare i film. Sarà che ho letto il mio capitoletto quasi ogni giorno dopo pranzo, sarà che la palpebra calava, ma nonostante non mi sia dispiaciuta questa lettura, mi aspettavo molto di più.
Pensavo e speravo che la storia sarebbe stata più avvincente, e invece mi sono ritrovata a dover leggere descrizioni molto lunghe, mille nomi che ho già da tempo dimenticato, nomi di città che non avevo idea di dove collocare (nella mia edizione, purtroppo, non ci sono cartine).
Nonostante tutto, sicuramente andrò avanti.
Per il momento, però, prenderò una breve pausa da Tolkien!

I've had this one on my TBR list for quite some time. I finally got it on my list for this month, and I'm glad that I've read it now, although this isn't really my genre. I don't plan to continue in the series, but I also no longer have to wonder what I've been missing.

The most difficult part of this book is in trying to follow the story and understand what is happening without becoming distracted by the weird names of characters and places. I don't fault the author for that, because it gives the story character. I just couldn't get into it. I skipped all the singing and poetry; some of it in English and some of it in the language of the characters. Again, I just couldn't get into it.

However, my favorite parts of the story were near the beginning when Frodo first gets the ring and has to decide what to do with it (I was hooked early), and I also liked the part of the story where the fellowship ends up in the Mines. I enjoyed reading how they tried to get in, and I felt claustrophobic as they journeyed through. I wanted desperately for them to be able to get out of there. Yet, in between those two parts, the story was just too long for me, and I would have preferred that this book in the series had ended when they made it through the Mines.

Even after they made it out, the plot seemed repetitive to me. Just as had happened before they reached the Mines, they traveled... they camped... they had to look out for the Enemy... they traveled... they camped... they had to look out for the Enemy... and the cycle just went on and on and on and on and on until I lost interest.

There's also no real closure to this book. I think most people know that going in, but then again, most series have clear endings and beginnings between each book in the series. This story doesn't seem to do that. It's more like one part of a 1500-page book. The climax was the suspense of whether or not they would make it out of the Mines. After that, nothing of interest happens other than being left to wonder if they were on some infinite path in which they will never arrive at their destination.

Overall, I didn't hate it, or I wouldn't have finished it. It's just not for me, but the quality of writing is certainly above most books. I do think it is important for readers to try different genres. You never know what you may discover, and any time spent reading a book is not wasted.

Geçen yıl Hobbit’i okuyup çok sevmiştim o yüzden Yüzük Kardeşliği’nden beklentim çok yüksekti. Altı günlük okuma maratonumu bugün bitirdim ve şuan üzerimden kamyon geçmiş gibi hissediyorum. Benim için çok yorucu bir okuma oldu. Hiç planımda olmasa da ikinci kitaba geçmeden önce kısa bir ara vermem gerekiyor.

Hobbit’in o akıcı ve kolay dilinden sonra Yüzük Kardeşliği’nin dili bana biraz zor geldi. Öncelikle çok fazla betimleme vardı. Yazar hayali bir dünya yaratmış ve bunun her karışını dahi bize anlatmaya çalışmıştı. Güneşin doğuşu, nehirlerin akışı, dağlar, taşlar, ormanlar kısaca her şey çok detaylıydı.

Betimlemelerin fazlalığı dışında beni yoran diğer bir şey de sürekli ama sürekli yürümeleri ve neredeyse kitap boyunca hiçbir olay olmamasıydı. Kitabın yüzde doksanı oradan oraya yürümeleri ve bu sırada çevrelerindeki her şeyi betimlemeleriydi. Epik fantastiğin olayının bu olduğunu biliyorum ancak beni pek sarmadı. Bu kitaptan sonra epik fantastik sevmediğime emin oldum.

Kitapta arada sırada geçmişte olan olaylarla ilgili bazı şeyler anlatıldı. Bu kısımları okurken gerçekten gözümü zor açık tuttum çünkü kendimi tarih kitabı okuyormuşum gibi hissettim. Kitabı okurken genel olarak modum esnemek ve uyumamak için kendimi zorlamaktı. Özellikle Tom Bombadil kısmında bileklerimi kesmemek için kendimi zor tuttum ve şarkıların hepsini atladım.

Yüzüklerin Efendisi filmlerini çok küçükken izlemiştim ve hiçbir şey hatırlamıyorum. Keşke kitaba başlamadan önce filmi izleseydim, en azından kafamda daha rahat canlanırdı. Filmlerin daha iyi olduğuna ve bu serinin filmler yüzünden ülkemizde bu kadar çok sevildiğine eminim.

Kitapta en çok sevdiğim şey kesinlikle karakterler oldu. Aragorn, Gandalf, Legolas, Frodo hepsini çok sevdim. Birkaç düşmanla savaşma sahnesi vardı -aşırı az olsa da- oralarda çok keyif aldım.

Son olarak şunu söylemek istiyorum: Bu kitabın edebi değeri, fantastik edebiyatın öncüsü olması vs. pek umrumda değil. Ben okurken aldığım keyfe göre puan verdim. Böyle bir dünya, böyle bir hikaye ve karakterler yaratılmış olması ne kadar mükemmel olursa olsun, benim için kitabın sıkıcı olduğu gerçeğini değiştirmedi. Man kann anerkennen, dass dieses Werk Grundlage für viel der modernen Fantasy ist. Man kann auch anerkennen, dass Tolkien eine wunderbar überwältigende und detailreich ausgearbeitete Welt geschaffen hat. Man kann auch die häufig auftauchende verschiedenartige Lyrik anerkennen und bewundern.

Abseits von einer Anerkennung für diese Tatsachen muss ich aber sagen, dass ich mit „Die Gefährten“ nur schwer warm geworden bin. Die Geschichte rollt gemächlich an und macht meiner Meinung nach etwas zu häufig Halt. Dadurch konnte ich mich nicht wirklich auf die Erzählung einlassen und empfand die Geschichte an vielen Stellen als zu lang. Viele Abschnitte waren interessant, aber ebenso viele nicht. Mir gefielen insbesondere Bree, Bruchtal und die Zusammenkunft der Gefährten, Lothlorien und das Ende. Moria war so mittelmäßig, Tom Bombadil fand ich relativ langweilig und auch die meisten anderen Teile der Reise etwas zu langwierig erzählt. Alles in allem zwar nicht schlecht, aber halt nicht -wie erwartet- großartig.

Dadurch, dass sich Tolkien aber so viel Zeit für seine Welt nimmt, kann er gut die Wirkung der verschiedenen Magiearten herausarbeiten. Die Wirkung des Rings auf die Charaktere kommt super rüber, wie sie sich nach und nach In Rage reden und nach dem Ring dürsten, nur um irgendwann erschreckt zu bemerken, was sie gerade getan haben. Die Elben und ihre Magie bleiben auch wunderbar mysteriös und interessant.

Was bisher -insbesondere im Vergleich zum Film- etwas auf der Strecke bleibt, sind Gimli und Legolas sowie die Entwicklung ihrer Beziehung. Insbesondere Legolas ist relativ unbeteiligt, am Ende des Buches wird einfach kurz zusammengefasst, dass „Legolas und Gimli jetzt Freunde geworden sind“. Fand ich schade, vielleicht kommt da aber noch mehr in den nächsten Teilen.

Insgesamt immer noch eine schöne Geschichte, viele positive Dinge kann ich erkennen und auch anerkennen, sie haben mich beeindruckt, aber nicht wirklich unterhalten. Trotzdem habe ich Bock auf den zweiten Teil und hoffe, dass mit der weiteren Zuspitzung der Geschichte auch meine Kritikpunkte etwas relativiert werden oder sogar verschwinden.

I have a tremendous amount of appreciation for the historical significance of this book, and the impact of J.R.R. Tolkien on the (high) fantasy genre. Nonetheless, I found most of this book to be dull, repetitive, and overwhelming. The sheer quantity of characters was hard to track, especially on audio, but while audio often draws me more into the plot and helps me to develop a greater understanding of the perspectives and voices of the characters, I often found myself tuning out, getting distracted, and totally losing track of the story. Frankly, I don't think that reading the hard copy would have made much of a difference.

Tolkien has contributed phenomenally to the field of literature and beyond. This book has spawned countless adaptations and has inspired the imaginations of generations of readers, even many who don't know the source of their beloved characters, plot lines, and quotations, perhaps including myself...but Tolkien's original, the proof text for future fantasy, just wasn't for me.

I must admit that I found The Fellowship of the Ring to be far more engaging than The Hobbit, or There and Back Again, and I did enjoy the relationships between Frodo and his friends significantly more than between Bilbo and the dwarves, and I thought that their adventures were infused with a greater degree of excitement. However, despite rewinding several times and listening to certain chapters over and over again, there are only a few scenes that I can remember clearly from either book, and I would be hard-pressed to summarize the plot of the book without considerable additional research and reminders.

I want to like this book more than I do. It feels like, as a lover of fantasy, having an untouchable adoration for The Lord of the Rings is required. And for what it's worth, the story itself is mostly solid - I love the whole classic 'ragtag team on a mission' thing, and if it's a little by the numbers, it's only because J.R.R. Tolkien is the man who made the numbers. This is the series that, for many, put the fantasy genre on the map. It's certainly responsible for a lot of how the genre has developed today.

What I'm saying is, I can see its worth. It's an important milestone in the history of fantasy. I get it.

But it's not an easy read. The writing, as you might expect, shows it's age a bit - the syntax is one step removed from reading like 'ye olde English'. The narrative is positively choc-a-block (and I'm not even exaggerating) with what I would normally dismiss as pointless description. Every valley, every hill, every goddamn tree is described in excruciating detail - in fact most of the book length, I'm certain, comes from this descriptive overkill alone. It's important, in a fantastical world, to give readers a good idea of what the world looks like; but, for me at least, I don't need an in-depth examination of every tiny detail. I also don't really need exact geographical locations every step of the way (I don't mind it every now and then, but it seemed like every time the characters started walking for any reason I was being given exact directions that, honestly, I couldn't care less about).

These aforementioned problems are probably directly responsible for what I consider to be The Fellowship of the Ring's biggest issue - the pacing. Because god damn are the first three quarters of this book slow. The progression from the start of the book to after the chapter called The Council of Elrond is nigh glacial. That's page 265, for anybody who's curious. Page 265 in a book that's only 398 pages long in the first place is a ridiculous amount of time to be slogging along. And it's not like the book gets hugely more exciting after that - it's still very much a slow, meandering journey, but at least after the council it feels like a slow, meandering journey with an end goal.

Now, I know I might be making it sound like I really didn't like The Fellowship of the Ring. That's actually not entirely true. Yes, I had issues with the pacing, yes, I found the writing to be tricky to navigate at times (so much so that I actually finished the last three or four chapters via audiobook, which helped me to enjoy the ending a bit more), but there were things I enjoyed too. When the action does get going in this book, it does so brilliantly - some of my favourite scenes were the fight with the Ringwraiths, the infamous underground battle in Moria, and the end when Boromir confronts Frodo over the ring and Frodo runs away and tries to leave by himself. The writing is tricky most of the time, but if you can get into the right zone it can be mesmerising too. And like I said, the story itself is a classic - an epic adventure to destroy a dangerous weapon and defeat the evil villain? I am all kinds of on-board for that.

So it has it's good points, and I'm completely certain that I'll end up finishing this series some day. I've heard that the other two books are much better than this one, but even if that weren't the case, I would finish them on principle alone. Just... not yet. Tolkien's writing has left me mentally exhausted. I don't want to go right into book two and try to force my way through because I don't think that's the way these books are meant to be enjoyed. I think The Lord of the Rings is a series you have to take your time with - and that's just what I intend to do.

P.S. This is very much a 'me' problem, but I'm not a fan of all the songs and poems scattered throughout the story either. Poetry isn't my strong suit, and I find it hard to appreciate a song when I don't know the rhythm the words go with.

I feel like I'm going to dishonour this book by saying this but I shall say it nonetheless... I like the movie more than the book. There, I said it.

When the movies came out when I was but a young'un, I had zero interest in them. Small Me was only interested in happy movies or horror movies; there was no in-between. And so whenever someone in my family would watch the movies, I'd be off to the side, playing with my toys and ignored everything (except for when a certain scene played where a certain Smeagol turned into Gollum in a very disturbing and dark montage that scarred me for life... Me. The little girl who gladly watched horror movies).

At some point in my high school years, my mom had managed to inspire me to at least try to watch the movies and so I did... and promptly fell asleep 15 minutes into it. When I woke up, the team was already in Moria and I gave up on it and resolved to read the books first before the movie so that I could maybe not fall asleep next time I attempted the movie.

Fast forward to almost a decade later (now), I had started the book finally (I was startled by just how much singing there was in it) and I thought to myself "maybe I should watch the movie alongside the book". And for a short while, I did that. Read some chapters, watched the movie up to the point that I reached in the book, repeat.

WELL. A week later, I had watched the entire movie (in small increments), LOVED IT TO THE MOON AND BACK, and I hadn't even met Aragorn yet in the book :)

I'm so sorry but also not sorry because if I had just read the book on its own, I think I would have ended up giving this one star for how little I enjoyed it. That said, because I had already completed the movie when I picked this back up again, I had the movie playing in my head while I was reading the rest and it helped me not be completely bored with it. Sadly, I am not inclined to complete the rest of the book series but, not sadly, I am continuing the movie series and I am glad to report that I am completely obsessed with them and I'm trying to spread them out as much as I can so that I can keep it going for longer. In short, I decided to use the time given to me by watching the movies.

This review was completely unfair to long time fans of the book series and I feel guilty by taking a whole review for the book to compare it to the movies. I've written before here on the blog that I feel weird about not having read The Lord of the Rings series. I love fantasy, I love classic novels, and these books are pretty much the perfect combination of those two things. I've meant to get around to them for years now and finally be a LotR person, but I haven't felt motivated enough to take on such a long and dense series. I did start my journey almost exactly three years ago with The Hobbit, which I did like, but didn't get any further with it at that time. With the Back to the Classics Challenge asking me to read a genre classic this year, I figured it was a good time to finally return to the series.

The Fellowship of the Ring picks up several decades after the events of The Hobbit. Bilbo Baggins has returned to The Shire and has been living a quiet life with his nephew, Frodo. He still has his magical ring of invisibility that he acquired on his big adventure all those years ago, and uses it from time to time to get out of sticky situations. His life is good, but boring, and he has started yearning to go off on another adventure. On his eleventy-first birthday, he decides to do just that. He leaves his magical ring with Frodo, and heads out into the unknown.

Meanwhile, as life in The Shire continued on more or less the same, the rest of Middle-earth has not been so lucky. An old evil, long since defeated, has risen again and is seeking to exert control over the country. His name is Sauron, and he has positioned himself in the dark lands of Mordor, where he is slowly building power and followers. He lacks one magical item that would assure his complete victory--a special magical ring. Gandalf, the powerful wizard that assisted Bilbo on his journey to defeat Smaug in The Hobbit, has been traveling throughout the country to learn more about Sauron and find ways to defeat him. He arrives back in the Shire to convey some startling news to Frodo. The ring he received from Bilbo is, in fact, the "one ring to rule them all" that Sauron is searching for. If the ring falls into his hands, he will become unstoppable and all will be lost. He tells Frodo that now he must undertake a terrible and dangerous quest. He must travel across the land to Mordor and destroy the ring by throwing it into the fires of Mt. Doom, where it was forged.This is the only way to defeat Sauron and save Middle-earth.

Frodo is daunted, but accepts the task. He sets out with a small band of trusted hobbits, including Samwise Gamgee, Meriadoc Brandybuck (Merry), and Peregrin Took (Pippin). His journey is immediately dangerous, as Sauron has already heard rumors about a Baggins from The Shire having the ring and has dispatched nine terrifying servants, the black riders, to overtake him. The party manages to evade them for a time, but the riders are always just a step behind the group, waiting for an opportunity to strike. As Frodo continues making his way across the land, he adds more adventurers to his party to aid him in his quest and protect him from Sauron. Among them are the ranger Aragorn, the dwarf Gimli, the prince and soldier Boromir, and the elf Legolas. Together, this fellowship fights their way across Middle-earth to try and destroy both the ring and Sauron for good.

This was a grand, epic adventure story, and I could immediately see why it inspires such devotion in its fans. Reading Fellowship felt like sitting around a fire at a medieval inn, listening to a master storyteller. I found myself wishing that I had stumbled upon it as a kid, as I think I might have truly fallen in love with it back in the days when The Chronicles of Narnia and The Neverending Story were making deep impressions on my reading life. As it was, I ended up enjoying it quite a bit, but there were some aspects of it that I struggled with.

On the positive side, the world of Middle-earth was extremely well-developed, with every town, river, hill, and plant having a long explanation behind it. It's not exactly groundbreaking analysis to say this. This is a high fantasy series, and Tolkien is known for his extensive world building. Even knowing this before I started the book, I was still surprised by the sheer amount of detail present in the setting. The story would frequently pause for long descriptions of land that the characters were currently travelling across, which were impressive and very well-written, often to the point of being overwhelming. It was very easy to picture what the various locations they visited looked like, and all the details made for a very immersive reading experience. Admittedly, it did get a bit boring occasionally. Still, this was probably the most intricately-crafted setting I have ever experienced in a novel, and I truly felt like I was in another world while reading.

The characters all had similarly detailed backgrounds, which were unveiled gradually throughout the story. Much like with the setting, all of this information felt overwhelming at times, but it also made the characters feel more real. By the end of the novel, I had a clear sense what everyone's thoughts and motivations were. I knew that Sam, when not thinking about Frodo, was probably thinking about food. I knew Gimli would be looking to prove his strength at every opportunity. I knew that Aragorn would always choose the noblest course of action in every situation. The characters weren't all necessarily three dimensional, but they were certainly consistent and easy to like. Frodo and, to a lesser degree, Sam, were the exception to this, as they experienced clear growth throughout the course of the story. One of the themes running throughout the text is the idea of unassuming people being capable of great deeds, and their movement towards bravery and selflessness develops this idea nicely.

On the more negative side, there were a few elements of the story that I didn't enjoy so much. As I mentioned previously, the amount of detail included was overwhelming at times. The plot was pretty slow-moving in general, and all the extra information slowed down the story even further. I eventually got used to the style, but I think that the pacing is a bit too slow for my taste in general. Also, there is a real lack of female characters. The elf Galadriel is the only woman to speak more than a few lines, and she is not present for the vast majority of the novel. There are so many interesting male characters to read about throughout this story, and this is a clear and obvious imbalance. I wish that at least one woman had gone along on the journey as well.

Still, I liked The Fellowship of the Ring and I can understand why so many readers have fallen in love with the series. It's classic high fantasy, and even though it shows its age in spots, it is still a fun reading experience. Due to all the world-building details and slow pace, it took me a while to get into the story. Once I did, however, I had a good time with it. Frodo's journey to destroy the ring spreads across all three novels in the series, so this one ends on a cliffhanger. I am looking forward to picking up The Two Towers and seeing how the story continues.

you need a good mental compass to navigate all the places they go. or consult the maps.

January 2026 review:
Before revisiting Fellowship of the Ring, I thought that much like rewatching the movies, I would come to realize that these books are perfect masterpieces that only get better with each read. And while I did enjoy this first volume more this time, I still agree with my last review; the story is windy and often confusing, both in the actual journey of the fellowship and the worldbuilding. The depth of middle-earth's lore is a double-edged sword. The world feels very lived-in with great history and culture, but the specificity of place-names and lineages is overwhelming and often not necessary outside of an appendix or glossary.

Since reading the books for the first time in 2020, I've rewatched the films multiple times, watched two seasons of The Rings of Power, skimmed the Silmarillion, and read lots and lots of neat tidbits and whatever of lore. And I think it greatly contributed to my increased enjoyment when reading passages where before I might've glossed over them. I know who the Númenóreans are now. And Elendil and Celebrimor and others. In my mind-movie Elrond and Galadriel switch back and forth between their original and younger actors.

I feel like I'll get banned from Goodreads if I declare that I think the movies are better than the books, but I'll just say that there's a lot of things that the movies did that improves the clarity of The Lord of the Rings, both with the themes and the actual story.
