I finally started my journey into The Lord of the Rings, courtesy of another buddy read. I probably would have never gotten to it if it wasn’t for this push! I’ve got some mixed feelings. If I were to give an overall rating, I would give it a 3/5 stars. Bear in mind, I have never watched the movies or formed an attachment to this series in any way. This is one case where I think I would have enjoyed the books more if I watched the movies first, and I intend to watch at least the first one before I go into the next book, which I will continue with eventually. Unfortunately, you shouldn’t have to watch a movie to get into the book that it is based off of, so the rating will stand.

“The Road goes ever on and on

Down from the door where it began.

Now far ahead the Road has gone,

And I must follow, if I can,

Pursuing it with eager feet,

Until it joins some larger way

Where many paths and errands meet.

And whither then? I cannot say.”

I started off pretty intrigued in the hobbits and Frodo and that quickly turned to boredom. 50% of the book, it felt like a struggle to get through. I got to Tom Bombadil and was like, this guy is pretty unique and then got bored again because that section lingered a bit too long. I think Tom in general is pretty interesting since he’s shrouded in a bit of mystery. I actually love when our authors don’t feel like they have to tell us every little bit about a character, because that’s true to life, we don’t know everything about ANYONE. Two of my favorite authors, Rothfuss and Hobb, employ this tactic. It can drive you absolutely mad with wanting to know more about specific characters, but that intrigue can build an amazing story. It’s good for us to use our imagination to complete characters in our minds. Then Strider came in and things started to get interesting. Up until this point, I felt like the character development with our forefront characters was so bland that I wasn’t connecting with Frodo’s group. In contrast, the world building is outstanding. Tolkien spends most of his time building this world up instead of developing his characters. For some people, this is exactly what they’re looking for. There’s a reason why people love Middle Earth, and it’s absolutely due to Tolkien’s time spent weaving its illusion. The lore and the songs were something that I adored because I have a penchant for subtle clues when building a story, if you pay attention to the words in the songs, they provide a lot of detail. I LOVE world building but my true heart lies in character development. When Strider came in, I felt like we finally start to get some depth to our characters and our merry little band of friends start talking more, rather than it feeling like we are just reading about them walking. It wasn’t until about 75% that I actually was INVESTED in the story and I felt like we were starting to experience enough action for me not to glaze over and have to reread paragraphs.

“Deserves it! I daresay he does. Many that live deserve death. And some that die deserve life. Can you give it to them? Then do not be too eager to deal out death in judgement. For even the very wise cannot see all ends.”

Don’t get me wrong, I knew that this was going to be a verbose novel. At times, it’s more than just verbose… it’s plain ole dry in that first 50%, at least to me. There’s always going to be people that have read more fantasy than I have, but I have a decent range. I read A Song of Ice and Fire before watching Game of Thrones and fell into the camp of wanting people to read the books before watching the show because I feel like the show is more enjoyable after having read the books. It is another series that is loquacious, but I can’t say that I ever spent 50% of the first novel glazing over. I say this because you get scoffs here and there about not having read LotR. I’ve read plenty of fantasy. This personally would never be the book I recommend to get someone into fantasy. Most people aren’t going to wait 50-75% of a book to see if it gets better. It makes me wonder how many of the people who have told me that they have tried fantasy and hated it was due to trying to start with LotR. That’s not to say that people can’t (in fact, I know many people HAVE) jump into fantasy by reading this first, but I would recommend something more universally palatable. That being said, Tolkien drops these little nuggets of wisdom that absolutely reminds me of why I love the fantasy genre. It’s a testament to the fact that fantasy is capable of being this magical journey while teaching us about ourselves and our world. We are capable of bravery in unlikely times, we can be compassionate when we least want to. Fantasy has always been so much more than it is marketed, it’s not just for “nerds” or dreamers, it’s for people that like looking deeper into themselves and humanity as a whole. Tolkien drives that point home effortlessly.

“Even the smallest person can change the course of the future.”

There’s no doubt that Tolkien was truly a pioneer of the fantasy genre. I am not debating that in the least. Throughout Fellowship, there were times that I was found myself with that Eureka! moment during a scene or when seeing certain terms or an expression, where it was obvious that another author’s book was heavily influenced by Tolkien. He’s the father of epic fantasy and there’s no doubt that the fantasy genre as whole would be much smaller without his influence. Gandalf’s awareness that absolute power corrupts absolutely is groundbreaking. To have a powerful being capable of taking more power into his hands and saying no is monumental. This certainly isn’t a new comparison but you can’t read Harry Potter, learn about Dumbledore and not think of that influence. This is just one of the millions of comparisons you could make.

“But I have so little of any of these things! You are wise and powerful. Will you not take the Ring?’ ‘No!’ cried Gandalf, springing to his feet. ‘With that power I should have power too great and terrible. And over me the Ring would gain a power still greater and more deadly.’ His eyes flashed and his face was lit as by a fire within. ‘Do not tempt me! For I do not wish to become like the Dark Lord himself. Yet the way of the Ring to my heart is by pity, pity for weakness and the desire of strength to do good. Do not tempt me! I dare not take it, not even to keep it safe, unused. The wish to wield it would be too great for my strength. I shall have such need of it. Great perils lie before me.”

All in all, I am excited to see where this journey goes, as it leaves on quite the cliffhanger and I am completely in the dark about what happens. I’m happy I did finally decide to read this because now I am able to have some narrative on the subject. Thanks to David, Pato, and J.M. for the push on this buddy read, I wouldn’t have done it without you!

My Informal Reading Notes on The Fellowship of the Ring:

Book One:

Prologue/Chapter 1:
• I am convinced that I have some hobbit blood in me, deep down.
• The Shire just sounds like an awesome place. But is its sheltered nature akin to childhood, like a paradise that you can’t go back to?
• I have to say that I love how, among all of the important prologue information on hobbit culture and history, there is an entire section devoted to smoking pipe-weed. I am also delighted to find that Merry wrote a book on pipe-weed.
• Frodo’s parents drowned and it’s insinuated that his dad, Drogo, was so fat he sank the boat or that his parents fought and pushed each other to their deaths. This is delightful.

Chapter 1/Chapter 2:
• When the story actually goes, and doesn’t just talk about the minutiae of Middle Earth, it’s really easy going. 40 pages in one sitting is more than I ever expected.
• So Bilbo is remarkable because he relinquishes the ring of his own will. This is something that Frodo doesn’t end up doing (though Sam does). What does that say about him?
• I’m unclear about what the power of the Ring is on people. It seems to fill Frodo with misery and pain, it eats away at Gollum, Bilbo's apparently fine but he just doesn’t want to let go of it…and this is from hobbits/Gollum who have more resistance to its powers. Would it just turn humans into mindless Sauron puppets? Is the pain and decay put on these folks the result of the push-pull of the Ring’s influence?
• So apparently Aragorn teamed up with Gandalf years ago to hunt down Gollum, and Aragorn literally dragged Gollum to Gandalf. I love this image.
• New detail gleaned from the book: Frodo looks down on most of the Shire inhabitants and views them with a sort of contempt (he thinks some kind of disaster would do them good) and is drawn to the outer world of elves and adventure (like Bilbo).
• Bless him, Sam just really wants to see the elves. This detail makes me like him more already.

Chapter 3/Chapter 4:
• I don’t really like that the Sackville-Bagginses ended up getting Bag-End after all. I feel like Frodo should have just left it to a friend. Or sublet it. But I guess they’re all proper about inheritance and stuff like that.
• Pippin and Merry come off way less buffoony than their movie counterparts do.
• Frodo complains about his pack being too heavy, and then Pippin accuses him of being lazy and fat.
• I’ve heard all about the notorious Tom Bombadil, but no one seems to mention the Good Samaritan Farmer Maggot. I surprisingly liked his bit.

Chapter 5/Chapter 6:
• Up to this point, I wasn’t having trouble staying interested in the narrative (with the minor exception of parts of the prologue). But once the hobbits set off into the forest, it was like the nightmare of reading The Hobbit and following every twist and turn that they take. It’s possible I’m more tired right now than I was when I read the other chapters, but it felt like a long, tedious bad dream. We need to get out of these accursed woods and to the Prancing Pony, pronto.

Chapter 7/Chapter 8:
• This wasn’t quite as bad as them getting lost in the forest in Chapter 6, but it was a whole lot of tree talk and “here’s every turn they took.” I don’t really know what all of the fuss is about Tom Bombadil, either good or bad. He’s just a jolly, batty forest god who is super hot for his river-lady wife.
• It might have been a placebo, but I felt more optimistic the moment that the hobbits finally left the forest behind. Maybe this was all a very unfortunate detour and things will get back on track now that we’re heading for Bree (and Strider!).

Chapter 9/Chapter 10:
• The fact that Book Frodo randomly jumps up on a table and sings a song as a diversion is so stupid, but I kind of wish that we had seen Elijah Wood Frodo do that as well.
• And also the fact that Frodo putting on the ring was just because he got too into the merrymaking and fell off a table during an encore of the song rather than the “perilous danger” approach of the movie is too good.
• Aragorn’s introduction isn’t nearly as smoldering as it is in the movie, but his presence and dialogue are a welcome change of pace from all of the other kooks we’ve encountered since leaving the Shire.
• I love how Frodo keeps putting off talking to Aragorn and Aragorn isn’t having it, so he just follows the hobbits into their room and sits down in a chair and they don’t even notice for several minutes.

Chapter 11/Chapter 12:
• These “walking” chapters are not exactly captivating, but they’re not nearly as bad as that forest episode. I think having Strider in the picture really helps, not only because now we have a character who actually knows what they’re doing and hustles the group along, but also because he’s a very different personality from the hobbits and that gives them something to play off of. The only way I can really stomach a “walking/quest” fantasy is if it’s anchored in characters who have good chemistry on the journey, and the companionship developing between Strider and the hobbits at least hints at that. The small conversations that they have along the road are definitely better than the endless descriptions of the road.
• I feel like we need to give a shout-out to the little pony that could; they bought him because there was no other pony available and they said he was a pathetic, weak thing, but then he got strong and climbed the mountain with them. The pony’s a trooper.
• It’s mentioned at one point that Strider doesn’t seem to sleep, and I was totally thinking the same thing. I’m not convinced Strider would ever feel comfortable letting one of the hobbits stand guard/keep watch without him, especially in the middle of the night, so I feel like he’s just developed some Ranger superpower to stay conscious for weeks at a time. Or maybe it’s the magical king blood in him.
• I have to admit, the hobbits thinking that there were trolls about and Strider’s immediate response being to pick up a stick and say, “Well, let’s take a look” is quite hilarious. As is him smashing the stick into the “troll” and yelling at it.

Chapter 12:
• Mostly all of the walking feels punishing. Tolkien really wants readers to feel how long and hard this journey is for all of the characters. It’s like going through the mental misery of a hike without having to leave your chair.


Book Two:

Chapter 1:
• Thank you so much, Bilbo, for that four-page song of nonsense you performed for everyone at Elrond’s house. Good on Aragorn for wanting nothing to do with it and making Bilbo write the whole thing himself.

Chapter 2:
• Gandalf kindly sends the horse back to Rohan once he’s in the Shire, but that seems a lot less nice and convenient when you remember that Rohan is basically on the other side of the world (okay, maybe that’s not technically true; I’m not looking at a map of Middle Earth and I’m not a Tolkien-phile, but it’s clearly weeks’ worth of travel). That’s like arriving in Seattle and saying, “Thanks for the ride, pal, now run along back to Orlando.”
• The very fact that Saruman and Sauron’s names are so similar—and really easy to confuse when you’re reading too quickly—probably should have been a warning sign that Saruman was no good from the start.
• I dig the idea of the three elf rings actually having the power for good and healing but, because of their link to Sauron, what they gained with those rings will likely be lost when the One Ring is destroyed. It adds credibility to why evil is so enticing. Could you imagine if Rivendell lost all of its beauty and pretty waterfalls when the Ring was destroyed because of that?

Chapter 3:
• Aww, Bilbo, it’s so nice of you to point out to Frodo that his journey to Mordor will be even worse because he’ll be setting out in the middle of winter and then being like, “But there’s nothing to be done about it! Too bad for you!”
• Frodo’s such a bleak, moody pessimist even before he starts off to Mordor. Bilbo asks him if he’s thought of any endings for the story he’s writing, and Frodo’s like, “Several, and all are dark and unpleasant.”
• Personally, I’m with Bilbo: “Books ought to have good endings. How would this do: and they all settled down and lived together happily ever after?”
• Elrond just straight-up dissed Pippin and told him it would be best for everyone if he stayed behind. (Though I guess since—in the film at least—he sets off the events in Moria and with the Palantir, he’s kind of right.)

Chapter 4:
• I was becoming quite attached to Bill, the little pony that could. Shame on the fellowship for just abandoning him at the gates of Moria.
• The image of Gandalf chanting a bunch of spells at the doors and then throwing down his staff in frustration, sitting, and not talking to anyone is so temper-tantrumy and delightful.

Chapter 6:
• The visual of the fellowship crossing into Lothlorien on a tightrope over a river, with only a higher tightrope to hold onto, is completely awesome and I wish it had been in the movie.
• Yay, Aragorn, for resolving the “blindfold the dwarf” conflict by having all of the company be blindfolded. A true king.

Chapter 7:
• Hey, there’s the theme I was talking about in Chapter 2! Galadriel says that Lothlorien will fade away if the Ring is destroyed, which makes its loss difficult for their people even if it’s technically the right thing to do. Props for exploring this dilemma.

Chapter 9:
• I love how Sam, Frodo, and Aragorn have all been aware for a while that Gollum has been following them on their mission but haven’t bothered to discuss it with anyone else. Maybe this is the kind of thing that merits a Fellowship meeting, to let the rest of the group in on the situation?
• What on earth was the deal with the great flying creature? The whole chapter was building up to them being pursued by something, and then this ominous black shape bats around in the sky, then Legolas shoots it and that’s the end. I assume it was a Nazgul, but the way that it’s written is so “Raiders of the Lost Ark ninja” that it felt almost comical.

Chapter 10:
• I miss the movie scene of Aragorn and Frodo parting ways. It gave the splitting of the Fellowship a stronger resolution, whereas the book just has Frodo take off, then Sam takes off after him and the rest of the company must infer that they’re alive and don’t want to be followed.
• However, Sam and Sam alone figuring out Frodo’s plan and catching up to him in the nick of time proves exactly why he is the Fellowship’s MVP and deserves to accompany Frodo.

The Lord of the Rings lore marked my childhood even without me reading it. Unfortunately, I was saddened to discover that my enthusiasm wouldn`t be sustained, even after reading the books. Possibly, some of it can be ascribed to the fact that I`ve already seen Peter Jackson`s adaptations countless times now. However, I am sure that the part of the reason why I missed the chance to enjoy such acclaimed, literary work was due to my personal disagreement with Tolkien`s writing style and choices.
It is, however, an unfair mistake not to pay tribute to one of the greatest architects of the whole new, fantastic universe and its complex, historically embroidered storyline. Honestly, well done for that. It was such a joy to read all the myths, legends, and songs about the Middle Earth and its past. The problem with Tolkien, for me, arises in the fact that his whole body of work is infested with classist, Christian ideas that are too elaborate for me to turn a blind eye. Understandably, Tolkien`s religious, Victorian/Edwardian background could be accounted as responsible for such inspirations. Nonetheless, I was disheartened by reading it.
In particular, I was bothered by the whole superiority of bloodlines and its blind glorification. Sam, for example, being brown-handed as a reference to his lower class, obsesses over the fair, superior elven nation. Even his speech and mannerisms are ridiculed compared to the well-spoken Frodo or Legolas. Which brings me to the heavily implied social ranking within the lore:
Valar>Maiar>Elves> Edain> non Edain>Orcs & other creatures of Morgoth
The hierarchy begins with `fair`, `white` Western nations, and finishes in non-western `dark`, `black` creatures. The books certainly have a questionable racial undertone that cannot be ignored. For instance, the fact that Numenorians are in many ways the literal master race. While Easterling and other Eastern folks (darker) are all under the sway of Morgoth and Sauron. However, they can be `saved` by the Western values and their `mercy` (Christian values, ideas). Such racial questions are debatable and should be, perhaps, left altogether to linguists, historians, and mythologists to discuss. It is certainly an issue to be mindful of when reading the books.
The lack of representation of women in the books is not necessarily a problem for me. However, it does imply poor understanding and portrayal of female characters. There are absolutely no women in Rivendell, in Lake Town, or in Thranduil`s halls. While it does not bother me, it is certainly bewildering and alienating..
Tolkien`s characters also seem to lack dimension to them. The antagonists like Nazgul, Orcs, or Uruk-hai seem to be mindless slaves who hate good for the sake of it? Not to forget Sauron himself, a witness of the fall of one dark lord, seems to repeat the cycle instead of breaking it? Evidently, Tolkien was a moral absolutist. Evil is evil, good is good. Distance from Eru (god) serves as a metaphor for the characters` evilness. The closer they are to Eru, they become inherently good, unable of committing any evil. The examples of Saruman or Boromir are inconsequential to this hypothesis, for they do not represent a gray, middle ground. Boromir redeems himself through repentance and salvific death and is therefore considered good. While Saruman fails to accept the salvation offered to him and thus, is considered evil. Some people, however, seem to enjoy such traditional good vs evil stories with heavy use of deus ex machina, which is absolutely fine.
I still, however, consider myself a Lotr fan as its influence and candid memory remains. I was excited to read about Tom Bombadil who was unfortunately omitted from the films!! Such a funny character, but my enthusiasm deflates as I read that he was supposed to resemble a god-like figure......

*A couple of disclaimers before reading this review*
1) I respected Tolkien and his works even before reading The Fellowship, so, please, do not believe I am insulting the author or the saga whatsoever;
2) The three star I gave here indicate my own personal taste and my personal experience while reading/listening to this book; I gave three stars to other books that I would never, NEVER compare to Lord of the Rings -this saga is beyond imagination, it just does not captivate me the way I wished, and, after all, Goodreads's rating range is very restricted, and we all know that the "3 stars" category is but a big melting pot.

Thus being said, I will not proceed with the plot because I believe the general outline is to be taken for granted -if not, I am sorry for 'discriminating'.
I will start with saying what I *did not* like:
a) the hours long description: I am perfectly conscious that Tolkien's main intention was to create a lore and a whole new world, besides the story is a child of its time, and back then long descriptions where everyone's cup of tea. Well, while some of them were actually interesting and useful to create the perfect atmosphere and to evoke that magical idea, but more often than not I found the narration to be slow-paced and dull because of them -I basically read without reading, and that is something I hate.
b) The random songs: no, not ALL songs. Although some were indeed quite long, and I might have skipped one or two, I am talking about the songs that popped out of nowhere in contests I found unbelievable, like when Bilbo stands up during Elrond's Council to sing in favour of Aragorn, when he could have just have *said* that.
c) Hate me for that, but some scenes where unrequested to me -Tom Bombadil was fun, and so was the Hobbit's journey, but had they been cut, probably I would have spared some energies for reading the second part.
I started with the best intentions, I really wanted to enjoy the book like everyone does, and I know this is just an introduction to the whole story, but while I read the first half almost avidly, I found myself wishing to finish it as soon as possible after Elrond's council -this reading consumed me.

But now it is time for the praises:
a) SAM: I am amazed at the characterization of this little Hobbit. His devotion, his intelligence that is so slowly revealed, his genuineness and his kind heart moved me and placed him to being one of my favourite characters ever. He evolves through the narration, but what is great is that our perception of him evolves with him, too, and we cannot help but change our mind on his personality.
b) The description of the Evil: blame it on WW1, but I believe Tolkien could have been a perfect horror author; the scenes where he describes the power of the Ring, the visions of the Eye, and most of all the scene in Moria when Gandalf reads from the book of the dwarves scared me and made me uncomfortable even while I was cocooned in my bed. There, the description are not "heavy", for instance.
c) The worldbuilding: as I said at the beginning, I have a huge respect for Tolkien, and the worldbuilding is one of the main reasons. It is so vast and complex that more than 400 pages of written paper are not enough to reveal one third of it, for there is a very detailed research on geography, cultures and races, and, above everything else, the LANGUAGES. There is a poem in Sindarin (I think) at the end of the 12th chapter that was so beautiful, so touching because of the structure of the language, and for me that is enough to bow. Chapeau!
d) The Elves: people often believe that the elves of Lord of the Ring are this ethereal, flawless, intrinsically good but posh creatures that guard the wisdom of the world -and this vision has been repeated many and many times by other authors- but nobody seems to think that Tolkien's elves are probably, deep inside, his most flawed race, and that is why they are so fascinating. Many times they make fun or mortal, and kinda despise their ways, they are full of prejudices and so so proud, but they have this aura around them that even you, as a reader, forget their words and forgive them, as if they charmed you with actual magic.

So, to be honest, this is objectively a four stars books... but I can't ignore the things I have mentioned in my rating.
The story is really beautifully written, with poignant reflections about how to face adversity but some chapters were too longwinded for me.

It's been some 15 years since I last read this book in German and this was the first time I read it in English. I thought hard about what it reminded me of and I think I finally know:
It reads like a first draft of a NaNoWriMo novel where the author starts out describing every single boring detail because he's worried he won't get to 50k with the plot he has, and then suddenly finds himself close to the goal but woth too much plot left over, so entire days or weeks are brushed over and everything seems to happen at once when hardly anything happened for the first half or so.

Many may disagree with me there and that's fine. I know why it is a classic and one of the pillars of high fantasy, but 'show, don't tell' clearly wasn't a concept Tolkien knew of or believed in.

We'll see what part 2 holds in store once I get around to rereading it.

What I will say is, seeing the movies wasn't the same as reading the book for understanding this foundational piece of Fantasy literature.

What stood out to me was the extent to which we have culturally embraced darkness as a metaphor for evil and light as a metaphor for good. The world of the Lord of the Rings reflects that, and one way to bring the genre of Fantasy forward is to interrogate that metaphor.
The world building was nice but seems unnecessarily long if I'm being honest. Overall the story was very wholesome but not something that had me hungering to keep going.

Poetic and melancholy, Fellowship is an undeniable iconic fantasy classic. While you can sense its influence on all that came after, it doesn't hold up as well as one would like. Filled with plodding sections and snooze-worthy descriptions of nature, this first entry in the series was in need of some serious editing. The characters are one dimensional and dull, most significantly the protagonist Frodo, who is singularly unremarkable. The fictional characters here unnervingly feel like fictional characters (@HarryStyles) - unreal and un-relatable. They don't possess choice or conviction, but rather are entirely held prisoner to the larger narrative of good vs. evil. Tolkien's prose is certainly beautiful at times, but its effectiveness is wildly uneven.

Two sections stand out, which are of course The Shadow of the Past chapter, and the chapters covering the Mines of Moria. The storytelling here is excellent and moving - but unfortunately most of the rest just doesn't compare to this quality. Tolkien's legacy is certainly aided by the aesthetics and ambience of the gorgeous movies, which definitely lent this offering some much needed gravitas. On to Two Towers!

This is my first Tolkien book, and I would say that I now understand much of the things I've heard about his writing style and this book in particular- both the praise and the criticism. Overall, I would say that I liked it. I would even say that I liked it enough to feel compelled to read the rest of the series as well as The Hobbit. Tolkien's imagination is truly something to behold; vast, diverse and extraordinarily vivid- too vivid for me to even begin to comprehend half of his descriptions with my limited visionary capabilities, I must admit, but I can appreciate the sheer strength and scope of his at any rate. The characters also were one of my favourite aspects. Tolkien crafts such a vast and dynamic landscape of endearing and intriguing characters, some homely and comic, some noble and stoic, some wise and thoughtful, some dastardly and manipulative, and ultimately with the protagonist, Frodo, he is able to provide a 360, panoramic view of these characteristics, for the protagonist, though emerging as brave and capable, is nevertheless subject to many of these temptations which have characterised the more villainous characters. Tolkien is able to converge this, in principle, rather simple story with ancient mythology so deftly that I must confess it is very difficult not to get wrapped in the tension and excitement of this epic tale. It manages to feel thunderous, enthralling and profoundly moving and consequential in a similar way to Star Wars or Harry Potter; there is a timelessness, an inherent profundity and archetypal essence to it that makes it irresistible. These elements were so strong and hypnotic that they proved sufficient to envelop me and I must say, I enjoyed the ride, and look forward to re-embarking for The Two Towers.
Due to the aforementioned elements, and some of which I have certainly not mentioned, The Fellowship of the Ring, for me at any rate, rose beyond my criticisms in many ways to ultimately become more than the sum of its parts, and therefore in many respects I probably reflect with rose-tinted glasses on the reading experience; for there was much throughout that I wasn't very fond of. I almost hate myself for espousing what I had thought before reading to be such a dull and vapid criticism, and so I apologise in advance, but there were chunks of this that I found indeed quite boring. For the most part, there was usually something relatively constant to keep be engaged, but they were certainly sections where I had to frequently shake myself awake. I am in awe at Tolkien's vivid imagination, but after a while I found the scenic descriptions grew rather stale and repetitive; I understand that the tale is supposed to be meandering, and so I realise that I'm projecting my own wishes onto the book, but I can't help it, because amidst it all there is a tale that I find riveting and genuinely quite enthralling, its just that its shrouded by one too many additional lanes for my liking. Tolkien certainly takes, literally and figuratively, the scenic route, and I would highly doubt that The Two Towers or The Return of The King would differ very much in this regard, and so I expect that I will probably feel quite similarly, overall, after reading them too.
It's certainly a tour-de-force of the fantasy genre, at least from the meagre pile of fantasy books I have read, and I appreciate the sprawling scope of this fictional universe, how dynamic it is, Tolkien's mesmerising flair for world-building and deft characterisation amongst many other aspects. Indeed, part of me wants to slap a five-star rating on it purely due to the grin I bore on my face during many parts of this, the excitement located sparsely but substantially throughout, but if I'm to really review the entire book, I must consider ALL of it, and for me a little extra haste would have been nice- but hey, then it wouldn't really be the meandering sort of experience it's clearly intended to be.

Of course I’ve been hit with the curse of watching the films before reading the books again, but what films they were! That was probably the biggest problem because for me the film was the ultimate Lord of The Rings and anything else is wrong.

The best way to sum up this book in my own way is that the many parts of the film that I loved were either different or not even in the book... and instead it was filled with parts that evidently were not good enough to even be included in the film... (My fangirl mum once told me that when she was younger she wrote a two page list of all the differences between the book and the film. I can see now how that is possible now.)

I’ll start with the good! The conversations between Bilbo and Gandalf, and then Frodo and Gandalf about the ring, it’s history and what is now brewing in the world were fantastic and really built up the importance of the journey to come. Oh and the writing has actually improved from The Hobbit!

Now for the bad... everything after that? Just kidding.... no not really. We’ll start with Tom Bombadil who after writing this I wish to never hear or see his name ever again. For he and everything that went on during his chapters made me want to tear my hair out. It was the most pointless sidetrack from the main story I have ever encountered in my history of reading. And the singing... please make it stop. It burns us. Ultimately I had to set the speed of my audiobook as fast as I could so my suffering would end quickly before I received any long lasting damage. I can see why there was absolutely no mention of this character and these chapters in the film.

Now let’s speed through the rest because by this point we’re about halfway through the book and in comparison to the film SOD ALL has happened. Right, every scene with Strider/Aragorn was brilliant, his character is epic!! but Arwen? Where you at? I miss you. Then meeting Bilbo again: ‘Hi there, just don’t start doing any sing- oh great... please just leave me alone.’ Skip along a bit more and we don’t even get the classic ‘Noooooooo’ from Gimli in Moria, in fact he didn’t even seem that bothered, shame. Now let’s skip to the end where we are completely missing one of the most iconic scenes in the entire film!? How’s that happened then? I mean I guess it will come at the beginning of the next book but that will be pretty bizarre.

Look, I’m nitpicking obviously, and having fun doing so too. Despite the many differences the book was still great, I mean it’s Tolkien’s Lord the Rings. But the problem is by the end, instead of appreciating the work of Tolkien, I was left appreciating more what director James Cameron actually managed to create from it. He created a masterpiece from something that in my opinion wasn’t quite there yet.

It pains me that I can’t give The Fellowship of the Ring 5 stars. Because I love The Lord of the Rings. I mean really love it. I’ve watched the films countless times, as I’m sure many other people have. My friends and I just can’t help quoting it at every opportune moment. We randomly growl at each other like Bilbo has just seen the ring for the first time in ages. We mimic Gimli’s hilarious laugh whenever anyone says anything remotely funny. We’ll sometimes say “Let this be the hour when we draw swords together!” instead of saying “Let’s go the pub!”. I flipping love it!

Now, I am acutely aware that I am subconsciously forming my opinion of Tolkien's classic compared to modern fantasy and I understand the problems with that. If had been alive and read this book when it was first published, would I have liked it better? Maybe. The issue is I’ll never know. Tolkien was clearly a pioneer of fantasy fiction and has been a huge influence on most fantasy writers ever since (for which he has my thanks and admiration), but when I review a book I solely base my judgement on whether or not I enjoyed it. Not whether the prose was pretty or flowery or complex.

This all sounds like I didn’t enjoy this book. I did! I gave it 3 stars. I thought it was good. Partly. There was a lot that was bad. What stood out to me the most is, that despite this vast world and lore Tolkien has created here, he was very limited on details. I was eagerly looking forward to Gandalf battling the Balrog of Morgoth. This is going to be epic! Then it wasn’t. What does the Balrog even look like, Tolkien?! It’s kind of on fire and has wings. That’s it. How big is it? What does it look like?! And Orcs. Not a clue what Tolkien had in mind for what the Orcs actually looked like.

And, character development is pretty non-existent for most of them. I feel like I only know what drives Frodo, Sam and Boromir. Everyone else is just...there.

And don’t even get me started on the car crash that was those Tom Bombadil chapters.

However, the only thing that will make me carry on is that it started well and ended well. The start was really well written and set the scene perfectly with just the right amount of exposition. When Boromir shows his true colours at the end was a particularly tense part and the awesome Samwise just can’t leave his friend to endure this horrendous quest alone.

Hoping it doesn’t take me as long to read The Two Towers.

When The Lord of the Rings is mentioned, one probably envisions the grand scale it entails. They probably see the Eye of Sauron, or the epic battles. One most likely thinks of Elves and Hobbits and Aragorn and Gandalf and, honestly, the movies. To no surprise. In the 66 years since The Fellowship of the Ring book came out, Lord of the Rings has become something almost grander than life and has far surpassed being a trilogy of books.

It's also important to remember that Tolkien was the father of this genre of writing. A world like Middle Earth had not been seen before, but, in the 66 years since, it has been seen endlessly. Countess other stories follow a similar arc, and just about every fantasy story will consist of Men, Elves, Dwarves and Orcs. Even the fact that I wrote the word as dwarves and not dwarfs is thanks to Tolkien.

This book, and it's two sequels, certainly had a huge impact on writing, and society in general. That is undeniable. I say all this to ask anyone who may be reading this review to please understand I am not reviewing Lord of the Rings as the entity it has become, but only The Fellowship of the Ring as the book contained within these pages.

With all that said, in my opinion, this book, as a book, without the context of what comes next or the movies or anything else - isn't very good.

This is my first time reading this book, and I fully understand if I had read this 60 years ago, I would probably enjoy the story far more. Seeing this magical world of Elves and Dwarves and Hobbits with this evil Dark Lord would absolutely excite me and I would love it. Even today, as I read this book, I did like that. I loved seeing the different areas of Middle Earth. I loved earning about things not shown in the movie. (To an extent.) The story and the environment were fun! When the environment was being shown and the story was actually happening that is.

Originally, Tolkien started writing this story as a sequel to The Hobbit, and as he wrote the trilogy over the next 12 years, it became what we know it to be today. When I listed the things people think of when hearing Lord of the Rings, I intentionally didn't mention 'a sequel to The Hobbit. Despite people recognizing they take place in the same world, I think it's safe to say most people will know one is not a sequel to the other. Not directly at least.

However, the first ten chapters, and 180 pages or so, are. That's the majority of book 1. It's written with a heavy focus on the hobbits, going into every tiny little detail, and families and their history and a lot of information that never comes up again and isn't really needed.

There is a lot of that in this book. There is a whole lot of information that simply never comes up again. Maybe 66 years ago when this was written, that was how books were. Admittedly, I haven't read many books from that time period. Today, it's not good writing. The book is 398 pages long, when it could easily be 300 at most. Maybe closer to 250.

I'm not just talking about scenes describing every family in the Shire. I'm talking about scenes like when Frodo wants to go get water, and gets to the river, and forgets his water bottle, and goes back and it's all described out for some reason. Step by step.

That leads to some pretty bad pacing in this book. It's not just the excessive details that cause that though. It's how the book itself is. There are 24 songs in this book alone. That's 24 times when the story was stopped dead for a song, with only 1 instance where I could think it actually somewhat made sense to have. That is with Frodo at the Prancing Pony.

Alongside the songs, the Company stops a lot. One of the most noticeable examples was after failing to go over the Mountains, the Company climbs back down and they start discussing what to do next. Moria comes up and after pages of this, they finally ask Frodo, who says they should sleep. So they do. Then they get attacked in the night. That attack was the first action in a long time. Besides, it stopped the story dead. It was moving along. Clearly their enemies were watching and trying to hinder them, and it was interesting seeing what they wanted to do, and then, nothing. They did nothing. They just stopped there and slept. There are so many times when the flow of the story is stopped dead because of them resting and sleeping.

The last big thing that ruins to flow of the story is continuously having character recount events we already know. Even in some cases don't know. There are two big instances of this. First, the Council of Elrond, in which the Fellowship of the Ring (the group itself) is created. Kinda. Not really. It's more an afterthought done in the last 2 pages of the chapter, which in itself is 30 pages, and then kinda finished in the next chapter. Even then it feels more like the others are coming because they are also heading that way, and not because the literal fate of the entire world depends on it.

So what are the other 28 pages of that chapter about? Frodo waking up and being told what happened at the Ford. Then the council starts and they say the entire history of the ring. The entire thing. Form start until Frodo brought it up. Elrond talks, and then Bilbo talks and sings (And it's even mentioned how he talks to much) and then Gandalf talks and says his part about the ring and the entire encounter he had with Saruman, and the history of Isengard and Orthanc. Not to mention Boromir speaks and Aragorn speaks, and did I mention they go rest then?

It's cool, and some of it is interesting, and some of it is actually useful. So what's the problem? Besides this book being called The Fellowship of the Ring, and the creation of said Fellowship being an afterthought, the entire 30 page chapter gets summed up into a 5 minute sequence in the movie. Which, yes I know the movie is a different thing, however, I think that comes to show just how much was unnecessary. Yes, some of the information told her was told elsewhere in the movie. (Gandalf visiting Saruman for instance.) Even then, I cannot help but feel as if so much of it wasn't necessary.

While what happened to Gandalf was important to know, the history of Gollum being captured and then escaped probably wasn't so important to go into full detail of. Nor was Bilbo singing, multiple times. All of this comes after almost 200 pages of just the hobbits leaving the Shire. Now I will give it credit, because before the council, the enormity of what Frodo possesses and what must be done doesn't really set in yet. Frodo and his friends have no idea.

The problem is that after the Council, when they know this ring must be destroyed, MUST BE, or the world will fall to darkness, and all free people will fall, even the Shire, and it still seems like they are taking their sweet time. THAT is why it bugs me that they sleep so much. Yes, they have to. Is it so important it must stop the story? No. Especially when figuring out where to go next, on this quest to save the world.

Going back, the second instance I was speaking of comes shortly after leaving Moria. In where Gandalf's death receives but a few lines before they're off again. Then when they meet the elves, Galandriel asks to hear the full story of what happened, and we are subjected to an 8 paragraph description of everything we just read.

I went into this book incredibly excited to read it. Beyond excited. I had just finished watching all 3 extended editions to the movies. I had watched HOURS of lore videos and behind the scenes videos. I felt it was time to finally read the books. After doing so, I'm not moving on to the next two. I can't. Clearly these books are not for me.

I'm incredibly grateful for what they have become. I am incredibly happy they became so popular. This book, as a book, has a lot of problems. I enjoyed the story. I enjoyed the characters. It was fascinating to see how different certain characters were to what I had seen of them before. The writing itself, the dialogue, the extensive exposition, the non-stop songs, and constant stops, just killed the story. By the time I was done, I wasn't enjoying myself anymore.

So I'll leave it at that. I think this book could use an abridged version. I'm happy it exists.

A truly thrilling story, this book is a beautiful work of art. The characters, the descriptions and the intricate plots make it worth your time (and its going to take a lot of that).
This book may, in the beginning, bore you thoroughly.But as you take the journey with Frodo and his companions, you will find it hard to put down. I, personally, have known very few who have been able to bear through the entire story, and each one of them is in love with Tolkien's world.

Moreover, the highly detailed world of middle-earth , (which has been named "The Most Complicated Fictional World ever Created"), is so carefully laid out and detailed, that it is sometimes impossible to believe that it is the product of the imagination of one mind only.

This is basically the mature version of The Hobbit. Instead of a hobbit going point A to point B to steal treasure, we get a more serious journey that decides the fate of Middle-Earth. And instead of getting 13 forgettable dwarfs, we get a smaller but more memorable cast.


Tolkien does an amazing job in breathing life into Middle-earth. He breathes life into it through the poems and songs, the character themselves, and in his descriptive imagery of the landscapes. Though it can be excessive at times, it does help in immersing the reader into this high-fantasy world that they otherwise wouldn't have taken as seriously. It's a trade off.

Because a lot of this book involves walking, the bulk of the tension is done through the fear of being caught by the enemy. It's this impending doom that keeps you engaged. Did Frodo really hear footsteps? Was Sam seeing something or was he dreaming? The payoff for all this anticipation is usually done by a riveting action sequence that reminds you of how dangerous this journey really is (Perfect example: Moria). In addition to that, It also makes you appreciate the fighters in the group.

One of the issues readers say LOTR has is how black and white it is. I didn't find this much of a problem (in this book). The temptation of power and its corruption are already interesting enough concepts for me. The only thing that I did feel was lacking is Sauron's backstory. If you're going to give us all this information about towns and kingdoms, give us something on the antagonist!

Gandalf? The coolest. Sam? That's the homie. Frodo? Eh.

Frodo is interesting in that he isn't the typical hero that we imagine today. He isn't stoic, or powerful, or competent. But he is courageous. What I can't find interesting is his personality. He doesn't stick out to me: he's just the ring-bearer. Sam is endearing for his loyalty, and an intriguing character because he is more talented than we are led to believe. I feel like Frodo is very much like Bilbo, but I already read Bilbo's journey. I need something different.

What is else do I want to say? Oh yea! I hate Bombadil. I actually almost dropped this book because of him.

This was my first time reading The Fellowship of the Ring, and I'm really glad to finally be getting around to reading this epic, classic series. I've "watched" all of the movies once each (by which I mean that I fell asleep in each one of them--which is not an insult, they are long but I generally always fall asleep watching things), and I had read The Hobbit much earlier, but I was largely influenced by my brother, who read these books when he was in elementary school or middle school and found them boring at the time. Now that I have so many friends who stand by them so much, though, and also as a Christian and someone who is very passionate about languages, I thought it was about time I gave them a go.

And I have to say--even though I love a lot about C.S. Lewis and the Chronicles of Narnia, one thing I increasingly struggled with with those books is just how painfully obvious and aware Lewis is of the allegory. Here, some beautiful metaphors are folded within a much larger story, which itself was apparently just the backdrop for these languages Tolkien wanted to create, and I really liked that.

There were some immediate aspects in the first few chapters that got me hooked--Frodo and his quiet, serious regard for Bilbo; his proclamation that he would give all the wealth he inherited just to see him again; of course, Sam's deep loyalty, which was the biggest thing I remembered from and admired in the movies. I also do love the old style of language, which is more grandiose and un-self-conscious in its epic scale than a lot of the language we use today, which I think is forced to be much sparser. Of course, at times that also makes the narrative very wordy, but in general I like it.

Also, having fully immersed myself in contemporaneous books due to working in children's publishing and focusing heavily on YA, I admit, it's a breath of fresh air to read such an entirely different style that also succeeds in its own right. The slow pace is definitely not a page-turning mechanism; and yet there is a lot that is being built here, the world, the characters, and yes, the writing itself.

It was also amusing trying to imagine this overlaid onto modern publishing standards, though. I don't think it would have gotten published, or it would have been heavily edited. We're used to much tighter plotting now, much less meandering for world-building. And while I admit that that is what I am used to and that generally works for me, I also liked having a change of pace here.

Overall, per usual, the parts I enjoyed the most were more character-driven, and I admit that, though I try, I am never super enthralled by long descriptions of scenery or anything like that. But I did like this overall and I'm glad I read it. I don't know if I'll keep coming back to it breathlessly the way some of my friends do, who have been fans since childhood, but I found a lot to be inspired by, both as a reader, and maybe especially as a writer and a hopeful linguist.

L’unico motivo per iniziare (e cercare di finire) questo tomo è la trama. È una delle storie più belle mai scritte per quanto mi riguarda. Tolkien ha creato un intero mondo secondario e indipendente dal nostro mondo, con le sue regole, tradizioni, lingue e luoghi. Il grande difetto di Tolkien è lo stile di scrittura. Fa spiegoni, mega riassunti quasi azzerando di conseguenza il coinvolgimento da parte del lettore. Le descrizioni sono lunghe e non fa uso del mostrato. Il testo risulta pesante. I personaggi sono bidimensionali e statici, non vengono caratterizzate attraverso i dialoghi e la narrazione (essendo tutto raccontato). Tolkien ha a disposizione una miriade di personaggi, tuttavia preferisce una narrazione parziale assumendo solo il pov di Frodo. Se la narrazione parziale da un parte fa mantenere all’oscuro la situazione attuale dei personaggi, come la sparizione di Gandalf per esempio, e conferisce un’atmosfera di tensione e curiosità del lettore, dall’altra parte questa viene rivelata con un mega spiegone di 6 pagine nel consiglio di Elrond. In realtà quella parte di storia mi è risultata gradevole in un certo senso perché si ricostruisce tutte le tappe che ha passato l’Anello. Per quasi tutto il libro il ritmo è lento con occasionali picchi d’azione. Si passa a un ritmo serrato nel passo a Moria fino al famoso “tu non puoi passare” per poi avere un crollo di ritmicità e un abbiocco pazzesco.

The descriptive narrative seems to drag on and on and the reading gets a bit lethargic up until the second last chapter, though the flight of imagination, construction of new linguistic codes and background mythology remains splendid and unmatched.

It goes without saying that Tolkien has created an amazing and expansive world filled with whimsy, magic and many different races. I adored exploring all of the different places with the characters, particularly Lothlórien and The Shire. Each race brought something unique to the story, and Tolkien did a fantastic job at making them individual and distinguishable. We are given so much history in this book and it was so interesting to learn of all the different events, wars, and what makes up Middle-Earth. That’s about where my enjoyment of this book ended.

I buddy read this book with a group of lovely people over on Instagram, so we all helped each other to keep reading. If it wasn’t for this, it would have definitely taken me over a month to finish. Tolkien has a habit of giving you fifty words to describe something when he could have used ten. He really takes his time to explain EVERY. SINGLE. DETAIL. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing; however, I just really didn’t enjoy it personally. The writing style is dense and made everything so slow going, and although I got used to it as I read on, I didn’t particularly enjoy myself. Tolkien also takes his time in describing mundane events such as The Fellowship walking or eating which I found really boring. He often repeats the same phrases to describe certain things e.g. a waxing moon, everything different is ‘queer’ which got super repetitive and annoying, though it could reflect the writing of the time.

I also couldn’t really connect with the characters at all. Though Tolkien gives us lots of detail, I don’t think his characters were given very much depth (pls don’t come for me). Despite this, I thought the relationships between characters were done well and I understood their intentions and motivations. I particularly liked Aragorn, Gimli and Legolas, but the main characters fell short for me. I did enjoy some of the scenes in this book, including meeting Aragorn at the Inn, and when they arrived at the gates of Moria, possibly due to the intrigue.

I really wanted to like this, but I was just bored throughout. We are buddy reading the next two so I will persevere and hold off until I can form an overall opinion of the whole series.

Una de las cosas buenas que tiene este libro es que, conforme uno avanza en la historia, todo mejora considerablemente. El interés por lo que se avecina se multiplica, los personajes evolucionan y el cariño que uno siente por ellos, también. Si le pongo un 3, y no un 4 o 5, es porque no puedo negar que en muchísimos tramos se me ha hecho pesado, aburrido incluso. Este es un libro de esos que requieren paciencia: le cuesta arrancar. El prólogo no es muy halagüeño. Los pasajes que describen el trayecto de la Compañía a través de ríos, montañas y toda clase de orografía se hacen, en ocasiones, muy lentos; es fácil perder la concentración si uno no tiene un buen día. Las páginas enteras de poemas y canciones (que además, al estar traducidos, no conservan la musicalidad original) pueden ser un reto.
Sin embargo, creo que merece la pena pasar por todos esos tediosos tramos y empaparse de la literatura de Tolkien; disfrutar de la magia presente en cada página; del mundo de los Hobbits, de los Hombres, de los Elfos y de los Enanos; de las leyendas e historias, criaturas y paisajes de la Tierra Media; del camino, de las decisiones y de la amistad que se forja entre nuestros personajes. Me quedo con muchas ganas de continuar la trilogía y de seguir descubriendo.

This edition that I listened to on audio is the 1979 NPR radio drama, not the complete unabridged book.
------------------

This version already scores major points in my book for including Tom Bombadil. As abridged as this show is from the original story, I'm glad they made room for Tommy Boy.

The style of this radio show has an intentionally old-school, pre-television tone to it, like similar shows of the 30s and 40s, from the cheesy musical cues/sound design to the style of narration. This could make or break the experience for many listeners. I was able to enjoy it for what it was, but I can easily see this being a turn-off for many.

The cast was a bit of a mixed bag. I liked Frodo's Average Joe tone of voice, American accent and all (played by James Arrington), which helped to emphasize how ordinary he is, which makes his courage and his journey all the more extraordinary. Samwise was played by Lou Bliss, and I strongly suspect that this was a female voice actor playing a male character, which gave Sam a scruffy prepubescent tone of voice that I didn't expect. Honestly, it wasn't bad, and it even added another dynamic to his character, a Coming-of-Age story. Elrond's voice actor was weird, though, like an elderly Jay Gatsby. I half expected him to start calling Gandalf 'Old Sport'. Everyone else was either just fine or mediocre.

Overall, I had a good time with this, and I will be listening to the rest of this show, but I'm glad I checked this out from the library, as opposed to buying it.

Note: The book is split into two books/parts. I am reviewing the first book.

Taking place many years after The Hobbit, The Fellowship of the Ring is another fantastic fantasy novel by J.R.R. Tolkien. (Heh, see what I did there?) The Hobbit was centered around Bilbo Baggins, and this story is centered around his nephew Frodo Baggins and his friends Merry, Pippin, and Sam. In the story, Bilbo has a huge party for his 111th birthday, and uses it to announce his retirement by vanishing with the Ring he found in The Hobbit. Gandalf the wizard, however, becomes troubled over how the Ring has changed Bilbo slightly, and after Bilbo leaves Gandalf assigns Frodo to guard the Ring and leave his hobbit-hole to destroy it. Frodo accepts, and he also leaves with the hope of finding Bilbo, taking Merry, Pippin, and Sam with him. Along the way, they soon discover they are being followed by an enemy who wants the Ring. Frodo is probably my favorite character, and he is both similar and different from Bilbo. Both left on a journey sent by Gandalf, but Frodo does not need as much motivation as Bilbo did, rather he is doing it almost willingly. He cares for his friends and is persistent. In short, I thought this book was a well written sequel to The Hobbit, but it had the same problem The Hobbit did, except bigger. It spent too much time on transitions from one place to another. The descriptions of Frodo, Pippin, Merry, and Sam’s journey through the land seemed to me rather dragged out. (Example: “The woods on either side became denser, the trees were now younger and thicker; and as the lane went lower, running down into a fold of the hills, there were many deep brakes of hazel on the rising slopes at either hand.” (Page 80)) You could skip that part and still understand what’s going on in the main storyline of the book. I recommend The Fellowship of the Ring (technically part 1 of it) to those who liked The Hobbit.

Note: This book is split into two parts. This is my review of the second part.

The second part of The Fellowship of the Ring, in my opinion, was much better than the first part. While book 1 focused on a whole lot of walking and not much else, book 2 admittedly has some of that too, but this part is where the story sped up a little. The story begins with Frodo waking up in Rivendell, the place where he was trying to get to in the first half. Frodo and pals rest up and get better, then continue their journey. One of my favorite parts is when they meet Galadriel and Frodo and Sam look in the mirror. It was very similar to the Mirror of Erised in Harry Potter. (“‘Many times I can command the mirror to reveal,’ she answered, ‘and to some I can show what they desire to see.’” (Page 377)) My absolute favorite part, though, was the ending. I won’t spoil it, but it was a great way to finish the book and set up the sequel. Frodo and Sam in particular have gotten a lot more character development. To conclude my full review of this book, I recommend it to anyone who is looking for a long, detailed fantasy genre book.

Just watch the movie. Now, before you yell at me, hear me out.

I have tried to read the Lord of The Rings many times, but Tolkiens slow storytelling never failed to bore me to tears in the first 100 pages or so. This time was no different, but I finally powered through. And I must say... I'm a bit disappointed.

Now, the world that Tolkien paints is rich and beautiful, and it is certainly impressive how much work went into it. But I doubt these books are going to be riveting to anyone but Tolkien fans who are already deeply invested in the world and story. If you approach this book with little background knowledge, the info dump will hit you like a pile of bricks, and you'll say: Why should I care?

The story isn't terrible by any means, it's just so drawn out and interrupted with weird, unnecessary interludes, that it made me wonder if it was really worth it.

Almost every major character breaks out in song or rhyme at least once, often with very little prompting. And Tolkien felt it necessary to include the whole thing, not just snippets or the first verse, entire, page-long poems. Lovely if you're a Tolkien buff and can't get enough of Middle Earth, mind-numbing for anyone else. The same goes for history facts that get dumped on you with little context to make them meaningful.

Descriptions of landscapes and artworks make up a BIG part of Tolkiens writing, so it really lends itself to a visual adaptation. There's not a whole bunch of dialogue and main story left if you remove all the descriptions, info dumps and songs.

Which is what leads me to say: If you don't care about all the super intricated details, you'll be just fine having watched the movies. Sure, you might not realize Aragorn is actually 80 years old, but as my friend said: "Ew, I don't think I wanted to know that!"

In the end, LotR is a fine piece of fantasy. If you love it, I see why. If you hate it, I get it, too. I'm glad it was written, and I'm glad to know about it, but I doubt it's a Must Read. Have a crack at it, and if it bores you like it did me, watch the movies and move on.

Is Lord of the Rings the greatest book ever written? Or the greatest English book? Or at least the greatest book of the twentieth-century? Certainly the book used to regularly top polls of this kind, even before Peter Jackson’s hugely successful film trilogy.

As my rating indicates, I do not think so. However can we at least agree that the British public think it is the greatest book? Again, no. Appearances are deceptive. The difficulty with polls is that they are influenced by the enthusiasm of the fan base.

The people who love Tolkien love him hard, and are therefore more anxious to phone in their votes. The people who love Great Expectations or 1984 are less fanatical in their devotion, and therefore less likely to bother phoning in their votes. So I can at least grant that Lord of the Rings is the book that inspires the deepest affection among books with a large fan base.

Conversely Lord of the Rings inspires great ire among those who hate it. "Not another f*cking elf," C.S. Lewis is reported to have complained. (Incidentally if you want to find the quote, do not type ‘f*cking elf’ into Google, or you will find links of a more adult nature suggested by the search. Is there really such a big market for watching elf sex?)

So I guess all that remains is to say what I think. I should probably say that it is possibly unfair of me to review the three books individually. Unlike the Harry Potter books, these are not part of a franchise. Tolkien intended the entire book to be released as one volume, but his publishers had other ideas.

Hence The Fellowship of the Ring is part of a book, and not the first book in a trilogy. It is therefore no use complaining that the book lacks an artistic finish, or that the next book has no beginning or ending, or that the last book begins assuming reader knowledge, and is dedicated to tying up loose ends. That is a reasonable criticism for the Harry Potter series, but an unfair one here, as this is all one book.

The story once more returns to Middle Earth (Tolkien’s fictional world) and The Shire, home of the hobbits. (They are not f*cking elves. They are hobbits. But we will see some f*cking elves later if you like that sort of thing.) The action follows on from The Hobbit. Bilbo, the hero of that book is still around, and he still has the ring that made him invisible.

However we now learn that this ring has extra malignant magical powers, and that it is being sought by the evil Sauron, a Dark Lord who wishes to enslave the land. Bilbo reluctantly gives it up to the good wizard Gandalf (another returning character), and it is passed on to his younger cousin Frodo.

Incidentally the casting of Elijah Wood might lead readers to assume that Frodo is a callow youth, but the book clearly explains that he is 50 years old. So we should view him as inexperienced in this kind of adventure, but otherwise quite senior. Frodo sets out with his loyal servant Samwise on a quest to destroy the Ring before Sauron can get his hands on it. They are joined by Frodo’s friends, Pippin and Merry.

After a number of episodic adventures the group meet a ranger called Strider, who is really Aragorn (a number of characters confusingly have two names in the book). Finally they arrive in Rivendell, a world of elves (I told you we would get to the f*cking elves).

Here there is a council, which leads to a mixed group (the fellowship) setting off together to destroy the ring. This comprises the four hobbits, Gandalf, Aragorn (or Strider or whatever), the dwarf Gimli, a f*cking elf Legolas and another human character, Boromir, who wants the ring for himself. Gandalf is apparently killed by a mysterious beast along the way, and Frodo and Samwise set out on their own to complete the mission.

Thus endeth the first book. While it is considerably better written than The Hobbit, I can remember my feeling of disappointment on reading it, as it felt like a re-tread of the earlier book.

There is the interminable trudging along through one adventure after another, ending in an occasional skirmish or battle. There is a powerful wizard who can solve all their problems, but who goes missing during the most important parts. When our heroes finally arrived at a council, I perked up hoping the book could now go in different directions, but no. Off they set on another long interminable walk.

There are some improvements on The Hobbit however. This time the quest feels a little more worthwhile. Last time Bilbo and the indistinguishable dwarves were out for treasure, during which they caused a dragon to attack a nearby town and almost provoked a minor war. This time Frodo is not seeking to gain a treasure but to lose one, and for the noblest of reasons. He is seeking to get rid of the Ring and prevent Sauron becoming more powerful.

There are also better reasons to explain Gandalf’s absence from much of the book. In The Hobbit, he sets our heroes off on an adventure, and then tells them he has better things to do, and leaves them to struggle through the most dangerous parts of the journey. Here he has genuinely good reasons for being detained, the last one being his apparent death.

Of course it is a fantasy trope that the wise mentor wizard will be incapacitated or killed at some key point in the story, so that our inexperienced hero has a chance to prove himself. This usually results in an improbable battle to the death with the wicked sorcerer in which our seemingly inept hero somehow triumphs. Lord of the Rings is more realistic. All Frodo has to do is to throw a ring in a volcano.

Perhaps it helps to keep Gandalf off the scene as much as possible, because this might remind the reader of the one big plot hole in all fantasy. If we have a powerful wizard, why on Middle-Earth do our heroes have to spend most of the story walking to their destination? Why can’t the wizard wave his wand (or whatever) and teleport (or fly them on broomsticks or whatever) to their location and end the book within seconds?

Viewed in this way, the episodic adventures along the way are just filler from a narrative point of view. The only thing that matters is whether Sauron’s forces can be beaten in battle, and whether Frodo can destroy the ring. Both of these aims could be achieved with magic in just one chapter.

However that will never happen because the episodic events provide the gravy of the book. We know how it will end and there is little suspense in that, so we are invited to enjoy the journey which is less certain. It is therefore necessary that magic is only used to achieve minor results along the way, and our heroes will continue to walk (often without horses) and to fight battles with spears and arrows.

Lord of the Rings is not a book notable for its progressive views. Tolkien reveres royalty and nobility. Even the hobbits are financially well-fixed the aristocracy of their area. The only lower-class character here is Samwise, a dull-witted reincarnation of Sam Weller from The Pickwick Papers. He feeds into the upper-class fantasy of having a faithful retainer who stands by his master out of love, rather than because he is a paid employee.

Women barely feature here. They are peripheral characters who give encouragement and support, but play no other part. None of the Fellowship are women, and we see little of women fighting in later books. There is an exception, which I will discuss when I get to that book. For the main part this is a Sausageship as well as a Fellowship though.

To some extent, one’s love of Tolkien depends on one’s patience for certain aspects of his style. He furnishes us with huge amounts of detail concerning his fantasy world, often pausing the story for long periods to furnish us with this history. He includes maps of the journey, and long footnotes about things we never needed to know.

This approach will excite the nerdier fans, and exasperate those who are not very keen on Tolkien. I am a little in-between. I shake my head at the sheer amount of solemnly-presented information about elves and orcs and past wizards and goodness-knows-what, but I also admire Tolkien for the amount of time he has spent plotting out his imaginary world in detail.

Tolkien also brings a quaintness often missing in fantasy. The gentle laid-back hobbits, the snatches of song and doggerel poetry and the general sense of innocence here is something that is Tolkien’s, and removes it from the clichés into which fantasy has fallen. Sometimes the innocence leads to moments of double-entendre:

'Master Merry's being squeezed in a crack!' cried Sam....Tom put his mouth to the crack and began singing into it in a low voice. They could not catch the words, but evidently Merry was aroused. His legs began to kick."

Oh, baby!

I may change my mind when I get round to reading the other two books, but I would say that Fellowship is the better one. It offers a more solid adventure story compared to the repetitious structure of The Two Towers and long drawn-out conclusion of The Return of the King. It is long and frequently dull, but there are some exciting parts and I can see its appeal.

Desde hace mucho tiempo he tenido pendiente El Señor de los Anillos, porque come on, estamos hablando del papá de la fantasía. Las personas dicen que es uno de los mejores libros que existen y por eso mis expectativas eran muy altas. Cuando empecé a leerlo no tenía ni idea de qué trataba porque jamás he visto las películas ni tampoco he escuchado spoilers sobre la trama, así que básicamente empecé con los ojos vendados.
Lastimosamente, La Comunidad del Anillo no ha logrado convencerme. Me ha parecido excesivamente tedioso y lento. Creo que lo que más me hartó fue la cantidad de páginas que el autor se dedica a describir el contexto y los lugares que visitan los personajes. Entiendo que Tolkien quería que nosotros los lectores pudiéramos visualizar sin ninguna duda como se ve la Tierra Media, pero llegó un punto en que sinceramente todo era igual y ya ni me importaba. Por otro lado, el autor se toma su tiempo en escribir muchas canciones que explican tanto los sentimientos de los personajes como la mitología del universo de Tolkien, pero para mí eran un somnífero.
Otro aspecto que no me gustó fueron los diálogos. Creo que eran muy superficiales y para mí sonaban poco creíbles y falsos. Tal vez tiene que ver mucho la época en que el libro fue escrito, pero yo sentí que las conversaciones eran muy acartonadas. Pero creo que lo me se me hizo más difícil de digerir fueron los personajes. Me imaginaba que esta historia sería una donde los personajes son los que le dan brillo a la trama, pero no es el caso. Creo que en general la mayoría son muy planos, poco interesantes, copias uno de otros, y por supuesto, aburridos. Y quiero que me expliquen, ¿cómo un personaje tan soso como Frodo es el protagonista? No lo entiendo. Me gustaría decir al menos que me cae mal, pero ni eso. Es tan nulo, que me daba sueño. Sin embargo, no todo está perdido porque a medida que más leía le tomé cierto cariño a Sam, el único hobbit rescatable de la historia. También me terminó gustando Gandalf y Aragorn. Los demás, que son bastantes, se pueden ir a la hoguera porque no me interesan.
A pesar de que parece que odié el libro, no fue así. La Comunidad del Anillos no es malo, para nada, pues tiene varias cosas muy buenas. Primero que nada, sabemos que las obras de Tolkien son el pilar para el mundo de la literatura fantástica. Gracias a él tenemos muchas historias que amamos, como Harry Potter o Juego de Tronos. Y aunque no pude disfrutar el libro como hubiera querido, no puedo ignorar este hecho, pues El Señor de los Anillos ha hecho historia y siempre se mantendrá como un clásico.
En segundo lugar, la magnitud del universo creado por Tolkien es increíble y muy complejo. Sí, es cierto que me aburre un montón, pero eso no cambia que el señor creó un mundo completamente nuevo, lleno de historia, mitología y criaturas muy ricas en contenido. Así que no puedo evitar admirar al autor por su imaginación y también por darle tanta profundidad.
En tercer y último lugar, creo que Tolkien tenía mucho talento para escribir, lo cual no es sorprendente si tomamos en cuenta que fue filólogo. Si bien, no me enamoré de su prosa y no está entre mis favoritas, es imposible negar que el señor sabía lo que hacía.
Así que por estas razones, tanto buenas como malas, he decidido darle un 3, ya que personalmente no lo disfruté, pero objetivamente es un buen libro. Sinceramente no creo que continúe con los otros dos porque el simple hecho de imaginarme pasar por esta tortuosa experiencia dos veces más me hace querer golpearme la cabeza contra la pared. Pero como dicen por ahí, nunca digas nunca. Tal vez en un futuro (muy lejano) desee retomar la historia.
Mientras tanto me conformo con las películas. Por primera vez voy a verlas y ya empecé con la primera. Solo llevo 48 minutos pero ya puedo decir que la estoy disfrutando. Es cierto que casi nunca una adaptación cinematográfica está al mismo nivel que su versión escrita, pero creo que este es uno de esos casos extraordinarios en que prefiero la película. Es cierto que hasta donde he visto han habido cambios y por supuesto se han omitido muchas cosas, pero es imposible que en menos de 4 horas (estoy viendo la versión extendida) abarquen la magnitud de la obra. Y pues me siento muy satisfecha con lo que estoy viendo. Tal vez me vea las tres películas y eso me motive a continuar con los libros.

A book about creatures and steeped in history on said creatures. When J R R Tolkien sat down to write this book he already had written a lot for and about the characters he illustrates and the world they inhabit. It's not clear at first he had no interest in writing this book. For him it was a chore to write his stories about Frodo, Bilbo, Gollum, the one ring, and the numerous characters and creatures that turn up in his fake history. As such it's a bit of a chore to read it. In his forward and introduction to the colletor's edition of The Lord of the Rings, complete with the appendices getting into how his words are pronounced and the timlines about the hobbits, J R R Tolkien himself openly admits he had next to no patience for stories nor tale-telling. His passion lay in history and culture, "be it true or feigned".
His mentallity toward his secondary world was more or less, "let's just look at these pretty words". The world Tolkien built is a fascinating one, has been for decades, but when trying to get through The Hobbit and The Fellowship of the Ring book 1, the joy of exploring this world with him is almost lost. In fact, by the time I finished reading The Hobbit and The Fellowship of the Ring: book 1, I felt his work to be dryer than the fossil of Lucy.
