This is my first time revisiting the Lord of the Rings trilogy since I was a child, and I was pleased to discover that I still liked it! I listened to the great audiobook read by Rob Inglis, and this is defintely the version I would recommend. The only other one I could find was full cast with sound effects and music (great), but the narrator was doing a fake English accent (not great) which was too bad to not be distracting, and I gave up on it after about ten minutes. (Seriously, why not just actually hire someone with the accent you want?? Generally speaking non-British people are awful at putting on a good English accent, so how did they not see this coming??) But the Rob Inglis audiobook is wonderful, and well worth the £12 I paid for it on iTunes after I couldn't find it on Youtube for free.

For the story itself, I'd forgotten how slow and dull most of the first half is; it's just four hobbits wandering around in some fields and forests. But once you get to the Council of Elrond it really does pick up (the film had the right idea about skipping all that walking nonsense, even if we did miss the wonderful Tom Bombadil, and the super creepy barrow-wights).

Another criticism is that a lot of the characters (especially Pippin and Merry, I thought) aren't as distinct as they are in the film. But Sam remains as jokes as I remembered, and I also came out with a newfound appreciation for book-Gimli in particular. I'm also pretty sure Legolas has no actual lines until 75% of the way through the book, and it got to the point where I was surprised to hear him speak for the first time. This review is going to be more about my experience with this book rather than about the book itself . Everyone knows the story . And there already has been said much about it . So I don't need repeat it .

The Fellowship of the Ring kind of a bittersweet novel . For about 40% of the book almost put me to sleep . But the beginning and the ending were really fun . That being said , this book is best as it is .

It would be really difficult for me to talk about this book so I'd rather write the review in two categories . What worked for me and what didn't .

Pros :

⭐ The characters . I loved almost every character in the novel . Apart from the hobbits , Gandalf was definitely my favorite character .

⭐ The plot . Good vs Evil . It's still my favorite theme for any novel .

“The road must be trod, but it will be very hard. And neither strength nor wisdom will carry us far upon it. This quest may be attempted by the weak with as much hope as the strong. Yet it is oft the course of deeds that move the wheels of the world: Small hands do them because they must, while the eyes of the great are elsewhere.” 

⭐ The Setting . Ah!! How I wish I lived in Middle-Earth with all those hobbits and elves and dwarves ?! Tolkein's world has endured more than half a century . And that's saying something .

“Many that live deserve death. And some that die deserve life. Can you give it to them? Then do not be too eager to deal out death in judgement.” 

⭐ The Quotes . Sounds weird?! Maybe . But I like quotes . And Tolkein has set a benchmark in writing great quotes .(not comparing to Shakespeare)

Cons

⭐ The plot was soooo slow . Maybe this book was meant to be a slow burn adventure . But I've been spoiled . Fast paced novels and character driven tight plots have made me lazy . Half the time Tolkein was describing the trees , or the birds or the winds . These descriptions were a welcome relief at first . But then it was too much too soon .

Tolkein's writing is fairly simple . Though a bit out of fashion it's easy to understand .

And lastly , I would say , this book/series is important . I mean this book almost single handedly brought the fantasy genre into mainstream . You'd have to give that guy at least that . And thus , I respect the slowness of the book . It's appropriate for the novel . Even I'm saying this . Fans of fantasy literature should read Lord Of The Rings at least once in their life .

And a special shoutout to Frodo , Sam , Merry and Pippin for reading this with me . It was really fun guys how we bonded together while reading this book .

Este 2022 quería regresar al puño y letra de Tolkien, proponiéndome un maratón con obras suyas (que a decir verdad no voy al ritmo pactado pero más vale despacio que no hacerlo) y me alegro porque, ya sabiendo a lo que me deparaba, he podido degustar sus páginas sabiendo de la lentitud que caracteriza La Comunidad del Anillo y ciertas páginas que suponen el mayor altibajo del libro, en las cuales sé que más de uno abandonó su aventura en esta trilogía de fantasía.

La verdad es que he podido ver en esta ocasión el encanto de Tolkien: su amor por la naturaleza, el perfeccionismo por cada detalle de la Tierra Media y todos sus parajes, el encanto fantástico de cada raza que pisa estas tierras y a la vez los horrores que se esconden en ella. Ha sido un comienzo de aventuras fantástico que, por desgracia como dije antes tiene esos altibajos, en especial destaco el que transcurre desde que nuestro protagonista deja la comarca hasta que llega a Rinvendel, que empañan La comunidad del Anillo haciendo en algunas partes tedioso de continuar su lectura.

Aún así, si tienes la paciencia suficiente creo que La comunidad del anillo es buen libro de fantasía aventuras con un universo muy rico detrás que puede apreciarse en sus páginas junto con un elenco de personajes a la altura. Everything is very epic, and while I appreciate that that's part of the appeal, it's also, for me, part of the problem. This world and the plot are so expansive that I have trouble keeping up with everything, and that's only going to get harder in books two and three, now that the Fellowship (and therefore the plot) have split. . . . And my favourite, Sam. He is the loyal friend who would prove himself worthy of trust despite being constantly underestimated. He is someone whose determination and keeness outshines his many flaws. Sam is a joy to read.

A very charming piece of excellent world-building and storytelling that is not without its flaws.

I find the world-building in this book to be great: the elves and dwarves especially come alive with cultures that seem real and meaningful. Tolkien achieves this through consistent application of a technique of presenting a mystery and then pulling the curtain back on that mystery, only to reveal --- more curtain. It is a fascinating and engrossing way to tell a story.

It's strange to see what aspects of the real world Tolkien wanted to abandon and what he didn't. For example, Bilbo and Frodo share the same birthday: September 22. The whole calendar is just borrowed from our current time. This doesn't seem like the sort of thing we should read into. For even if Tolkien really thinks, as I think he does, that Middle-earth is *our* Earth, it still doesn't explain why our current calendar system would exist in that time. I don't mean this as a criticism, but today's fantasy works try to escape our current social norms so much that they even invent their own swear words. Yet, Tolkien is content is apparently uncritically lift our calendar system --- and that's really interesting.

I also think that Frodo is probably the best developed character here. Still, I want to praise how subtly Tolkien develops the other characters. It isn't like Gimli, for example, is given a chapter dedicated to him, but Tolkien chooses to develop his characters in the background in a way that other authors couldn't really pull off. Gimli might change or have his motivations revealed in a exchange with Legolas, even if the exchange is brief. This makes small, perhaps seemingly meaningless conversations seem more important.

However, I do have my complaints. I think there are huge parts of this book that are dull. The chapter concerning the Council of Elrond is too long by far and is way too much of an exposition-dump. Tolkien could have chosen a way to spread that information out a little more evenly. Moreover, the back half of the book is filled with some important and exciting events -- but they are few and far between. The first half of the book is a slog in its own way, but there's something exciting about the beginning of a mysterious journey; the second half sees the characters begin their journey by stumbling. They go from one boring event to another, although there really is some exciting and unmissable stuff squeezed in there, too: it's just not enough.

I recommend this charming fantasy work to anyone who loves interesting world-building and characters, although there are some serious problems with the pacing.

It's impossible to give this book a rating. If it weren't for Martha (and Rob Inglis, the audio book narrator) I would never have gotten through it, because Tolkien and I don't see eye to eye about language. I, for example, believe in the power of brevity, and am not obsessed with the power of meter. I can't deny the amazing amount of language and world building, and it's all stellar, but reading about people telling stories and singing/ chanting myths is deadly dull. Tolkien tells a good story, but he writes a boring book.

For me, the largest take away with this book is that it is meant to be read at a younger age. This is one that I did not read as a child, so I am nostalgia-free as an adult. The world-building is impressive and the importance of this book for later writing cannot be argued; however, the book as a whole is somewhat dull. There are great segments of action, but the payoff requires mountains of pages of descriptions of walking and bemoaning. It is very Dickensian in the way chapters can be spent on an insignificant moment.

As with the movie, I feel that this could be much more concise and interesting without the hobbits.

I do ultimately recommend the book, but suggest reading it at a younger age.

Die Filmen waren gesehen und die Neugier, wie die Geschichte der Hobbits und die des Ringes wohl geschrieben klingen würde, nahm immer mehr zu.

Im Rahmen des SuB-Abbaus nahm ich all meinen Mut zusammen und begann die Reise.

Bevor ihr eure Reise mit Frodo, Sam usw. beginnt, rate ich euch, vorher "Der Hobbit" zu lesen, da die Geschichte darauf aufbaut und man im Buch sehr viele Andeutungen zu ihr findet.

Tatsächlich hatte ich große Angst davor dieses Buch in die Hand zu nehmen. Besonders die Schreibart machte mir Sorgen, obwohl ich nicht einmal wusste wie sie war. Das die Geschichte sehr komplex ist, zeigten die Filme, weswegen ich mit einer gehörigen Portion Respekt an dieses Buch heran ging.

Einmal aufgeschlagen, kam ich dann sehr geschwind durch das Buch und hatte nur selten Probleme der Geschichte zu folgen. Was sich allerdings als Herausforderung sah, war die Verfolgung der Route welche unsere Freunde im Buch zurück legten. Stetig wurde man penibel darauf hingewiesen wo man sich befand und wo man hin wollte. Ich verlor hier sehr bald die Orientierung, da ich vor lauter links, rechts, Osten, Süden, Norden oder Westen, nicht mehr wusste wo ich mich überhaupt befand. Als Hilfe war hier wohl die Karte am Anfang des Buches gedacht. Da diese aber nicht den kompletten Weg zeigt, welchen unsere Helden zurück legen, empfand ich sie als nutzlos.

Zu Anfang erfährt man so einiges über Hobbits, was einem schon mal zum Schmunzeln brachte. Dabei steckten diese Informationen voller spannender Hinweise, die gut durchdacht waren. Man merkte einfach das der Autor seine selbst erschaffe Welt liebte.

Im Buch stehen des Öfteren Gedichte oder Lieder, welche nach meinem Geschmack nicht unbedingt in das Buch hinein gemusst hätten. Ich konnte selten etwas mit ihnen anfangen und überflog sogar das ein oder andere.

Die Geschichte an sich finde ich sehr interessant, da sie zeigt, das selbst kleine Dinge über mehr Macht verfügen als so manches großes. Auch der Drang den Ring zu besitzen, spiegelt für mich aktuelle menschliche Situationen dar, in denen jeder mit Hilfe von etwas die Macht ergreifen möchte.

Ganz ehrlich? Außer an die markantesten Figuren im Buch, kann ich mich an keine weiteren namentlich erinnern. Wie auch, wenn man förmlich mit Namen und Orten überflutet wird, die man teils nicht einmal aussprechen kann.

Das fehlen eines Personenverzeichnisses ließ mich zusätzlich sauer aufstoßen. Denn wie sollte ein Neuling, wie ich, sich im Buch zurecht finden, wenn man das Buch zum ersten Mal las? Mein Glück war es die Filme gesehen zu haben, da mir so einige Charaktere im Kopf blieben.

Das Wesen aller Personen fand ich ausgezeichnet dargestellt. Es war überraschend wie stark oder schwach einige Charaktere waren. Gerade Meriadoc Brandybock blieb mir im Gedächtnis, da er im Buch sehr ernst wahr und irgendwie reifer wirkte, als erwartet.

Die bemerkenswerteste Person war für mich jedoch Gandalf, da er mit Mut, Wissen und ein wenig Magie, ein Hindernis nach dem nächsten meisterte und dabei stehts für das Gute stand. Zudem würden ohne seine vielen Kontakte, so manches Erlebnis nicht möglich gewesen.

Besonders spannend war der Vorspann, in welchem J.R.R. Tolkien über seine erschaffene Welt und seine Bewohner schrieb. Hierbei die Geschichte der Hobbits zu erfahren, machte das Buch nur noch interessanter. Denn dabei erfuhr man welche Stärken und Schwächen ein Hobbit hatte.

Da ich eine ältere Ausgabe besitze, ist das Cover ein anderes als bei der Neuauflage. Allerdings konnte ich nicht wirklich erkennen, was es zeigen sollte. Der Ring mit dem Auge, war für mich noch verständlich, aber die blauen Schattierungen ergaben für mich keinen Sinn bzw. ein Bild.

Den Namen des Autors und den des Buches in ein schwarzes Feld zu drücken, empfand ich nicht gerade schön. Hier hätte ich mir ehr etwas verschnörkeltes gewünscht, was ein wenig der Elbensprache nahe kommt.

Für Anfänger der Reihe ist es sehr schwer den Weg der Helden zu verfolgen, hier sollte man mehr mit Karten arbeiten. Das gleiche gilt für die Namen aller Charaktere, die ruhig ein Verzeichnis füllen dürfen. Ansonsten eine interessante Geschichte voller Überraschungen.

Unpopular opinion: the movie was better than the book.

As someone who was fond of the movies in middle school, I decided to FINALLY give the books a shot. Though it wasn't a complete mistake, I was left feeling very underwhelmed and frankly, bored at what Tolkien's words had to offer.

Instead of focusing on character dynamics and development, this novel focused solely on plot. The characters were left feeling two-dimensional (except everyone's homie, Sam), and at times, it was easy to forget who was even on the journey with the fellowship (sorry, Merry and Pippin). I'm really disappointed in this aspect because the immense trust and unbreakable bond that was built between the members of the fellowship was to die for and left your heart and soul aflutter.

But that's not even to say that the plot was particularly great. I, for one, commend the Peter Jackson for his story cuts in the movie. Right off the bat, for example, the film kicks the journey into motion directly following Bilbo's birthday party, but in the book, Frodo sits around for NINE YEARS waiting for Gandalf to come back and tell him to get a move on. The sense of urgency and danger was severely lacking in this book and instead was filled with a lot of unnecessary landscape descriptions, background information and odd characters (who tf is Tom Bombadil?).

The only reason I didn't give this a lower rating is because I recognize that it is the source material that Peter Jackson transformed into the movie I know and love. I wish I loved this, but I just didn't.

I really wanted to like this book. I know how important Tolkien is to the fantasy genre, but they just weren’t what I thought they would be. I saw the movies when I was younger, and loved them, but I heard the books could be a hard read so I put it off. I just watched the movies again and decided to read the books because I wanted to delve deeper into the story and the characters. I found there wasn’t much deeper to go. These are the first books I have read after seeing the movie first. Maybe books just aren’t as good when you do the movie first. Tolkien goes into so much detail about what paths they are taking and how the trees look and what not. He does not go enough into what the characters are thinking and feeling. It got kind of dull. That being said, I still have huge respect for the impact he has had in the literary world.

Honestly, I think that book I (which Tolkien himself titled “The Ring Sets Out”) is spectacular. The world building he accomplishes — whole also establishing the groundwork for a great and thrilling story is brilliant. Tolkien manages to balance a great awe and wonder of the world of Middle Earth with the genuine sheer terror of The Black Riders, and he excels.

However, Book II (The Ring Goes South”) is where The Fellowship of The Ring deteriorates. Yes, the world is fascinating and brilliantly made, but the journey from Rivendell to the split of the Fellowship at the River Anduin is so painfully boring that I can’t possibly give it a pass.

I do appreciate that Tolkien essentially founded modern fantasy with this novel, and I support the statement, but I do think the overall telling of the story lacks severely in pace and progress. I don’t hate The Fellowship of The Ring — largely because I absolutely adore Book I — but I definitely don’t love it. I merely have, I suppose, profound appreciation.

I'll admit, I saw the movie first. And, yes, I still like the movies better. (Yes, I know, I'm one of *those* people.)

I am awed by the scope, depth and detail Tolkien has infused into his world. I've rarely encountered a fantasy world that springs so completely into life and just takes you along for the trip. That trip, however, does tend to be a little long-winded. I've had a hard time getting into the story, whereas the movies just swept me along.

I am still, however, of the strong opinion that Tolkien is a must-read for any hardcore fantasy fan.

An enjoyable read, full of charm and a lore-rich world. It's influence on fantasy is obvious even for someone who doesn't have much interest in fantasy. Moments of the novel feel straight out of a cRPG game (LOTR obviously influencing D&D, which was then turned in to games like Baldur's Gate, etc), and even the characters and their interactions feel like something you'd see in an RPG.

I am a bit confused though, as to why people herald this as a literary masterpiece. The characters are barely fleshed out beyond "elves hate dwarves" and "hobbits are hobbits!" and there seems to be character growth at a snails pace, something which probably shouldn't happen so slowly in a 500+ page novel (though of course, this is only 1/3 of the complete story). It's almost like you're expected to have a complete working knowledge of Middle Earth politics and history before you start reading if you want to understand every reference to a place name or historical character or event, etc.

Tolkien's overly detailed descriptions are mind numbing at times, and made me start doing what I do in the more dialogue dump heavy bits of RPGs; skim read and just pick out the important bits. Tolkien's pleasant writing sometimes ascends to beautiful pieces of prose, but seems to always be bogged down in describing every blade of grass or snowflake on a mountainside. At least the songs and poems were enjoyable enough, even though they were quite dense in the first half or so of the book.

I haven't seen the films since they were released, and even then I don't remember anything about them beyond the things that have been turned in to memes or parodied endlessly in pop culture - but I was surprised there was no "You have my sword" "And my bow" "And my axe" bit in the books, it's extremely anti-climactic in the book. Particulates that stand out to me include the more shallow expression of character personality. More modern books of powerful impact, like this trilogy was in its day, labor to have the reader understand the protagonist in a deeper manner. Today we seem to hunger to see heroes with passions and faults, like we have, still succeed against the challenge they face. We want inspired by characters we relate to. Although we may strongly admire a character for what they have done, do we really have an intimate kinship with them? I think that is my biggest lament of this writing.

J.R.R Tolkien wrote a memorable beginning of a critically acclaimed trilogy in The Fellowship of the Ring,which revolves around two Hobbits saving the world of Middle-earth. The title of the novel refers to the forming of a band of “heroes” to destroy the ring of the dark lord Sauron. The Fellowship of the Ring is a very used and cliché example of the fantasy genre, and it paved the way for similar book series’s such as Game of Thrones, without the violence. It’s a very complex book, but if you can get past the first 50 pages it becomes much better.
Set in Middle-earth, a fictional world full of magical creatures such as elves,dwarves, and orcs, it tells the tale of two Hobbits; Samwise Gamgee and Frodo Baggins. The book starts out peacefully in the area of Middle-earth called the Shire, which is the home of the Hobbits. The setting shows the peace our protagonist feels at the beginning of the story, before he is given the quest to destroy the Ring. The book expands on this peace, saying how Hobbits have multiple breakfasts, and they are very content with their lives. But, Frodo is soon tasked by the wizard Gandalf the Grey to destroy the One Ring, to end Sauron’s dominion in the land of Mordor. It’s a perilous journey, and the Frodo will be hunted by Sauron as Gandalf says to him “He desires it-but he must not get it” (Tolkien 55) Sam and Frodo leave their homes in the Shire, they soon find out horseback riders in black are hunting them, giving them their first glimpses of the world outside the Shire.
The protagonists of the trilogy are Samwise Gamgee, a gardener and servant, and Frodo Baggins; a Hobbit and the nephew of Bilbo Baggins, the protagonist in the Fellowship of the Ring’s prequel The Hobbit. Frodo is a very easygoing and kind Hobbit, and doesn’t want anything to do with the Ring, until Gandalf and Sam convince him to take it and destroy it. The journey to destroy the Ring in Mordor is perilous, and a fellowship of all the races of Middle-earth forms to help the Hobbits on their quest. Sam becomes Frodo’s saving grace and protector, helping him out of harm’s way, cooking the meals on their journey, and his best advisor. Sam is crucial to Frodo succeeding, as he would have a much worse time getting to Mordor without him. But, there isn’t a lot of conflict between them in this story, and there are a lot of details Tolkien included that I don’t think move the plot forward. He also made characters that don’t do anything remotely crucial to the plot.
Finally, Frodo isn’t a great hero or an excellent warrior, but just a plain Hobbit, like his uncle Bilbo before him. His character expands on the nature of the Hobbits and how they are like people, and how an ordinary person can become a hero chosen for a perilous quest. Tolkien created a path for other fantasy novels to be written, yet his work is unparalleled in detail and storytelling. Those who have read any fantasy novel and enjoyed it should read this, as it is a classic of the fantasy genre and one of the original books that make up that genre. While having an excess amount of detail, it still is a fantastic book and Tolkien wrote this to entertain and enthrall readers in a magical world. The message he tries to convey to the readers is that anyone, even the littlest person, can be a hero. Frodo was made to remind us of ourselves, normal people who can make a difference in the world. The Lord of the Rings trilogy is one of the most successful book series of all time, so obviously Tolkien’s message worked. The Lord of the Rings may be a boring book at times, as the detail put in is so immense, but it is a book everyone should read.

In the Fellowship of the Ring, Frodo Baggins is left alone in The Shire, after his cousin, Bilbo, departed. Around the same time Gandalf, a powerful wizard, gives Frodo Bilbo's powerful ring, Frodo begins to realize dark things are going on outside of The Shire. He decides with the help of Gandalf to depart in secret. Two Hobbits, Sam Gamgee and Pippin Took, decide to join Frodo on his journey. They proceed to journey across Middle Earth, pursued by the Black Riders, servants of Saruman. Saruman is chasing the Fellowship due to Frodo's possession of the One Ring. The fellowship meets many people along the way, including Tom Bombadil, Aragorn, and eventually many elves and fair folk.

I really enjoyed the immersive nature if Tolkien's writing, it really made me feel like I was in the book. He spent a lot of time on small details, which could be tedious at times, but I enjoyed. I also enjoyed the overall plot of the book, I just thought it was a great idea, and that it was really cool that an author could dream all of this up.

I didn't like how slowly paced the book was. It really took a while to get to the action, and there was a lot of travel without anything interesting going on. It definitely got interesting at some points, especially the end, but I felt that the times that weren't interesting outweighed the times that were. However, I think the second book will be better in this regard, as Frodo and the Fellowship are almost upon Mordor. Overall, I liked it, but I hope it gets better with the next two books.

It took me 4 years and about 2 or 3 restarts to finally finish this book. It's painfully hard to read and I got easily lost in Tolkien's endless descriptions. Yet, it is such a wonderful world to be lost in.

Don't get me wrong. My last update (and my rating) probably give the impression otherwise, but I actually liked this book for the most part. It just was too drawn out for me to get sucked into. I was super into it the first half and then my interest just kind of fizzled. I know the drawn-out-ness is just J.R.R. Tolkien's writing style, and I felt the same way about The Hobbit, but it was just really hard for me to get into it for the second half. Maybe someday I'll read the rest of the series, but I don't think anytime soon. I might commit the reader's crime of watching the movies to get inspiration to read the books to read the rest. Like I said, I really want to love this series, and can completely understand why other people do. I just have to be in the right type of mood for Tolkien's excruciating detail.

Tolkien created a pretty amazing world. And I'm not just talking about Middle-Earth. We live in a world now where our imaginations are free to roam the most epic realms of magic that the human mind can envision and I don't know if such a world would exist without Tolkien. It would probably be here in some form but it would most certainly be different and it might not have surfaced so soon. So for that, I'm eternally grateful to him but I did have some issues with the first part of his trilogy.

Now I would imagine had I been one of the six people in the world that hasn't seen Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings films yet I would have had a better time with the book but that's not the case unfortunately. At times I found it very difficult to engage with a story that was veering off on irrelevant tangent after irrelevant tangent on its way to a destination that we've known about since the earliest chapters. While it is effective world-building having the characters halt their journey repeatedly so we can get a glimpse into the lives of the inhabitants of Tolkien's universe, it's not really effective story-telling.

World-building can be accomplished without sacrificing the plot, George R.R Martin does it all the time, but when a third of the chapters in the book are dull and inconsequential from a narrative perspective it starts to become a problem. It must have been very tough to try and tell a story in a fictional world as vast and unfarmiliar to its readers as this one and I think that a lot of High Fantasy writers that were influenced by Tolkien have learned from his mistakes. But at the end of the day they were still mistakes.

I think his prose is beautiful and the world is pretty incredible even if I do have my complaints about how it was unveiled for us. So I enjoyed most of the book, and knowing what's coming I think I'll probably enjoy the other two in the series a little more but some of those narrative issues aren't easy to get over.

The Fellowship of the Ring is a good book, but not as amazing as I was expecting based on its popularity and the near-universal acclaim it has received since its publication. Perhaps that is an unfair assessment since this is really only a third of the story (and I’ve yet to read the rest of it). This work was obviously a labor of love for Tolkien and the years, thought, and energy invested in this imaginary world are astonishing. The backstory and invented history (with all its races, languages, names, songs, and folklore) lend the world an air of realism absent from most fantasy novels. Unfortunately, the time devoted to it also tends to overshadow the main story itself. When you could skip substantial portions of the text and not really miss anything important, then it’s probably a little bit of overkill. The parts that were good though, were really good: Gandalf’s confrontation with Saruman, the journey through the mines of Moria, and Frodo’s clash with Boromir at the end all stand out as exceptionally good storytelling. All in all, I enjoyed the book and look forward to continuing the story in The Two Towers.

I first began trying to read through the Lord of the Rings in 1989, though I don’t think I succeeded until 1994 or 1995. In kid time that seemed to take decades. Since then I read through the trilogy one other time around 2003 or 2004. I decided it was time to revisit them, though my reading was interrupted by both a change in jobs and a move.


SUMMARY
Years after the events of “The Hobbit”, it is learned that the ring found by Bilbo Baggins is actually the “One Ring” forged by Sauron and possessed of his awesome power. Bilbo’s nephew, Frodo Baggins, begins the quest to destroy the Ring under the supervision of Gandalf the wizard. Later he is joined by seven other companions and they make their way southeast, toward the dark land of Mordor (where the Ring must be destroyed) and the wars in Gondor where men hope to survive against Sauron’s armies.


OVERALL: 3.2 out of 5
More than most books, “The Fellowship of the Ring” is a journey the reader undertakes with the characters. Tolkien is in charge of providing the scenery.

Someone might mistake my rating as an indication that I consider the book mediocre, but that would not be accurate. I love the characters, history, and setting, and I think the series is stronger as a whole (as Tolkien wanted it), but there is an issue in the technical execution that bothers me. It’s subtle enough that I did not even realize it until I had finished the book.

The reader isn’t left with any memorable scenes of great importance. When I think of the book, I don’t remember the fellowship fighting orcs or Gandalf making his stand against the Balrog- I remember scenes of traveling and discussion. The books drips with tension, but the only “intense” scene that stand out in my memory is when the Ring Wraiths are pursuing Frodo near the beginning.

I think this is because Tolkien is a somewhat flat author. He describes action in the same way he describes anything else; his writing does not change based on the scene. It’s an impressive feat, but I don’t think its final effect is a positive one in terms of a reader’s memory.

There is a ton of good stuff in the book too. The history and lore, the general ambiance, and as I said before, a lot of tension. The desperation of the characters grows until it reaches a fever pitch in the final chapter.


RATINGS BY CATEGORY
CHARACTERS: 3 out of 5
Tolkien did not describe his characters in great narrative detail; they are established through their actions and mannerisms. Some elements, such as Aragorn’s romance with Arwen, are only hinted at in the main text. Still, this allows a very natural form of character growth that is enjoyable.

Some characters, like Sam, seem to jump off the page. Others like Boromir are more mysterious. No one fits into a neat two-dimensional template though.

My only real complaint is that it is easy to think of the hobbits as children; they don’t really talk or act like adults (Frodo is a bit over fifty years old). I think that was Tolkien’s way of demonstrating how simple and innocent the hobbits are, but it would have been nice if there was one hobbit who is more world-wise (Merry comes very close, but is mostly forgotten once the rest of the fellowship is introduced).


PACE: 3 out of 5
There are some people who don’t like Tolkien’s writing and claim that it’s a travelogue that focuses more on scenery and history than what is happening at the moment. I would disagree; the descriptions of the land and weather match a specific English style that reminds me of “The Thirty-Nine Steps” written by John Buchan and published in 1915, except I like Tolkien’s work much more.

There is a certain magical ambience in every page of the book that no other book possesses. There are imitators, but Tolkien achieved this effect with no apparent effort.


STORY: 3 out of 5
This is the book that started it all for many readers (I do realize there were fantasy epics composed prior to this), but on its own the story is simple. The book can’t stand on its own at all, ending on a cliffhanger as Frodo decides to take his journey alone (though he’s persuaded to accept his servant Sam’s company).

When I think back on it, much of the story feels almost anti-climactic. There are all kinds of menaces and challenges faced by the companions, such as the Ring Wraiths, the orcs of Moria, and an ancient demon, but none of these moments stand out in my mind. I believe this is a problem with the technical execution.


DIALOGUE: 3 out of 5
Most of the dialogue is well-written, though there is an abundance of songs that I’m just not interested in. Tolkien does an excellent job of keeping the reader’s attention during long speeches and page after page of back-and-forth conversation, frequently between large groups of speakers. That is not an easy task for any writer.

It is also possible that the songs and poems, though I groaned as each began, are contributing more to the magical other-worldliness than I realize. I did not skip anything.


STYLE/TECHNICAL: 4 out of 5
As I said, Tolkien achieves a kind of magical ambiance throughout the book. It has to be experienced to be understood and isn’t easy to explain.

His narrative is of one flavor though. What I mean is that episodes of travel, and the descriptions of land and weather, are provided in the same pace and style as the action scenes. This isn’t bad writing (in fact it is quite impressive), but it leaves a reader without the peaks and valleys (in terms of intensity) that most books rely on.

There are few things which I feel more conflicted about than Lord of the Rings. On the one hand Tolkien created a remarkable world which millions of people have connected with, including myself. It’s his abilities as a novelist which I struggle with. His wooden prose and melodramatic despair towards modern society are my primary points of contention. His writing, while occasionally memorable, falls flat as often as it evoked grandeur.

In the Hobbit Tolkien wrote a whimsical boy's own adventure. The ‘adult’ world of the Fellowship of the Rings feels almost more juvenile than the Hobbit because it feels like the oddities are reduced. Tone is more measured, the charm is lessened and the evils are harder to comprehend. The Hobbit felt like a world with different societies; goblins, elves, shapeshifters, spiders, dwarves and men, which each have their own logics Bilbo must navigate between. A lot more feels achieved in the Hobbit with a far shorter page count.

While I prefer Bilbo too, Frodo is a worthy enough successor. Unfortunately he is somewhat sidelined after the enjoyable beginning. While Tom Bombadil is maligned, I enjoy this quirky episode, it feels like a continuation of the Hobbit before we get the overlong infodump at the Council of Elrond which shifts the story into a more dour direction. After this dull meeting the hobbits, who are the characters with the most amount of charm, go out of focus. The rest of the story transforms into an underwhelming sword and sorcery romp. Tolkien is no Robert E Howard; his prose is too stilted to be effective in the pure action. He is better when the static comforts of Middle Earth contrast with its fearful visions, but there’s little enjoyment to be had in the second half of this novel.

The Lord of the Rings and in particular the Fellowship of the Ring cast a spell over me as a child. I suspect a lot of people can relate. This enchantment has sadly broken now, but I still do appreciate the cozy adventure story he has created here even if his more 'serious' additions to a classic adventure story merely lengthen the text and expose his flaws.

The writing style just didn't click with me, and I honestly why as I loved The Hobbit.

but I enjoyed it enough that I will probably continue to read the rest of the series.

I think the theme of this book is greed. One reason for this is that while the "fellowship" is traveling Boromi grow increasingly greedy, wanting to use the ring to destroy Sauron. And as Gandolf advised the Ring leads Boromir to desire it for himself.

I know: people are crazy, crazy, crazy about this book. The whole series of these books. As good as the Bible, they say.

And maybe that's actually a pretty good comparison. The Bible. Because similarly, it's another really really long book that everyone in the western world seems to claim to have read, but when you do actually read it, most of it is a real slog. Furthermore, the people who really do seem to enjoy reading it aren't enjoying it on its own merits, but out of reflected reverence for its fandom in general, so to speak. They're so enraptured with its message that they're blind to its reality. And that's OK: if it makes them happy, more power to them.

Don't get me wrong: the characters, the imagery, the mythology, the overall story – and all of these are timeless and wonderful. But, frankly, no thanks to the raw text that presents them.

For example, and even though this criticism is already well documented, but the first, what, 150 pages? 200 pages? — All of the hobbits' initial wanderings around the outer edges of the Shire and dealings with Tom Bombadil – literally nothing of any importance to the remainder of the plot happens there. It's no wonder most adaptations of the story cut it out entirely. There are other slightly less long but similar passages later, for example, like so much of the aimless wandering before they finally into the Mines with Moria. The whole book feels like sections of 100 pages at a time about walking and camping and snacking on Lembas bread, or relaxing and feasting and sleeping late in elf towns, and then, when something really cool finally happens, like when they enter this amazing and cool and awe-inspiring dungeon carved into the base of a mountain by armies of dwarves over centuries and centuries, the narration rushes through that in 20 or 30 pages to get back to the wilderness-wandering and bread-munching without wasting too much time on anything that's genuinely interesting.

And the singing – oh God, the endless singing. I see what Tolkien was trying to do there, imparting a greater sense of culture and lore to the story, but for the reader, it's torture. And really good books don't torture their readers.

So anyway, I utterly respect the contribution this book has made to the genre of fantasy fiction, not to mention role-playing games and fantasy films and TV shows. And for its time, it was undoubtedly groundbreaking.

But now that I've actually read it, when viewed from the context of more recent and more refined fantasy books, I can agree with my friends who said, "You know what? The movie really was better."

I love the endless ways it has permeated popular culture to the point that it has almost become actual mythology (hobbits, balrogs, rivalries between elves and dwarves, etc.), and there are, of course, the memes to consider as well.

But reading it? Actually buckling down to read "Lord of the Rings" has taken me four lifetime attempts, and this is the first time I actually powered through "Fellowship." I don't hate it, and that didn't really come as a surprise to me. Tolkien's writing style, ceaselessly academic, never met an ancient-literature trope he didn't attempt to force into his modern fantasy epic, with poetry-kenning being one of the most egregious. A slow, wonderful beginning to an amazing series. I grew up loving the movies, had always wanted to read the books, but had always been daunted by the size and intensity of the world-building. I wasn't sure if I was going to be able to handle the material, or understand it.

Fortunately I was wrong. While maintaining a much slower pace, the book is gorgeous in it's description. Every place of Middle Earth has been revealed to the most minute detail, to the effect that every setting becomes it's own character, which lends itself to the novel. While the characters at times feel a little two-dimensional, the world and magic of Middle Earth is a transformative aspect. Tolkien's language is also breathtaking, and I thoroughly enjoyed reading passages over and over again.

However, I do have to admit that I didn't enjoy this book as much as I was hoping to. It really is a travel story. And although I love a travel story, there is only so much I can read about a group of dudes walking through the woods at one time. I had to take several large breaks from the book, just to keep from getting fatigued, and sometimes I didn't have a real drive to get back to the story. I am definitely going to be reading the next two novels in the series, but I think I might take some time away from Frodo and Middle Earth before returning.

So what's my only issue with this book? The pacing. Now the best thing about it is that unlike Joe Abercrombie's The Blade Itself which took 90% of the book to be over before they told me what the purpose of all of it was, this book gave me everything in the second chapter and yours truly is extremely grateful for that. However, once the journey started, I did ended up meeting someone the movies omitted which was an interesting experience by itself but the book more often than not felt like it's taking this journey with stride. Basically it felt like a video game where I'm stopping at villages, triggering events to learn more about something, meeting new people and leaning new stuff which goes in accordance with the whole "Journey" aspect of their quest, but while it would work epically for a video game, it makes the pacing in the book incredibly slow.

Kind of like it makes me wish they'll go faster in some places or just shorten the lengths of the chapters detailing their stay at certain places because I know that there are more interesting things to follow. Later I learned that Tolkien actually intended for the story to be one huge book instead of 3 smaller ones which makes sense why he's taking his time getting Frodo and Co to reach certain areas, of course it doesn't make it any faster but yeah, still worth mentioning. The one thing I can say without a doubt it massively succeeded in doing was remind me of how much I love the series; the lore he created, the world he built, the characters and their journey. It's too bad that the book couldn't give me the same enjoyment the films did.

There's really isn't much to say about this because the pacing or maybe the way it was written might be a more accurate description of my ONLY problem with it, kind of ruins it a bit. It definitely doesn't lessen my love for the world at all so while I'm not sure I'll be continuing with the books, I might (still undecided). I need to marathon the movies, it's been years since I last saw them and I need a big refresher, personally I think they're really awesome.

Before I get into my review for this book, I just want to put it out there that Peter Jackson missed out on a fantastic opportunity to make The Lord of the Rings trilogy into a musical. Its been almost 15 years since I last read this books and I forgot how much freaking music there is. I swear, Frodo and Co. break out into song (or poetry, depending on how the mood strikes them) like every 10 pages. It almost reaches Disney princess levels of randomness and it made me wonder what it would've been like to see Viggo Mortensen, Ian McKellan, Orlando Bloom, and Elijah Wood break out into song every 15 minutes or so of the movie. I'm still laughing.

All joking aside, my second excursion into the world of Middle-Earth hasn't been as rosy as it was the first time around. With more years and a BA in English under my belt, I noticed more flaws in Tolkien's writing than I did the first time and came to appreciate some of the stylistic choices Jackson made in the film adaptation. While Tolkien is a master of world-building, the story itself sometimes left something to be desired. There were many points, especially early on in the book, where Tolkien lingered too long on the day to day minutia of Frodo's quest, with unnecessarily lengthy descriptions of the countryside and forests. I typically don't mind slow plots, but these rough patches were slow enough to even test my patience. I also greatly detested the character Tom Bombadil.

That being said, I still love this book and the characters. Tolkien isn't the grandfather of modern fantasy for nothing! There's so much history that went into creating these books and once the Fellowship got together and started on their journey, I was sucked in and didn't stop until I reached the end of the book. With the fantasy genre overly saturated with heroes' quests, prophecies, elves, and The One True Darkness, this series may come across extremely cliched and unoriginal, but its important to remember that Tolkien INVENTED a lot of these cliches, or else, immortalized certain tropes within the fantasy genre. As an unconditional lover of fantasy novels, I owe Mr. Tolkien and his series a lot and I look forward to seeing how the rest of the series hold up to my memory.

The second paragraph of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Fellowship of the Ring says Bilbo Baggins ”was very rich and very peculiar and had been the wonder of the Shire for sixty years, ever since his remarkable disappearance and unexpected return.” I was interested in how the “shadow” of Tolkien’s The Hobbit hangs over the events of The Fellowship of the Ring, so this is less of "review" and will focus on The Fellowship of the Ring as a bridge between the Hobbit and The Lord of the Ring trilogy. The most obvious connection is that Frodo Baggins is the Ring-Bearer become Bilbo gains procession of the Ring from Bilbo who found The Ring in Gollum’s cave island. At Council of Elrond, Bilbo tells the story publicly for the first time of how he found the Ring for the first time. Bilbo apologizes to Glorin who was one of his Dwarfs he traveled with in The Hobbit for not telling the truth at the time at the Council. Gimli is the representative of the Dwarfs in the Fellowship of The Ring. Other examples of the events of the Hobbit appearing in The Fellowship of the Ring are Strider/Aragon and the Hobbits on their way to Rivendell in The Fellowship of the Ring passed by the Trolls that Gandalf turned into Stone in The Hobbit. One the more fascinating connections between The Hobbit and The Fellowship of The Ring that I did not remember before I re-read The Fellowship of The Ring is that Balin from the Hobbit is Balin, Lord of Moria, who tomb the Fellowship finds in Moria. This few examples above out of many more show how The Fellowship of the Ring (a good book in its own right) connects the story of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Ring trilogy. Some of the more interesting characters in the Tolkien’s universe are introduced in The Fellowship of the Ring such as Galadriel, Samwise Gamgee, Strider/Aragon, Boromir, and other characters.

The sections I don't so much care for so far all involve Tom Bombadil... I kind of hate Tom. The interesting part of Tom is how powerful he is and how unaffected he is by the woes of the ring and the dangers of Mordor, but he's also totally nuts, and (for me at least) not in a fun way. Tom comes across to me as incessantly annoying. I guess to some that's part of his charm, but not to me!

Overall I think the way this book and J. R. R. Tolkien changed the face of fantasy literature and film (much later on of course) is truly admirable. He crafted a world that inspired so many other stories all over the world and this is the beginning of an epic adventure. However, I also think it's sometimes a bit of a boring adventure and there are some moments I just think weren't great at all. It's a solid book, probably too long for what actually happens, but it's a cornerstone of fantasy and I'm glad I've finally read at least part 1! 3*s

This is one of those cases where I really wish there were two separate rating systems on Goodreads - one for quality of the book and one for my personal enjoyment of it.

Because on the one hand, I REALLY respect this book. The world-building is insane and obviously the most important aspect of the series to this author. He created a history, a language (several languages?) and an entire catalog of folk songs and poetry to weave into this tale. This book is a foundation stone for an entire genre of epic, high fantasy. The world is beautiful and the descriptions are poetic. The good guys are Noble and Tragic and the bad guys are freaking terrifying. It scratches all those epic legend itches while still providing a sentimental underside of poetry and pastoral beauty.

But, guys, it was SO hard to get through. Like, I’m not afraid of lengthy (is this book really only 400 pages???) or hyper-descriptive books and sometimes I really enjoy them, but Tolkien’s style of writing (at least in this book) is just not for me. The constant singing and poetry recitals was incredibly irritating and you can tell that Tolkien put in a lot more labor on world-building and cultural description than actually giving his characters personality. Now, that’s not like incredibly unusual in speculative fiction (where sometimes the authors get so caught up in the magic system or the world specs that they forget how to write people), but it’s a major bummer to someone like me who thrives off of good character development.

All my favorite books have a really heavy emphasis on complex, interesting, (dare I wish for humorous?) characters and I really think that’s where this book fell flat for me. The characters are all so noble, and occasionally, so very, very tragic and their struggles are epic and sometimes very emotional, but I just don’t get a sense of personality from them. Does that make them great headcanon fodder? Yes! Is it an excellent use of archetypes? Hell yes! Is it the best method of writing to please me in particular? Nah, not really.

So yeah, five stars for being a lovely, wordy, epic fantasy tale built on an insane amount of world-building and cultural crafting. But three stars for having the story pacing of frozen molasses and all the damned singing.

I’m going to continue with the next two books, because I promised my sister-in-law I would give it a go. And honestly, with how much I love fantasy, I really feel like I should have read them. And I do think I’ll like them better as the story becomes a bit more frantic and the pace picks up a bit. But, oof. I highly doubt I’ll be reading Fellowship again.

See The Fellowship of the Ring in the best light and you will see what makes it special to so many. These two quotes are a bit long, but no spoilers:

Frodo looked up at the Elf standing tall above him, as he gazed into the night, seeking a mark to shoot at. His head was dark, crowned with sharp white stars that glittered in the black pools of the sky behind. But now rising and sailing up from the South the great clouds advanced, sending out dark outriders into the starry fields. A sudden dread fell on the Company. ‘Elbereth Gilthoniel!’ sighed Legolas as he looked up. Even as he did so, a dark shape, like a cloud and yet not a cloud, for it moved far more swiftly, came out of the blackness in the South, and sped towards the Company, blotting out all light as it approached. Soon it appeared as a great winged creature, blacker than the pits in the night. Fierce voices rose up to greet it from across the water. Frodo felt a sudden chill running through him and clutching at his heart; there was a deadly cold, like the memory of an old wound, in his shoulder. He crouched down, as if to hide. Suddenly the great bow of Lórien sang. Shrill went the arrow from the elven-string. Frodo looked up. Almost above him the winged shape swerved. There was a harsh croaking scream, as it fell out of the air, vanishing down into the gloom of the eastern shore. The sky was clean again. There was a tumult of many voices far away, cursing and wailing in the darkness, and then silence. Neither shaft nor cry came again from the east that night.

That's some all time epic action.

True-hearted Men, they will not be corrupted. We of Minas Tirith have been staunch through long years of trial. We do not desire the power of wizard-lords, only strength to defend ourselves, strength in a just cause. And behold! in our need chance brings to light the Ring of Power. It is a gift, I say; a gift to the foes of Mordor. It is mad not to use it, to use the power of the Enemy against him. The fearless, the ruthless, these alone will achieve victory. What could not a warrior do in this hour, a great leader? What could not Aragorn do? Or if he refuses, why not Boromir? The Ring would give me power of Command. How I would drive the hosts of Mordor, and all men would flock to my banner!’

And just the kind of turmoil our characters should be in. Boromir's intent to use the means of evil despite Gandalf's warning of what it will turn him into. Frodo's self doubt. Sam's loyalty. Classic archetypal conflicts.

So, it's hitting all the right notes right? Well, sometimes, maybe too seldomly. First of all, I regret to inform you that the lore master's lore is superfluous and dull. Everyone gets a song(and often more than one), various dwellings and provinces are rattled off with a frequency that will leave you wondering if you should consult a map... again, a whole exam's worth of history of ages long gone, family lineages and a dozen other things besides. All of it is consistently not worthwhile, there's no wonder or beauty here.

Second, Boromir's quote and all the rest like it are very few and far between, there's probably less than five instances of a character hitting on something human and genuine. Most of it is painted with a very broad and shallow brush. Imagine how a 12 year old would explain it to you, that's about as subtle as this book is. Evil is evil and nothing else, Elves are good and wise, cause just look at them! And down we go, down along racial lines actually, which is a little discomforting. Not that I'm about to make an egalitarian plea for the dwarfs, that's best left to every Western RPG ever striving to be taken as "mature" and deep. But, all in all, I think I'm with Boromir. He's the only one in the whole book to so much as question the wise elves and Gandalf, the only one to betray that perhaps evil isn't something altogether alien and originated from hate and malice only. Except of course, it is stated at the end of that scene that the ring is in fact having an effect on everyone around it, so Boromir too had in large part been possessed.

But hey, the last quarter is markedly better than the rest, that bodes well for the last two books. I wish I had better tidings for you halflings, but now you must go forth in search of The Book of the New Sun and Harry Potter! And maybe even A Book of Ice and Fire if you want something livelier and fast.

I have to say, I have very mixed feelings on this. The writing's good, solidly entertaining, but the plot is very bare-bones and slow. The world is interesting but there is So Much info dumping. Then there's the fact that there are only four named women in the whole book: a greedy old shrew aunt of Frodo's; a woman whose purpose is to look pretty, keep house for Tom Bombadil and feed the male heroes dinner; Arwen the elf whose only character trait is her beauty; and Galadriel, who is actually pretty cool but who apparently still can't be an active participant in the adventure. It's very clear this was written in the 1950s, and it pisses me off. There is no reason women can't hike cross-country, fight monsters, live rough with very little food or rest, get gross and sweaty, be tough and brave and *human*. Women and female elves/hobbits/dwarves/orcs are so unimportant in this story world that they aren't even mentioned. Middle-earth is a fantasy that says to me, "You're a girl, we don't want you here, you are useless." I can't relate to a world that's uniformly male, where female characters are set pieces and nothing more. I'm also uncomfortable with how Tolkien constantly uses words that went on to become anti-LGBT slurs. In LOTR, a bundle of sticks is a f*ggot, a shallow ditch is a d*ke, and anything weird, strange or abnormal is "queer". It bothers me a lot. I've never felt so Othered while reading before, even though the words aren't used in hateful contexts. Queer is MY word, it's part of who I am, and it is not weird or bad or abnormal. There's also the fact that the villains are always described as black and the good are white, which is a well-known trope that subtly promotes racism, even unintentionally. All these things bother me about this book/series/franchise. I want to know more about the Girls and Women of Middle Earth. About time they got to have some adventures too! And white straight men are never allowed to complain about diversity again. If they want to see only themselves in their media, they can pick up LOTR and leave the rest of us alone.

I first picked up this book about 15 years ago when the hype for the movies was strong, but when they hadn't come out yet. I couldn't get past the first third. I found Tolkien's writing to be too meandering, his world building and descriptions to be dull and the scenes in which the plot actually advances to be rushed. With all the book's descriptions of lineages and the history of places, in some ways it felt more like reading a chapter of the old testament than part of a fantasy novel.

I've recently returned to the book thinking that my adult more settled mind would appreciate this style more. I did finish the book this time, alas my opinion remains broadly unchanged.

Contrary to what its high rating on here and the universal praise it seems to receive almost everywhere else suggests, this is a book for people who enjoy this rather specific writing style that is certainly not found in popular fantasy books of more recent craft.

Two minds have I upon reflecting on my initial reading of this novel so greatly praised among those who dwell within the forests, now much diminished, and upon the vast plains of North America and still those who make their habitation on the island of the rains, Britain, which dwells within the great ocean, called by some the Atlantic.

Okay, so that initial sentence is horribly written and could have easily been expressed with much greater brevity: I'm of two minds about The Fellowship of the Ring. On the positive side, I love the overall plot, many of the characters (particularly Frodo, Sam, Aragorn, Gandalf, and Glóin), and the action, adventure, and magic. On the other hand, Tolkien's prose is all too frequently exceedingly laborious and even pretentious (as in my opening sentence above). Except for the hobbits, almost all of the characters speak, even in informal conversation, as though they were delivering great and important oratories. And then there is Tolkien's fondness for listing the names of mountains, rivers, countries, marshes, bogs, etc. of which we readers really have no inkling where they lie, and he also loves to give us additionally useless and coma-inducing information like what the names are in Elvish or this or that language of men or dwarves. He seems unable to tell us about a walk through a forest without listing the mountains to the west and the vast wastelands to the north that once were ruled by King Insert-Vaguely-Celtic-Sounding-Name. It's this exacting level of detail in his descriptions as well as the overly formal manner of speaking of so many of the characters that really make reading The Fellowship of the Ring a labor.

I did, however, so enjoy this novel that I really want to move forward and read the rest of the trilogy, and yet I dread having to slog through Tolkien's exhausting, boring descriptions and long-winded, bloviating dialogue. I think I will, eventually, read the next to novels, but I'm going to have to take a rest and move on to other books to cleanse my reading palate. In contrast, I recall when I first read the Narnia books and the Harry Potter novels, I could not wait to begin the next volume in those series. Such is not the case with Tolkien's trilogy, and for that reason, I would have to rank the former two as better than the latter.

I feel so conflicted about this... I'm loving the story itself, but I just feel like the writing isn't that great. It's not gripping me or sucking me into the quest. There's a fine balance between reading a story and experiencing it, and right now I'm just reading a story that's very good and exciting in theory, but it falls short of it's potential. It felt like a chore reading this, but not enough for me to abandon the books and just watch the movies instead. I do think I'll take a little break before staying book two though...

Drużyna Pierścienia to pierwsza część z cyklu powieści Władca Pierścieni autorstwa J. R. R. Tolkiena wydana po raz pierwszy w 1954, a w Polsce w 1961 roku. Historia zaczyna się sześćdziesiąt lat po wydarzeniach z Hobbita, ale jest poprzedzona prologiem, więc nie jest konieczna znajomość tej książki aby ogarnąć wydarzenia z pierwszego tomu Władcy Pierścieni. Wszystkie wydarzenia związane są z Jedynym Pierścieniem, który odziedziczył Frodo po swoim wuju Bilbie Bagginsie. Gdy okazuje się, że niesie on ze sobą niebezpieczeństwo Frodo postępując zgodnie z radami Gandalfa wyrusza wraz z trzema przyjaciółmi na wyprawę w celu zniszczenia pierścienia, a po drodze dołączają się do nich inni członkowie tworząc tytułową drużynę.

Tak jak się spodziewałem, książkę czytało mi się trochę lepiej od Hobbita. Jednak nadal coś blokowało mnie przed jego swobodnym przeczytaniem. Lektura zajęła mi dużo czasu i często nie mogłem się skupić na tekście i pewne fragmenty powtarzałem nawet trzy razy. Wolałbym tego nie pisać, ponieważ chciałbym zachęcić do przeczytania tej książki, ale jednak prawda jest taka, że czytało mi się ją dość ciężko.

Tym razem historia również wydała mi się ciekawsza. Może dlatego, że całość nie działa się tak szybko, ale mimo wszystko historia ciągle szła do przodu. Najwolniej czytało mi się właśnie w tych momentach, gdy drużyna miała dłuższe postoje i narady. Mało pamiętam też szczegółów, gdy akcja działa się zbyt szybko. Całość była chyba zrównoważona gdzieś po środku. W tej części zagrożenie wydaje się jakby odległe, trochę mityczne i tajemnicze. Mam wrażenie, że im bardziej poznam wroga, tym ciekawiej będę śledził wydarzenia.

Podziwiam autora oraz dobrą pracę tłumaczy przy licznych elementach lirycznych. Ogólnie nie uważam tego dzieła za coś nadzwyczajnego, jednak potrafi ona niesamowicie rozbudzić wyobraźnię i nie wszystko tutaj dzieje się według schematu. Również kolejna część zapowiada się być jeszcze lepszą od poprzedników. Mimo, że z pewnym trudem, chcę poznać dalszy ciąg tej historii już nie za względu na popularność tego dzieła, lecz na dotychczas poznane wydarzenia. The Ring must be destroyed.

And Frodo is its bearer.

The first time I read this book, I’ll confess I found it tedious work. It didn’t help that the first film had just come out and the pace of the novel seemed tortuously slow – Tolkien seems to love telling us the minutiae of every single road and stream in his beloved Shire and I spent most of the first five or six chapters all but screaming at the Hobbits to just hurry up and get to Bree!
However, on re-reading it I have to say I was curiously absorbed. Perhaps it’s because this time I didn’t have the pressure of wanting to get all three read before Two Towers came out (which yes, I did manage) but this time it was far less of a chore. All the passages about Hobbit family trees and such were still pretty dull and I’d forgotten that it’s something like 17 years between the birthday party and Frodo leaving the Shire, but the chapters with Tom Bombadil were really quite interesting, and I was struck with curiosity about this enigmatic character, rather than just willing him to shut up and let Frodo get on with it.
Rather than feeling like it was lots of walking and talking and not much else, I found the constant threat of the Black Riders quite sinister and it gave an edge to it that I hadn’t experienced before (a good lesson not to rush through reading things like this). I won’t deny that I was still keen for them all to get on, but it wasn’t in a particularly frustrating way, more in an encouraging way.
After reaching Rivendell and meeting my favourite character (Boromir) the story stays interesting, though I do feel that both Legolas and Gimli could have done with some more ‘page-time’ to get us a little more invested in them. I appreciate that Elves are supposed to be a bit mysterious and Gimli is just a nice throwback to the Dwarfy fun of ‘The Hobbit’ but nonetheless they felt very much like secondary characters to the Hobbits and Men, and of course; Gandalf.
Something I enjoyed very much about our Grey Wizard was that he is at once immeasurably powerful and wise and at the same time vulnerable and lost. Even without the previous book to reference, we know from his tangles with Saruman, the Wolves, the Black Riders and the Moria Goblins (and ultimately; the Balrog) that he is a being of immense personal power. We also know from his conversations with Frodo, Aragorn and Elrond that he has great knowledge of ancient lore and has travelled through more of Middle Earth than any other member of the Company of the Ring. And yet time and again he admits to being out of his depth, not only making us frighteningly aware of the gravity of the situation, but also making the character that much more likable and identifiable.
Another definite point of interest for me, as someone who had seen the film first (I know, I’m a Philistine!), was that our two Men are on a very different mission in the book. The film gave the impression that all were committed to getting Frodo and the Ring to Mordor while in the book, Aragorn and Boromir are only escorting them part of the way as they journey to Minas Tirith with the newly-remade Narsil (Anduril). Their intent is clearly more focused on the larger-scale military situation right from the start, something that makes a lot more sense to me, given the upbringing both men would have had. Aragorn might be a little more learned in such things than Boromir, having spent so much time in Rivendell, but he is clearly happy to leave things like magic rings as the province of Gandalf. He later assumes leadership of the Company with great reluctance after the Wizard’s fall, and criticises his own decisions on several occasions. Again, it makes the character feel very human, and I found him a lot easier to like and identify with; someone who wants to do the best for his people and for the world in general but is confused and scared about how to do it.
As to Frodo and the Hobbits (surely a rock band waiting to be formed?), they are still a bit tedious, and I have to say that for all that Sam is a likable character, I’m a little sickened by the slavish devotion he has to Frodo. In the film it’s implied that his loyalty is almost all born of friendship and of Gandalf’s instructions to him, where in the book the master-servant relationship is made uncomfortably clear. I appreciate that the two do genuinely care about one another, but it’s definitely one of those aspects of the book that marks it as a product of its time.
Another of these is that the romantic story of Aragorn and Arwen is all but nonexistent in this book, practically the whole thing being relegated to the appendices at the end of the trilogy. One of the few real failings of these books is the lack, not so much of female characters themselves, but of any motivation based on romantic relationships. Any psychologist will tell you that sex is one of, if not the most powerful motivator of the human psyche, and you don’t need to be writing naughty scenes to include that in a story. At no point in this book does anyone spare a second thought for a romantic partner and nobody’s actions seem to be motivated by any kind of romantic or sexual relationship. The adventure continues reasonably well without it, but I do think the absence of such motivation makes the characters less believable as real.
All in all I found myself enjoying this book far more than my initial ‘I’ll give it another go’ attitude would have expected. I still think a bit more of Saruman and Radagast would have been nice, and I maintain that it doesn’t matter how much Professor Tolkien was in love with a romanticised concept of England, we do not need to know everything about everyone and everywhere in all Four Farthings of the Shire. It would have been good to have some more of Aragorn and Arwen and I’d have liked a bit more of the interplay between Aragorn and Boromir myself, given that I do like the Numenorean story (and don’t be pedantic – they are both descended from Numenorean aristocracy), but – spoiler alert – at least I don’t have to deal with the emotional trauma of Boromir’s death until the next book!

I’ve returned to Middle-Earth for the first time in nearly 6 years. The Lord of the Rings – novels and movies alike – were seminal experiences in my teenage years and revisiting the brilliant world created by Tolkien was a joyous experience. His highly descriptive style is extraordinarily effective at materialising Middle-Earth in the reader’s mind, yet every time I read the books, I am conflicted. For me, the worldbuilding and endless descriptions of the landscape, on more than one occasion, feel overwhelming and pull me away from the intrigue and the plot.

Nevertheless, the story is engaging with either new lore constantly being dropped or unforeseen trials presenting themselves to our characters. I especially love how Tolkien creates urgency and tension in the various chase scenes throughout the book. Firstly, the fear of the Black Riders drives much of Frodo’s decision in the first half and forces him to go into the Old Forest (although I love Tom Bombadil, this section is always a slog for me to get through). Thereafter, their race from Bree to Rivendell is one of the most riveting sections. And iconically, the detour in Moria as the Fellowship is being chased by orcs and the Balrog is the best ‘action’ scene in “Fellowship”.

I am happy to report that for the first time in my many read-throughs of the series, I actually read the poetry/song bits rather than just skimming through them. I am, in no way, an avid reader of poetry, but I found that most of the poems in the book were fine.

I’ve read some criticisms of the dialogues of the characters in LOTR, arguing that each character’s voice is the same. That didn’t bother as much. In fact, many of my favourite segments were dialogue heavy – ‘The Shadow of the Past’ and ‘The Council of Elrond’ being two of my favourite chapters. One of the reasons maybe being that Gandalf and Elrond do a lot of narrating and maybe their narrative voices do not tend to go as deep into landscape description as Tolkien’s own. 😁

If this completely unprompted rereading of Tolkien's first LOTR book has taught me anything: it is that I like the ideas more than the writing. I consider myself to be part of that rare camp which grants the first part of the trilogy as the literary peak of this verbose mountain. Furthermore, I actually think the Tom Bombadil scenes can be rightly labelled as a significant highlight of the entire series (*gasp*). Never cared about Lord of the Rings as a kid and have never been a fan of the movies, so any type of hazy, nostalgic, golden-eyed reminiscing does not exist in my deeper psyche.

What I see in these books is an admirable (and extremely thorough) attempt to create a universe. What stands out to me as the real crowning achievement of such an endeavour is the natural depictions and the Nazgul chase scenes. I seriously think the entire series could have consisted of these 'Black Rider' trailing episodes, with Frodo and his hunted friends weaving in and out of temporary safe zones to evade the hunters. This combination of relentless anxious suspense coupled with depictions of the natural environment is a very intriguing mix. Tolkien allows Frodo and his buddies to take some time out and smell the roses. But not too much.

This back and forth emphasis on surviving danger and embracing the surrounding landscape is a unique way of depicting fantasy, to me it is much more effective then the plot heavy action of the following books. Maybe I've grown some type of morbid fascination with environmental representation in writing after sifting through Thoreau's journals for years now (a permanent bedside fixture). Tolkien himself reminds me much of what I like about HDT, and it is curious that more literary comparisons between the two writers does not exist.

Either way a decent read. Not a die hard fantasy fan by any stretch, but I applaud the writer for seriously stretching beyond the bounds of a simple adventure story: perhaps a fact of Tolkien's writing that needs to be more appreciated rather then briskly acknowledged.

Well, I finally got around to starting one of the most beloved fantasy series ever. And my feelings about it are certainly mixed. I didn't find myself loving it, but despite occasional frustration I didn't dislike it either. Hopefully I can make my thoughts on it somewhat comprehensible...

First off, the writing is very dense and can be hard to wade through. For most of the book, there was a lot of landscape description that probably wasn't necessary. For most of the middle of the book, I frequently wished that there was more dialogue and fewer details of trails and rivers. The character development(especially of the hobbits) could probably have been much better without all this setting description taking up space. The hobbits' personalities became more distinct towards the end, but up until that point they sort of blended together. I did feel vestiges of individual personalities in the others, like Aragorn, Boromir, Gimli, Gandalf, and Legolas, but none of them felt like fully realized characters to me. Hopefully they will be developed more in the other books.
For me, most of the book alternated between being quite interesting(the beginning, the ending, and a couple other parts) and being tedious(much of the Old Forest part and the "Council of Elrond" chapter).

The Fellowship of the Ring does have its good points though. The way Tolkien developed the world of Middle Earth was very impressive, and there was some nice prose. Really, my favorite part was the final chapter. I thought it was much more successful in its character interactions(the one between Boromir and Frodo was especially well-done and tense), developing the Ring aspect, and creating atmosphere than the rest of the book was. The ending really did make me interested to read the next book of the trilogy, and that is very much to Tolkien's credit. Hopefully, the next book will continue in this vein.
