Bookish Reaction: The Fellowship of the Ring (Spoilers Might be Present)

Hiya Guys, Ria here with another bookish review type thing. Here I have The Fellowship of the Ring: the first book in the Lord of the Rings Series by J.R.R. Tolkien. This book is considered a modern day classic and Tolkien does change his writing style for the trilogy, so it is a little bit more confusing so this is what I got out of it.

Plot: Here we have the main character Frodo Baggins, he is the nephew of our beloved Bilbo Baggins, who is now a millionaire and everyone is kind of jealous of him in BagEnd. Bilbo is now WAYYYY older, like 110, and the book starts out at his 110th birthday. Here he just has a couple of thousand people at his party. All the Tooks and the Baggines and the Brandybucks, and any other names you can imagine. Bilbo has a rather interesting and expensive party. At the end of this party he disappears before everyones very eyes. Frodo, inheriting BagEnd, is faced with the difficult decision of what to do with the Ring Bilbo had left for him. Gandolf tells Frodo many years later, for some reason, that this Ring is a all powerful piece of jewelry that controls other rings around Middle Earth, made by this awful guy named Sauron. Sauron apparently is this very dark being and no one really knows what he looks like. In the Movie, he is a eye, because in one of Frodo’s dreams that’s the only thing he sees. In the book, however, he is kind of a being no one really knows. Frodo, along with a overhearing Sam Gaimgy, set out on a adventure that they will never forget. Somehow Pippin and Merry join them before the adventure begins. This is a good change of pace because there was more Hobbits….and they are trying to avoid Isingaurd….which doesn’t happen in the movie. Anyway they get more friends along the way, like Legalus (the Gorgeous Woodelf in the movie), Gimli (Gloin’s Son), and Aragorn (Son of Airathorn - some powerful human being) and they set to bring the Ring to Mordor, where they will destroy it in the volcano once and for all. Meanwhile Sairamon (probably spelled his name wrong) wants the ring too, the white wizard, and they are trying to avoid him at all costs.



Characters:

Frodo: Not as loveable as Bilbo, but has more sense than him. He is kind of a blah character in my opinion. He doesn’t know how to keep care of himself (even though he knows what he has to do and what not) but therefore this is why Sam is here to save the day.

Sam: Sam is kind of the hero of this tale believe it or not. He is a common Hobbit and doesn’t come from money, but he seems to know exactly what to say and who to say it to when he is up for bat in this story. He seems to do a lot of sneaking around. He is extremely loyal to his master Frodo and probably would follow him to the ends of the Earth….well Middle-Zealand…

Pippin: Kind of the most childish Hobbit out of the four in this story. He is kind of carefree and doesn’t understand the height of the situation the characters are in. He seems to just make more problems for the characters with his childish whelms, he kind of the comic relief of this tale.

Merry: He is as young as Pippin but kind of understands more than Pippin for some reason. He is more technical with his thinking, knowing where he is going how to get to certain places. Although he is not as childish as Pippin is, he still grows a lot in the story as it progresses.

Aragorn: Kind of the lousiest ranger in all of Middle-Zealand….he kind of is he never knows where he is going in this book. He takes them too north, even though he supposed to know the land well, and then they have to walk more. I thought this was kind of funny because my professor described him as the normal heroic figure, when Frodo is kind of the more reliable character. Personally I thought he had his flaws, so it made it so not even the more model like heroes seemed to be perfect.

Legalus: The Gorgeous elf, what do you want. He walks on water, he kind of flawless and he is really only there because they want to show Gimli and his relationship grow, being the dwarves and elves do not have a great relationship because of the war. He makes for great Rowan Whitethorn memes apparently.

Gimli: He is the son of Gloin, who is one of the many many dwarves that traveled with Bilbo in the first book. Like I said for Legalus he is only there because of the relationship growth between him and Legalus. He is very funny in my opinion he made me laugh on several occasions in this novel.

Gandolf: Well, he is the wizard….enough said I already talked about him in my Hobbit Review, the only thing really different about him is that he gets captured by Sauramon (probably still saying his name wrong) and it forces the other characters to become more strong.

Sauramon: The white wizard who is a total D-word. He wants the ring so he can defeat Sauron, but he just wants power for himself. He wants to be the rainbow wizard, or the wizard of many colors….Agh so many characters.

Sauron: The main antagonist….enough said I explained him in the plot.



Conclusion:

This book is rather confusing in my opinion. I wanted it to be a better storyline, but there is sooooo many plots and points of view and so little time.
I give this book 3.5 stars, for confusing and having such long chapters

This is going to be a review of all the 3 books - Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers, and The Return of the King. The Story is complete only after the third finishes and I felt the books were kind of haphazardly parted into three, where it should have been one.

That said, I have kind of mixed feelings for this EPIC tale. True to all the rumours, the story was magnificent, grand and extraordinary. The few thing I did not like in the story included
1. The wired names of the cities - Although I feel the mix of languages was necessary to depict the difference and variety of races, but they felt so difficult to me, it was hard to remember and hence interfered with the "mind map" of the story. This stole a bit of glimmer from it.
2. The Grand description of cities and places - At many point I felt that the author simply was not interested in the describing the places, rather he resorted to telling how would you feel once you see it, although this worked for the first few times but after that it became tiresome. Every next place was grander then the last and due to the "description" I felt kind of saturated and it really became extremely tedious to go through the passages at that moment.

Apart from the above 2 things the story of the Ring was ABSOLUTELY fabulous. The beginning, the travels, the events , the wars and the ending... everything was so carefully crafted. No loose ends, nothing happens abruptly.

The one thing for which I am confused whether it was a good thing in the story or bad was that every character is either plain GOOD or plain EVIL, well apart from Smegul. I think that this is what gave the story so much of the Grandeur and Epic feel, but at the same time I felt that it was very unrealistic. I won't grudge that though, it was part of the story telling.

One of the best things about the story I felt was the ending. The author could have ended the story with the fall of Souron, but he did not. There was so much more to the ending after the crowning of the king. The problems did not end there either. The scrounging of the Shire and the rise of Hobbits was the greatest part of satisfaction in the story. I am not sure if I can say the ending was happy, but it was definitely PEACEFUL.

I won't be commenting on the different parts of the story because firstly it would be needing another 3 part book to explain and secondly because it took me about 5 months to get through all the three books and I am not sure I remember every detail correctly. This story has been my longest read till date.

This is the second time I read “The Fellowship of the Ring”. The first time was at the age of 13 or 14 maybe, around the time when more or less everyone reads Tolkien. Somehow there were no sparks between us at that time, and I never continued reading beyond the first part of the trilogy. Fifteen years later I was annoyed by the same elements that bothered me before, so there must be some continuity to my personality. It’s something. This time around though, I knew that I would finish what I started. Maybe I have become more patient or more persistent with age. That’s something as well.

J. R. R. Tolkien is prone to long and slow starts. I learnt that much at least from “The Hobbit”. And in all honesty: it was tiresome. But it was half as bad, given the context. Against a total of more than 1200 pages, I can live with an elaborate introduction of roughly 250. Sure, I can only handle that many forests, hiking trips, meals and bursting into song before I go amok. A song about bathing? Really? Fucking kindergarten! Though I was maybe more profoundly irritated by the sheer randomness of the first half of “The Fellowship”. All the events and episodes between the Party and The Prancing Pony are, for my taste, too easily interchangeable and/or omittable and too loosely set into structure. They lack causality. They lead nowhere and are even now, having read the entire story, of no relevance for further events. Except maybe to show that Middle-earth has its very own Jar-Jar Binks for one thing, though not that stupid. But why exactly would one want to do that of all things is still a mystery to me…

The story does gain momentum after the Council of Elrond. But it is still the first phase of a work in progress, and comes down to setting the stage and introducing the characters. Those are, for now, types with specific functions within the story and in their own world. The wise guide/organiser, revealing less than he knows and knowing still less than he would need to. The formally central but essentially passive figure without any personal engagement or quality, slipping into events through circumstances beyond him. King Arthur turned Atticus Finch. The devoted and loyal soul, who needs to put more faith in himself and break out of his shell. The representatives of two ever-conflicted groups who are to show the true meaning of having an open mind. The noble yet proud one as an incarnation of misjudgement. The two who have not the slightest idea what they are doing, but are doing it anyway full force.

But it works very well. Tolkien has found a good recipe to begin with, the right ratio of wide brush-strokes and miniscule detailing. There are enough debates and contemplation to provide the necessary background and knowledge, but they are still kept natural and necessary for the characters in their own “reality”. Arda and Middle-earth are a setting, and as temping as it might be to spread out all their splendour like a fan, their presence is trimmed down to the measure of the characters, to what they know beforehand and what they need to find out. Not the reader. Just like the characters are gradually exposed through their place in their world and in connection or contrast to the others. Which altogether is a brilliantly nuanced feature. But to that you get later. And slowly. Prior to that I felt like in midst of a litter of hyper-somethings tumbling around – too chaotic, too simple, too blunt, too thoughtless, too petty. This contrast to the rest of Middle-earth and its people is not only relevant for the core of the story and its development, but also one of the essential moral concepts, especially toward the end. Though this explains none of the apparent stand-alones or loose ends. But, I happen to be quite good with acknowledging the significance of things while still being repulsed by them. You know, nasty hobbitses, we hates them. No wonder my impersonation of Gollum is spot-on.

I last read this first part when I was still at school and then, I couldn't put it down. It's still one of the best adventure stories ever written, but with a more mature outlook I can find plenty that I don't like.

Today's impatient readers would squeal "info dump" right away at the prologue, the rather over-long introduction to the Shire and Hobbits. There is a lot of unnecessary information here that Tolkien may have planned to expand upon but never got round to. It doesn't really do anything for the book and could quite frankly be safely left out without ever impinging on one's enjoyment of the story. Although one has to bear in mind that originally Tolkien wrote the Hobbit stories for his own children with little thought of publishing them, the Fellowship of the Ring begins with a prologue about the Hobbits and the Shire that gives away the ending and informs the reader that all the main Hobbit characters are going to survive the adventure and live to a respectable old age.

This means that whenever things look dark for Frodo, Sam, Meriadoc and Pippin, the reader only needs to recall the opening pages and let out a sigh of relief. They'll be fine, don't worry, all will be right in the end. It is perhaps this aspect of the work that dates it the most.

Tolkien was clearly a man possessed. It took many decades to write the Lord of the Rings' 6 books, published later as a trilogy. Admittedly, he was rudely interrupted by WWII and bringing up a family, carving out a career and dealing with paper shortages, but the length of time it took to write the core of Lord of the Rings meant that he could "wallow" in the world he had created, making it an endless mire in which future readers could lose themselves and their patience in the quicksand of Tolkien's never-ending "history" for the races of people he'd created.

There's just too much of everything: too many names of people who play no part whatsoever in this book or any of the following works, too many story threads that lead nowhere and too many references to "the good old days, when High-Elves" still walked in Middle Earth. Too many lengthy descriptions of landscapes. It grates after a while.

The near total lack of female characters in the book - and when they are mentioned there's always a negative quality to them - leaves one with the impression this book was written by a misogynist. Plenty of women worked to help the war effort in WWI, when Tolkien fought in the trenches as a young man - and they did so again in WWII, when he was of mature years. Why then, when there were so many real life examples of heroic and brave females in times of war all around the author, did none of these excellent examples make it into his books? It is the main downfall of his work.

And a man who shamelessly plundered Scandinavian as well as northern German mythology should have remembered there were Valkyries and brave Queens and warrior princesses among them who'd have made mince-meat out of the nine Ring wraiths just for the fun of it, rather than doing it as a sulky "he doesn't love me, so I don't want to live" act of defiance of a spoiled teenage brat from Rohan.

Since Tolkien plundered mostly Nordic myths, one is also left with the impression that only the strictly "white" or Scandinavian types are of high birth and spirit, namely the Elves, while everybody else is never quite good enough to live up to their example. Orcs and other races in league with Sauron are always dark of skin, slant-eyed, ugly and barely able to speak let alone write, sing or interested in anything other than destruction. Hm...that makes The Lord of the Rings pretty racist at the heart of it, methinks.

Perhaps my favourite part is the Tom Bombadil story-line, which introduces a mysterious woodland character to us, a person perhaps as powerful as the Dark Lord himself, only Tom Bombadil is a force for good, not evil. It is never really made clear what he is and whence he came from - perhaps one reason why this character and the Hobbits rather interesting stay with him is left out of the Hollywood movies?

The humour, of course, stands up to the rigours of time and is as fresh today as it was when this was first published. Tolkien always maintained that this was not an allegory and had no hidden meaning beyond that of being an adventure story, but one has to remember that he belonged to a generation that had seen so much horror in WWI and been taught not to show their feelings that it is evident to me he suffered from survivor's guilt and spend his entire life trying to live up to what he imagined his (dead) friend's expectations of him would have been.

There is an underlying restlessness in all six books that makes one positively want to put on one's walking boots and fetch one's walking stick before turning to a new chapter, but particularly in this one, where the Fellowship of the Ring sets out pleasantly enough, but soon encounters deadly peril. Most songs in the books reveal great joy at finding something, and even greater feeling of loss when the thing we valued most is taken away for good. Every Tolkien song that deals with setting out on a quest ends in melancholy or sadness...Not an allegory, my foot!

For Tolkien as a young man, just like hundreds of thousands of other British men, would have set out in high patriotic spirits to defend his homeland from the Bosch...only to find themselves thrown into the very midst of hell, a Flanders that could rival Mordor at its worst any day. I can just picture their fresh young faces, as they are sitting on a train to Dover, singing a cheeky song or two, just like Peregrin and Meriadoc. The smiles, and high jinks, would soon come to an end.

Tolkien's restlessness made him move house more often than other people change their socks, and from the posthumously published books we can see that he started lots of projects but hardly ever got round to finishing them. He is just like Frodo and Bilbo who, once they have discovered there is a Road outside their front door, they want to have adventures. But when they find them, the adventure with the Ring proves too much for them. Their hearts are wearied and tainted and sadly neither of them can be at rest in Middle Earth every again. They must leave the land they fought so very hard to protect...but Tolkien could only leave in his imagination, not in reality, having a wife and kids, a chair at university college etc. There was no white ship at Grey Haven to take him to the promised land and lessen the pain of losing all but one of his childhood friends, seeing blown-up bodies all around him and knowing that if the enemy's not stopped, their wild hordes will overrun England, that green and pleasant Shire.

So, six months later (almost to the day) I've finally read this book. Do I get my official geek cred now? It took me six months to read 290 pages... an outstanding rate which far outpaced my initial expectations!

Look, I recognize that this was one of the originals. There is brilliance in here, I know it when I see it... I just didn't like it. I thought... just get out of the Shire and it'll get better. Then it was just get out of Rivendell. Finally it was 'just get to Moria'.. and you know what? It got a little better then! Things started to move forward and then JRRT starts throwing more detail at you and songs in Elvish until you realize you're re-reading the same paragraph three times and it still doesn't matter!

I suppose if you're a huge JRRT fan and love his works (of which there are thousands of and I am grateful for) then this book is for you. Just trust me in that it doesn't get better as you read it. It's the same chore while reading page 8 as it is reading page 278.

For those of you still on the fence, I will include a paragraph which perfectly captures the essence of The Fellowship of the Ring -

"...They stand tall in our dreams: Baraz, Zirak, Shathûr.
'Only once before have I seen them from afar in waking life, but I know them and their names, for under them lies Khazad-dûm, the Dwarrowdelf, that is now called the Black Pit, Moria in the Elvish tongue. Yonder stands Barazinbar, the Redhorn, cruel Caradhras; and beyond him are Silvertine and Cloudyhead: Celebdil the White, and Fanuidhol the Grey, that we call Zirakzigil and Bundushathûr.
'There the Misty Mountains divide, and between their arms lies the deep-shadowed valley which we cannot forget: Azanulbizar, the Dimrill Dale, which the Elves call Nanduhirion.'"

See, if you love this level of detail in the first book, then by all means read it, read it and love it. If, however this is the type of thing which can wait for book four (see: Dorne, GRRM) then perhaps you might want to pass on this one and enjoy the movies instead.
The classic saga, the quest of the mythic journey--Tolkien fills the pages with poetry and charm and adventure and life that make this a fantastic reading experience.

I went into this book prepared to love it. I'm a self-proclaimed supernerd, so I figured this would be right up my alley. I guess I was a little let down. It wasn't what I expected it to be.

The plot was fine, but hard to follow. There were just so many things going on and lots of little side-quests and things that just confused me. And seemed to serve no real purpose.

Also, we don't get to see much inside any of the characters (with the possible exception of Frodo). We never learn what makes them tick, or how they really feel about being dragged along on a huge quest. Sure, the author gives a good description of how they act, but I want to know how they feel.

One other thing. This book was flat-out hard to read. I almost never say that. I love reading (duh) and devour books much more complex than any of my classmates. But this was one of those rare books that didn't hold my attention. I kept getting distracted because the book was just dry. It felt like walking through Jello. I was counting the pages until I finished.

So, if I so clearly hated the book, why the 3-star rating? I have 3 words for that: a freaking awesome world. I mean seriously! I really loved the whole universe it created. I want to know all about the cultures and the histories and the traditions of all the different species, cultures and towns. That part got me thinking. It's like why I love Star Wars. That movie series has a pretty good plot, but it's basically a futuristic cowboy movie. But the galaxy it creates. All the worlds and cultures and everything just make me want to watch more. And more. And more.

So yeah. I liked this book. I didn't love it. I guess I set my expectations too high.

Hace muchísimo que quería leer la saga El Señor de los Anillos. No hace mucho que me familiaricé con el género épico fantástico, y cuando lo hice, no empecé con los clásicos. Hablando con un amigo de George R.R. Martin y de su narrativa, surgió una discusión. Me dijo que no podía decir que Martin fuera tan bueno ni que su saga fuera estupenda sin haber leído a Tolkien. Ni bien tuve dinero para poder gastar en unos cuantos libros, compré los tres tomos de El Señor de los Anillos y comencé a leer La Comunidad del Anillo.

Éste primer libro, aunque muy bueno, me dejó un tanto decepcionada. Debo decir, antes de empezar a hablar sobre él, que tampoco había visto las adaptaciones de la saga a la pantalla grande, así que fue todo nuevo para mí.

La historia comienza con los preparativos para la fiesta de cumpleaños del viejo hobbit Bilbo Bolsón en Bolsón Cerrado. Toda la Comarca se entera de tal festejo y se rumorea que contará con grandes sorpresas, tales como los fuegos artificiales del mago Gandalf. La intriga crece cada vez más, pues Bilbo es un legendario hobbit que en su juventud realizó un gran viaje, del cual volvió con varios tesoros. Llegado el día del cumpleaños y luego de que los asistentes recibieran inmensos regalos y observaran los fuegos de Gandalf y otras maravillas, Bilbo comienza a dar lo que parecía tomar forma de un tedioso discurso... pero que es interrumpido abruptamente por la desaparición de Bilbo ante los ojos de todos los huéspedes. Pasados unos días, Bilbo no retorna y Bolsón Cerrado queda a cargo de Frodo Bolsón, su sobrino y heredero. Frodo recibe a Gandalf, quien parece ser el único que conoce las verdaderas intenciones del viejo hobbit y le indica que Bilbo le ha dejado un brillante anillo de oro, y le advierte que no es un anillo común y corriente.

"(...)Tres Anillos para los Reyes Elfos bajo el cielo.
Siete para los Señores Enanos en palacios de piedra.
Nueve para los Hombres Mortales condenados a morir.
Uno para el Señor Oscuro, sobre el trono oscuro
en la Tierra de Mordor donde se extienden las Sombras.
Un Anillo para gobernarlos a todos. Un Anillo para encontrarlos,
un Anillo para atraerlos a todos y atarlos en las tinieblas
en la Tierra de Mordor donde se extienden las Sombras...."


Desde el principio, la historia te atrapa, los personajes te seducen con sus encantos y te llevan con ellos en sus andanzas. Tolkien escribe muy bello, la narración está plagada de imágenes muy vivas y largas descripciones de la naturaleza que te trasladan al lugar de los hechos. Todo ésto es lo que más destaco de éste volumen de la saga: comienza una gran historia muy bien contada.

Lo que menos me gustó fue la inocencia de la cual está repleto. Tal vez, si lo hubiese leído unos años atrás, me hubiera gustado mucho, sin reparar en ésto. Pero no fue así, y aunque los problemas se presentan inesperadamente durante el viaje de nuestros protagonistas, involucrando éstos criaturas misteriosas y envueltos en sombras, todo queda en la nada cuando ellos se salvan de alguna manera maravillosa, por la aparición de algún otro personaje que pasaba por el lugar. Me parece que ésto arruina toda la construcción enigmática previa al problema, resulta un desenlace muy poco creíble y repentino.

De todos modos, aunque ésto que les acabo de contar me molestó un poquito, continué leyendo el libro con muchas ganas de pasar al siguiente y así poder saber el destino de sus maravillosos personajes. Creo que desde que apareció, Aragorn fue mi favorito. Un personaje misterioso pero más ligado a los hombres que el gran Gandalf.

Otra cosa a destacar es que el mundo está construído maravillosamente y que lo habitan millones de personajes no humanos muy interesantes y que son presentados sin muchos rodeos ni descripciones, para que uno se imagine cómo son éstos seres. Se le da mucho lugar a la imaginación del lector de ésta forma.

En fin, La Comunidad del Anillo sienta las bases para lo que es una gran historia de fantasía épica que se construye a partir de su mundo y los personajes que lo habitan.

As everyone else said, it feels really weird to write a review for this book. I mean not only is it really hard to capture why this book is so beloved but the truth is that it is so beloved you probably know everything about it. So I guess instead I'll give you a warning before you try reading this book because many people have come to it with big expectations and have left bored. The truth is this book is very dense and heavy, it can be a lot to take in. But you can't be a passive observer when reading this book, instead you have to actively engage with it. The level of detail is so insane that you can build your world, your Middle Earth, in your head while Tolkien describes it. It'll go on for pages and you'll either love it or if you just skim it lazily you will find yourself hating it. If I was ever tired, or not really focusing on what I read, I found myself missing out. As a reader, you are basically a hobbit. You are completely clueless about the extent of this vast and timeless realm that others before you have and will travel. Instead you have a narrow understanding of the world and as you explore this fantasy you can either allow it to expand your horizon or just make you feel overwhelmed.

This book is full of little encounters that take a great deal of time to read through. Sometimes they feel pointless. But you'll have to dig a little deeper to find the more nuance messages about power that Tolkien is trying to convey. There's a reason the heaviest burden has fallen on the smallest of creatures, why nobody who is much stronger will accept it. There's a reason some have near mastery and ultimate power over their own realm but will not participate in the conflicts of the outside world. And there is a reason that somebody as small as Sam, who is really just a silly hobbit, can be at times as wise as the experienced travelers and warriors he goes with.

Basically, this novel and the entire series is an adventure. But if you just passively read it you will honestly get lost in the pages and pages describing the different types of trees in a forest and really miss out on what Middle Earth has to offer. Instead, if you live through Frodo's experience as a witness to everything, and try to understand the actual stakes of the novel and empathize with the characters, it will completely transport you into this world. Because we are so used to our heroes being brave and strong that we forget how much we are vulnerable creatures who fear the dark, spiders, and heights. Frodo is us. The hobbits are all us. I know it's a bit dramatic to say but imagine how we'd feel if the fate of the world was rested on our shoulders and we faced death. Because that's how Frodo feels. It is so much realer to read this fantasy novel than about real heroes. I know that's a weird thing to take from reading these books, but that's how I truly felt at the end. I felt empowered.

The early hobbit chapters are charming, what follows is tedious and adds little to the overarching narrative. It adds to the world building and the homage to the verses of old texts such as the oddest, Beowulf and the eddas and as such it has its place, but I would rather have done without. The same can be said about the many songs. Some add to the theme, some I can’t see the point of.

I was likewise unpleasantly surprised by how much tell and not show there is. ‘Grimly and Legolas share a boat for they had become fast friends.” That’s not great writing for people accustomed to prose. In verse it served well enough. I additionally noticed the way the landscape is described. It reminds me of stories from the 19th century, travel logs, where descriptions of lands the reader has never been to and may never visit or see in image. It tried to instill awe yet a curious lack of details and a detached reporting style made it fall flat.

So why as much as 3 stars? Well, my love for the story, mostly instilled by the film trilogy, and a memory of liking the following books better along with appreciation for the cultures shown ans the themes it touches upon as well as the real world impact it has had makes it a worthwhile reading experience.

The Fellowship of the Rings helped turn fantasy into a respectable genre. As with most good books that would otherwise be called genre fiction, I wouldn't say it's fantasy but literature that happens to be fantasy. The prose is good and well-written. The rambling parts make sense as to why they're rambling and there's a great sense of the story being retold. The heros are faced with a parade of perils and each is interesting and different with a new feel to each.

Chances are, two readers wouldn't come upon the same image but I feel they would come upon the same idea.

The book ended abruptly and some of the song-asides were longer than I wished but Tolkien had set himself the challenge of writing a long story. His first volume of it was surprisingly enjoyable.

It is with great trepidation that I write this review, knowing that the great majority of readers will likely not agree with me. I consider myself a fairly well-read individual, and I am well aware of Tolkien’s legacy as the “Father of Fantasy Fiction”, however, I struggled through this novel.

In no way am I minimizing his contribution to English literature, as I realize that his imagination is above reproach, his rhetoric, truly impressive. However, I truly detest monotony, and this novel is laden with it. I trudged through the overly-detailed descriptions of the geography. The characters seemed to languish during the prolonged events, and very little progress was made through the entire novel. Also, the ever-growing list of names for the same character or location was exhausting! I just can’t understand why so many aliases were necessary, other than to create complete confusion.

To some degree, I feel that the same effect could have been accomplished (even to adequately set the elaborate scene), in ¾ or less of its current length.

When all is said and done, I cannot, in good conscience, rate this novel less than 3 stars; the impact of his work on literature, and as previously mentioned, his extraordinary imagination, are priceless.

Frodo Bolsón es un joven hobbit que recibe de parte de su tío, Bilbo, un misterioso anillo dorado con un inimaginable poder, que a su vez, está tan cargado de tanta maldad, que cualquiera que lo usase sin la más mínima mesura pronto se vería seducido por sus virtudes al punto de ser arrastrado hacia su propia perdición. El mago Gandalf, amigo y consejero de los Bolsón, advierte al joven heredero del gran peligro que se avecina con el regreso del Señor Oscuro Sauron, propietario legítimo del anillo y de la gran contienda que se librará cuando sus ejércitos en la tierra oscura de Mordor, partan a conquistar el mundo en caso de que dicho objeto mágico sea recuperado por su dueño.

Es entonces cuando Frodo debe asumir la misión más peligrosa de su vida: dejar su cómodo hogar en La Comarca e iniciar una travesía por los sitios más inhóspitos de la Tierra Media hasta las Grietas del Destino en Mordor, con el fin de destruir el anillo dorado. Acompañado de sus amigos Sam, Pippin y Merry, en adición de Gandalf y otros integrantes como Aragorn y el elfo Legolas, el grupo conocido como La Comunidad (o La Compañía) del anillo deberá partir hasta su destino final para escoltar al mediano Frodo a fin de consumar su encargo.

La primera parte de la trilogía del escritor J.R.R. Tolkien es un trabajo enriquecido no solo por su prolífica capacidad imaginativa y detallada descripción de los lugares y eventos, sino por el romanticismo que evocan los trágicos versos narrativos de las leyendas pertenecientes al amplio trasfondo mitológico de la obra. No se trata solo de una serie de historias dirigidas al público infantil (recordando que Tolkien inicialmente las escribió para sus hijos) sino que es en igual medida disfrutable para los lectores más grandes.

The book was hard to read for a number of reasons. (Spoilers ahead)

(1) Tolkien was terrible at suspense. Even if I hadn't watched the movie, it was fairly obvious that Gollum was the spy. That could have been more cleverly worked in. Boromir's coming betrayal was also much too obvious. Tolkien left no room for doubt.

(2) Though this book is more fantasy than adventure, the fact that we're going through death and peril on a mission also makes it an adventure novel. But the action was so slow. Maybe all 3 novels could be condensed into one great one if Tolkien had skipped over all the unnecessary details and smalltalk.

(3) The characters did not stand out in the way they did in the Hobbit. Though you can clearly tell everyone apart by behavior, they aren't very colourful characters who keep me interested. I'm not invested in the characters.

(4) The writing wasn't exceptional in any way. It didn't read like a well told story. Just Tolkien grasping desperately for words to share the mystical world he had created. It was apparent to me that the point was not to build and tell a story, but to describe the world in which it happened. He was too focused on background and setting.


All in all, it wasn't a terrible read. I've read far worse, but it was a great disappointment.

First of all, can I just say: What the hell is up with Tom Bombadil? I had the impression that he's a much-beloved character (at least in some circles)---but good lord, he makes even the elves seem hardly sappy at all by comparison! That whole section of the book was completely ridiculous---no wonder they left it out of the movie versions.[return][return]One aspect of the book that the movie didn't fully capture, though, was Tolkein's portrayal of power-lust, especially through the characters of Saruman and Boromir. The ring represents a somewhat different temptation for the halflings (particularly Smeagol and Bilbo), a sort of unhealthy obsession with material objects, similar to that represented by Voldemort's horcruxes in Harry Potter (which also symbolize power-lust and a neurotic fear of death). The discussions between Gandalf and Saruman, and Frodo and Boromir, which were much better in the book and the movies should have used more of that dialogue or at least stayed truer to its spirit. They really helped bring out some of the basic themes of the novels more explicitly, but in the movie they were really watered down and generic by comparison, which really weakened the impact not only of those particular scenes, but of the movies overall.[return][return]I've also heard it complained that the movies tried to force non-existent and vaguely hinted at romances to the fore, but I actually thought strengthening some of the romantic storylines was one of the better changes made by the adapters. It helped emphasize the values at stake, and in some cases actually tightened the plot and cut out unnecessary characters. For example, it was much better to have Arwen meet Aragorn and the hobbits on their way to Rivendell instead of some other random elf who played no further role in the story, rather than just having her be present at the feast given for Frodo after his recovery and then occasionally dropping subtle hints that Aragorn is in love with her. Tolkein basically just told us that there was a romance between them---the movie dramatizes it. Sam's interest in Rosie the barmaid also gives him a stronger reason to want to return to the Shire other than just that he longs for a peaceful, quiet life of gardening, and thereby raises the stakes for his character. I know the peaceful quiet life of gardening was really the whole point for Tolkein, but let's face it, he was a bit fruity on the subject (as witness the whole Tom Bombadil fiasco).

The Fellowship of the Ring has been on my reading list for years. Like many others, I greatly enjoyed The Lord of the Rings film trilogy. (As a side note, I saw The Return of the King in the theater five times). I have been less enamored of the film adaptation(s) of J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit, but I haven't lost any of my love of the original trilogy. I'm glad to have started on my own personal journey to read Tolkien's source material.

If you talk to just about anyone who has read The Lord of the Rings books they will all tell you how much they enjoyed the books and how dense and difficult they are. It's a huge barrier of entry for many readers, myself included, to explore Tolkien's world. It becomes very, very apparent very, very early on in the reading of The Fellowship that Tolkien loves the world he has created; its detail is entirely unmatched by any other fantasy book I have read thus far. It can also be totally superfluous to the story, which at times nearly brings the story to a grinding and unwelcome halt. I found myself intrigued by this fantastical world Tolkien had created with all of its geographic locations, historic monuments and events, and ages of time. It's overwhelming, and that's not always a good thing. Although I was intrigued with Tolkien's detailed world, whenever Tolkien did wander back to his story I remembered why I was actually reading the book.

The story itself is a grand, albeit simple, adventure. It's a basic but bold story of good and evil. When the story was flowing I was enthralled and entertained. Having watched the films, it was a fun exercise to identify all of the areas and elements that were changed for the film adaptation. (Most of them, quite frankly, were desperately needed; perhaps more on that later). Tolkien's dialogue feels flat but can often be profound. Most of his characters are in desperate need of time—time to speak, act, and generally be characters. With the amount of walking and waiting that goes on in the story, you would think Tolkien could have taken more advantage of the time he insists you spend with the characters to actually tell you more about them or better yet show you who they are. Instead, we’re left with brief encounters and brief explanations of motivations. It leaves characters that should be three-dimensional stuck in a somewhat two-dimensional frame.

The Fellowship of the Ring, along with the other books in the series, must be recognized for their contribution to literature and book genres in general. Tolkien created a living, breathing place, even if his characters don't do as much of those two things as they should. While reading about these magical places, I wanted to go to those places. An author can't accomplish a feeling like that without providing a commensurate amount of detail. However, there is a balance in setting a scene, creating a world, and telling a story. In The Fellowship of the Ring, Tolkien falters on the storytelling tight-rope.

I will finish The Lord of the Rings trilogy. I enjoyed The Fellowship of the Ring, but I wanted to love it. I enjoy the Fantasy genre and feel it's only right to pay my dues to the monumental books that created it. Thus far, the story has been worth experiencing even if it sometimes feels like Tolkien's secondary concern.

Upon first sight, one can find the book intimidating. That's alright, many books are more than 531 pages long. But, what "many books" don't have, is the detailed, and intricately crafted world that The Lord of the Rings series boasts. One need not fully realise the world initially, but doing so greatly increases the enjoyability of the novel, and one can forgive the endless barrage of sleep-inducing songs and poems.
The plot, just like in The Hobbit is a standard Hero's Journey template. In fact, it can be described in a few words. Bilbo Baggins, a hobbit, vanishes from his hometown, the Shire, on his one-hundred-and-eleventh (or eleventy-oneth for more ardent fans) birthday, after a huge party. His nephew of sorts, Frodo Baggins, inherits all his property including the hole in which they lived (hobbits live in holes. Don't you know that yet?) and a perfectly circular, gold invisibility ring. Now, although I describe it as an invisibility ring, it has great, hidden powers of evil, with whose help it continually tries to get back to its maker, the Dark Lord, Sauron, who resides in Mordor. It is up to Frodo to take the ring to safety, and make sure that it is destroyed. This can be done only by casting it into the fires of Mount Doom (really Tolkien? You thought up such imaginative names for everything else, and all you could come up with for Orodruin was "the Cracks of Doom"?). Despite the unintentional laughter which this may incite, it is treated surprisingly seriously.
His journey is divided into two parts in The Fellowship of the Ring. One is to Rivendell, home of elves, and the other one from there to the breaking of the titular fellowship. Two things surprised me most, one was that the most iconic line in the films, "One does not simply walk into Mordor," is entirely absent, and the other was the abrupt ending. Half-a-star gone there.
The plot moves along briskly, with beautifully prosed descriptions that titillate the reader's imagination, and fairly interesting and likable, albeit unidimensional, characters. Indeed, I would have even forgiven the occasionally god-awful dialogue too, seeing all the pros of the storyline, had it not been for the songs. The Songs, I should call them, the Dreadful Songs. Characters randomly burst out into musical melodies which would make even Shah Rukh Khan cower, beholding their amazing plot-stopping properties which surpasses even those of his.
Gollum (my favourite character) has a mere cameo appearance, though I hope that Tolkien has done something about that in the other two books.
Oh, and a note: Gandalf, the wizard's death scene was short, and lacked the power it should have had. The mourning that followed ventured not into the minds of the Fellowship, but stayed outside, describing the beauty of the Lothlorien woods. This I disapproved.
Characters are simpler than in The Hobbit, something which I didn't find much of a problem, but definitely counts as a step backwards, however, I did take issue with the stereotypical differentiation between good and evil. Black = evil. Good = white. I like more of the grey stuff, if you take my meaning, although this is just a personal preference.
The greatness that this book often achieves undoubtedly overshadows most of the qualms that one can have about the book, and makes the shortcomings seem forgiveable, but the abrupt ending was a cause of why this book isn't "amazing" And the songs. Don't get me started about the Dreadful Songs.

What Tolkien is doing here reminds me of Borges in the best possible way. That is, fictional scholasticism. But whereas Borges would focus on one scholar per story, Tolkien is an entire humanities department. Fictional history, politics, culture, poetry, song, geography, lineage, and more are fully realized. It's very easy to believe in a world that has its own Dante or Homer. The existence of the world pours out from every page and it's fairly impressive. That should be enough but this is an adventure novel and he's not as competent at nailing that part. This novel doesn't quite have the pace for it. You can marvel looking at the provided map thinking "wow it's a long distance they need to close to this next place they're trying to go" but then it'll be inconsistent whether the actual trip is interesting to read. His prose can vary in quality and that can make or break these sections. He is adept at describing environments, but the dialog tends to fall flat with awkward stiffness. You still have to wonder at the originality of it though. I'm not much of a fantasy reader but the idea that there's a genre based on cloning Lord of the Rings sounds nonsensical to me. It misses the point of the originality of his vision, and you can't just lift the sword and sorcery elements and call it a day. It's not the fantasy elements that makes this what it is and I can only imagine how hollow those works are. In any case it's clear this is deserving of its status despite whatever stumbles and stretches of boredom there can be. Despite inspiring generations of genre fic this still feels like literature to me. Decent recommendation.

The Fellowship of the Ring is told truthfully to how most adventures would happen: slow. Normally, I would get bored out of my mind trying to read a book as slow as The Fellowship of the Ring, but because of its vivid imagery, as well as great rhyming songs and poems, I was always interested, and thinking about what J.R.R. Tolkien was trying to foreshadow. The poems and songs were definitely my favorite part, because some were just lighthearted, as you might hear on a long, difficult journey, some were beautiful, glorifying scenery and characters, making them seem beautiful and mysterious, and some were serious, giving off the impression that something important was trying to be conveyed. Though I personally loved this book, and am even more excited to read the next books in the series, I would only recommend this book to be read by someone with a high attention span, or for it to be listened to on tape instead. Like The Hobbit, however, The Fellowship of the Ring lacked much character development, though it dived much deeper into the workings and reasons behind each and every part of the plot. Few books have peaked my interest as much as The Fellowship of the Ring, and though I have only read the beginning of the Lord of the Rings series, I feel that it has been given too much recognition for being such an amazing tale, and so far it isn’t even in my top ten series, much less my favorite books. Finally, something that I wanted to add was that there is a huge amount of detail and intricacy in some areas that other areas are completely lacking of because Tolkien created the LOTR series to be a place where the elvish language (which has multiple dialects) could exist, which explains a lot about his style.

What really annoyed me was that Tolkien indulges in describing rather unneccessary stuff nobody wants to hear that much about while other by far more interesting events are handled within five sentences. There was for example a scene in the books (left out in the movie) where the Hobbits walk through the woods and are attacked by a barrow wight. The whole incident was covered in a few sentences and I still have no idea what really happened nor what a barrow wight actually is.

In the movie however, this part of the book is covered extremely well. A lot of the walking was left out and many things were altered which I appreciate very much. It gives the movie a faster pace while still keeping all important elements of the story.
Another point I really like about the film are the side plots. In the book you only here about Gandalf's problems once he reaches Rivendell. Meaning that a whole lot of plot (of several characters) is stuffed into that one chapter where everybody tells his story. In the film these events are shown when the actually happen. For me it is a lot more interesting this way.

Another sub-plot that was shown in the movie (but did not exist in the book) is the love story between Aragorn and Arwen. Although I am not a fan of unnecessary love stories being thrown in somewhere to attract a wider audience, here it was done very well and blends in perfectly with the rest of the story. As I felt like the whole book could use a bit of sub-plots, this was a very welcome sight in the movie.
This is of course also true for the side plot where Saruman is shown doing work for Sauron. For me this really helped to get more into the story and to understand what is going on in Mordor and what their goal is while this was basically not mentioned in the book.

I'm not sure whether I got used to Tolkien's way of telling things or the book really got better, but after the council in Rivendell it is far more enjoyable to read. The movie however, doesn't let you down either. All the incidents along the way are covered pretty well in the movie. The only time I was a little disappointed was when the fellowship reached the woods of Lothlórien. I had pictured it to look more magical, but all of this was forgotten once they came to Caras Galadhon. This was more wonderful than I ever could have imagined. Very well done Peter Jackson+Team!

The only thing the film lacks are certain bits of history that would have made places like Moria even more impressive. I am aware that it had to be cut out in order to prevent the movie from being five hours long, but in the film pretty much no info was given about certain stuff.

The Lord of the Rings is the typical saga of fantastic books that you have on your bookshelf for many years but you've never dared to read them due to lack of time, or laziness, or because you are not interested in the subject, or because you don't feel like it, simply. In my case, a little of everything. The movies are my favourites of all time, but the books have never caught my attention so far until now... It took me months to finish the first book.

So, we open the first page and see a small text about how the rings were distributed. I think that from there, Tolkien caught my attention and I kept reading. There are notable differences regarding the movie and sometimes I can understand why, but other times I was wondering how certain parts of the book don't appear in the movies or change completely although I am here to comment on the book, not the movies, of course.

I won't deny that the prologue of the Hobbits was impossible to read. With every word I was looking forward to the end and the real action that made its presence act quite late, by the way. There are passages in the book that are tedious and difficult to read. In spite of this, I don't mean that Tolkien is an author who wrote books that can make even the smallest being on earth fall asleep; there were just some moments from the book that bored me and I didn't feel like reading them. Another thing that was difficult to assimilate were the random names of all characters and places, giving little information about them - I don't know if I had to read another book before or I simpy don't understand what happens, but the author gives names randomly as if I had to know them already (the characters do, obviously).

I also have to admit that I skipped all the poems and songs because I couldn't find the rhythm and I felt like a robot reading. It is an unimportant fact but I had to say it.

There are better parts in the film than in the book, in my opinion, as it can be: the Council of Elrond, Hobbiton and Moria. Instead, there were other parts in the book that amused me more and that have given me more emotions and made my imagination fly more easily, such as the Lothlórien Forest chapters.

All in all, my note for The Fellowship of the Ring is a remarkable one. There are two parts (at least in the edition of my book): first and second part. The first is slower and more boring than the second one but that doesn't mean that it isn't of interest because it tells many additional things about Hobbiton and there are many more details of Bilbo's escape and the preparation of Frodo and the ring's long trip.

If you want to start in fantastic literature, The Fellowship of the Ring is a book that I highly recommend despite my criticisms, since Tolkien is one of the parents of fantastic literature and who better than him to teach you the magnificent Middle-earth and the fantasy world in general.

Tolkien begins this classic trilogy by effectively bridging the related work, THE HOBBIT, and moving the story into new and exciting adventures. Bilbo Baggins is celebrating his eleventy-first birthday, coincidentally also the 33rd of distant cousin Frodo. When Bilbo agrees to leave his ring of invisibility to Frodo, Gandalf the Grey, wizard and chief counsel of all that should be done, discusses with the younger Baggins the importance of keeping its possession a secret. Frodo and his trusty helper, Sam, leave their home and trek out through Middle-Earth, careful to guard their ring and keep it out of the hands of those with evil aspirations. After a close-call attack, Frodo awakens with Gandalf at his side and many more surprises to be unveiled. At a meeting of the Council of Elrond, led by the elfin leadership, discussion of Frodo's ring and its origin takes up a great deal of time. Sauron, the Dark Lord, has succeeded in gathered all the Rings of Power, save one. The One Ring, being that which Frodo possesses remains out of his grasp and keeps him from ultimate power. Agreeing to trek across Middle-Earth to destroy the ring before Sauron can obtain it, Frodo and a small collection of fellow hobbits, men, and dwarves begin the long and daunting journey. Meeting friend and foe alike as they commence their journey, the small fellowship run into trouble and comic happenstance along the way. From a willow tree that takes no prisoners to a pack of wolves, and even the Black Riders who seek to intercept the ring, Frodo faces adversity at every turn. Tolkien pulls readers in from the get-go and takes them on a long and winding trip through Middle-Earth, sure to dazzle all who have the patience for the journey, which is nowhere near complete by the end of this book.

Tolkien creates imagery that cannot be discounted by any reader. However, this attention to detail can bog the casual reader down, with its nuances and specificity. I admit to listening repeatedly to certain sections to retrieve their full meaning, paying special attention to ensure I understood the themes presented. I am neither a science-fiction nor a fantasy reader with any regularity, making this read an additional challenge for me. Tolkien has not only a way with words, but with the language of the fantasy genre. His creation of words, worlds, and characters of all shapes and sizes makes for a read like nothing I have encountered before, even in George RR Martin's classic series. I struggled and stumbled, but this should not be seen as a problem with the story, but simply its reader. I shall prevail, though my pace may leave even Frodo waving his hand to encourage continued momentum.

Kudos, Mr. Tolkien for this entertaining and masterful piece of work. And so we trek onwards on this journey.

Technically a 3.5 stars, and I’ll get into why.

Everyone knows that the Lord of the Rings is good. A strong argument could be made that they are the most influential fantasy books of all time. I love all things Middle Earth. If I was rating these books purely on my enjoyment, they would all get 5 stars.

Despite this, there is one thing these books lack, and that is women. To say these books fail the Bechdel test is an understatement. Sure, this might make me sound like a bitter feminist, but I just prefer to read novels with at least some women in them. There are loads of other great classic novels from this era and earlier that have great female characters, so that’s no excuse.

Therefore, I have developed a new rating system for these books. For each named female character that appears on the page, it gets half a star (historical/mythological figures and legends don’t count). If they have at least one word of dialogue, it gets another half a star.

In the Fellowship of the ring, 4 women appear on the page: Lobelia Sackville-Baggins, Goldberry, daughter of the river, Arwen and Lady Galadriel, for a total of two stars. Arwen has no lines of dialogue, so an additional 1.5 stars for a total of 3.5 stars.

The second half was better than the first, so the trend was improving. I think I'll actually read Two Towers at some point in the future.

This book is one for those who love tales of adventure, mystery, and suspense. J.R.R. Overall this was a good book but it, like all the others, had flaws.

Though the book was good it moved to fast in the beginning. For those who read this book before The Hobbit, you will agree that readers did not get a good enough look into Bilbo Baggins. After one chapter of being introduced to Bilbo Baggins, he leaves without much explanation and leaving readers wondering much about Bilbo. Bilbo should have been given a deeper look into before he left in the beginning.

I love action but after Bilbo left to much happened too quickly. Many years passed in a matter of two chapters without explanation then a not so long and perilous journey took up the remaining chapters. Along the way Frodo and his fellowship are attacked by wraiths and a malevolent willow tree, nearly get trapped in a ghost tomb, accidentally expose the ring, nearly get killed in the inn they were staying in, again face the wraiths, Frodo nearly gets killed when someone tries to take the ring, then Frodo and Sam leave the group and head for Mordor just in time for the book to end.

The book-to-movie adaption was decent,but as always there were flaws to create a more film-like feeling. In the beginning of the book Bilbo uses the ring to disappear, but Gandalf adds some special effects to hide Bilbo's use of the ring; but the movie depicts Bilbo just disappearing inexplicably. Another simple and unneeded change was that the sword of Narsil was broken into two pieces in the book versus six pieces in the movie. The movie also cut out some chapters, but it obviously did not effect the story line much

The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring was an okay book with flaws that could be pardoned by some people. These flaws include the lack of much needed description of beloved character Bilbo Baggins and the uneven passing of time in this book. Now imagine if this book was just a little longer because it was more descriptive and spent more time on each event.

It took until about halfway for this book to get going, at least for me. And throughout, given my ADD, I have trouble with the great detail with which Tolkien tells the tale. All the intricate history that Tolkien conjures up is too much for me to process and I find myself just wanting to know what happens next and not every little fact about geography and lore. I don't mean to sound unappreciative of his creative intellect, but it's just not something I have enough mental RAM to handle (it feels much like I'm going to be quizzed on this stuff later, rather than as a cheery side-note to the main plot). The only other complaint, if you could call it that, that I would make is that the climax points are far too brief. We get page after page devoted to describing our main characters walking through various lands and setting up camp, and staying watch, and waking up and setting off again, etc. But when the action finally starts to get good, we usually get only a few pages before things settle down again. All that being said, when the book is good I enjoy it thoroughly. I must say, that I may not have enjoyed this book without first having watched the movies. There are many names and places to remember and keep in mind, and having seen the movies helps me to envision these better. It was interesting, though, to read the book, having first seen the movie(s). And as I read the book, I would pause and watch the movie up until that point in the book. This experience has given me less respect for the movies, though, at least insofar as Peter Jackson (or whoever has most to do with the adaptation) made changes that seemed unnecessary (e.g. who said what -- which in some cases is crucial to a particular characters' development). In fact, the movie was so much different from the book so frequently that it bothered me greatly and I found myself sighing and getting uncomfortable when certain parts in the movie were drawn out way longer than in the books, or when minute details were sufficiently different (or simply omitted) to the point of distorting the flow and feel of the story. This is the very same feeling I got while watching the first part of the new Hobbit film, and why I vowed not to watch the other two installments. But that's a different can of worms. It may be that my being upset with Jackson for changing things having to do with the Hobbit was based on ignorance, because this now seems to be nothing new for him in his involvement with these books (at least if the differences between the books and movies holds for the other two volumes). In any case, I'm hoping that, like the latter two films, the next two books are better than the first. The story having been established, I hope it reads much quicker as the many details are kept to a minimum from here on out.

Why did I award 3 stars to the first part of Tolkien´s famous trilogy?

I found The Lord of the Rings a bit ponderous and long-winded. I started reading it in university in the early 70s and read all of book one and a third of book two and then got bored with it and put it aside. A year or two later I tried it again. Again I read all of book one and got to about the same point in book two when it got boring and I put it aside. Never did read all three books. The movies were a bit ponderous too.

So...I actually put a lot of thought into this review. I really, really wanted to like this book, but...Oh, yes, here comes that major but...Tolkien is not that great of a writer. He spends way too much time focusing on trivial things that really don't add anything to the plot. All the songs and poems were not necessary. In fact, they just dragged the story out that much longer. He also seemed to leave a lot of stuff out. I was ready to read a battle scene at the end of Book 1, but got nothing. However, we can focus on every little detail of every character. Also, he uses "said" for every little bit of dialogue. Find another word! Seriously! Said! Said! It's really annoying! Make it stop!
Okay, let's talk about how important this book is. Without Tolkien, we probably would not have the great fantasy works of today. Harry Potter, His Dark Materials, and A Song of Ice and Fire would probably not exist. So, points for that!
I actually did like the universe of this book. Very creative and engaging, but, again, the writing was not that great. If you are to ignore all the "saids," the dialogue is very well done. I actually like stories with a lot of dialogue. Still more points for Tolkien!
I am always jealous of writers who can come up with very original worlds. I can never do it and I always admire writers who can. It takes a lot of creativity and guts to be the first to do something. You simply don't know how people are going to respond to it. It really did pay off for Tolkien and many others!
There was no action!!!! Why!!! What?!?!?!? How in the world can high fantasy be lacking so much in action. Oh yeah, Tolkien does plenty of telling us about the action, but no showing. Details are necessary, but it was just too much for me.
Again, the writing...Yeah, the writing is what kills this book for me. I really, really wanted to like this book, but it was just there. Just there and nothing more. I have not watched the movies, but this book did not make me want to go out and see them. It just did not do it.
Did I hate this book? No! Did I love it? No! Why did I read it? Because Tolkien is the fore founder of this genre and how could I not?! Overall, not bad, but not good either. It was just okay.

Seen as the definitive fantasy novel by many-a-reader, I myself have a love/hate relationship with LOTR.

I bought this book a while ago with the intention to get round to reading it at some point, and when it popped up on my second-year university reading list I was more than happy to give it some priority on my TBR pile.

Firstly I want to start off by saying how much I admire Tolkien's ability to describe. Whether a book is hit-or-miss for me depends entirely upon an author's skill with description, and Tolkien excels in that area. The way he conjures up the image of Middle Earth is just beautiful and he creates such a strong image of the world, a must for any fantasy novel. However, the description, I feel, is also this book's downfall. There's just waaaaaaaaaaay too much of it. I understand that as a fantasy/adventure it is imperative that there's a lot of description of the world and what's happening, otherwise you're just not going to have the foggiest what's going on, but honestly, I feel that it really dragged the book out and got a little boring in some stages. It was pretty slow-paced.

The best parts of the book was the action, 100%. I absolutely LOVED the chapter where the Company enter Moria and meet the Orc's for the first time, it made all the description worthwhile, but that's pretty much the only action-packed portion that the novel has to offer.



In terms of liking characters, I'm half and half. Aragorn and Sam are absolute BABES, and I also loved Bill the Pony (he's cute dammit). Apart from the fact I'm pretty Hobbit-sized myself, it's hard to identify or connect with anyone, but most of the main characters are very likeable.

I've heard that the films are really different from the books, but with most fantasy I find it really helps to watch a film/tv show alongside reading to help create faces/places in your mind. I'm sure the songs are omitted from the films which is a shame as these were a brilliant part of the book and so cleverly put together. I definitely think I will give the films a go, and possibly re-read the book afterwards at some point in the future to see if I enjoy it any more. I'll probably commit the ultimate readers sin and prefer the film as it's bound to be more fast-paced and action-filled than the novel. (and HELLOOOOO sean bean/viggo mortensen/orlando bloom)

I will definitely also aim to read The Two Towers and The Return of the King because of the ending of the first book *insert frowny face*

As a little parting note, here's my favourite song from the first book:

I sit beside the fire and think
of all that I have seen,
of meadow-flowers and butterflies
in summers that have been;

Of yellow leaves and gossamer
in autumns that there were,
with morning mist and silver sun
and wind upon my hair.

I sit beside the fire and think
of how the world will be
when winter comes without a spring
that I shall ever see.

For still there are so many things
that I have never seen:
in every wood and every spring
there is adifferent green.

I sit beside the fire and think
of people long ago,
and people who will see a world
that I shall never know.

But all the while I sit and think
of times there were before,
I listen for returning feet
and voices at the door.

This is the first time that I have re-read the LOTR trilogy since the moives were released nearly 20 years ago. I thought it would be interesting to see how the well the books have aged. Fellowship has always been the weakest of the three books for me. This go around was no differnet. There are good and weak points to this novel.

I will start with the things that I liked. The first is that this is a very rich story. Of course, this is part of it's downfall too. There is a lot of history that only a Lord of the Rings scholar would be interested in or would be able to follow. The lore of the ring is one thing. But every character's history is handed down to the reader. Is it rich? Yes. Is it very hard to follow? Well, if you don't want to take notes, yes.

Along these lines, one of the biggest complaints I see from people is that Tolkein should have handed this story to someone else to write, and I can see that perspective. There are a lot of flowery yet empty descriptions. But for me that wasn't too much of a turnoff. In mentally building a scene, I like to have it painted before me. Still, there were times when I was edgy to get the narrative moving. There were other times when I was downright bored by the lack of action.

Bringing that thought around again, however, it leads me to proclaim that this narrative is more believable in that fashion. Classic fantasy books have balls to the wall action from cover to cover. This is not the case here. As such, this is more believable as a story that does really exist somewhere and Tolkein merely related that story to our world.

The action is not overly sensational. Nothing is "over" anything. Of course, this is what makes people like it less.

The ending of the book is dreadfully slow. This is something that I take issue with. Someone else mentioned that there is no character development, and I think this is true. But I also think it's true that there doesn't need to be character development in what equates to a journey of a ring with a various number of escorts. The "character development" is essentially what you learn about the ring and the powers that exist to get it.

One thing I particularly do not like is the excessive songs and poems. I think they add little to the story and only serve to derail the reader who genuinely wants to see the story develop, not take another detour into history or a different tangent altogether. I wouldn't mind songs entirely, I don't think. But some are 3 pages long and read very dry.

OK, so those are my complaints, which started out as what was supposed to be a positive. Well, the positives are that the book is very enjoyable if you don't want a big strong lead character to destroy every foe in his wake. You likely will not sit down and get back up again when you're done. The book doesn't read that fluidly from cover to cover. Some things take digesting.

I would recommend this book for just about anyone. Of course, you should read the Hobbit first, as it is the prequel to this series. The Hobbit is a bit more enjoyable than the first read but a tad younger in its target audience, I believe. This first part of the Lord of the Rings is a solid first step, but moves a bit more slowly and contains a fair amount of info not needed to really get at the unfolding narrative in front of you.

I liked the ending, the breaking of the fellowship was was caused by the ring effecting the other members. I don't think Frodo and Sam will do too well on their own though... Its a pity they couldn't bring anyone else with them.
I'll have a break before reading the sequel.

I started writing this review a little late, so I'm already about halfway through the novel. Although the beginning was a bit slow and I had to work a little to get through it, it quickly picked up pace. Because of the movies, I was expecting things to happen a little faster I suppose, so that's my own bias clouding the beginning of the book.

He is full of mystery and very enigmatic and his relationship with Goldberry is something to wonder at but they seem such a wonderful couple. What truly draws you in is how they live so simply and yet you know that they are full of power and knowledge. It is a fascinating and well constructed juxtaposition.

It is also fascinating how much detail Tolkien put into his world. He knew every twist and turn and town and road and forest. It takes a strong mind to create something so vivid and I applaud him.

My only complaint thus far is Frodo. He seems to be a lacking a certain sense of personality. While he is described as wise and brave, there have been few instances which prove these qualities or any others. Perhaps my expectations for him as the protagonist as too high, but I hope to see him develop quite a bit more as the novel goes on.

Update: 7/11/2016 FINISHED!

I love the feeling of accomplishment that comes with finishing a book, particularly a large and somewhat difficult book. Add to that the fact that I've been putting it off for some time and the satisfaction only increases.

Side by side with those feelings are as always the question of what next and the feeling almost of emptiness as something that has taken up so much thought and time has now ended.

Naturally it's all answered by picking up a new book tomorrow and that's exactly what I plan to do. But out of respect for the finished novel, I never start a book on the same day that I finish the previous one.

Instead, I take the remainder of the day to let it settle on my mind, and I lay here, for the first time, my thoughts and revelations.

As out of practice as I am I made a huge mistake going into this book: I compared it all the time to the movie. Having watched the movies before I read the books, mistake #1, it's only natural to have those images and characters in my mind. When one starts comparing the book to the movie and judging it based on those comparisons is when the problem starts. Too late I realized that this is exactly what I was doing.

Since this is my primary focus, let me just get it out of the way and then maybe I will be better able to take the book for what it was, on its own.


The company did not all intend to go with Frodo to Mordor as they seemed to in the movie. Instead, each intended to go along with Frodo only for as long as his path followed the same road. All along Frodo knew, on some level, that he had to go on to the end alone. Which strengthens his character, which I'll come back to.

Aragorn and Arwen are not explored at all except for one or two brief mentions and then only an allusion to a relationship unknown to us. I had expected, again at my own fault, that the books would delve deeper into.

An actual difference that I enjoyed. Tolkien is so detailed in his writing that it covers so much where the movie failed. Not only did it open my eyes to truly how far and how long they traveled but it also provided a deeper understanding of the world that he tried so hard to build. The feel of the land so to speak. The relationships between borders and species as well, it all becomes so real, it feels natural as if you had known about these rivalries all your life and it just fit together as it always had.

Galadriel has a Lord. She is always represented as an immensely strong and powerful she-elf and above all the rest. Although the book made less mention of the Lord than of her, I would've liked it better had her independence and superiority been made clear.


Let's move on.

These thoughts aside, the book follows in Tolkien's form, just as The Hobbit did. I had the same issue when I read that book as I do now. It is all description, the characters moving from here to there and running here and fighting or hiding there. The characters are less developed than I would like, and there is little life, for lack of a better word, in the novel. There are not very revealed relationships. It is a history more than it is a novel, a story. Without the amazing tale that it is, I think that type of writing, clever and sophisticated as it is, would have no appeal to me. I would not like to say that it is boring, not in the slightest, it just doesn't have enough humanity. Enough character.

Which is a strange thing to think is important to me, not being a fan of these things in my own life and experiences. But I suppose that's why we turn to books, isn't it? To find things that we don't in our lives, and live through someone else's eyes for a while, to see what a different life might be like, leaving it behind or taking a piece with us when we finish.

At least there's two more books for me to worry about first ;)

The reason this got three stars is because well...it was slow.

I mean I loved...LOVED...The Hobbit but this one was a lot slower. There was so much build up, especially in book one. But I think that Frodo was a great character! He was just such a lovable character and I also loved the fact that Bilbo Baggins was also in this, even though it was for a little bit. Bilbo holds a special place in my heart.
