So this is going to be one instance that I like the movie better. Simply because the pace is faster and there's less singing. Still the story is fantastic, and Tolkien creates a beautiful and slightly terrifying world with wonderful characters, who interact beautifully with each other and the world around them. This classic tale of good versus evil might start slow,, but once they make it to the mines the story picks up speed, okay kind of still slow, but less slow than the first one hundred pages.

I'm torn. I don't know how to rate this book because I both liked and disliked it, and I wanted to love it.

The plot and world-building are phenomenal, as are the characters, but the descriptions can get a little out of hand and make parts of the story feel unnecessarily long-winded. In other words, the story is great, but the narrative is rather lackluster and dry. I found myself skimming through several more intimidating passages, mostly in the first half of the book. There's a whole lot of travelling there that can become slightly repetitive and too slow-paced for a supposedly action-focused story. It simply wasn't as engaging as I thought it'd be.

I don't like juxtaposing books to their movie adaptions, but in this particular case it's hard to avoid drawing comparisons between the two. In my opinion, the movie succeeds in capturing the plot's most essential elements and presenting them in a very gripping manner, without bringing out the more uneventful chunks of this first installment that made it frustrating to get through.

Of course we know that a lot of material was left out of the Peter Jackson movies.
That is what makes these books worth reading: there is more to discover.
A little too much, actually.

Each of the three Lord of the Rings books are actually divided into two "Books" which gives the overall story a bit of a split personality.

Book I begins with Bilbo's party and ends right before Frodo arrives at Rivendell.
What is surprising is about 90% of this portion of the book is nowhere to be found in the movies.
This is anything but a prose version of the movie.
What you get instead is an adventure full of subplots that the movie doesn't even hint at.
Most of it is fun to read and it recalls the fairy-tale-adventure feeling that Tolkien did in The Hobbit.

But the momentum hits a wall in Book II.

At the beginning of Book II you are greeted by the Council of Elrond which makes the movie version look like a quick chat.
It goes on and on and on and on.
And it is here where Tolkien introduces the issue that he is most criticized for: dense history.
Names upon names upon names are dropped giving a strong sense of a solid history...that you have no clue about.
To the average reader, this is difficult to get through. You simply have no idea what they are talking about.
That would normally be fine. Backstory is not as important as the main narrative. But the main narrative drowns in this stuff.

Also adding the lackluster second half is that about 99% of it makes it into the movie. So the familiarity may encourage some skimming and scanning.

What I like most about reading The Fellowship of the Ring is the little subtle differences that work better in novel form than film.
Boromir's betrayal and the hints leading up to it are slightly different. The idea of Gandalf being the leader and his death leaving them uncertain as to how to continue. Most importantly is Frodo's reason for leaving the Fellowship. His thought process is more specific than the more feel-good message at the end of the movie.

All of this definitely makes for a more fully developed legend, but not a seamless one.

I enjoyed it, but the pace was a little slow for this 21st century millennial. The book just kept...happening, but very little contributed to the plot. Also occasionally felt a little lost among all of the places that were named.
Shire, Rivendell, Moria, Lorien... and the journey continues.. Frodo and Sam made me smile.. No wonder the movies depictd them as friends, I too would have preferred that..
I honestly loved the plot line and the story itself. I'm really excited to see how the story porgesses, but I felt like there were to many details and I was bored a lot of the time.

I think one should review The Lord of the Rings as a whole, that is, a single book, the way Tolkien wrote it, and not in three different parts, because The Fellowship of the Ring is... not that good?
Sacrilegious to say to modern fantasy fans, but I think a majority of (new) people who love LotR do it because they watched the movies and not because they read the books, so they assume they are the same thing, THEY ARE NOT EVEN CLOSE. Because the latter is quite dissapointing if you come from the big screen adaptation (also I read it in spanish, which means Tolkien's essence is lost, so I only got the story part of the book, and not the whole package, a concept that is shared by Cortazar about translated works).
Many of the memorable scenes that give great characterization to the Fellowship are NOT there, like Boromir teaching the hobbits to fight, Legolas and Gimli accepting to help Frodo (and my axe!), or their constant bickering (they become instant best friends after visiting Galadriel, and I get why they do, but it's still much more boring that what happens in the movie), Aragorn is far too righteous, Arwen... is not really a character, like at all, and Boromir is just an ass, and guess what happens to him? I think the hobbits are great, and that's probably because Tolkien envisioned them as actual people, and not just high concepts of kings and warriors. Gandalf is also pretty good, the grey that is, but the other one doesn't appear here yet.

Far too dull, unromantic, far too much meandering, too preachy, and way too much flexing at his own lore, Tolkien is similar to those authors who spend pages upon pages telling you about how much research they did for the book, except he does it by telling you tidbits of past events that he made up, like wars or elven kings and queens, or namedropping a million different places that aren't relevant more than to make the world seem more expansive, sure, if you read the Silmarillion you may pop-off when recognizing things mentioned in this story, but other than that it really doesn't add anything, and it's not like I want the story to be 100% efficiency, I love lore and random stories, but he does it WAY too often, just like he feels the need to add a song (or a couple) in pretty much every single chapter, it just makes the whole thing bloated.
Also Tolkien was, as he said himself, "a meticulous sort of bloke" so he spends several dozen paragraphs describing the road, how it turns into x form, if it crosses a river, or a hill, if there was stones here and there and so on, so more than half of every chapter is spent describing the road, and the other moving the plot forward, sometimes not even that. I found it particularly funny how even one of Tolkien' self-proclaimed 'scholars' said that the 'Council of Eldrond' (the longest chapter in the story and in this book) is dull, he said "nothing happens in it" (but of course then he proceeded to praise it, because I don't think you call yourself a scholar of an author if you didn't enjoy them). There's also the likes of Jorge Luis Borges finding the story tedious, but Borges was a grumpy guy, so you shouldn't mirror the opinion of someone just because you respect their intellect, form your own opinions.

I still love LotR as a story overall, but I doubt it would be as highly praised if it came out today as a first book (just talking about the Fellowship)—takes way too long to start, takes way too long to get anywhere, 90% of the chapters end with the characters going to sleep and waking up in the next. And you can't accuse those that criticize it as 'not getting it', it's precisely because we 'get it' that we complain about it. Anyway, this is only a third of the story, so I'll be reading the rest next.
"But a book like this couldn't come up today, because Tolkien invented modern fantasy!", did he though? Having read the likes of Dunsany or Eddison, I find extremely hard to see anything particularly inovative in this work, it's not the first depiction of self-made languages, nor of modern elves, dwarves, magic artifacts, not even of epic fantasy. He doesn't even prioritize characterization over plot like modern authors do, as except for the hobbits every character is more of an arturian depiction of a man rather than an exploration of human psychology, so what did Tolkien invent really?
As much as I enjoyed some parts of this, reading it felt more like work than enjoyment. I may read the next book in the series, but it will likely be a bit before I do so.

I gave this three stars 1. because I really do appreciate Tolkien's ability to create this world, and 2. because I always feel bad giving books low ratings on here. I don't know; I guess I'm an optimist about books. But as for the story itself, if we're not including the fascinating Middle Earth deal, I'd give it a 2 or 2.5 stars tops. There were parts of this books that I think are five star material, if you will, but they were few and far between. The exciting parts were great... this book generally just lacks action. There was a whole lot of history I had no context of and WALKING. Like 75 percent of this book was the fellowship walking- and with very little dialogue and very few super entertaining character personalities if I'm being honest. As for the history part, I tried to explain this to people I know who have read both this series and the Asoiaf series like so- Asoiaf has a shit ton of history added to it as well..... however, I think it was integrated much better. For one, you have a context of the world (via houses, backstories, knowing who is related to who, etc.). With Lord of the Rings, I feel like unless you studied the Appendix (not sure if the Fellowship book by itself has that, but I rented the book that has ALL THREE PARTS IN ONE BOOK SO IT'S LIKE 1000 PAGES PLUS A LONG ASS APPENDIX) you would be lost. Maybe reading the hobbit first would have helped, but I tried reading that twice and got like a third of the way through and got very little backstory, so I can't imagine there was a ton. And as for the characters, don't get me wrong- I did like a bunch of them. BUT, I few like very few had personalities. Merry and Pippin were like the same person, and mostly ignored. Frodo is cool, but not super duper entertaining. I loved Aragorn, Gandolf, and Gimli- Boromir was fairly well developed as well. And the elves were cool as shit. But throughout the story, I found it hard reading this plot line of them just walking when the characters were failing to amuse me as well.

I don't know, man. I feel like I'm breaking the rules by saying this isn't the greatest series ever, because everyone who reads it seems to think so. It's not that I hated it either... I've seen some before and remember liking them, but I was pretty young. I so wanted to say this book was amazing, but A+ for Middle Earth and just meh for the overall storytelling.

I wanted to like this more than I did, but the freaking constant bursting into song just got on my nerves, and I guess I'm realizing more and more that I much prefer interesting dialogue and action to detailed descriptions. The story is obviously awesome and shaped modern fantasy, but book II just ended up being too long-winded for my taste. I'm obviously going to read the other books, though.

I decided to read LoTR again because I had the suspicion that now I've read a lot more old books, I wouldn't find Tolkien's writing style so dry and difficult to read. I'm happy to say that I was right, and enjoyed FoTR a lot more the second time around. In fact, I found it very readable. Part of this may be due to reading it at my own pace, whereas last time I read it for a read-along, so I was meant to read only a few chapters each week. Interestingly, the first time I found the songs a welcome break from Tolkien's narrative style, but this time I found the songs annoying as they interrupted the flow of the story.

I still have a few of the same problems with FoTR as in my first read, though. As everyone will agree, there aren't enough female characters, which is frankly just strange and inexplicable. I wouldn't expect a man in the 1950s to make half his characters women, but I would expect more than the few that appear very briefly, especially given the large cast of characters in total. There don't seem to be any mothers in Middle-earth either, as they're all dead.

I also take issue with the structure, as a lot of what happens is retold to us by the characters instead of us seeing these events happen, and there also isn't an obvious climax to FoTR. Perhaps this is because Tolkien intended LoTR to be one long novel, not three.

I'm leaving my rating at three stars, even though I liked FoTR more the second time, because I should've really given two stars the first time and was just being nice. I've gone from not really liking it to liking it quite a bit. Now I wonder if and when I'll reread The Two Towers.

the movies are significantly more dynamic than this book is, which is mostly remarkable because it is effectively an academic linguist's attempt at constructing a world that highlights the particular traits of his research ability. there isn't much of a story here, in other words, nor are there fully fleshed out characters - instead, what there is is the creation of cultures, languages, and background setting to a staggering degree. in terms of world development this is unparalleled, but it doesn't necessarily translate into the most gripping of narratives - the fact that tolkien devised three separate languages for the purposes of setting out the history of a world that there isn't really space to get into (and that these languages then also have era-dependent dialects which he seems to all know fully as well!) makes this less of a novel and more of an exercise in the appreciation of the variety, flexibility and force of language. the peter jackson movies in many ways distill a wealth of ideas into an actually engaging narrative that creates personal character-driven stories, whereas what this is a mere peek into the formidable imagination of a single man, condensed into print-length.

i'll also say that there was significantly less singing and "stop it's time for a hobbit meal" in this than i had in mind from my discontinued attempt to read this a decade ago, but nonetheless i spent about half the time reading it flipping over to the maps included at the back of the book to try to figure out where in the hell we are, only to realize we haven't really moved past the area we were in 50 pages ago but it's called something different in Elvish than it is in Dwarfish or Mannish or the common western tongue (which of course is not the same thing as high elven or the language of mordor or anything they speak out in the west). as i said: the imagination sings in this, but in execution, it's not the most pleasant thing to navigate as a casual read.

I was very excited to begin The Lord of the Rings series by J.R.R. Tolkien after re-reading his companion novel, The Hobbit, back in June. This book, the first in the series proper, revisits old characters (Bilbo, Gandalf, Elrond) and places (The Shire, Rivendell), while introducing the reader to new people and places to fall in love with.

The main character this time around is Frodo Baggins, Bilbo's adopted nephew. When Bilbo tires of the Ring, he entrusts it to Frodo. But when Gandalf arrives with disheartening news, Frodo realizes that the Ring is more a curse than a gift, and sets out to destroy it (clearly easier said than done). His gardener, Sam Gamgee, is too loyal (and too fond of elves Frodo might encounter on his journey) to let him go alone, and cousins Meriadoc "Merry" Brandybuck and Peregrin "Pippin" Took aid in him in the early phases of his journey. But quick into their travels, the four Hobbits are faced with a menacing enemy, a black rider vigilantly seeking out Frodo and his Ring.

Throughout their journey, the Hobbits receive aid and counsel from several interesting characters, including many breeds of elves (such as the powerful half-elf Elrond in Rivendell, the wise and powerful Glorfindel, the wood elf from Mirkwood, Legolas, and the beautiful Celeborn and Galadriel), the mysterious yet chipper Tom Bombadil, the wizard Gandalf, cunning, brave Men (like ranger Strider/Aragorn, and Boromir from the North), tenacious dwarves (like Gloin and his relative, Gimli), and even other Hobbits, like those near the Brandywine and in Bree. After the climactic Council of Elrond, Gandalf, Aragorn, Boromir, Legolas, and Gimli join the Hobbits on their quest.

But during their travels, the Fellowship faces much adversity: there's environmental factors, like the foggy Barrow-Downs and the bitter snow of Caladhras, not to mention ferocious new enemies, like Orcs and a terrifying Balrog in Moria, as well as the decietful, nimble Gollum, who stalks from the shadows. Also, there is the grave news that concerns powerful Saruman the White.

Overall, The Fellowship of the Ring was a good start to the series. It definitely has "First Novel Syndrome", as in, "this is the first book in the series so there's a few information dumps and lots of getting to know people." But there's also poignant moments, where the reader really feels the peril of the Fellowship's journey. Each experiences loss and grief, and questions what it is they're going on the journey for. And by the end, great, sometimes unexpected, friendships are formed. The reader really grows attatched to the characters in a special way, and that encourages me to go on with the series and see what else they go through.

The Fellowship of the Ring is the first book of perhaps the most influential fantasy saga of the 20th century. It shaped literature itself and set new standards, which some still stand nowadays. But, like every book, it has flaws.

Most of the 'bad things' in TFotR are, as far as I know and believe, due to the writing process. The first part of the book is slow and sometimes feels offtopic with the rest of the saga. It seems(and so I've been told) that Tolkien didn't knew how the story would end. And it makes sense. The appearance of characters like Tom Bombadil show that the author wasn't sure which road the story would take. That would also explain the lots of 'nothing' that happen in the first part. The Hobbits in the beginning appear to take forever to get to Bree, that in the map appears to be very close. I do believe that this slow pace is also responsible for the constant comments about Tolkien adding too much details, being wordy. Sincerely, I don't believe that is the case.

The second part is more warm, that is, more things happen. But yet it has other problems: Characters. In the beginning we were following only four characters, but now there are nine. Save Gandalf, that was introduced in The Hobbit, and four hobbits that we knew from the first part, the others are somehow dull and empty. Little effort is made to add true personality to them. At some points it's impossible to say who is talking until the author reveals that information for you.

Also, the book feels a lot like 'passing on the baton'. In the Hobbit we had Bilbo, and now there's Frodo. We had a lot of dwarves, and now we have Gimli, son of Gloin. We had Thranduil and now we have Legolas. We had the 'soon-to-be-king' Thorin and now we have the 'soon-to-be-king' Aragorn. Again, the writing process. Feels like Tolkien was more concerned with writing a close-sequel, and not in telling a different, and more complex story. Which brings me to another topic: The first part, and actually almost the entire book, is more focused in the setting and not in scale of the events. That does change in the second part, but only a little. What is interesting it that this changes completely in the others books. The scale, the wars spreading across Middle-Earth, take a more central role in the story.

But even with all that TFotR is an amazing fantasy story. The lore of Tolkien's Universe is tremendous and few come near writing greater stories. This is just the first book, and I personally avoid looking to deep at the first book of a series. The first book is always a introduction and therefore may be a lot different to the rest. It is important to remember that this book is only a part of a much greater sum, even if it is the smallest part.

The plot seems much too thin; they are on a journey throughout most of the book. The magical qualities of the ring are too ambiguous: it seems more dangerous than good. The reader of this book was very good; and the language was excellent, with tens of interesting names and felicitous prose throughout. I also enjoyed reading it during the darkest weeks of winter, because the story is set in a cold clime and the theme is dark. I may eventually read books 2 and 3, but I'm not willing to do it now. There are too many other books which don't require such a strain on my willingness to suspend disbelief.

Overall, I liked this book, but I didn't love it. Given it's popularity, I was expecting more.

The story was interesting, but the writing was too flowery (to the point that whole passages lacked real content) and the pacing was too slow for my taste. I found myself skimming over paragraphs and skipping all of the songs. I liked the character Sam the most, though I felt that the other characters were lacking depth. Most of the characters didn't feel like fully fleshed out, well-rounded characters, but more like stereotypes of their races. The world of Middle Earth had great scope and sounded really interesting, but was not explored in as much depth as I would have liked. Also, the different races and their histories weren't well explained, given how important they were to the story.

Maybe my expectations were too high. I also haven't read The Hobbit, and I have managed to avoid seeing the films; maybe that is why it took me so long to understand the world that was being presented in this book. Things felt slow and repetitive until the ring got to Rivendell. The second half of the book was tremendously better. Again, maybe that's just because I had adjusted to the language, and had a clearer sense of the geography and history of Middle Earth. A problem that could have been avoided, I'm sure, had I started with The Hobbit. I understand the impact this book had on the fantasy genre and greatly appreciate it. I'm excited to read the next one.

The Fellowship of the Ring by J.R.R Tolkien kicks off one of the most prolific fantasy trilogies of all time, The Lord of the Rings, part of the legendary series including the Hobbit and the Silmarillion. Having just finished the hobbit I already understood the culture of the characters, as well as the medieval and mythical setting where fear is ever present in the minds of the weak. Author J.R.R. Tolkien manages to have the Hobbit flow straight into the Lord of the Rings, except for a time lapse of 60 years. The protagonist is still Bilbo at the beginning, back from his journey and now the wealthiest in the shire, the home for the small dwarf-like creatures. It is his birthday, allowing for a natural flow of conversation to recap the missed years of his life. A young hobbit, Frodo Baggins, is introduced as the adopted kin of Bilbo, as well as the new main character for adventures to come
Frodo is given responsibility of taking the all powerful ring that was earlier found by Bilbo. With the assistance of Gandalf, a wizard, he understands that to keep the power away from the evil dark lord Sauron, he must destroy it in the fire of Mordor, an area far away and under enemy control. Sauron and his frightening army of black riders share the role of antagonist with the evil desires for the powerful ring. This is the theme of the story, as the characters each fight off the desire to use the ring for personal gain, and strive for what is best for the world. Originally, Frodo is accompanied by Gandalf and two other weak hobbits, who prove to be enough support through the safe beginning of the journey. After weeks of travel, they reach the council, where the wisest and most worthy make decisions of importance. It is decided that Frodo is to accompanied by 8 others. The fellowship includes Frodo and 3 other hobbits, Gandalf, two men of great importance, a dwarf and a powerful elf. All of these character are round, being thoroughly described. At this point the reader picks up on the worrisome mood of the book.They move along at a slow pace, evident through the 540 page book where little happens, but is described well. It fails to be suspenseful until the last 100 pages, where there are battles and betrayals. One of the men, Boromir (a dynamic character), loses his fight to the desire of the evil ring, almost killing Frodo. Unfortunately, this fate comes to almost all who possess the ring, likely Frodo will not be able to destroy it when the time comes.
There are two more books to share this journey, but I feel the three books would be more interesting if compiled into one shorter version.

Many readers will hate me for this; it is a 'cult' novel, and has a strong fanbase...

When I was a teenager, my friends kept telling me I had to read it, yet I was busy with classics, so, I left it till when I finished my first degree: what a disappointment!

It's nothing more than a piece bien faite. Well written without anything that stands out in terms of style; to be honest, I think it does not have its own style altogether; I cannot hear the personality of a narrator here, but the anonymity of narration for narration's sake.

In terms of content, it's a let-down as well: there is nothing on these pages that is not in ink, nothing that transcends the literal meaning of the words (apart from a vague reference to Nazism, but since the end of WWII, any text dealing with conflict by default refers to Nazism; it is as a foundation stone of modern sensibility as is breathing part of our lives). Dear Talkien disappoints me here, having read his studies in Anglo-Saxon literature, I expected to learn something from this book, yet I walked away without anything at all.

My friends told me that 'Talkien had created a whole mythology.' Here I have to correct their understanding of mythology... It is not talking about fairies and elves or inventing fantastical creatures. Mythos is an Ancient Greek way of explaining the metaphysical (as well as the laws of physis) through narrative and allegory, per se a higher form of communication than logos: Greek Myths are parables of laws of physics, of proper spiritual understanding, Narcissus does not become a flower to entertain the reader, to choose a simple one, he is chosen by the gods to teach humans that egocentrism only leads back onto itself, and has no outlets that may affect the workings of Cosmos: his story is a moral parable. Blake, in 'The First Book of Urizen', 'The Marriage of Heaven and Hell' and other of his greater poems creates 'his own mythology' (if mythology can be seen as belonging to an individual), yet he was uneducated, Oxford mind Talkien does not even consider that; academically, quintessential mediocrity: putting funny names and faces to characters does not constitute mythology.

This sad, it is not a bad read, if you wish to spend time abdicating your role as a thinking being, go ahead.

In my teenage years, I read The Lord of the Rings, and I really loved it. I was 17, it was the first real, adult fantasy I had read, and it was amazing. I came back to it over a decade later, and if I'm honest, I've been left cold.

Tolkien was first; that's the comment made by any reader who holds these books dear to his (or her) heart. It's true, he was, but it also shows the remarkable degree of development that's happened in the fantasy genre in the past sixty or seventy years, and just how dry these novels really are in comparison.

You have to read them in the context of their time; I'm an English student, I know that, it's called historicism, and reading these with the period in which they are written in mind does them no favours either. Tolkien's work is full of social Darwinism; Sam is the common man, but comes across as a border-line learning disabled PG Wodehouse caricature, whereas his 'master', the hobbit with money, is clearly represented with an Oxbridge accent and stifled middle-class sensibilities. It makes for a painful read, and demonstrates Tolkien's inability to deal with the voices of real people (or hobbits.)

It's not all bad, of course. The story is epic in scope and scale, and once you get past the light-hearted and folksie bits in the shire (which are ham-fisted and badly written), and towards the great events around which this epic tale pivots, the whole thing does get better. Moria, Lothlorien, Rivendell: these are creations of fiction that live and breathe, and the great lords and ladies who inhabit them leap off the page. Aragorn, Frodo, Merry, and Pippin are inherently likeable characters. I should like Sam, but I find that I pity him, for the reasons described above.

What Tolkien has done is created a world with history. The myth and legend that the characters aspire to really do give depth to the world, and it makes the whole thing more memorable, with a sense of incredible danger that builds as you, as the reader, really start to feel that Middle Earth is worth fighting for.

Overall, I was a little disappointed and I wish that I'd left this one as a memory. It makes me sad to say it, but it's true.

Oh yes, and one more thing. The mark of a bad author, I was once told in a post-grad English lecture, is the beginning of words, or paragraphs with the word 'suddenly'. It's demonstrative of a lack of creative technique, or ability to build tension in prose. Now, Tolkien was clearly a very imaginative man. I think he just missed that lecture. Next time you read it, you'll see what I mean...

Criticizing LOTR is like criticizing the Beatles: its influence is so pervasive that any negative comments are subsumed in the vast ocean of gushing praise.

For me, reading LOTR was a misery and a chore. For most of the book, I forced myself to keep reading. The dialogue is stilted and effete, and as the story goes on it slows to the pace of frozen molasses.

However, this first volume is the best part of the story. With the exception of the inexplicable Tom Bombadil digression, the first half builds great suspense and comes to a climax at the book's midpoint.

Of course, that means that the second half of the book is an anti-climax, and things get much worse when you get into The Two Towers.

I do like the movies, however. Fundamentally there's a good story here; it's just overwritten and in fact, badly written in places. Tolkien wrote it over a long period of time, with numerous hiatuses, and it shows. Parts of it are well done; parts of it just crawl.

Tolkien has created an amazing fantasy world that allows the reader to escape from everyday nuisances, boredom and routine. Having read The Hobbit in my my early teenager years and having seen all Lord of the Rings movies, I was looking forward to be dragged into Middle Earth once more.

The book started with a rather boring (and wordy) introduction by the author which I felt compulsory to read to refresh my memory about the Middle Earth. It took me about a week to chew myself through it until I could finally start with the book itself.

All in all it is not such a bad book considering the time Tolkien lived and the style of the books at this time. I did enjoy jumping into Middle Earth again and at least the first part of the book was quite smooth for me to read (the everyday life of the hobbits, the start of the journey of the hobbits and of course the part with Tom Bombadil who was my favourite character in the book). Still, I was looking for something more sophisticated, deeper and way more adventurous; even though I didn’t mind the long, uneventful parts where the hobbits where making their way to the first ‘checkpoint’, the Prancing Pony. For me, the book started to fail once the whole company got together as Tolkien didn’t seem to know what exactly is the purpose of all the members of the Fellowship nor how to use them to keep the reader still interested. . . There were several occasions I forgot that there were nine of them on the journey as quite often many of were not mentioned on a whole page or even longer.

The characters seemed extremely superficial, even stupid and arrogant. Feels like Tolkien took the most obvious and simplest characteristics of humans and applied them to different characters in his book, leaving nothing for the reader to discover in them or to dig deeper. The dialogues didn’t make much sense most of the time in the second half of the book and all the emphasis seemed to be on descriptions.

Oeh, these descriptions… They were probably the worst part of the story. Tolkien really loved descriptions and giving his readers proper geography lessons of his (imaginary) world. Even many dialogues (or monologues) were just geography lessons… I understand descriptions are necessary in a book but it seemed Tolkien didn’t have much faith in his reader – most of us who love to read have a great fantasy and the ability to see even the undescribed. The Lord of the Rings books certainly is one of the most imaginative fantasies ever written, but, at least for myself, I can’t say it’s one of the best, or even the best, because it’s not. Indeed, I think it’s actually far from perfect, especially the last part, but I’ll get to that.

The story itself together with the characters is very imaginative, I guess you’d say epic. And the character progress is nicely done, but in my estimation that’s about it. Just that and that thanks of the depth and his imagination. But just these three things never won the war and sadly there’s not more to it, quite the opposite. The worst thing in Tolkien’s books is his writing style. It’s quite terrible to read it sometimes – he can’t express himself properly, the plot is not build and way too serious and that even in parts where they should be “merry-making” and it also looks that it’s never been edited. Each book is far too long; many parts could have been shortened and some left out; the chapters are not thought through – too long and the storylines should’ve been alternated more frequently, because if one fourth of the book is formed by just one storyline and then another big part of the second it’s incredibly boring. And more – take this plus the incredibly long descriptions and parts added just to stretch the story – and the result is even worse. Too bad that he didn’t find someone to help him with the books, because as they’re I really couldn’t enjoy them and surely I’d never recommend them to anyone. I think it’s almost better to skip the books and rather just watch the films.

Oh, I almost forgot back to the characters – Frodo was better than in the films, Sam’s just stupid and irritating, but Merry and Pip were the best, not so stupid as in the films, brave and good guys. The rest was just OK I guess nothing special. Just the female characters were one dimensional; he really couldn’t empathize with them. One last thing there was a huge amount of weeping worse than in a very bad second-rate soap-opera; nothing against sensible souls, but this was annoying.

To summarize it – this is not something I enjoyed and something I’d not read again. Tolkien had a great mind, but was not a great writer.

Akhirnya saya baca juga novel pertama dari trilogi Lord of the Ring ini. Salah satu buku fantasi paling dikenal, tapi yang belum saya baca. Padahal ngakunya pecinta novel fantasi.

Buku pertama ini ternyata merupakan gabungan dari dua "buku". Saya kurang tahu apa dulunya, saat pertama terbit, memang diterbitkan sebagai dua buku atau bagaimana. Buku pertama di sini menceritakan kehidupan Frodo di Shire. Saat dia pertama kali memperoleh cincin itu dari Bilbo, hingga pada awal perjalanannya ditemani 3 orang temannya: Sam, Merry, dan Pippin. Di bagian ini juga ada semacam "rekap" dari novel "The Hobit".

Jujur buat saya bagian pertama ini terasa membosankan. Saya ngantuk banget pas baca. Apalagi di bagian rekap "The Hobbit"-nya. Walau saya belum baca novelnya, tapi ringkasannya bikin ngantuk. Keseluruhan perjalanan awalnya Frodo juga kurang begitu menarik.

Untungnya masuk di bagian dua ceritanya jadi lebih menarik. Terbukti saya hanya butuh 1,5 hari untuk menyelesaikan bagian kedua, padahal saya butuh 4 hari lebih untuk menyelesaikan bagian pertama (walau yah, ada unsur sibuknya juga sih).

Sampai akhir, ceritanya menarik. Saya suka dengan Gandalf. Dia bukan tipikal penyihir tua yang bijak. Terbukti dari sikapnya yang kadang bisa sarkastis (seperti waktu dia bilang akan memakai kepala Pippin untuk membuka gerbang).

Saya yakin buku kedua akan lebih menarik dari buku pertama ini. Pasti konfliknya akan lebih tajam di sana sih. Apa di sana sudah akan ada Gollum yah? (iya, saya belum nonton filmnya juga).

This is the fist volume of the famous Lord of the Rings trilogy. Overall it is a good fantasy epic with a big bad guy, a party of hero's, and a main character that starts off as a nobody but is destined to be the biggest hero of all. This formula has been used for decades in the fantasy genre and it started here with this book and the Hobbit. Middle Earth is an interesting fantasy world, packed with enough to tell a great story but not bogged down by too much going on. The reason I rated it 3 stars was because I am not a fan of how Tolkien writes. I always seem to have a hard time reading this and have to put it down every so often. I have read it many times and I just feel its his writing style and not the story that that did not age well.

Tolkien's first work in his magnum opus and according to many the magnum opus of the fantasy genre is an engrossing tale that is only hampered by Tolkien himself. The first act drags and has no sense of urgency at all. This problem is accentuated by a section containing Tom Bombadil that is nothing more than sheer filler and a good example of why editors are important. The story picks up in the second act in Bree, and this is where the book is enjoyable, as the pacing through Bree, Weathertop, and Moria is flawless. Unfortunately, Tolkien slams on the brakes at several parts of the third act, making one wonder whether or not he wants the reader to have fun reading this book at all. Anytime the novel gets any forward momentum and becomes enjoyable, Tolkien throws some detour in the story, which brings everything to a halt, and the book becomes boring again. I wonder whether or not it was Tolkien himself who originally said, "I had fun once. It was awful."

By itself, the story is a good one, accentuated by massive amounts of lore and backstory Tolkien has built into the world of Middle Earth to make it more believable. Tolkien just needs to stay out of the way of it with unnecessary detours that kill the pacing and make what should be thrilling a rather dull affair.

In the past two weeks I have attempted to read The Lord of the Rings, the Fellowship of the ring. I would say that I was successful in that venture and for that I am extremely proud of myself. When I first picked this book up, I didn’t quite realize what I was getting myself into. These books are extremely complicated and I found it hard to get into the story because I was unable to connect. I really liked all the details that JRR Tolkien put into the story line (I mean he made up an entire world) but since I didn’t know any of the back stories I was just so easily confused by all the details jumbling together in my head.

The style that Tolkien writes in is a beautiful way to write and I greatly admire his ability to have such an imagination and create something so complicated. He also found a way to gather a huge fan base that follow his stories like they are the best thing ever. Maybe if someone sat me down and explained it all in as simple of a way as possible, then I would be able to grasp the story line and really attach to the book. However, I was trying to read this book in a matter of a week and a half, and I barely had the time to watch the movie. So that might have contributed to my problem of not really enjoying the novel. Maybe over the summer I can find an expert and a month of unaccounted for time and try again. Sadly unaccounted for time is not easy to come by…

All the details in this story create something that doesn’t exist anywhere else. For many readers this is the best thing a book can provide. However most of the time, I tend to like books that I can connect to. That way I understand a little bit better, and just out of a moment of laziness, easier for me to read. Even though the details create what seems to be a beautiful story, I just couldn’t grasp on because there were too many for me.

This book is a much larger undertaking than I realized when I first picked it up. I would only suggest this book to people that already have some understanding of the story, or they have someone that can talk to you and explain the complications whenever you need them too. Although I did have people to somewhat explain the story, we just had too much to cover in such a short amount of time that not everything could be fully understood on my part. I did enjoy the basic story and I think I would have liked the details too if I had been better able to understand them.

I certainly appreciate the importance of this book; its influence is so far reaching and the scale of it cannot fail to be impressive. Not only does Tolkien present an entirely new world with its geography mapped out in minute detail, but it is coupled with cultural and historical background, even a carefully crafted new language.

Impressed as I may be by the grandeur of the novels framework and the depth of the authors imagination, I found something lacking its delivery. So many pages were spent describing landscapes and ancient battles, but the characters themselves were barely more than one dimensional. They were lost in the minutiae; we learn little of their psychological states-insights into emotions and thoughts are minimal at best, though their family history is laid out in full. The fellowship marches on, prepared to die along side one another, and yet they don't know their comrades; their conversations amount to little more than bickering about what direction to proceed and what's for dinner.

So whilst I can appreciate how the book continues to be a phenomenon, and how it's consistently considered to be one of those 'best loved books', unfortunately, a painstaking 400 pages later, it hasn't made my list of favorites.

By J. R. R. Tolkien
Chris Reichart’s review
March 31, 2013


What would you do, if you were given a quest to go to the most evil part of the country to destroy an even more evil ring? This is the decision the main character, Frodo, has to make in the book, Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring by J. R. R. Tolkien. Frodo, a hobbit of the shire has to face many challenges as he and three of his other hobbit friends go on a quest to destroy an evil ring. "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Rings" is a fictional work. I would further classify it as fantasy. "The Fellowship of the Rings" is by J.R.R. Tolkein. This is the first book in a series of three. "The Lord of the Rings" is written in third person omniscient. The author's purpose in writing this novel is to entertain the reader. This is evident because of the fictional characters, creatures, settings, and events that were meant to amuse the reader. The author used a writing style of older English. He used a lot of old fashioned words such as "thy" and "arte". The audience for this book could be a child or an adult. I would see the person that is the ideal reader as your stereotypical nerd. The book is told as a narration because it is telling a story through a description of events.
The theme of this book is good versus evil. This is portrayed trough the protagonist, Frodo, trying to destroy the One Ring. The antagonist is Sauron. His goal was to use the One Ring to conquer Middle-earth. Frodo is a Hobbit is a hobbit who is trying to destroy the One Ring. Unfortunately, because this is only the first book of three, the reader does not find out who is successful. The book is told as a narration because it is telling a story through a description of events.
Overall, I thought the novel was very good. I did, however, find it hard to read because of the older writing style. Some of the language was different than some that we use today. This was partially due to the fact that the story was set during the Middle Ages or the equivalent of the Middle Ages. I liked the diversity of characters and creatures. This book is honestly similar to none other that I have read. I don't really read a lot of fantasy book though. I couldn't change anything without ruining the entire concept of the book.

Everybody's been a part of one of those discussions: Books that are better than the movie - or movies that are better than the book. There's certain books / movies that tend to turn up a lot in the latter category: The Shining, The Silence of the Lambs, sometimes old crap like Ben-Hur and Gone With the Wind, stuff that nobody REALLY cares about.

I had one of these discussions recently around a campfire, and I did not mention The Fellowship of the Ring. I was too scared to say that the film was better than the book, even though I definitely think so.

I dislike Tolkien for almost the very same reason I dislike Proust. Whereas Proust deals with the vast minutiae of reality, Tolkien deals with the vast minutiae of a completely made-up world. The funny thing is, I can actually relate to Tolkien's world (which, with its mythical creatures and heroic deeds, is clearly totally absurd and unrealistic) better than I can relate to Proust's agonizing over colors and slight breezes.

My problem, however, is not with Middle Earth. It's those damn DETAILS! It's like Tolkien feared that the main questions his readers will have on their minds while they read his books are things like "Well what was the name of the homeland of that dwarf that he just briefly referenced? And what are the names of the dwarf's kinsmen? And THEIR kinsmen?" or, "He described how that river sounds, smells, feels, tastes, and looks... But what is it thinking about right now?" or, "Remind me for a third time, please: What were the names, locations, and foreign diplomacy histories of all of eleven Hobbit villages?"

The nice thing about a film is that it doesn't have any of this stuff. Oh, don't think that the insufferable nerds who make those things wouldn't put these details in, if they could! Luckily, common decency doesn't allow for that sort of thing. Don't get me wrong: I'm equally in favor of both film and literature. I don't put one above the other. (I realize that, this site being about books, many people here would put literature first; well, those people are dicks.) Anyway, to make a long story short, that's why the film of Fellowship is better than the book.

While Tolkien was busy figuring out the ludicrously intricate histories of every single species in Middle Earth (and not just the anthropomorphs - if there are termites in Middle Earth, I'm sure they'll get their fifteen pages of fame. I haven't read the second or third books yet) - anyway, while Tolkien was busy with this, he forgot to give his characters stuff like emotions, depth, and personality. They HAVE emotions, of course: Tolkien mentions that they do. Why wouldn't they? Everybody has 'em! But Tolkien didn't actually GIVE them those emotions; as in, write about the emotions, and make it seem real. As far as personality goes, Gandalf, Sam, and Frodo's evil relatives are the only characters who seem to have any. The rest are interchangeable. Hobbits don't act differently from other hobbits; elves from other elves. Tom Bombadil might be worth mentioning, if he weren't horrible, and awful, and excruciatingly annoying, and by far the worst character in the book.

Still, the trilogy that Fellowship begins is considered an all-time great for a reason. Its world is compelling for the same reason that the genre it helped create is compelling: We like to read about magic, strange creatures, epic battles, heroes and villains, and other such nonsense. It's escapism. It's not a naughty word; Tolkien even uses it in his introduction.

I don't think my views on Tolkien are unfair. From what little I've read of the fantasy genre, there seems to be a lot of the same fictional histories that irked me so much in Tolkien: descendants; ancient battles; powerful but extinct forces; all that ponderous, meaningless stuff that some people apparently go nuts for. However, not every author forgets to give his story some substance and emotion in the meantime. For that, Tolkien had no excuse; he was just a bad writer.

(Oh yeah, one more thing: The songs. I hate them. I hate them, so, SO much. I think the thing I hate about them the most is that for some reason, I can't just skip them. It would save me SO much time, since about 10% of the book is composed of songs; but I just can't do it. I have this irrational fear of skipping stuff, as if it will ruin the entire book for me, or like I'll be stripped of any right to say that I've "read" it.)

Brief review. I felt slightly bad about the relatively low rating I have given the frontrunner of modern fantasy, but I think it should reflect how much I enjoyed it and was compelled to carry on reading it. I am probably on well trodden ground, but here goes.

Tolkien is not that great a writer. He creates an incredibly complete world with myth and history and a great deal more, and there are legions of Tolkien scholars who have ensured the consistency of the whole thing and noted the precious few places that there is a mistake. I think that Middle-Earth is certainly one of the most complete universes I have come across in fantasy. Unfortunately, what I have seen of it is still not enough. I think the books occupy a strange middle ground between a universe where you can know everything - there is a truly complete history - and ones which are content to leave you wondering. Westeros and Essos, by way of comparison, are certainly less fleshed out than Middle-Earth. Much of the history is not written, but just alluded to; many of the languages really consist of just a few words in comparison to Tolkien's tour de force that is Elvish. Yet in reading, the impression you get is not significantly different. There is still a great deal of unknown surrounding Middle Earth, and filling in the gaps with cryptic references to Valinor and Light, not to mention anythng east of Mordor, is no more satisfactory than ASOIAF's oblique mentions of ancient kings. In both cases the reader feels that there is so much more to be said.

The characters of the Fellowship are often equally bland.

There's a whole thing on heroism I'll talk about once I finish the trilogy, since that was why I started in the first place. In any case, I think this book was impressive in its scope and historical importance, and contains enough that you won't dislike reading it, but I didn't find it exciting by any other means.

I'm a fan of the movies and so I decided to read the book and get the full story as it was originally intended. It was hard - the movies are so ingrained in my head that I struggled to accept the deviations in plot and character development. However, I learned a lot about what I would call the "LOTR theory", meaning that I could better understand character motivation, how and why the actor(s) played things the way they did, and connect the dots between major plot events to create a full historical timeline.

Again, I struggle to see this as an independent literary work because I saw the movies first and know them inside and out. I'm looking at this as a supplement to enhance my LOTR knowledge and fill in some of the gaps that I had after seeing the movies.

This is effectively my review of the entire LoTR trilogy:

While I did enjoy reading the Lord of the Rings, I felt it was bogged down with endless descriptions of landscapes, that godawful unreadable section with Tom Bombadil, and on the whole just too much unnecessary wordiness. It needed some tough love from an Editor, and could have had it's word count slimmed down by about 30% and lost nothing.

And the singing. Good god, ALL THE SINGING.

A word about the magic system: after reading Robert Jordan and Brandon Sanderson, I find the super vague and undefined magic system highly annoying. Why was Aragorn able to go toe-to-toe with Sauron through the seeing stones without losing his mind while Gandalf could not? What do the rings actually do? Why is Sauron so powerful? Why is the One Ring so powerful? What does it ACTUALLY do? What can Gandalf actually do? As far as I can tell all he is is a glorified flashlight. *sigh*

Now that I've made the LoTR superfans mad, let me say that I do believe that LOTR is still a good read, and there is some great character work here. The books are compelling anytime Frodo/Sam/Golam are the focus, not to mention Gandalf who is too old and cranky for your bull$hit, thank-you-very-much. However, this is one of those instances where it's hard to put the genie back in the bottle, and in this case the authors that J.R.R. Tolkien have inspired have taken the genre and made better books out of the ideas he birthed. Kudos to him for his imagination, and for blazing the trail, but I won't be rereading these again anytime soon, if ever.

** Edit 15th September 2024 **

It's been three years since I last read this book, more than 20 since I fell in love with the Peter Jackson movies, and nearly 25 since I was first introduced to the books to begin with. I have always struggled with the novels as I love the story they create, but I dislike how those stories are told. As an avid fantasy fan, I feel like a Christian who loves the story of his religion but struggles to see any value in The Bible itself.

After a recent binge-watch of the extended movies, combined with the comprehensive knowledge of ChatGPT on these stories, my passion for this world was renewed. I fell in love with it beyond just the movies again, becoming fascinated with the world-building and its rich history. Having something I could question when something got confusing was incredible in helping me fill in the gaps in my knowledge of this world.

This put me in a new frame of mind where I wanted to revisit these books to not just read them, but study them and immerse myself in richness of Tolkein's writing. I deliberately slowed down my reading, stuck to the physical novels rather than the audiobooks, and kept ChatGPT handy for clarifications and explanations.

And you know what... I genuinely got a lot more out of this re-read than I ever have before. I believe more than ever that this is an absolutely fascinating story worthy of its legendary status.

But, is it a good novel?

Unfortunately, the answer remains the same; not really.

I can't ignore that I needed to study this book rather than simply read it to get any more enjoyment from it than what the movies provide. I also can't ignore that if it were not for the movies, I probably wouldn't have enjoyed even this re-read as much as I did. I hate even to admit this out loud, but in these three books, Tolkien simply isn't performing the job of a good storyteller.

Sure, he is fantastic at crafting an unbelievably rich world, the overarching story is incredible, and his use of the English language is beautiful. But the line-by-line, chapter-by-chapter job of telling a story is not up to the standards of storytelling that I consider all that competent.

He writes vast paragraphs of information about the history of his world and descriptions of things that aren't necessary to the flow of the story, but has a disturbing habit of leaving out descriptions about the things that are necessary. As a result, I often found myself feeling like I was skipping over essential events in the story when, in fact, it was the author doing this. This is because there might be pages upon pages of lore fed to you in great detail, but an event vital to the story will pass in a mere paragraph or two.

There is no better example of this than the time spent in Moria (coincidently, where many of my re-reads of this book have ended), especially the Balrog scene. In my copy, from the first moment the Balrog comes into sight to the moment that Gandalf says the line, "Fly, you fools!" is two pages and two lines. There are literally songs in this book with a higher page count. In those two pages, here is every line of description we are given about this Balrog:

What it was could not be seen: it was like a great shadow, in the middle of which was a dark form, of man-shape maybe, yet greater; and a power and terror seemed to be in it and to go before it.


Its streaming mane kindled, and blazed behind it. In its right hand was a blade like a stabbing tongue of fire; in its left it held a whip of many thongs.


The dark figure streaming with fire raced towards them.


... the shadow about it reached out like two vast wings. It raised the whip, and the thongs whined and cracked. Fire came from its nostrils.


The fire in it seemed to die, but the darkness grew... it drew itself up to a great height, and its wings were spread from wall to wall...


That's it! Meanwhile, a mere chapter before, there is a literal diagram of what the runes on top of Balin's tomb looked like. Which of these things is more important than the other to the flow of the story? A description of the tremendous evil creature that should terrify us about the fates of our heroes, or the dwarven runes upon the tomb of a character who has no bearing on the rest of the story?

In two pages, we are introduced to a great evil so powerful that only Gandalf can face him, and then . It should be a monumental moment in this story, one with all-time high tension and just as high emotion. Instead, it is fed to us as fast as possible, free from either tension or emotion, so that Tolkien can return to doing what he enjoys most: exploring the world he has created, especially its history.

The Lord of the Rings is a story that exists as a vehicle for Tolkien to explore the world he has created. In my opinion, world-building should only exist to enhance the experience of telling a good story. These books have the balance the wrong way around, which is why no matter how many years pass or how many times I come back to this book, I struggle to make it to the final pages.

I came to this fresh from listening to Andy Serkis read The Hobbit, and I loved what Andy brought to that story. I was keen to experience the same revitalisation of The Fellowship of the Ring. Once again, Andy Serkis delivers a masterful performance… but Andy can only do so much.

Before I explain, let me say that I love the story of Lord of the Rings. I love the characters, their world, and so much more about this series. However, my definitive version is the extended version of Peter Jackson’s movie trilogy, not the books. I know, that is blasphemy to many people, but unfortunately, I can’t overlook the storytelling flaws in this book.

The major one is pacing. This story starts with an enormous info dump that made me false start on this book so many times over the years when reading it. There are many more info dumps littered throughout the book, though thankfully, they are a little more subtle in the future, but they still affect the pacing. Most importantly, though, story pacing is achieved through plot progression, and when you plot out the relevant plot points covered in the first two-thirds of this book, there’s not as much as you might think, as most of the things that happen along the way are side adventures or world-building. These things might be interesting, but they don’t help plot pacing.

The second issue for this reader was the song breaks. I hated all of them when I was younger, but Andy Serkis has done a great job bringing these songs to life, and I now see them as an interesting way to create the tone of Middle Earth. In The Hobbit, it added to the charm of the story. Here, however, I felt there were just too many.

In the forward to the audiobook, Tolkien described how the Lord of the Rings almost happened organically. It started as a history of the languages he developed, and slowly, the story formed over time. The problem is that it reads that way. This book is wonderfully rich and detailed, and there’s a great story in there, but what is missing is that last link that distils that great content down into a great novel. (This is where I think the Peter Jackson films come in and provide that final edit).

So overall, I can honestly say that I enjoyed this reading of The Fellowship of the Ring much more than previous ones. Most of that was Andy Serkis doing a masterful job that was so good that I was tempted to give it a 4-star rating. However, a lot more was because I was picturing the Lord of the Rings movies that I have seen often enough to know almost by heart as this story was playing out. It allowed me to overlook narrative failures I might have got hung up on before, as I could picture the movie's interpretation and not what the author said. So it ends up as three stars. For the sake of the epic story being told and what it did for the genre. I wish it could be higher, but I can’t bring myself to give it any more.

While all of us seek refuge from that evil Shadow that has covered the world, it is such a pleasure to escape to Middle Earth! To revisit a land where good and evil are clear, where trust in your friends and hope in a better future are enough to defeat the Enemy, is one of the most charming escapes that literature can bring in these dark days.

The Fellowship of the Ring, the first chapter of the Lord of the Rings, is indeed a charming introduction. A read that at times flows like the sun over water, with simplistic themes and a straightforward narrative. However, some of the qualities that make it such an easy and universal book, result outdated and maybe even show the limitations of not only Tolkien's storytelling, but the story itself.

I am not talking about the unidimensional characters (although some insight into everyone's likings and pet peeves would be appreciated, if only to give a more distinct voice to each of the characters), the very outdated lack of diversity in gender and race in the characters, or the terrible unbearable songs. No, although works such as A Song of Ice and Fire have shown that fantasy is not an excuse for dull reflections on the human condition and the ways of the world, a critique of a foundational text such as The Lord of the Rings should dwelve into what made it so important. when judging such an important cultural reference, one should look at how this book is able to bring so many readers, for so many years, under its charm.

The Fellowship of the Ring is a nice dip into a fantastic world, but it fails to inspire the fear and hope that the darker The Two Towers and the gilded The Return of the King do. At times, with months-long debates on the proper course of action (just as certain trolls in the Hobbit!), our heroes seem to not be in a rush to defeat the Enemy. After all, the Fellowship's greatest foe in these pages is the Shadow under Moria, and that one gets left behind, so the stakes nor the risks don't ever seem too high.

Just as Dune or the Foundation trilogy, The Fellowship... shows that the creativity needed to forge a world with multiple cultures (each with their own gods, heroes and languages across millenia) does not always translate into vibrant characters or innovative narratives. Furthermore, The Fellowship's tale of selfless heroism fights against its own narrative, one plagued by plot holes, melodramatic dialogues and a character development as thin as obvious when it exists.

Many of the most exciting sequences in The Fellowship... lack emotional impact in the first read, as they usually need careful re-reading. In chaotic scenes, actiones and words are difficult to place, and the outcomes not always clear. Tolkien's extensive geographic descriptions often confound more than clear things up. Perhaps recognizing this limited ability to describe scenes, some sequences stop mid-air, allowing some character to try to explain what is happening and why. This clumsy over exposition makes more evident certain plot holes, either by over explaining peculiar happenings or grossing over them.

The biggest problem of The Fellowship... appears through this overexposition. The characters (and the amazing footnotes) repeatedly mention how their path originated in happenings of long ago, from greater forces of good and evil. They talk about these events with a tone of reverence which -combined with the nostalgia for a world that was purer and perhaps better- give these background stories much more life that the actual members of the Fellowship. It's like the characters were bad actors, reading a bad script of the true Fellowship's tale. In this book, the farce, the actors fail because they must leave the scene, or win because they must advance the story, and not because the story takes us there. Perhaps a slower, more mythical narrative (such as that of the Silmarillion or the footnotes), or a faster and more emotional take (such as the masterful screenplay of the movies) -but certainly a more defined style- could make more justice to the true Fellowship.

I look forward to revisiting the next two books, as I'm sure the most important messages of The Lord of the Rings still live there. It is however a pity to see that The Fellowship of the Ring has almost nothing to say about the importance of ecology, of friendship and honesty being the base of a just society, of having mercy on lost souls, and even on how we must learn to let go of the stories of old, and accept the lively heroics and sins of our contemporaries. As Aragorn loves to say, alas.

I'll admit, I was about to give this book a two star for having a rather simple story with an incredibly slow pace; but then I had a last minute epiphany. This book was revolutionary for its time in creating a setting that is so vast and so complicated, that it ends up undermining the story, which I think should be the driving force.
The setting in of itself, is very impressive, and it is clear that Tolkien put many hours into developing it. Filled with its own languages and cultures, each containing their own lineages, lore, and myths, it's actually daunting. This incredible setting is what became a template for years to come in the fantasy genre.
However, the story is totally undermined by its setting, containing a simple plot, description that is used lavishly, lore that seemed pointless, and bits of prose that didn't seem to add to the story much at all (the chapter of Tom Bombadil was without question the most random chapter I've read, one that I thought should of been omitted entirely).
So what shall I compare this book to in this short review? If you'll take this rather crude comparison, I compare this book to an underprepared calzone, having an outside that crisp, grand, and greatly satisfying, but a core (the story) that is cold and unsatisfying, leaving you in the end with somewhat of a bad experience.

the reading in this is more slow going than the hobbit. the history and planning that comprise this trilogy are really just staggering. tolkien made up a world and its people down to the most minute detail. my only gripe about that is i think that he replaced character development with meticulous detail. after finishing this book i really have no idea about the heart and soul of the characters. i mean, they were all so sad when gandalf fell off the bridge and down, down, down, into the deepest mines of moria, but why? sam had the best reason— he was gonna miss those fireworks! i mean, yeah, because fireworks. frodo said he was going to miss his beard and his eyebrows and stuff. so…yeah…wut? why was gandalf such a great guy? i really don’t feel like i know. i also feel like i know nothing about gimli or pippin and merry. gimli barely pipes up the whole book and although i understand that pippin and merry are loyal, what else are they? i think the characters are portrayed amazingly in the movie, but because of the writing, the direction, and the actors. i read somewhere that the actors were constantly going to peter jackson during filming with characters questions or suggestions and i really love the directions they all took. it doesn’t feel like it strayed from what tolkien wanted, it just went to a deeper level. that being said, i want to live in rivendell. and lothlorien. or anywhere the elves live. okay, i just want to be an elf. i want to spear orcs with my bow and arrow and be immortal and have long hair that is almost always beautifully braided (probably by awesome elf magic). i also felt like the way that tolkien writes really conveys the hopelessness and seemingly endless length of the fellowship’s journey. that kind of sounds like i’m saying that he writes really dully and boringly. not at all! but they’re constantly on the move and not constantly getting attacked. the getting-attacked parts are definitely exciting. the trudging-through-forests-without-paths parts aren’t exciting for the characters or readers. in all, i feel like this book (and probably the other two in the trilogy) are so introspective that they’re meant for the movie screen. the things that tolkien envisioned are so specific that seeing them instead of just reading them is really how they are meant to be conveyed. i’m usually not a big “THIS BOOK SHOULD BE A MOVIE!” person, but in this case, yes. totally.

Many of the characters are interesting, the Shire is very well realized, the Council of Elrond is magnificent and portentous, the mines of Moria are thrilling and dangerous, and there are occasional moments of surpassing beauty. I get all that but at the same time Tolkien is a really uneven writer and I felt the book suffered from a lot of pacing problems and baffling storytelling choices, often fixating on aspects that seemed unimportant or trivial while rushing by things that should have been more drawn out. The worst example of this to me was a scene that lays out in detail the order in which the Fellowship is going to get into boats they've gotten from Lothlorien and the middle of that description, Tolkien reveals in a quick aside that Legolas and Gimli have overcome the prejudices of their races and become good friends. What an abysmal storytelling choice! I sure would have liked to have seen them become friends rather than be told that it had happened while the boating arrangements were explained in detail. Moments like that weren't enough to completely ruin the book for me but they definitely hampered my enjoyment significantly.

This is my third journey through Tolkien’s trilogy. I first read it way back in the mist shrouded past of 1978. It was unlike anything I had experienced before, and I fell under Tolkien’s spell. Now, returning to it nearly a quarter century from my last reading of it in 1999, I find that much of the old magic is now lost on me.

The great strength of Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings (of which The Fellowship of the Ring is the first book) is its unparalleled world building. Tolkien created a world that is deep (nearly fathomless) and richly layered. All throughout he hints at ancient history, lost kingdoms, and legends now all but forgotten. These bits of lore surviving in snatches of song, old barrows and standing stones, collapsed towers, and the stories of grim rangers captivate and enthrall Frodo and his hobbit friends, just as they enchanted me and captured my imagination when first I read it.

The problem with The Fellowship of the Ring is almost everything else. It opens at a glacial pace, literally taking years from book’s beginning for the hobbits to leave the sleepy confines of the Shire to begin the quest that defines the books. Even when Frodo and company finally do hit the road there is far more verbiage given over to walking, eating, and singing than to anything resembling adventure. The threats they do encounter in the book’s first half are more there to build tension and a growing sense of dread rather than to charge your adrenaline. Even after reaching Rivendell, forming their fellowship, and setting out on their perilous quest, the bulk of the story consists in more walking, singing more songs, long descriptions of countryside, and longer monologues filling in history both ancient and recent. Of course, there are spots of action peppering this verbiage stew, but they were far sparser than my memory recalled.

The book has other issues. There is a lack of serious character development in this initial volume. The stark divide between good and evil in the book’s central conflict is fundamental to the story, but I no longer find this morally unambiguous divide between good guys and bad guys as compelling as I did at 14. Despite my love for Tolkien’s richly realized world, and my nostalgia for how much this book meant to me as a young reader, I simply couldn’t look past these flaws.

“One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them, One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them.” In this heart-pounding, blood-pumping novel written by J. R. R. Tolkien, whom we all know can write one heck of a book; you will lose yourself in a mythical world, where the fate of humanity lies on the courage and strength of 4 young hobbits. Frodo is our hero. Also know as Mr. Baggins, he has the full responsibility, and he alone must carry “the burden”. The burden of The Lord of The Rings. However, this story would not be complete without Frodo’s dearest companions. These heart-warming, yet strangely peculiar figures accompany Frodo in his perilous journey.

With the devastating news that Frodo holds one of the world’s greatest perils, he must take action, and fast. When he plans to leave the Shire, a beautiful and calm hobbit town, he brings his one true companion with him, Sam. They set of on this grand journey to destroy The Ring and rid the world of its danger, yet they could not do it without more help. That’s where our beer-drinking friends come in play. Pippin and Merry discovered news about the ring through Sam, who had been spying and plotting to join Frodo on his exhilarating journey. Through rough terrain and exhilarating battles, the young hobbits follow their path. In the Elven city of Rivendell, the Fellowship of the ring, also know as the Company, is united. Four hobbits, three men, one elf, and one dwarf; these are the heroes who must bring down Sauron and save the world.

Along with action, mystery, and sorrow, J. R. R. Tolkien shows readers a whole new side to adventure. She truly shows us 2-D characters, not loose-leaf-like. So many different characters – from Gandalf the wise old man to Pippin who only knows to drink and blabber - to connect with. The world created through her astounding writing is truly boggling. Every inch of land walked, new nail-biting adventures await the Company, and not only were these adventures truly amazing, but also extremely detailed and titillating. Not only do I now know which is the next book I’ll read, but I also know what tomorrow’s lunch topic is going to be! Two birds with one stone baby. B

J.R.R. Tolkien is arguably one of the greatest fictional authors of all time. I can totally understand why so many are captivated by the epic adventure and rich description of Middle-Earth. The Lord of the Rings series has indeed been a pinnacle in shaping the fantasy fiction, with modern authors such as J.K. Rowling clearly feeding off of Tolkien's successful methods.

However, the book is not as powerful as it once was. This is no fault of Tolkien, it is simply the fact that the development of modern day fiction has surpassed it. Upon it's initial publication the book would have certainly offered something completely fresh - world far richer than any previous fantasy. Yet considering I have read the entire Harry Potter series, and a range of other fantasy books such as Eragon, this book offered me nothing new or particularly exciting. The book definitely felt as if it dragged on and the lengthy descriptions of the world and of Middle-Earth history often were hard to conceive.

Having said this, Middle-Earth is certainly one of the most believable worlds I have ever experienced, and is well in line with the Harry Potter series. Several moments of the book did really stand out of me, particularly in the Shire, and these helped to balance out the less interesting or monotonous points.

Overall I found myself quite disappointed with this book, particularly after the success of the movies. I still appreciate Tolkien's importance to fictional writing, and applaud his world building, for it is one of a kind. I will still be reading the next two books in this classic trilogy and hope that they make a better impression on me.
